is a first-person shooter (FPS) that's surprisingly varied and story-heavy. The variety of gameplay and settings as well as the engaging background story succeed in driving you through this game at breakneck speed, leaving you wanting more when it's over.
is set in an alternate history related to World War 2. In 1946, the nazis have managed to develop highly advanced technology that may win them the war. You play as agent William "B.J." Blazkowicz who's fighting for the allies, trying to stop the plans of the nazi's main threat, General Wilhelm "Deathshead" Strasse.
In the game's introductory chapter, not everything goes according to plan and the nazis win the war in 1948 when the United States capitulate. Blazkowicz spends 14 years in a psychiatric hospital. When nazis shut down the hospital in their own charming way, slaughtering the patients and the personnel, Blazkowicz is rudely awakened from his catatonic state. They'll soon wish they hadn't done that…
The story that follows is captivating and exciting, and will take Blazkowicz to all sorts of places around the globe. He meets interesting characters who show a lot of personality, considering the short time you interact with them. All in all,
is quite story-heavy for an FPS. When I was browsing reviews, I noticed several reviewers asking themselves "Did I just watch a movie or play a game?" (either in a good or a bad way). Now that I played through the game myself, I certainly understand that sentiment. Whether that's a good or a bad thing is entirely subjective, so I leave it up to you to draw conclusions.
has 5 basic difficulty modes, a chapter select option to replay earlier chapters while keeping all your current perks and weapon upgrades, and a way to unlock four more difficulty modes. These bonus difficulty modes all come with a twist, for example all health and armor pickups are removed from the game or the game is set to the hardest difficulty mode but you get more health points and unlimited ammo. Add to this the fact that you need to make a decision at the end of the first chapter which influences the whole game after that (although not immensely), and
certainly offers replayability.
Overall, the gameplay is very smooth. The only times I got frustrated was when jumping came into play. Blazkowicz can't jump much higher than his boots. You often need to press the jump key three or four times before he actually manages to jump up a tiny ledge or a small crate. When you drop down a very short distance and get shot at, you may want to jump back up to find cover but since jumping is so awkward and getting shot in the back depletes your hit points very fast, it usually means having to reload the last checkpoint.
You'll see a fair share of combat, of course, but
is more than a mindless shooter. There are times when a sneaky approach is advisable or necessary. There are even parts of the game where there's little to no combat involved and you just need to collect some items and perform a few actions to further the plot.
The gun action is great. You start out with a knife and a pistol, but you'll soon come across fantastic weapons like energy weapons and a rocket-launcher upgrade for your assault rifle. Or for your assault rifle
, as you can dual wield almost all of the weapons. Basically, there are only ten or so weapon types but you can customize most of them and turn them into something else entirely, which makes you feel like the game has twice as many weapon types.
Sneaking can be fun. Sometimes you're thrown into a location armed with nothing but a knife, so a sneaky approach is required, at least until you come across some guns. Also, the nazis have commanders who will raise an alarm that will draw more nazi troops into the fight, so you want to stealth kill these commanders as often as possible.
The problem with the sneaking, though, is that it's somewhat underdeveloped. There are no actual mechanics to the stealthy approach like moving around silently or hiding in shadows or keeping an eye on a detection meter. It doesn't even matter if you crouch or not. You just need to make sure you don't get in the field of view of a nazi because he will spot you no matter what, even from huge distances. Also, while the NPC's do become hostile when they actually
you stealth killing one of their buddies, they aren't alarmed at all when their patrol route takes them right next to a couple of dead nazis whose throats you just slit.
There are 32 combat perks to unlock, divided into 4 categories: stealth, assault, tactical and demolition. Unlocking perks requires you to perform a related task. For example, a stealth perk may require you to stealth kill 5 commanders and an assault skill may require you to kill 20 opponents while dual-wielding pistols. Unlocked perks add a passive skill like being able to reload weapons faster or being able to spot collectibles on the map.
I only encountered one bug in
and it turned out to be well-documented. When you reload (or are forced to reload because you died) in the first building of chapter 14, all the lootable items disappear from the area. So all the health and armor power-ups as well as all the collectible items are gone. The only way to fix it is to reload the chapter (not: reload the last checkpoint). This is no problem since it's at the start of the chapter anyway, but until you figure this out it may leave you frustrated and googling for answers.

In the entirety of games,
's graphics are, of course, far above average. That being said, for a relatively recent triple-A title I wasn't overly impressed with the graphics. This isn't a game where you'll feel the need to be making screenshots the whole time.
The music is varied and fits the game's atmosphere perfectly. Sometimes, the music is quiet and tense whereas other times, the soundtrack consists of pounding hard rock.
Sound effects are okay. The shooting sounds are satisfying enough, although I have played games where the guns sounded a bit 'heavier' and more realistic, causing
's guns to sound a tad underwhelming in comparison.
The voice acting is very decent. Blazkowicz doesn't say a lot but when he does grunt a one-liner through his teeth, it's usually rendered in a way that sounds serious and funny at the same time. The other voice actors manage to speak their lines with care and professionalism, although some lack the ability to add genuine-sounding emotions to their characters.

- Steins;Gate is one of the best stories I ever read and definitely the best time travel related one.
Story: [Spoiler free]
The story is set in Tokyo (Akihabara) July 2010 and told from the perspective of Okabe (surname) Rintaro (given name), a 18 year old university student. Okabe unintentionally invents a time machine based on a remote controlled microwave oven and starts experimenting on it in his "lab", which is actually more like his student flat where he hangs out with his friends. As he can be very childish he has an alter ego Hououin Kyouma, a self-proclaimed mad scientist, longing to destroy the secret organizations, who rule the world from the shadows. As the story progresses Okabe finds himself in a desperate fight against the outcomes of his own mistakes, various conspiracies and eventually fate itself.
The concept of time travel here is based on modern physics and explained in great detail. The best part about it is that it's very consistent and leaves (almost) no plot holes, depending on how you interpret some details.
The story will invoke a wide range of different emotional situations in the reader ranging from sadness, a hearty laugh, thrilling tension to pure epicness and possibly affection and horror.
Though the story features a lot of references to Japanese pop and otaku culture most of it should be easily understandable to everyone as there’s a tips section explaining them. I won’t deny that these references, as well as the protagonists alter ego, might appear cringy to some people, but in my opinion this is much less the case in the novel than in the anime adaption (which is also 10/10).
Tough a lot of the characters from the wide and diverse cast will first seem very stereotypical, all of them have a great backstory and will grow on you fast. The character cast, mainly consisting of women
, is probably also a point where it’s rather obvious that this novel is more targeted to men than women, though I guess it should be really enjoyable for both.
The story has six endings, of which one is considered the true ending. What ending you’ll get depends on the various choices you have to make during the game. These choices are all made by interaction with your cellphone, e.g. how do you reply to an email or do you answer a call or not.
If you want to reach all endings you probably have to rely on one of various guides (search for Steins;Gate flowchart) or try and error a lot. Some endings differ considerably in length so I recommend to make sure you read at least one of the longer ones (chapter 10).
Music:
In my opinion the music is superb and I instantly get goosebumps from listening to the main theme “Gate of Steiner”. But even so I can imagine one getting annoyed as some tracks are played quiet a lot, while others are rather rare to hear. Especially the main theme is played a lot as there are various variations of it, but this wasn’t a problem for me as I f*ing love all of them.
The only thing I didn’t like was the fact that here in the steam version, they changed the Gate of Steiner variation in the main menu from the normal(?) to a piano version. I’m not even sure if the original main menu track is still in the game.
Miscellaneous:
The character sprites as well as the backgrounds are really good and look better than many newer visual novels. The characters also have lip synchronization to match the magnificent voice acting.
The UI is well made in general, though the standard text font is rather bad. This can be fixed with the general improvement patch from the “Committee of Zero” (google it!). The keybindings are not customizable.

It's rough, but that's expected. What is unusual about IM is the commitment of the team. I bought this on the promise that I would eventually get an awesome combination of some of my favourite shooter elements. FPS games are my favourite but one of my least played, because my standard for FPS games is fairly high. I bought this game at a time when arcade shooters like Call of Duty were on the rise and that trend doesn't seem to be slowing.
I can't write a review for an early access game, but what I can do is say that I trust the commitment of the devs to delivering on their promise. If you're tired of shooters with unsatisfying gunplay, with superficial RPG mechanics that don't mean anything, with bad map design, poor story designed by some board of directors along with their marketing department and if you crave a challenging co-op experience reminiscent of Rainbow 6 co-op, then give Interstellar Marines a chance.
Currently they're refining the mechanics that will be used in co-op through vigorous multiplayer testing, giving you a chance to play and test the game while they work on delivering the cooperative meat of the game later on. It's not perfect, but I'm confident that investing in Interstellar Marines will be pay off far more than you ever expected, if you just give it your time and support.
At the end of the day, it's all...for the love of the game.
/Long-time supporter of IM

This game got me really excited, after playing for some time. At first it was a little bit difficult to get into the game, but I like it that you don't get everything pushed in your face. So I had a great time figureing out how the game works.
After i understood how the death mechanic works and that you will lose all your relics on death, which are the most important items to boost your character, i got really excited. So in this game death gets punished, which is great. I had some exciting moments when i survived near death or some frustrating moments when i died and needed to start over. You keep your character (even though you can play a hardcore character), your level and your gold and will lose your keys (to open certain treasure chests) and your relics.
I did find some minor bugs, but the devs are very active and releasing regulary patches.
There are some DLC's which will 'complete' the game. With the basic game you can access 4 out of 7 acts and you can not play every character available. For now I find this way of handling the DLC's okay, because you can reach the max. level without the dlc's. Im not sure if the endgame content is limited to dlc users, but I will add this detail once i reached the max level (150).
If you like Diablo you will enjoy this game as well. Just the fighting mechanics are kinda like in The binding of Isaac.

And for whatever reason I can't get access to the Servers (living in germany). So I ended up playing on multiplayer alone with the peer2peer option, because i was too lazy to open the port.
All in all I really enjoy this game so far!

The stages are vibrant, dynamic, and well-themed. Each course is based off of classic Sega worlds and areas, with fitting music to match. I felt so damn pleased when I started up a race in Shibuya and heard "Let Mom Sleep" come on. I mean, I was almost sold right then.
The vehicle swap mechanic is horrendously fun and introduces interesting aspects, particularly with some shortcuts in the stages causing you to swap vehicles and adapt your playing immediately. Or run face-first into a wall because you forgot how planes work.
The game has clear progression and unlocks, with levels for characters unlocking mod kits that tweak their stats, in case you love a character but find their playstyle impossible to deal with. It's also great if you love seeing bars fill up and being told you did something good and earned a reward, and don't even care what the reward is.
It runs smoothly and looks fantastically stylized. Also, it has local multiplayer, which, while common on console games and their ports, is not something I ever take for granted. That is a selling point.
But, to be honest and a little glurgey, it also brings back a lot of good memories. Regardless of how one feels about some of their mistakes, Sega has been around a long time, and has touched on a lot of innovative and fun ideas and characters in their years of making games. Some of them were expanded upon, some of them have collected dust for a long time. But this game addresses them. Cynically, I guess one could say it's just milking their old franchises for cash, but with the care and detail put into the characters and stages, it feels different, different from the random, purely visual cameos in some more forgettable games. It feels like this is someone's way of saying that even if these worlds and series never get a new game, even if they only exist in rerelease compilations and cameos, they haven't been forgotten. Sega has fans on the inside.

One day you find yourself marooned on a distant planet, a rimworld some would call it.
The literal butt end of ruled space that is akin to a pit stop in hell.
You are far from what you would call home, a nice glitterworld where all of your fantasies can come true.
Here your only friends are a giggling pyromaniac and some guy who thinks he is some sort of space knight.
All the other people you have meet have been drooling tribals who keep on looking at you with slightly hungry eyes.
Or space pirates who just want to maim, kill and burn everything, including you.
Also squirrels are also the most terrifying creatures imaginable, having seen a horde of them eat a man alive.
There are also very angry robots that keep on trying to blast you into atoms.
If this place has ticked any of the 'come here for a tourist visit' boxes then the people who did tick them should be rightfully sent to a 'corrective facility'.
However for some reason, somehow this place is home too you.
Heck you will be damned if someone is going to move you off of this rock.
Those that tried now have their bones scattered across your couger pen, but thats a story for another time.
While your new associates did take a while to get used too, they do seem to be pretty nice people.
You think.
Maybe.
Deep down inside they are.
At least you thought that until the day when you woke up too the sound of manical laughter as the pyro sets your bed on fire, with you still in it.
The space knight had also inconveniently decided to have a mental breakdown and start bingeing on all the potatoes you spent all summer growing.
To say you were angry was an understatement.
There was alot of repressed rage to be let loose at that moment.
Now all that remains of your 'Comrades' are being roasted on a small campfire in what now remains of your once glorious house fort thing.
The 'a mans gotta eat' saying feels a little corny thinking about it right now.
Did i also mention that you are a cannibal?

Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed, in case you can't tell from the title, is a racing game, and the sequel to Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing. In this game your car transforms into a plane or boat depending on what the course calls for at certain points. As you play the game you earn experience points, and when you level up, you earn a new mod for that character. Mods are changes to how your character's vehicle handles. Because you have to level up each character individually to unlock all the mods for all the characters, it can either be something that adds replay value for you, or be an unfun grind. Aside from the usual grand prix and versus modes, there is a quest mode as well, where you complete challenges to earn stars that allow you to unlock more characters, mods for characters, and of course more challenges. Some of these challenges can be really difficult at times, and to top it off there's also an extra difficulty to unlock that makes these challenges even harder. While the game doesn't have as many power ups or courses to choose from as Mario Kart games have nowadays, the gameplay is solid, and the courses often have multiple paths you can take that act as shortcuts. So far in these Sega All Stars games, I think this one has the best fan service. It's also the best looking and best sounding game in the series. This game is available for multiple platforms, but I recommend getting it on Steam assuming you have the specs to run it, since the Steam version has more exclusive characters than any other version, including an exclusive DLC character.

Do you like anime? Do you like otaku culture? Do you like the concept of a bunch of otaku friends exchanging banter between each other while slowly working on their time machine which takes the form of a modified microwave, all the while making countless references to japanese memes (which all have their contexts conveniently explained via an elaborate in-game glossary) and anime/manga?
That's the first 10-20 hours of Steins;Gate. There is substance, but it is buried beneath stacks of references that nobody outside of its target audience will appreciate in any way. If you do not like the characters, The plot of this has absolutely nothing for you, for reasons that I cannot really go into without spoiling the game.
Steins;Gate is incredibly slow, and if you're not into all of its references/nods to otaku culture, or if you're not captivated by the seemingly endless sci-fi buildup about quantum physics, then you're going to be in for an extremely rough ride.
If you like the characters by chapter 3, you will probably really enjoy this. If you hate them, you will not enjoy this. If you cannot suspend your disbelief far enough to accept the levels of stupidity the protagonist will go solely for tangling the plot into a mess that he needs to fix later, then you will not enjoy Steins;Gate. That is my biggest issue with SG--the story feels like it is carrying the characters. It doesn't feel like they make logical decisions with any amount of sense behind them, but rather they make decisions because the writer realizes that they can't continue the story unless they do something irrational and stupid. The foreshadowing is too blatant, and the actions the protagonist takes are too careless to feel any amount of sympathy for him.
I can only explain something like this with an example, so the following is an extremely minor spoiler which happens in the beginning hours, before the tone shift of the 6th chapter, so just know that in advance:
So basically, these characters hesitate to alter the past week of their lives, and are even relieved to find out that they do not succeed in doing so... but then immediately afterwards they are completely comfortable with changing the past 16 years for their own personal gain.
If you can find it in your heart to feel sorry for a group as incompetent in this one, then go for it and buy Steins;Gate. You'll probably love it. But if anything I've said has made you wary, you may want to look somewhere else. Steins;Gate has a lot of flaws in its writing that generally makes it hard to swallow unless you either are willing to suspend your disbelief by a considerable margin, or you're genuinely engaged by its slower moments of banter and sci-fi talk.
It is a fine game, although there should be more customization and a lot more features to be added. This game is only fun with friends.

Played when it first came out. I wasn't impressed then, and I certainly am not impressed now.
Pros:
- Relaxing, when everything is running and operating correctly.
- Gameplay is good, if you don't encounter bugs.
- Cool concept!
- A lot of grind, but it's rewarding.
- Educational for the most part!
- Is actually a very pretty game!
Cons:
- Crashes, bugs, and glitches galore. I had to restart around 5 times on my first playthrough(s) due to game breaking bugs where my equipment would disapear, and I didn't have any money to buy replacements without taking out a loan. There was a glitch where my truck dropped off the face of the game world, and another bug where the player model would get stuck on nothing. Every time something like this would happen, it was easier just to restart my progress.
- Feels very empty. There isn't a whole lot to do, and it just feels like the player is wandering the world in Cormac McCarthy's "The Road". Which would be really cool, if the player was supposed to feel that way while playing this simulator.
- Very strenuous. I ran this on a system with 8gb VRAM, 16GB RAM, with DX12 and I got some massive frame drops at medium graphics settings.
- Driving is not great, I had a pretty hard time driving around with all my equipment. I found it very difficult to stay on the road without crashing into something. It really doesn't help when the world renders about three feet in front of your car. Overall driving and the rendering feel like a PS2 era game.
Verdict:
Would not buy again. This is the only game I've refunded on Steam, and I'm pretty disappointed because it seems like it could be a really good concept. If the Devs fixed the issues of the base game instead of focusing on paid DLC, I think that I might buy this game again.

Every piece of me wanted to rate this game a 10/10 but I knew that was wrong somehow. It took me awhile to figure out what it was holding me back, but after some replaying and hearing my friend’s experiences I figured out what it was.
I'll start with the pros of this game
- Finally a good online for the DBZ Universe
- Good replay-ability
- Great character customization
- All the skills you could hope for
- Level up system
- Just enough grinding to keep you interested
- Tons to do with friends or by yourself
- And the graphics somehow make everything feel better even the negative things
- More...
And here are my cons
- Bad launch day servers
- PVP is not balanced
- SSJ is about spamming skills not powering up....
- All playable characters are EXTREMELY WEEK compared to custom even the ones you have to wish for
- Unsecure servers (Hackers/Glitches/Exploits)
- And here is the main reason that weighs on me why this game does not get a 10/10... The storyline, first time I played through the storyline I felt like wow that's pretty cool I get to see every one of the Z warriors right? Well the fact is not only is the story line short, but it is weak in plot and the worst part about is that the fact that your character is basicly NON EXSISTANT! I would go back in time wanting to be part of the Z warriors hear Goku say wow your strong lets battle sometime, but no every person I run into is like wait was someone just here? I understand it's to balance the timeline and all, but it still felt overall lacking and the main reason I can't give this game a 10/10.
So in short this game is amazing it gives you almost everything you can want in a DBZ game from skills to characters, but it lacks just enough where it matter to earn a 9/10 it would be lower but the game is great enough to carry its own slack of having a poor storyline where you feel nonexistent and some non balanced moves and exploits/glitches.

As others have stated, Titan Souls appears to try and combine the difficulty and precision of the Dark Souls game with the bosses only style of Shadow of the Collosus. This was exciting to me at first, until I saw the execution.
One hit kills never make for fun gameplay in my opinion and should only be reserved for a boss mega attack. Even then, being killed by such an attack should be reserved as a punishment for doing something you can verify as being entirely your fault for not dodging/preventing. However, Titan Souls' bosses not only get away with insanely fast movement and shots (with absolutely no projection in most cases), but they also tend to lead their shots, making it nearly impossible to dodge unless you are very far away from the enemy and not doing anything else the moment they choose to fire.
Given the time it takes to charge a shot and the incredibly narrow windows with which to hit the boss, it seems to come down more to luck than anything else, which is never a good game mechanic. I can't say I didn't have fun with some of the bosses, but most were unnecessarily tedious to keep going back to from the save points only to be crushed in a few seconds and then have to trek back all over again. They corrected this for the final two bosses, but that doesn't make up for all the other times I had to schlep on back to a boss.
I really really wanted to like this game, but completing it felt more like a chore than an exhilarating adventure. As such, I cannot recommend this game to anyone at full price. Wait for it to go on sale, as it is very short (took me ~2 hours) and frustrating.

-- I am sad to say that after only 4 days of playing. I do not ever see this game making it much further than it has. Though I could be wrong. You see there is enough gimping of players to keep them spending real money for digital money in order to do things. So what is the real incentive to "finish" the game? If ya ask me it is finished. Effectively landing it a "pay to win" view from me. The Devs, the staff, and the company are making money off of the game and it is 'not done'? For example, after being handed defeat after defeat by players with better equipment than is/was available to me. I took some time and have done several hours of research on how the match making system is suppose to work... and it does not seem to work the way it is supposedly intended to work. Why do I say this? Well, when I build a vehicle that is under (key note here ---UNDER---) 2k PS, and I am getting matched with players that are in the 3k to 3.5k range. There is no hope of being able to win a fight. Additionally, being pitted against players that have several -blue- quality items gets the same result. That is no real chance of winning. My team might win a few times here and there. But that is only if others on my team are similarly outfitted to these other players. So here I am, after a couple days of play, I manage to get a couple -blue- items, and yet I am pitted against players that have multiple -purple- quality weapons. And again my team might win a few times here and there. But that is only if others on my team are similarly outfitted to these other players.  Then I come to find out that there are other limitations like the acquisition of scrap, as a resource. So much for trying to build anything, without spending real cash?  So here we have an "unfinished" game. At least according to the Release information; Closed Beta: April 5 2016 and Open Beta: May 30 2017. In which players can spend real money to get more things to use in the game that have direct game altering effects, and a match making system that does not seem to be working towards balanced matches. Which could be seen as a incentive for players to spend money to get better equipment so that they can have a chance at winning... thus the pay to win concept.
Please do not get me wrong. The game is enjoyable. I just will not be spending any money on it and will not be suggesting it to anyone else after seeing how it appears to work. Good game, great idea, loads of expansion potential. Closest game to "Steve Jackson's = CAR WARS=" game I have seen in a very long time. But the pay to win aspect... yeah that killed it for this driver.

This should be a neutral review, but I don't think it deserves a negative one, so I guess I'll recommend it. I feel this way mainly because the story is far too short for the reader to really get attached to any character, including the protagonist. This is supposed to be a story about love, but it fails to elicit romantic feelings and doesn't give the reader much of a chance to even feel motivated to salvage the relationship between the MC and his girlfriend. What I do like about it is that it portrays a disabled person in a positive light and debunks the myth that a disabled person is inherently unable to take care of themselves. Many people think that once someone becomes severely disabled that they can't do anything for themselves, when it is far from the truth, and many disabled people learn to lead independent lives.
Bonus points for including a queer character.
It has a lot of room for improvement, but I didn't hate it. It could be enjoyable for some who like shorter stories or someone who doesn't care much for romance.

I'm going to attempt to keep this short.
Oh boy, this game was an interesting one.
I completed Blind Love in a span of ~2 hours - not too bad for a cheap visual novel, I must admit. The novel has a total of four different ending you can get (of which I have gotten all four of). One major issue I had with the game is how very little dynamic there is between each ending. There's a pretty limited amount of choices you can make, and again, four different outcomes; the ratio of choices and outcomes overall makes the game
sensitive to your choices. This can make it difficult to achieve one ending in particular; you really have to figure out the mechanics of the game in order to get the ending you want. I think this game overstretched too simple and short of a story. Two or three possible outcomes would have better suited this VN versus four due to just how short the game really is (i've seen one person on the community hub get all four endings in 11 minutes). More on dynamic - the characters. The one character I, for some reason, seem to really dislike is the main character's girlfriend. Even though she is perhaps made out to be a protagnist (could the main character be considered an anti-hero?), I just really seem to dislike how she is personified, and she leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Perhaps it's how the devs decided to portray her PTSD and military past; I don't know.
The art style is one thing that really saves this game in terms of it being something to have in your Steam library. In short: it's beautiful. Major props to Kopianget, ReddArt, and Michaela Laws for the amazing art in this VN. The use of a monochromatic color pallet really has an impact on the story, I think. One thing that I really think the dev's missed out on is having a short scene at the beginning in bright, happy colors; this would allow for a grave contrast between the colorful life the main character lead, and the one he is currently stuck with. I think they 100% hit home in the art catagory. It's beautiful, and allows for a sense of sympathy to be strung through the audience.
There is one thing that I am still left questioning through this entire game: what was the goal?
[ending spoilers after this point]
What was this game trying to prove?
What was the point?
In conclusion:
Despite all the negativity I threw towards this VN, I still highly recommend it. It's pretty short and sweet - and, not to mention cheap. Why not spend the $.99? The love story will either leave you heartbroken or warm and fuzzy - or, perhaps, somewhere inbetween. You can't go wrong!

The more I play I find more scenarios, I find new options, new maps, new mods, new people, new factions. The List keeps going, getting more interesting over time.  I love getting immersed in my colonies, wondering how my colonists live and sometimes I find myself adding myself or friends / family into the game, giving them their proper skills with Prepare Carefully (A GREAT MOD) and just seeing how it would play out.

As the enemy advanced I lost all hope when the messages showed up. 4 of my 7 colonists came down with the plague and instatntly headed inside and went to bed, expecting treatment. The raiders knocked down two colonists and killed the remaining one, then they decided to kidnap the two downed colonists and retreat. The four colonists that got the plague were still waiting in the infirmary. Little did they know, no treatment was coming. They all decided not to get up and either starved or died from the plague. With that out of the way I will say that I first heard of Senran Kagura while browsing /v/ years ago and the art grabbed my attention. When I heard it was coming on PC I figured may as well get it to see if the actual game is any good. I remember it released during my final night shift for the week back in summer and I snuck my laptop at reception so I can download it, because no internet down in the basement where the staff stayed. I tried it out after getting a few hours of sleep as I had the next two days off and I pretty much wasted those two days playing only this, stopping only for a short trip to the kitchen to get some food off the head chef and the occasional bathroom break. Needless to say this game occupied several weeks of my free time back then, so add another 30 or so hours of offline playtime to whatever my current online playtime is. Now on to the actual review.

For a game about ♥♥♥♥♥ ninjas destroying each other's clothes the story was actually surprisingly decent. It's nothing groundbreaking but it had its moments and all the characters had a decent amount of character development.
You have three main campaigns to play through with 25 missions each, an extra campaign that you unlock once you finish the first three and a special surprise once you finish it, but I won't spoil it. Aside from that every character also has their own personal side story which consists of five missions per story. Since the PC version comes with all the DLCs included you also get two extra characters which are normally not playable in the main story, so that's another extra ten missions.
Overall there's a lot of content to go through, but if you don't care for story you can pretty much skip everything and get to the action.

The game originally released on the PS Vita so next gen AAA graphics are out of the question here (not that I expect graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ to be playing this). The PC version runs at native HD resolution so nothing is upscaled. It also runs at native 60FPS so the FPS police can sod off. I'd say it's rather lacking in the Anti-Aliasing department but you can easily fix that with something like NVIDIA inspector (or whatever equivalent AMD has). One thing I noticed, at least on my end, is that vsync is bugged in regular fullscreen mode. Regardless of how I tried to force it on I kept getting screen tearing. This stopped being a problem when I switched to borderless window.
The final thing I need to mention is that the system requirements posted on the store page are VASTLY overblown. This game will run just fine even on a toaster (I tested it).

The soundtrack's pretty good, lots of metal, some of classical music and a lot of Japanese influence. The voice acting is also great but it's only in Japanese (I shudder to think what a dub of this would sound like). I'm no music critic, so I won't bother going in-depth here.
I would say this might get repetitive during extended plays if you aren't a beat 'em up fan, but in short bursts it's an absolute blast. The missions are mainly comprised of annihilating hordes of enemies Dynasty Warriors style and fighting one of the other girls.
The combat is not overly complex and it won't take you weeks to master it (unlike something like Devil May Cry), but it's really fun. You have a total of 22 playable characters to choose from and they all have their own unique movesets. Some also sport even more unique gimmicks which apply only to them. Every character also has three different states to choose from: Flash, Yin and Yang.
Flash is your default state. Yang is your shinobi transformation which completely heals you, makes you stronger and allows you to use hidden arts. Yin is essentially berserk mode which greatly boosts your own damage but you take a lot more damage as a result.
Each state also slightly alters the character's moveset and you unlock more moves naturally as you keep playing and level up.
There's a shop where you can buy clothes, accessories and other things with the money you earn from missions and a lingerie lottery to play when you have nothing else to waste your money on. There's naturally a dressing room where you can dress up your characters however you want (and you can do some fun things in there as well).
I won't bother talking about clothes destruction, you can figure that out by just looking at the screenshots and I don't really want to spoil everything now.
There is also multiplayer which I unfortunately didn't get to experience thanks to no internet at the time and it's currently pretty much dead unless you can get a friend to play with you or want to fight against bots.
Controls wise with a controller it works fine. The Vita's touch screen features are sort of emulated via the mouse. I haven't tried the keyboard controls so I can't comment on them.
It's pure unadulterated fun, the port is fine and it triggers women and normalcucks alike. What more can I say about it? Wasted over 30 hours playing this in a basement that felt like an oven back in summer. Now I wasted another 30 just unlocking everything and having an absolute blast. Get it, it's great.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is the newest fighting game in the Dragon Ball Franchise that has run about as long as the anime and video games have been available. It's the first in franchise history to make the jump to PC, and honestly, it's about time. I could go on for hours about how much I've been waiting for this game and how much I love it, but instead I'll give the condensed version.
Side Note: I'm a bit biased as I am a HUGE Dragon Ball fan, and I'll start by saying that if you're not a fan of the series, you probably won't like this as much as a fan. The game is catering to a very specific player base, and it does this well.
PROS:
+Game looks gorgeous, the graphics could have come straight out of the anime/manga.
+60 FPS at max settings on a DB game = SSSSSOO MUCH YES
+ Gameplay is simplified, but not as bad as Ultimate Tenkaichi was.
+CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION - This one is huge, fans have been screaming for a proper character creator for years now, and UT's was pretty lackluster. DBVX's CaC system is extrememly open ended, and all of your 12-year-old DeviantArt OC fantasies can now come true. What's especially nice is that the custom characters are unique - each race has it's own strenghts and weaknesses, and working around them is an interesting challenge.
+Story is decently engaging and interesting
+TONS to do - Story mode, parallel quests, master quests, tournament mode, item customization, standard battles...plenty to keep the player engaged.
+Takahata101 is a CaC voice. Look up Team Four Star or DBZ Abriged and thank me later.
+It's DBZ. DBZ is just fun.
+You can use a controller - THANK GOD, I don't even want to think about trying to play one of these games with a keyboard and mouse.
CONS:
-Port is rough around the edges - game WILL crash if it tries to hand too much, or even just in loading screens - it's clearly built for console, specifically XB1 and PS4, and this is probably why, but it's not really an excuse, given that the new consoles are so similar to a basic gaming PC.
-LIghting engine can get harsh and obnoxious at times
-AI can be a MASSIVE pain to deal with - getting bum rushed by every enemy on the field at once is not fun
-Always Online - We've all seen the connection error issues, and there are times I just wish the first connection attempt at the start screen would fail just so I don't get kicked out later (which I think is stupid). I know Namco Bandai is working on this, and I'm glad, but I wish they had included an offline mode of some sort.
-Game is HARD - this could be a good thing, and for me it is, but it's not always very accessible. Granted, it's not as frustrating as Battle of Z was, but it's still a pain sometimes.
-Get's REALLY grindy at times - drop rates are a thing, and items YOU NEED for some quests or items don't always drop the first time, forcing you to grind the same mission several times. I just got done grinding two missions to get parts for a Z Soul and it was really irritating
-The story is pretty convaluted - any non-DB fans are gonna get lost easily - this is some tricky stuff
Overall, I like this game. It's frustrating at times and the crashing or logging off is annoying, but my experience has been general positive. I enjoy the game, and I would thoroughly recommend it...to a fan of the genre. Anyone that isn't a DB fan or doesn't care for the fighting games isn't gonna enjoy themselves much, but if you fit those two groups, this is well worth the buy, especially on PC. I truly hope they keep bringing these games to Steam, it's a whole new platform NB can open up to.

Simple but hard, Titan Souls is a boss rush game sitting right on the edge of being frustrating yet rewarding. Its pseudo pixel art style, orchestral music and overall cosy soundscape come together to form a ruined fairytale realm where time stands still.
The protagonist is a tiny archer with exactly one arrow, which needs to be retrieved after shooting. Theoretically, one well placed shot is enough to defeat or at least trigger the next stage of a boss. That one-hit mechanic works both ways and the only defence available is the dodge roll. Therefore, knowing the tells and learning the patterns for each boss is crucial. That doesn't always suffice, as some attacks have a high variance in scope and timing. As a result, that small bit of uncertainty sometimes leads to rather lucky instead of deliberate shots. In the end, approaching a titan is often a mix of puzzle gameplay and dexterous control.
This game certainly requires a high level of frustration tolerance. While the bosses are varied and interestingly designed, the most enjoyment comes from the relief after overcoming the difficulties in seemingly unfair duels. The will to endure is a prerequisite to a satisfying experience in Titan Souls.
Difficult to get into at first and lacks a bit of action, but once you get used to how the game works it's pretty unique and good fun.

But you also need to know that the devs are still working on this game, unlike Loadout. Maybe they will stop later, or something, I dunno, but at the moment, they are definetly still around working on the game. I mean they posted something on the 22nd, it's not like their last post was 2 years ago.
The game itself is fun. You have a bunch of classes to pick from, each has their own skills, you can give them a cute little hat and name them suger♥♥♥♥♥♥if you want. You run around a big plane with a few obsticals, and you have to kill wave after wave of monsters, and fight a boss at the 6th wave.
There are problems, like the many insta death hazards (acid mucas and spikey bouncy balls of death), and the inventory is clunky, but besides that, at least in my opinion, it's still a fun game.
Just be warned, don't grow too attached to your character. Updates in this game can easily ruin them. I'm one of the few people who don't mind this, and are just happy to watch as bosses are eaten alive by my skeletons and demonic arm babys. I'm sure there are people really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that their level 80 character was ruined by the mana update, but to me, this just isn't the type of game to get attached to a character you've been building up. But really, this game thrives on Rogue-Like elements, while also letting you build up a character. When you die, you lose all temporary stat changes, and relics you found, rendering you to a soft weakling with only your base stats to defend yourself.
But that's also a part of the beauty of this game, when a character's stats are lost, ore lost entirely, just build back up again! The leveling is fun and diverse, and there's enough classes to try something new if you're sick of always playing as the same class.
If you're new, you might wanna buy it. I mean it's six bucks, what do you really have to lose? Three bags of Lemonheads? It's a fun game, all things considered! Burning sh*t, poison, playing as a flying pygmy demon from hell, if you like RPG's, you might like this.
... Also I've never did the multiplayer, mostly cause I didn't want to make an account on some website, but I hear it's broken to f*ck.... So yeah.... Also the voice acting isn't great...
Overall, 6.5/10, could use alot of improvment, but still a fun game in the end.

This is weird. I enjoyed this game (quite a bit at times), but I am having a hard time recommending it.
First of all, the game is very short for the asking price... but since the value is decent enough
and the entire presentation is downright great, I can let this one slide.
The entire game revolves around the Idea of 'What if we make a Boss-Rush Game with SotC-Art, except the
player and every boss dies in one single hit'.
And while that does make the game unique and occasionally creates very memorable moments,
it can be very frustrating. The penalty of each death is that you respawn at a spawn point and
have to walk back to the boss you were trying to beat. So essentially just a loss of time.
The Problem is: For the amount you will die and the way death just... feels in this game,
there needed, and I mean needed to be an automatic respawn at the start of every single boss fight.
The way they chose to go here just is.. highly frustrating. It takes away from the meat of the
game and heavly discourages experimentation with your approach to combat.

To sum it all up, this overall good (great at times even) game has a few design flaws that take

Everybody else should be very cautious and maybe test the water before.

Around the time just after the Update 11: Deadlock Gamemode was released I would have recommended this game in good conscious, but that was two years ago.
After that said update, the addition of new game modes, crouching, tactical cover, and an additional weapon - made me think this game was really coming together. The developers have proven they are dedicated to the player base; and were willing to talk the talk, and walk the walk. After Update 11 came out my choice in purchasing Interstellar Marines felt entirely justified.
Gameplay wise, Interstellar Marines is very unique. There is no minimap, or ‘x-ray vision’ capabilities. The game is totally immersive - realistic - focused around shooter instinct, reflexes, and awareness. Players must rely on vantage points, shadows, weapon control, and tactics to survive. Any notion of quickscoping, drop shooting, jump shots, or other miscellaneous antics are out the window. Mechanics wise, Interstellar Marines is one of the most realistic first person shooters available, and it provides a competitive challenge.
Unfortunately, the failure of the Hell Week campaign to revitalize the game was the last chance for Interstellar Marines. With lack of funding, ZPS had to layoff most of it’s staff and is operating barebones. Although there are promises of continued development, many avid fans have left, or remain skeptical. Due to the slowing in development I cannot recommend this game.
There is a sad story here that goes even deeper. In today's indie game scene it’s easy to sell out. Interstellar Marines is an uncompromised artistic vision. ZPS hasn't sold out to anyone (which is why they had a hard time funding the game). The soul of IM is there, but the body isn't.
ZPS, you guys are awesome. I only wish things could have turned out better because you deserve it. You never gave in, and always kept trying.
Somewhere inside me, I still believe, but I cannot lead people astray.
I do not recommend this game; if only I could.

Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed, in case you can't tell from the title, is a racing game, and the sequel to Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing. In this game your car transforms into a plane or boat depending on what the course calls for at certain points. As you play the game you earn experience points, and when you level up, you earn a new mod for that character. Mods are changes to how your character's vehicle handles. Because you have to level up each character individually to unlock all the mods for all the characters, it can either be something that adds replay value for you, or be an unfun grind. Aside from the usual grand prix and versus modes, there is a quest mode as well, where you complete challenges to earn stars that allow you to unlock more characters, mods for characters, and of course more challenges. Some of these challenges can be really difficult at times, and to top it off there's also an extra difficulty to unlock that makes these challenges even harder. While the game doesn't have as many power ups or courses to choose from as Mario Kart games have nowadays, the gameplay is solid, and the courses often have multiple paths you can take that act as shortcuts. So far in these Sega All Stars games, I think this one has the best fan service. It's also the best looking and best sounding game in the series. This game is available for multiple platforms, but I recommend getting it on Steam assuming you have the specs to run it, since the Steam version has more exclusive characters than any other version, including an exclusive DLC character.

Wow. The sheer amount of storytelling involved in this game amazes me.
Short Review: 9.5/10
Longer Review: My story began as a humble hunter, alone in a rimworld. I had nothing but my shelter and bow, just trying to survive. I hadn't been alone long, when a young lady that was being chased by a gang of feral tribesmen crossed my path. I offered her shelter, and fought off the gang. It didn't take long for a romance to bloom, resulting in a vow of matrimony. For a while, we lived happily, expanding my once lonely cabin into a refuge for the lost. Unfortunately, tragedy struck. My wife was out gathering berries for the night's meal when a grizzly bear found his. I heard the screams from the refuge, and quickly grabbed my bow and rushed to the woods. As soon as I saw what was happening, I drew my bow, and fired. And fired. And fired. The bear finally went down in a bloody heap, now missing its eyes and right paw. I sprinted to my wife. She was alive, but bleeding out quickly. The bear had torn off both of her legs. I carried her back to the refuge and spared no expense or expertise to help her. The refuge doctor was able to save her life. We had no way to contact a rescue ship to get her to a glitterworld, but we had to do something. For years, she lay in bed, being hand fed while we came up with a solution. Finally, we made a breakthrough. Our doctor had finished his research into prosthetic procedures, and immediately prepped her for surgery. After several grueling hours, the surgery was complete. The next day, I awoke to my wife bringing me breakfast. She was walking again. Joy filled my heart.
Then we accepted a pyromaniac into the refuge and he burned the place to the ground. The end.

It has been a while since I have been so critically negative on a game as I am with LOUD on Planet X. You cannot begin to imagine how disappointed this makes me feel. I am a big fan of music and generally of music games especially when they try and do something unique. This is basically a musical rhythm shooter. In a way it attempts to borrow from great games such as Crypt of the NecroDancer and the more action-y parts of Rock Band and Guitar Hero in order to forge something unique. But sadly it just does not work. At least not on PC and without a touch screen. I wonder if this game would work as intended on mobile devices.
The best critical praise that I can offer for the game is that the track selection is brilliant. I haven’t heard of most of these bands and I am quite thankful for being introduced to them through the game. Call me musically naive but unless you work hard on keeping up with the indie music scene in another country I imagine that the two scenes are very different. I’ve already decided that I am going to purchase some of these tracks and albums on iTunes and in a way given the game has had that effect on me – and I imagine others as well – then in a way the game is a success for those bands.
The keyboard controls are putrid. The key set up is 1, Q, A and Z. You almost have to play with the keyboard turned sideways for that set up to feel comfortable but then you have a keyboard jutted out towards you. Sadly, the Xbox One controller that I use isn’t much better as you spend far too long trying to groove around from lane to lane. This is the single greatest issue with the game and is the primary reason why the game in its current state is unplayable. If you can’t control a rhythm game in an appropriate fashion then you have a dud game.
I’d love to see the devs work on their game and release something more playable. Until then I cannot recommend this game unless you’re in it purely for the music.

Electronic Super Joy is the sexiest, most infuriating game I have ever played. The humor is sharp and the music is awesome, and while there are many platformers that are "challenging," Electronic Super Joy feels more like Super Meat Boy on LSD. Infinite checkpoints (complete with sexy moans and oh yeahs) make sure you're never too far off course, and the gameplay is tight and constantly changing. The final boss in particular is a nerve wracking experience in that I personally both loved and despised, for it took me far too many tries to finish even though I knew what I had to do.
This game is not for the faint of heart, and there were plenty of areas that made me stop and take breaks after many frustrating failures. At the same time, the game is not strictly a barebones platformer. Many mechanics are implemented through out such as changing gravity and a constantly changing move set, but there are plenty of moments where ESJ becomes more like a bullet hell shooter, keeping the freshness around even after I felt I'd seen it all.
It feels unfair to compare this Meat Boy, for the platforming has a very different feel than many games of the genre, nor is it as nearly precise, even though it demands it. This often led me to most of my frustrations as I found it harder and harder to play out what I was supposed to do, for the controls can be extremely touchy, even with a gamepad. There were plenty of moments where my palms were sweating less out of nerves than frustration, but these sections are not common and did not ruin my enjoyment.
Plenty of modes are offered as well, including an endless runner that I enjoyed a bit more than I should've. There are also four bonus levels that you can unlock once you find all the collectable stars, but they pose a challenge that far exceeded my abilities, as I only managed to complete one of them. I got half way through the second before being driven insane by some of the obstacles, and the other two including I tried a few times before calling it quits. Completionists will enjoy the increased challenge, but for me the fun quickly waned.
All in All, Electronic Super Joy is a fantastic but flawed game that far surpasses most games that come out of the indie scenes. Strikingly unique but with a familiar feel, this game will leave you with a lasting impression and a sense of accomplishment time and time again.

I wanted to like this game so much, the music is great, the concept is fun, presentation is clean.
BUT
Pet Peeve: 4:4 songs are *also* all divisible time signatures, thus, a hit on a half, quarter, or sixteenth should count. As this is a rhythm shooter primarily, it literally behooves the player to shoot on the 16th, but that's somehow "wrong" even while it's on beat (the majority of the songs in this game are a flat 4:4)
The keyboard keys are 1, q, a, z (try to imagine how your hand sits to hit those on beat,) and the studio has literally done absolutely nothing to make it accessible on a gamepad, which is criminal considering that without a touchscreen, this game is basically unplayable. *Maybe* a gamepad or a rhythm controller like a Rock Band guitar, could be mapped to make it better, but the control mapping functions are completely stock, have labels that are not related to game functions (so you don't know if you are mapping a button to "top lane" or to "Loud mode" or what,) and the stock gamepad mapping is basically unplayable as shipped. A simple gamepad control scheme would make this game great, but it apparently wasn't worth it to the team to map one, or even make it easy for us to do it ourselves.
Good music, neat idea, unplayable game. Seriously, take the couple of hours to map some worthwhile controls to the *primary* control method available on PC's before you just ship♥♥♥♥♥♥to Steam, where we'll be playing with gamepads or mouse n keys. There may come a day when Telltale Games fails to hit one out of the park. There may be a time when Telltale tells a tale that is bad, or even worse, boring. Rest assured, it is not this day. This is another great foray into someone else's IP, and they deliver yet again on the promise of a tale well told.
Not to avoid full disclosure, I really enjoyed Borderlands 2, even if I was  a late adopter. I really dug the whole vibe, and it fit really well with the whole Space Cowboy scifi subgenre that I formatted my mind too when first I saw Cowboy Bebop in 1996. So I am a fan of both Telltale Games and Borderlands. Honestly I find it very difficult to reccomend the game despite being a huge DB fan.  At the time of writing it has multiple server issues, which cause crashes and booting from the game even during single player.  The fighting system is fairly boring without a huge amout of depth or strategy.  The charecters are limited to very samey combos with little unique flare in terms of mele ( for example on the game pad there is a single combo that lasts longer and thus dfoes mroe damage making it the best one in every situation).  The ki batsts have been altered so you can't charge them anymore so they become an easily dodged medium range attack that is again the same for every character.  Teleportation is now based on a stamina bar which is also used for dashing so you have to choose between moving around the map at a reasonable speed and ebiong able to dodge your opponents attacks, ( this can run out mid mele too which is very frustraiting).  Each character has their own set of special moves and finishers which are very pretty and feel good to use the first few times but quickly become broring as you'll end up using only one or two per character.
The game's much touted character creater is paddling pool deep. you can chosse from five different races and then male or female which all have differnt attributes, which, at first glance looks varied.  However on further investigation of these classes one is very diffuclt to play on account of having speed penalites, and of the other four, only the saiyans have access to transformation techniques which make them the obvious choice as thay have more power and thus more damage.
To add to this the single player is agnosising, there are several fights where opponents whon't react to yor attacks, but you react to theirs meaning they can stunlock you and defeat you in seconds.  There are multiple stage fights where if you lose you must do all of the preciding fighs again  ( in trh saiyan saga you must battle  5 saibamen with allies , five mroe saibamen without allies, Nappa with piccolo, Nappa without piccolo, then Nappan and vegeta all in a single health bar and lsoing rests the whole thing).   One last gripe about the single player there are several fights against multiple opponents, you can only attack and dodge the enemy you are locked onto meaningyou can be attack from behind or the flanks by enemies off screen and cannot teleport put of their attacks, you just have to wait from them to finish fall to the floor get up change locked on taget then you can carry on.
TLDR the games is shallow, poorly designed, and only gets by on it IP. don'y buy it

Red Alert 3: Uprising is a standalone expansion to the original Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3. I played the game before buying it again on Steam. Much of what I said in my review of the original game still stands: this is a fun game and if you like real-time strategy games -- and especially if you like Command & Conquer -- you should get this.
For an RTS, though, this is a little strange as the game is entirely focused on singleplayer. This is perfect for me, but I expect those who enjoy the competitive aspect might find it less appealing. The game introduces some new units to every faction. There are also four new campaigns with new actors to add to the original campaigns, and each of these is more or less comparable to the original campaigns.
The game adds replayability by the inclusion of a Commander's Challenge: these are challenge maps where the object is to finish each scenario using a limited subset of the total tools available to you. As you complete challenges, new units will unlock, offering more possibilities. I like the inclusion of this mode and it adds a competitive element without the need to go against other humans, as you're essentially competing against the computer and yourself.
In other words, this is an interesting expansion that quite literally expands on the original Red Alert 3. If you liked that game and are hungry for more singleplayer content, you should purchase this pack. If you don't care about singleplayer, there's no reason for you to buy it; you should stick with the base game.

Blind Love is easily one of the best examples of how a visual novel can achieve narrative brilliance. The artwork is done in black and white, making a sketched interpretation of the world. This style leaves the the world etched, not permanent. A concept brought more to life by the story and dialogue options. The voice work is executed with professionalism, yet, there are points of vocal uncertainty, audibly matching the artwork's guessing at reality. There is this perfect harmony brought by these two halves. It feels that at the same time you are experiencing the game, the voice actors are as well. It feels like a shared experience. It feels genuine.
There's a part of the story I have to point out since it is directly responsible for making this one of the best VN's I have read. At one point early on in the story, in the months after Alex's accident and getting into a routine, it's revealed he's a writer and working on a novel. There are dialogue options here that frame a turning point for his main character and the novel as a whole. The same dialogue options here mirror two later ones in the ending of the story for Alex's relationship with Sera. Maybe I'm alone here in believing this story offers this view of how everyone has their own battlefield; Alex and his blindness, Sera and her PTSD, Josh and Tyler, Alex's main character and his love, etc. I'm sure that term and examination has been used before explaining love and the path to it or even from it, but this was done with such precise subtlety that as I read it, the honesty of this story was far more emboldened.
Blind Love feels authentic, a property all stories should strive for and this story succeeds so beautifully. It explores the reality of personal difficulties and doesn't handle them with care, instead leaves real choices up to the player and allows real consequences to then occur. I absolutely recommend this game.
Worth the money. Get it.

RimWorld is a self-proclaimed "A sci-fi colony sim driven by an intelligent AI storyteller".
It is a god-game in which you take care of a group of colonists, give them orders and ensure their well-being.
Throughout the game, the storyteller will trigger random events - some good, some bad - to keep you on your toes.
Similar to other god-games, RimWorld is a rather indirect experience. Most of the time, you will plan strategies, issue orders and check up on everyone to see if they have any needs.
Progress manifests through a larger base, more technologies and better weaponry. Depending on your scenario, you will begin with bow and arrow or simple bolt-action rifles, and end up with power-armor and rocket launchers.
In the default setting, the goal is for you to repair a spaceship found somewhere on the planet, repair it and flee said planet.
To be honest, this goal is more of a pro-forma goal, as I personally believe the goal is just to build a base and enjoy yourself.
The description of the game mentions "an intelligent AI storyteller". What this means is you can choose between three different storytellers as of version A17.
These storytellers have varying "personalities", which events trigger how often. The "classical" storyteller is designed to provide a steadily increasing challenge, the "relaxed" storyteller is aimed to provide a more laid-back experience (my personal favourite), while "random" storyteller is - you guessed it - more random.
In addition to choosing which storyteller you like, you can also set a difficulty, which affects how much of a curveball they are going to throw you. If you're unlucky, one of your colonists might have a heart attack while a generator explodes, igniting your warehouse in which you store your highly volatile chemical fuel, all while a group of heavily armed raiders land in rocket pods and promptly begin murdering everyone in sight. But hey, at least sometimes a squirrel tames itself.
I personally did not have a problem with understanding the game's core mechanics. The in-game tutorial does a great job at explaining the gameplay basics and the controls and after an hour or two of playing around, you'll get the hang of it. I should mention that the game does have a very active subreddit (/r/RimWorld) and a somewhat extensive wiki, which are great sources for additional knowledge.
All in all, I consider this game to be easy to pick up, if you do not go overboard in the beginning and settle in the middle of an ice desert on extreme difficulty on your first run.
Even though the game is in early access, the game has excellent modding support. After several hours of playthrough, I did install a few mods, which just extended the game in a way I enjoyed it. One mod, for instance, allowed me to create prosthetics myself (in the vanilla game, anything more complex than a peg leg needs to be purchased from exotic goods vendors, if they have them available). Another allowed me to set up a temporary camp instead of a permanent settlement, which I enjoyed.
If you can have fun with a game that does not provide explosions and action 100% of the time, then you can have fun with RimWorld. The game is easy to pick up, yet has a surprizing amount of depth and complexity once you get into it, that you can easily sink whole days into it. I mean, in which other game do you hear questions like "Is it feasable to create an organ farm or should I sell my slaves directly?" or "How can I stop my drug-addicted cook from killing his wife?"?

The backgrounds of the characters made it seem very realistic and it flowed quite well from start to finish as everything linked back to their experiences that were explained at the beginning of the game. At certain moments your heart would ache and you would feel sympathy for the characters because of what they have been through. I don't generally write reviews, but as I'm approaching 250 hours in this game, I felt like I should say something.
TL;DR: Many people hate on this game, but I believe that this is still a good game, just not as good as it once was or could be.
So, I've played this game since its alpha stages, and about 6 months into my experience, it went to beta. I guess, compared to many other veteran players of this game, a newcomer. I was not around when there were still tiered cubes, 3 weapon types, etc etc, so I guess that people are just salty that those things went away. If you are just starting this game, though, you don't need to worry about any of those things, as you would've had no experience with them anyway.
The complaints about loot crates, however, I can fully support. The chances that you will receive a legendary weapon/equipment/movement type are 0 to none. They are extremely rare. You COULD buy them from the shop, but good luck grinding hard enough to get the amount of Robits required to purchase one. I have never received a legendary from a crate, and I've played for nearly 250 hours. A friend of mine, however, started about a month ago and already has 2 Laser Leviathan Carbon 6 and a Missile Launcher. How does that work, FJ??
Anyways, on to the good parts about this game.
The most obvious reason you'd want to play this game is because of the absolutely TREMENDOUS amount of customizability. You build your vehicle robot thing from the ground up-you literally have to build a chassis, add movement parts, weapons, radar system, etc etc until you have a beast of a war machine. This is an excellent concept that I love. The only downside is that some good parts are very rare and very expensive.
Another positive aspect of this game is the combat baalance. Every few updates, some type of build becomes the new meta, but these are very easy to counter. One of the best examples I can think of is drones. Little blocks of thrusters and lasers that were extremely fast and extremely annoying. These were easily countered by tanks with large amounts of health and a flak cannon. On the note of the flak cannon and weapons, there are many types of weapons. There are lasers, plasma cannons, flak canons, rocket launchers, and many more. There are also many movement types. You can build hovering vehicles, helicopters, jets, propeller powered planes, cars, tanks, mechs, and insane combinations of all of them!
Anyways, I think this game is pretty good, but could be better. I'd give it a 6.5/10.

This video sums up my review:
Skip to 2:40 - 3:25
----
If you're interested in hearing how great this game
, check out the latter half of this review. This'll hopefully be good feedback for the devs, if they decide to read this.
----
The game starts you out with a couple of bossfights. Edit: Actually, the entire game is only boss fights.
That's not really a problem (though is something they could've improved upon). Here's the real problem.
The first one is somewhat manageable, but the next two definitely feel like they were designed for people who've somehow already mastered the system after only one battle - or in other words, the devs who are already very used to the controls and timing.
Everything is a one-hit-kill apparently, so you might find yourself restarting constantly a few times just trying to figure out not how to get smashed by the cube boss.
The game has a lot of potential - as the graphics and sounds are all fairly good. The graphics and animation are the reason I bought the game.
Edit: After looking at the community guide and seeing what more bosses are like, yeah, there's a huge amount of lost potential here. A lot of the graphics and animation are really amazing. On top of that, a lot of the bosses look very creative.
Unfortunately, the gameplay just doesn't check out.
----
Before people go on about how I'm just a bad gamer who dislikes hard games, that assumption is wrong.
This game would have definitely been more well received...
1. If it wasn't just boss fights, and there were actual creative Zelda-like normal enemies and areas to explore.
You know what makes me sad about Fez? It has
enemies and bosses. If that game had actual combat, it surely would've been something amazing, just like Super Paper Mario.
2. If the game actually had a difficulty curve, instead of dropping you into what feels like endgame bosses.
Imagine if the first area were more forgiving and you at least had 3 hearts or whatever. The second and third cube bosses had weaker versions, while the ones you encounter here are the endgame hyper versions.
The game would've been overall more playable, and people would only be dropping out (if at all) near the endgame instead of the very start of your game.
Instead of a playerbase of only people who put up with that stuff or really like a challenge, you could have a playerbase of pretty much any gamer.
----
After looking around on the community hub, I also came across that quick kills guide, which kind of immediately trivializes many bosses by showing you a way to beat many of them without the boss being able to get much of its attacks in.
Honestly, it would've been better to throw these bosses in a more Zelda-like game with a little bit of back-and-forth, where you're going to have to actually survive the boss's mechanics for a bit, but you're also not a one hit kill.
Perhaps that's the reason Link's arrows don't just instantly kill bosses for shooting them in the eye.
Oh, and I'm not kidding at all about making it
not an instant-kill game. It's actually very important.
I guess I can't imagine enemies like that eyeball cube not being an instant-kill, but perhaps the sequence where he "rapidly moves towards your direction to crush you instantly" could simply be one of his attacks, instead of what he does all the time, where he's otherwise normally slow and more manageable.
In the mean time, the cube would have more than just one health, so you wouldn't be able to cheese the boss from the start, and will actually have to fight it even if you look up a guide.
A simple change like that also allows the laser attack to remain as an instant kill too.
Overall, it'd feel much more like an actual boss fight that way.
----
I'm definitely looking forward to anything the devs of this game might make in the future, if they learn from the flaws of this game and improve upon them.
If I have to be really nitpicky, I think the magnet arrow thing is a little awkward or strange to use, and that they should try slightly different mechanics for the weapon. Perhaps I only had a problem with it because retrieving the arrow forces you to stand completely still, in a game where you should be constantly moving, so I can't do what I intuitively want to do, and retrieve it while walking.
That on its own isn't a big issue though. Perhaps it wouldn't have even been a problem if there were a difficulty curve that teaches you to deal with it being this way.
----
I understand that the devs like the difficulty of Dark Souls and the idea of challenging gameplay.
But I think that could've been retained by pushing it into the endgame.
Maybe it's because I'm tempted to compare this game to the likes of literally any other 2D game, rather than 3D game.
Maybe it just didn't feel fun to actually try and solve bosses beyond the slime boss. I had fun fighting the slime boss, because it felt manageable and I was able to learn how to beat it blindly.
As soon as I got to the eyecube and brainfreeze, this feeling was lost. Maybe it's because the slime boss actually had pseudo-health, so I thought I was actually damaging it when I wasn't. The heart of the slime boss kind of came out of nowhere for me, but I understood that that's what I was supposed to do immediately.
I also had a good idea of what to do against eyecube and brainfreeze, but against them it felt a lot more difficult to actually properly land a hit on them, or to even retrieve your arrow after you lose it.
It was with those two bosses that I could tell that trying to land the hit on them would be stupidly difficult and require crazy timing. (Until I saw the quick kills guide that is).
Compared to... I Wanna By The Boshy... it just didn't seem like it'd be as fun to actually overcome those walls.
I played IWBTB all the way to the Kirby levels where your screen is constantly flipping, which I only dropped out of halfway in after getting tired by the screenflip mechanic.
In IWBTB, it was at least fun enough for me to overcome the rooms involved and progress.
If I had to say why, perhaps it's because there's a much more instantaneous respawn. I forget how close you respawn to where you die in that game, but I do remember it being very instant and quick to get back to where you go.
That kind of thing helps balance out a difficult game, as you at least get to keep going at it constantly. I've ran TF2 servers where a lot of instant-kill happens, and I always couple it with instant respawn to make up for that. Respawn times just aren't fun in an instant-kill environment.
So yeah, it was a little annoying having to wait for that very small few seconds or so to run all the way from spawn back to the boss I was trying to figure out.
Edit: And it looks like my intuition isn't wrong here. Other people have complained about it too. Maybe it's a good thing Momodora put checkpoints right outside of boss rooms?
The thing you want to capture is the frantic feeling of hitting a boss with difficult timing while dodging it, not so much being dropped out of the fight quickly for every little mistake or thing you need to learn.
----
By the way. Mouse support?
Good thing I just happened to buy a controller last week. But really. Does this game really not have mouse support.

It happens. When it happens repeatedly, submit a bug report, email the company, talk to Customer Support if you're brave enough, but unless the game is something as dysfunctional as Journey of the Light or Soda Drinker Pro, don't go leaving poor reviews and hating on the developers because you found a bug or a glitch.
