OK, so this is the part that, after many hours in-game and countless patches released by developers, made me write this review.
Long story short: I bought the game mid-June 2015, noticing a fun indie title with overwhelmingly positive (back then) reviews. Well, ♥♥♥♥ me, I bought a 4-pack to play with friends, bought the DLCs, told friends to buy DLCs (or bought them myself then gifted) so we can play the whole thing together, that sort of thing - you know the drill. Tried playing - nope, had to portforward, as peer-to-peer wasn't available back then. OK, no big deal, added one rule to firewall and all is good. Tried again - massive synchronisation problems, invisible monsters, traps working out of sync from the server. Game was basically unplayable, because it seemed like each player was seeing different game. So the game was shelved, hoping that errors will be patched, network protocol will be fixed and so on.
Fast-forward to 2016: things are unbelievably and utterly ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don't think I've ever seen more horribly broken piece of network software than Hero Siege and believe me, I've seen some seriously ♥♥♥♥ed up brain-damaged♥♥♥♥♥♥working as a professional and fairly low-level programmer and hobbyist gamedev. Out of morbid curiosity, I would like to peer into this abyss of shoddy sourcecode, knowingly that there could be an unspeakable, lovecraftian horror lurking inside, waiting for another soul to consume.
Think about everything that can go wrong with synchronising the state of two game clients (or rather: client and server) in a game like this and it will go wrong, plus a lot more.
All of this was observed while playing side by side, so that I could compare in what state the server sees the world to what is displayed on the client by looking directly on neighboring computer screen.
What's really fun is that some of these problems are directly caused by game engine sucking big time on efficiency front and that networking is seemingly tied to the graphics engine, doing stuff like positions recalculations with each frame redraw. When FPS on server starts dropping for some reason (many monsters and items on the screen) while on the client FPS stays high,♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan in the most spectacular fashion.
And don't get me started on playing on properly powerful machine. I comfortably played Diablo 2 (which looks better than Hero Siege BTW) on PentiumII 333 MHz. ♥♥♥♥ing hell, even on 6-core 3.2 GHz CPU this game can noticeably lag while opening chests (when many coins are being spawned on screen) or starting another wave of monsters! We have GPUs for a reason, and that reason is not "standing idly while CPU works its♥♥♥♥♥off on graphics processing".
What's even more disconcerting is the current idea of dealing with the problems of desynchronisation. In news posting from 8 Jan 2016, developers stated that they want to move the responsibility of checking whether client was hit by a trap or a monster to the client itself.
Seriously. Let that thought sink in for a while.
Or else you'll be having immortal players all around, faster than you'll be able to say "you are free to cheat as you like and we won't even bother checking♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
To add insult to injury, developers are incompetent on the security front. They got hacked (cracked), not once but
and it resulted in mass banning of players by the crackers. I do not condone cracking, though it made me think about security practices applied in Panic Art Studios and whether they, for example, store players' passwords in plaintext. Though seeing how they want to fix problems with their networking by blindly believing input from clients, maybe I shouldn't be surprised.
Oh, did I mention that sometimes you'll spawn in town as another character class? E.g. you play a Pyromancer and someone else is Viking. Then sometimes when moving to town you'll become a Viking. Luckily this is only temporary but still it boggles the mind on how deep is the rabbit hole.

I first came across Titan Souls in its Ludum Dare 28: "You Only Get One" form a few years ago. The game had a simple and elegant premise: There are four Titans that you must hunt down and kill; to accomplish this task, you are given a bow, with only one arrow that can be telekinetically called back to you, and the ability to dodge roll. Much like its inspiration and one of my personal favorite titles, Shadow of the Colossus, Titan Souls's battle design focuses on ascertaining how to locate and reach the Titans' weak points, then deciding when the best time to attack would be. Unlike SotC, however, both you and the Titans die in only one hit, producing a much more tense and twitchier experience. Overall, I had a good time with it, and I was not surprised when it eventually went on to win multiple first-place awards in the game jam.
Fast-forward to its commercial release — there are more Titans to defeat, more environments to explore, and the overall aesthetic is much more polished. On the other hand, aside from being able to aim in 360 degrees instead of just the cardinal directions, as well as being able to run a bit quicker by holding down the roll button, the core mechanics are essentially unchanged. This is all well and good — no need to fix what isn't broken — save for one major, inexplicable lapse in player-friendliness.
For whatever reason, when you die, you don't restart right at the beginning of the boss encounter, but rather at the last activated checkpoint on the world. This was tolerable in Ludum Dare version, which only had three Titans to fight and could be completed in around 10 minutes, but now there are over 15, all of them still able to kill you in one fell swoop.
I pondered to myself for quite some time as to why the developers would keep such a frustrating punishment in the game, but all I could think of was pseudo-artistic ideals like savoring the journey or whatever — stuff that would certainly be nice to do if most of us didn't also have to worry about wasting our time. Indeed, I am convinced that at least a quarter of my four hours of playtime was purely spent on backtracking to bosses.
The difficulty curve in this game can also be a bit erratic. Aside from the opening quartet and the final bosses, you can take on the Titans in any order, and some are decidedly more tricky than others to defeat. I went in a counter-clockwise fashion from the start and I found that the Titans got easier by doing so, and it didn't really feel like it was because I was achieving greater mastery over the controls either; it was more that the bosses farther along the clock were speedier and had smaller vulnerability windows.
As a final insult to injury, almost all Titans also have achievements tied to killing them in a specific way, like doing it in under 10 seconds or cutting off all parts instead of a few. You do unlock the ability to re-fight all Titans (plus a few additional play modes) once you've beaten the game, but you still have to keep backtracking to them. I'd be willing to try my hand at the achievements if the game would just let me get right back into the fight after dying, but in this state I'd rather spend my time elsewhere.
That all being said, it is incredibly rewarding to finally get those split-second victories, and while traversing the same areas repeatedly just to return from a loss is irritating, at the very least it is all pleasing to the eye. Some of the Titans use 3D models which actually mesh really nicely with the 2D environments, and the true final boss (haha, pun) has one of the most striking visual designs I've seen in quite some time.
In the end, while I personally felt satisfied with the game, I can't wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone else unless they are sure they can stomach spending the same amount of time backtracking to bosses as they do actually fighting them.

This is the most frustrating game I've played, and it's not just because you constantly and repeatedly die in every single fight. It's because of how this is implemented through the mechanics of the game which makes it unbearable. I can't believe it took me 3 hours before I rage-quitted, I should've done it way earlier.
Titan Souls supposed to be a sort of game where you learn the attack patterns of your bosses and exploit their weakness in order to triumph, using your skills both in-game and IRL. But in this case, it can't work, since your entire repretoire consists a single arrow which you can fire and retrieve, and a dodge roll. Also, every battle is instant-death based, meaning your learning curve is based on trial and error (or to be more specific, rinse and repeat and not observation or skill polishing.
The lack of a progression system makes it even worse. You are stuck with your single arrow, and your 1-Hit-KO health throught the entire span of the game. When defeating a boss, a sort of soul-absorption ritual appears on the screen. For every gamer this signifies leveling up, or acquiring EXP, but here it's just for appearance, without any meaning gameplay wise. No shops or coins, no weapons or items, just a single arrow, and a dodge-roll.
To be added to this is the excruciating trips throughout the landscape, in low speed, even while "running". While the scenery is gorgeous, it misses the point entirely, due to the lack of narrative presence or items to enhance these trips. There are no pre-battle save points, only ones for specific areas. For a fighting-based game, the battle-to-walk ratio is extremely unsatisfying.
On a positive note, The music for each battle is good, even great at times. It's utterly pointless though, because even the longest battles are about half a minute long. Another positive aspect would be the diverse nature of the surroundings and bosses. Every fight is different than the other aesthetically, and most of the bosses are designd to fit their enviornment. But as mentioned earlier, this is only for shows, and in no way enhances the experience.
Overall, I do not recommend this game for playing.

Nutshell: 11/10 - A true classic FPS game, plus it works FLAWLESSLY on windows 10.
Setup: 12/10 - So, to begin, I love how it only took 2 seconds to install for me, this game is only 6MB in size, this means, or course, it will take little to no time to install, and you should not worry about hard disk space.  Second, on to what I'm really impressed by, is this game is likely an MS-DOS game (like most 3D games of it's era on PC) however, it ran PERFECTLY, no crashing, no bugs, no exceptionally low framerates, runs like a charm! The fact I could just click play and go, was more than enough for a 12/10 rating on this section of this review, it's the easiest-to-set-up game of it's era I've played so far.
Controls: 9/10 - Keep in mind, this game is incredibly old, and is from an era where there were no standards for control schemes in FPS games, in fact, not everyone had a mouse back then. I suggest looking through the controls of the game to edit things to your liking if the controls aren't the way you want them.
Graphics (compared to games of it's era): 10/10 - So, this game dates back to 1992, there's not many games I can really compare it to, so, I compared it to Star Wars: Dark Forces, System Shock, Doom, and Quake, I would not really call anything released later a fair comparison, but, compared to these games I mentioned, the graphics look amazing, really well-done for 1992.
Graphics (Compared to modern-day games): 0/10 - Obviously, this game doesn't compare to modern games, why did I bother mentioning this part of the review? Cause some graphics-hogs out there still will ask me this, don't let this portion deter you from buying this game, it's great.
Overall it's a nice little game to spend using your spare steam wallet funds on, absolutely worth the money, and a great piece of gaming history here too.

This is a very good and enjoyable game with some flaws. Would definitely recommend trying it out. Your initial impression may be that it is P2W but it most definitely isn't - everything is available in the in-game market for coins which you can earn by crafting and selling what you craft. It's a good idea to buy at least one of the vehicle packs just to give you a decent start in the game.
This is still in early beta and the devs are updating this regularly so things can change quite significantly. Dev support is very good at the moment and has been all the way through development.
Pros:
- very fun gameplay, fast and furious
- building your vehicle is a game in itself
- alot of possible vehicle combos that can suit your own playstyle - fast buggies, slow tanks, cannons, missiles, machineguns
- art style works very well and is quite atmospheric
- the 'meta' vehicles change often, so there's never one 'killer' build.
- your mistakes and those of your opponents can be ruthlessly puinished!
Cons:
- can be difficult to get started as you are limited in part count on your vehicle and access to fuel for PvE missions until you start levelling up with the various factions
- higher tier weapons can feel out of reach at the start
- low storage count in your inventory can be frustrating later on without spending coins to upgrade it
- vehicle part limit doesn't advance in pace with the number of parts you can get from the factions (this needs a re-balance IMHO)
- matchmaking can be a bit weird sometimes especially outside of peak hours for your region (being actively worked on as a priority by the devs)
Disclaimer: I've played this since Alpha outside of Steam, although had a long break after the closed beta server wipe and returned to the game for the Steam release.

Bridge Constructor is a nice and simple way to waste some time. The story in the game is very straightforward. There has been a devastating earthquake that has destroyed the bridges on the islands of Camatuga and the player is in charge of their rebuilding. The problem for the player is that the available budget for the bridge constructions is very tight, so it is not possible to make too advanced solutions or to use the more expensive materials as much as would be ideal. After building the bridges, they have to be tested by letting some cars and/or trucks cross and if the bridge collapses a rethink of the design is needed. When all bridges on Camatuga are functioning for trucks, the game opens up for tests using heavy tanker trucks on the newly constructed bridges, with an often sad and explosive result prompting a redesign of the bridges.
Sometimes the statics of the bridge constructions seem a bit off with collapsing at unexpected places, but usually some engineering common sense and experimenting will solve the problems. It would have been nice to be able to play some of the levels with unlimited budget in order to test some truly exotic bridge designs, but the game is good enough as it is.
This is not a game to spend full evenings with because of its repetitive nature, but it is a relaxing game to play for a couple of minutes now and then. Quite a bit like sudoku.

You don't talk about the history of FPS games without mentioning the very first revolutionary title in the genre. Although the store page says 1994 I believe the game was released in 1992. Hovertank 3D and Catacomb 3-D were both titles using the same engine but in a more primitive form. Suffice it to say that Wolf 3D was an enhanced version back then. This was before Doom so we can consider this game the grandfather of all FPS titles.
Nazis and treasure. That's all what Wolf 3D stands for. We shoot guards and collect treasure in 6 chapters consisting of 60  levels referred to as floors since there's an elevator at the end of each level representing the exit. Lots of secrets can be found along the way - our job is simply to press the use button on paintings on the wall (or sometimes in between them). These often hold even more treasure. There's one secret level on each floor along with a bossfight.
If only there were some cool achievements included in the Steam version! The game runs under DosBox, however, I recommend that you download the ECWolf upgrade which features the option to select a greater resolution as well as customizable controls. Similarly to Doom a so-called Brutal version is available with enhanced graphics, much faster gameplay and new animations (including gory ones).

I was initially really, really torn over whether I should recommend this game. I'd say it's not a good game, but it is a good proof-of-concept, the concept being that both the player and the bosses die in one hit. This is something that was on my mind right before I came across Titan Souls, what it'd be like to get rid of this sort of health grind in boss battles and just simplify it all down to the most important thing: figuring out where and how to hit the boss and then doing it without making too many mistakes. And on that front only, the game delivers.
The bosses (18 of them) vary in difficulty and concept. Like regular game bosses, some rely on getting the perfect hit and some are puzzle bosses where you need to figure out what to do. Some of them are challenging for the right reasons, others for the wrong reasons (luckily only a couple of such on normal difficulty), some others are easy. A lot of them really work well and are fun to fight despite the fact that they can be killed in only one hit, which of course sounds easier than it is. Expect to have hundreds of deaths. There are also no upgrades, weapons, powerups etc. just an arrow that you need to retrieve if you mess up and a roll for defense. I enjoy this simplicity.
Walking is a common complaint for this game. Each time you die, you're respawned at a checkpoint outside the boss' arena that is shared by 1-2 other nearby bosses and you have to walk for 5-10 seconds back to the boss. As someone who hates it when games do this, I honestly thought it wasn't that bad. I think I can see why they did it in a way, because with no health on the bosses, meaning there's nothing to reset in most cases, you'd barely notice your deaths, in which case you might as well have no dying at all. So the threat of walking encourages the player to avoid the boss' attacks more as they attempt to figure out what to do. Still, it's a fair complaint and something that a lot of people hated. There is also lots of walking around the overworld where there is absolutely nothing to do except walking to the next boss. In three cases they put in a simple environmental puzzle that prevents access to the boss, but that's all.
The presentation is subpar. The main character makes me think of Dora the Explorer, it looks entirely out-of-place in an ancient world filled with ruins. The pixel art style is incredibly bland. The world is composed of a forest area, snowy area and volcano area. How riveting. I did not feel invested in the world, the character (i.e. the player character, as there is no other person alive in this empty world), or the story. If I did, I'd probably enjoy looking around a lot more than I did, even if there wasn't anything to collect or help with the gameplay. If you want a presentation that's very, very similar to this, but beautifully done and more interesting, play Hyper Light Drifter (it's also got excellent gameplay to go along with it).
Some other annoyances pile up. In a few cases I could've sworn the arrow should've hit and yet it didn't. Stupidly, there is no pause button, presumably because Dark Souls didn't have one and this game is really shallow when it comes to its influences (also somethingsomething Shadow of the Colossus). Aiming long distances with such a tiny character can be frustrating because even the tiniest movement of the joystick can make you miss. A slightly longer arrow might help there visually. You also can't fire an arrow instantly upon the press of a button, which makes split-second reactions impossible. This wouldn't be so annoying if some bosses didn't require these split-second reactions, especially in hard mode.
Ah yes, hard mode. So many bosses fall apart here. They are either almost the same as they were in normal mode since any changes made to them are negligible, or they ask for ridiculous precision that ultimately comes down to pure luck, or the game just accepts that what it's asking for is ridiculous (e.g. two of the bosses literally have areas around them you can stand in that allow you to completely avoid their attacks while still being able to shoot at them). I really did not expect such terrible and amateurish design decisions after the fairly well made boss designs in normal mode. Well, except for the "last" boss that is like this, with movements that are ridiculously fast and unpredictable, making it close to impossible to hit them reliably, especially with the delay on shooting the arrow. I was honestly amazed that such an unplayable boss made it into the game but hard mode showed me that's really what the devs think counts as a challenge and it ruined the game for me.
Oh yeah, some people also complained that the game is too short for its price. It did feel short, but I bought it on sale. I don't know the exact length since I often made pauses and left the game running in the background, but I'd put it between 3-6 hours. With hard mode being terrible, there is only the no-roll mode to play after you finish the game, which I haven't tried.
In short, if you buy this game, you should expect it to feel fairly simplistic and unpolished, but the one-hit premise is nice and the boss battles are mostly well designed around that idea. So the basics are there and they're made well if you're curious what playing against bosses like this would be like. If that's enough for you to overlook the game's numerous flaws in pretty much every other area, you will get a fairly enjoyable experience. I enjoyed it, but objectively, especially after finishing hard mode, I can't call it a good game.

With they super ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game server, to the very clunky combat system, the game got way more than it deserved in its steam rating. I'll run through some pros and cons.
Pros:
You can make your own character!
You have multiple races to choose from!
The graphics are pretty decent...
Cons:
The difficulty curb for the main story jumps all over the place. One fight you can absolutely stomp stuff into a hole, then on the next one, your opponent is so fast and powerful that you can't even touch em.
Because of the above reason, you're trapped into grinding the same parallel missions over... and over... and over again.
Enemy bosses have a rather vast innate guard (basically this keeps anything you do from staggering them, which is an essential mechanic for anyone that wants to do more than frantically run away from them while hoping to hell that your beam attacks hit them. (they usually don't since you can't stagger them first)
Now this stagger issue that the bosses are more or less immune to rules out all but one playstyle, which defeats the point of being able to choose one at the start. You CAN stagger them eventually, but because you can't stagger them while you're trying to stagger them, you get ripped apart while you're working their guard down. What's worse is that when you finally break their stagger immunity, they get it back in a few seconds. This means that you have to grind lvl's until you're a great deal stronger than what the mission would normally require.
The community is more or less non-existent. So have fun playing by yourself most of the time.
That brings me to the ally AI. Compared to the enemy AI, your team mates have a severe case of autism. They actually get in the way more than they help... when they decide to help and not just float there doing nothing while you get tag teamed by the extremely responsive enemy AI.
The combat, while it has its charm, it's so slow and clunky (while the enemy ai is not bound by this slow clunky BS) that you'll find yourself getting pummeled. Not because you suck, or that you messed up, but that to do anything... ANYTHING!!!!!!!! other than what you are currently doing, you have to stop doing said action, sit there a moment and then proceed to the next action. Want to blast your oppenent away from you with a kick, teleport behind them and unleash a super instead of following up with another kick? Nope. The game just can't keep up with it. It is however possible for the AI to accomplish. There are a lot of things the AI can do that are impossible for you to do (because while you have to stop everything you're doing to do something else, the AI can seemlessly slide into any action they want). That really brings the game down a great many pegs.
The only time you're truly on even ground is in pvp combat... kinda. Bout the only match ups you're going to find are against people 40 lvls over you... Good luck with that.
Skill just isn't a factor, since they built it around a really poorly designed RPG system. Your stats determine who is winning the fight, now your talent. I've gotten really good with my character in the game, so I can't really use me sucking as an excuse. Like I said, you're go from obliterating someone (then they power up and go back to full hp (with more hp than they had before), you don't... because ♥♥♥♥ you.) to getting flattened in a matter of seconds. Just because your stats aren't high enough to do any dmg to their powered up form.
The voice overs are horrific.
The AI can literally break out of anything you get them stuck in, things you couldn't dream of doing because it just isn't possible for you. For example, if I get stuck in an enemy super, I can't use any form of attack, even my escape attack is unreachable... not for the AI though, not only that, while you can only use your escape everynow and then, they can spam it over... and over... and over again. Oh yeah, it does a good chunk of dmg, so you'll die to it... a lot.
Finally, we come to the most irritating thing about this game. You have to grind... for anything... ever. Want some of Frieza's cool attacks? Welp, get ready for 10 hours of grinding the same mission over and over again and hoping that its extremely, and I mean extremely low drop rate finally comes through for you.

I'm a die hard DBZ fan and I wanted to love this game. But, no one likes a game where the enemy isn't bound by the game's rules like you are. Can I get a stagger guard that replinishes every few seconds? Nope. Can I do anything in any situation? Nope. Can I magically heal to full hp 8 times in a single fight just by going SSJ? Nope. Can I get infinitely faster and stronger in a single fight by powering up? Nope. Does my power up last indefinitely? Nope.
If you want a good DBZ game, go out, buy a PS2, then buy DBZ Bukokai 3. They haven't been any good since that one. Oh, the voice acting and graphics in budokai 3 are waaaaaaaaay better.
"TLDR" - You are bound by the game's clunky rules, the enemy AI isn't... not even a little bit. So buy Budokai 3 if you want to enjoy a good DBZ game.

The game worth it? Like a long time id Software fan that I am, I can tell you just one thing: yes.
If you have played Doom before then you are acquainted about what Wolfenstein3D has to offer you, but it’s a little different beings Doom's ancestor. The game have the same formula, you start in a point and have to reach the end of the level fighting enemies into a huge maze floor, because Wolfentein3D had no heights difference like Doom (not even a single step), and sometimes you’ll need a key, or keys, to get to the exit. It has fewer weapons than Doom, the enemy sort is short too, but we are before the roots that bring us Doom. The game is challenger in the higher difficulty levels, and worth it like a piece of the videogames' history, not only Doom but all along the FPS history itself.
Now, about compatibility. The game comes with DOSBox, it's an emulator, it runs old PC games just like playing them on their original hardware. DOSBox runs into Windows 10 with no problems but I suggest to play it with a modern source port. My favorite is ECWolf, the game runs smoothly on my old laptop with Windows 7 at full screen resolution and high framerate, besides you can configure your keyboard better than with the original game engine. ECWolf have excellent Steam integration so you don’t need to configure anything to start playing, ECWolf searches automatically for the game in your Steam library, and the Steam Overlay works perfectly with it. ECWolf needs a little trick to works with the Steam Overlay, but no big deal. Even there's a free Android version of ECWolf, so you can have it portable too.
Like a plus, the Wolfenstein3D Steam community is friendly and they are always there to lend you a hand or give you advice if you need it. Better than lifetime support ;)

This is a very good and enjoyable game with some flaws. Would definitely recommend trying it out. Your initial impression may be that it is P2W but it most definitely isn't - everything is available in the in-game market for coins which you can earn by crafting and selling what you craft. It's a good idea to buy at least one of the vehicle packs just to give you a decent start in the game.
This is still in early beta and the devs are updating this regularly so things can change quite significantly. Dev support is very good at the moment and has been all the way through development.
Pros:
- very fun gameplay, fast and furious
- building your vehicle is a game in itself
- alot of possible vehicle combos that can suit your own playstyle - fast buggies, slow tanks, cannons, missiles, machineguns
- art style works very well and is quite atmospheric
- the 'meta' vehicles change often, so there's never one 'killer' build.
- your mistakes and those of your opponents can be ruthlessly puinished!
Cons:
- can be difficult to get started as you are limited in part count on your vehicle and access to fuel for PvE missions until you start levelling up with the various factions
- higher tier weapons can feel out of reach at the start
- low storage count in your inventory can be frustrating later on without spending coins to upgrade it
- vehicle part limit doesn't advance in pace with the number of parts you can get from the factions (this needs a re-balance IMHO)
- matchmaking can be a bit weird sometimes especially outside of peak hours for your region (being actively worked on as a priority by the devs)
Disclaimer: I've played this since Alpha outside of Steam, although had a long break after the closed beta server wipe and returned to the game for the Steam release.

But Steins;Gate is one of my all time favorite anime. If I made a top 10 list for favorite anime, it would easily make it to the top 5. The premise was interesting and the thrills were, well, thrilling. The real magic lies in the characters and their interactions. It lies in the great character design and chemistry. It lies in the OTP to end all OTP's. It lies in its ability to make you laugh and cry. It lies in the GLORIOUS SCIENCE. IN DA MADA SCIENTISTA, SO COOOOOOOR (SONUVA♥♥♥♥♥).
But I digress.
So I decide I'm in the mood for Steins;Gate. I'd finished the anime twice but I had never really played too much of the VN. As I mentioned, I'm not too much of a VN guy so I was never really interested all that much. But for some reason, it just popped into my head that I wanted to play it. So I started playing it some. And slowely the magic came back to me.
And thus began a journey.
I spent the next three WEEKS playing the VN. I was entranced just like I was with the anime. Seeing and interacting with the characters in the VN feels a lot different than just watching them. Almost all of my free time was spent progressing through the worldlines. During school and work it was constantly on my mind. It's one of those series that makes you fall in love with the characters and really care about them. Like they're your friends, and that you're right there with them.
Three weeks of science and hard work went by and I was finally nearing completion. Feeling all of the emotions all over again. Feeling my heart wrench and going between laughing and almost crying, I was going to end the journey that I had started three weeks prior. Then I get to the ending aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaand........
I get Mayuri's ending.
Mayuri and Okabe are now in an intimate relationship. My reaction is as follows.
"WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ DOES THAT EVEN MEAN?!?!?!?!"
"MAYURI SHOULDN'T EVEN KNOW WHAT SEX IS. SHE'S OFF LIMITS. NOPE. SORRY. KEEP KNOCKING, NOBODY'S HOME. YOU'RE NOT GETTING INTO THIS TEMPLE BOYO."
The last three weeks had been for naught. Because while Mayuri is supreme, she's not my best girl and she sure as hell isn't girlfriend material. Just beautiful cinnamon roll, nothing else. I spent the next fifteen minutes throwing it around in my head. All that time spent, and all I had to show for it is the exact opposite of the ending I was striving for. But I wasn't ready to quit. I'd go to war for Makise Kurisu, and you're damn right I did. Like Cryaotic I glared at my laptop and declared "no, that's not my ♥♥♥♥in' ending."
So I did what anyone else would do.
I got in my car, drove to the gas station and bought about 4 liters of Dr.Pepper. I was gonna reach Stein's Gate if it killed me, and I was now hellbent on getting all of the other endings and achieving the goal that I so desperately had tried to achieve.
I started going through all the easy to get alternate endings. That took about two days. It was 3 endings, and all of them were simple to get. Then came the last two endings, Makise's and the true ending. Stein's Gate. These were not simple. I had to start from the very beginning of the game to achieve these. Before, I had made strategic saves so I could go back and reach the alternate endings when I wanted to, so getting them just meant loading a save. But I had no saves in place for getting the true ending, so I had to start fresh.
This also took two days.
I drank more Dr.Pepper in that space of time than I ever have in my life. I was skipping as much as I could, having to reload countless times when I ♥♥♥♥ed up and missed a flag. I compressed down three weeks into two days. I wasn't really thirsty, but I just kept chugging that Dr.Pepper. The thought of Makise Kurisu kept me going through it all. Seeing everything again reminded me of how far I'd come. And finally, after all of this. After playing this game for almost an entire month, I reached the true ending.
I could finally rest. The emotions running around inside of me subsided.
All was well. Everyone was safe. After all of my effort, everything was right where it was supposed to be. The legend of the mad scientist Hououin Kyouma, and how he refused to be triumphed over and challenged the universe itself, was over. It was a ballad of love, betrayal, pain, joy, and defiance in the face of overwhelming odds.
I had finally reached Stein's Gate.
10 out of 10 would screw up their kidneys with Dr.Pepper again.

TLDR: Standalone Real Time Strategy game following the events of Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3. You don’t need the base game to play this, but in my opinion, you should probably play the base game before trying Uprising. 7/10
If you’ve played any of the Command & Conquer (C&C) games, you should know that they’re a little bit silly in terms of overacting and racial stereotyping, but fun in their gameplay. The Red Alert series in particular is less about being realistic and more about having crazy units battling each other (Russian war bears, Japanese Samurai, Allied sonic attack dolphins). They also have a long standing tradition of full motion video cutscenes at the start of each mission starring a bunch of familiar faces. None of the actors are huge stars but you should definitely recognize a few. The women wear low cut tops and short skirts while the men are stereotypical badasses.
*Spoilers for Red Alert games*
The Red Alert series of C&C games takes place in an alternate history, created by a foolish time traveler who thought he was doing the world a favor by going back and taking out Adolf Hitler before he rose to power. Unfortunately, the time traveler never took into account that Joseph Stalin’s Soviet Union would rise to power in the mid-20th century, and without a powerful Nazi war machine to oppose them, the USSR rolled across Europe and Asia conquering everyone in their path. Instead of USSR + the Allies versus the Nazis, it became Allies versus USSR. In Red Alert 3 (the game right before Uprising), the Empire of the Rising Sun (Japan) came out of nowhere, challenging the Allies and the USSR with their super advanced technology. The Allies manage to barely come out on top, and Uprising takes place very soon after the victory.
Red Alert 3 Uprising, like other Command & Conquer games is a Real Time Strategy game divided into 4 separate campaigns, 1 for each of the 3 factions and a fourth campaign which follows a single character as a pseudo RPG (like the Tassadar missions in Starcraft 1). Since Uprising is just sort of a standalone expansion, each campaign has only 4 missions. Be advised that the game is quite difficult (except the RPG campaign, which is kind of just for fun/story). Just like Supreme Commander Forged Alliance, you are tossed into the thick of it without any easy “learning missions.” If you’ve played any of the previous C&C games, the mechanics are very similar. Almost everything is done with your mouse “right click.” You may find that the resource gathering is a lot simpler in Uprising because the resources are in fixed locations. You don’t need to send your vulnerable ore harvesters out into the middle of nowhere gathering minerals.
Pros:
+The pre-mission cutscenes are enjoyable as always, with recognizable actors hamming it up on screen.
+There is a lot of variety in gameplay, not just in the large number of different unit types, but also the occasional “commando” missions where you’re sneaking around behind enemy lines.  The money flows pretty freely in the game so you can afford a bunch of very powerful units, and every unit in the game has some sort of secondary/special ability. Every mission takes about an hour, so even though each campaign only has 4 missions, it takes about 12 hours to beat the game. Not bad for an expansion.
Cons:
-The game has no multiplayer, though it does have a skirmish mode where you can play vs the computer 1 on 1.
-As mentioned above, the game is quite hard, and this really shouldn’t be the first Command & Conquer game you play. The difficulty might turn off new players.
Overall the game is a lot of fun, and if you enjoy old school Real Time Strategy games, you should enjoy Uprising as well. If you have the other games in the series, play them in order. Unlike a lot of modern games with multiple campaigns, the campaign endings in the Red Alert series are mutually exclusive. If you win with the Russians, you conquer the world and Russia rules all. If you win with the Allies, the Russians are completely defeated, etc.

Decent casual puzzle game.
The "roatate to connect" puzzle has been done many times. You can get it for free on basically any device with
, and my personal favorite is
(the flash version)and
. So how is Curvy different?
Curvy sometimes has more than one shape on the same puzzle; on many other puzzles of these types, all tiles must be connected to each other, but here they may form separate groups. The tiles are on a hex grid, which makes the smaller connections move around quite a bit visually as you rotate them, and makes for pleasing shapes. However, the interface looks bad on my screen: the green won't go away, and it is so pixelated and non-antialiased that the color graduations look very ugly. For best results, I recommend setting the colors to "flat". Note also that the more difficult puzzles are initially locked, making me grind through the easier ones (and it doesn't tell you when the next set unlocks).
It's not my favorite game of this type, but it's not bad either. Recommended.

Never previously did play any games of this franchise, granted; it does mark an important history in gaming overall and I've seen footage and heard about it many many times. FPS never has been a big part of my life, nor will that change in the future for that matter either - nonetheless, sometimes I do step into foreign areas just to spread my wings from time to time.
Wolfenstein: The New Order succeeds where so many other FPS franchises fails in capturing my interest. It does attempt to write up a reasonably good story to keep the player invested in the characters as well as what's going on in the game generally. Each mission feels equally as important and even some support characters keeps me wanting to come back for more only to learn their backstory and outcome in the game.
It DOES more for the player than Call of Duty or Battlefield, it's not just simply a mindless mainstream shooter to milk the cash in off its own name for those whom cannot get enough of endless slaughter á la WW2-ish envoirement, with little to no effort in keeping the player from coming back for seconds because they never invested time nor energy for a "Good" game aside from the core of its design - point and shoot.
New Order perfectly reboots the franchise into the 2010's era as a modern reincarnate of itself - connecting not only past experienced gamers already familiar with this universe, but also manages to intrigue new faces with craftmanship of a game not relying or hiding itself behind explosions, blood or the all too tiresome halfassed multiplayer experience that so many other shooters go for.
It is an experience of a game - A FULL GAME! One that quite frankly took me by surprise without much expectation and pleasantly so I might add.
At the end of it, this game contains more than I initially bargained for and I'm happy it does, however; it doesn't make the game flawless despite my high praise. New Order keeps you coming back for the story yes, more importantly the gameplay does include a fun variety of stealth and shooting that of which the player decides how to lean towards. My 1 major complaint comes in the form of balancing issues from a difficulty standpoint. Despite not having sold my sould into the FPS genré entirely, I would call myself an accomplished gamer and can adapt with ease for these kind of titles - even though my aim much like in bed, sometimes fall short >_>
Regardless, there were clear difficulty peaks in certain areas that despite having had no issues with the game as a whole up to these points, were outright unfair and infuriating. Dying for absolutely no reason and without the game giving me clear directions of what its intention was for the course of action. I played on the default difficulty all the way through but sometimes it felt much higher than it should have been for yor average gamer just trying to beat the game.
Sadly, this is the reason why I won't go back for more and replay it for higher difficulties and it does effect my score of it. I've been able to push through shooters before on much harder settings for Uncharted, Unreal, Doom among other titles - but this one isn't worth the additional time and frustration.
Overall I feel like some areas SHOULD have been tweaked a bit more and that would have been enough for me to grade it slightly higher, it just falls short to accomplish what it set out to be - a great game. It is however still very much so an enjoyable experience and I would truely recommend it to anyone curious enough about this new installment of the series.

A perfect combination of Telltale's impeccable storytelling with Borderlands' genius writing. The proof that a first person shooter franchise can have material to build a rich story with many emotional and ingenious turns that would leave the player amazed and disgusted at the same time.
Often we rate games for the level of immersion we are put through. Good characters, good story and good way to reveal it. This game has it all. Every decision is crucial to the player, even if the outcome is sometimes the same (or it appears to be, but looks can be deceiving). The game makes us care for every character, good or evil, and throws us right in the middle of the field to make our own destiny.
As with other Telltale games, this one is a true masterpiece, and makes me excited to think about the future of the Borderlands franchise. Don't worry about the sub-par Pre-Sequel, that game was not made by Gearbox. This one was, and it is very clear in the way that everything fits. The genius of Anthony Burch is palpable in every scene and every line of dialog.
As a fan of the Borderlands franchise, and of other Telltale games, I loved this one and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a wonderful experience.

This is a wonderful quick-fix for Diablo 2 fans, and for the money you'll get a solid deal.  Don't expect an incredibly deep game or story, and don't expect something truly amazing - this won't be a game you keep coming back to years later.  But for what it is, it's a fair deal and it's definitely worth the price.
- Local co-op, always a big plus in my book.
- Random loot, random levels, and lots of difficulty options after you "win", offering a fair bit of replayability.
- The first two DLCs added enough fun that I don't consider them a waste of money (this is rare in my book).
- There are a lot of interesting classes out of the box even if you don't bother with DLCs.
- You can reset skills, but the cost is high enough to make you have to think about it.
- The loot system feels all wrong to me - by level 50 I'm still finding that my level 20 gear is better than anything I've found since.  I expected something more like Diablo 2 or Borderlands where a white level 50 is far beyond any level 20 item.  It seems like loot level has very little to do with loot quality, which makes the item hunt boring fast.
- Does gold ever matter?  I thought D2's gold system was broken....
- The game becomes a grind very quickly - I'm not sure I'll bother playing anymore, though I do want to know if loot ever catches up with my level.
- There are a variety of annoying bugs, like loot dropping in places you can't reach.  If loot mattered more, this could be tragic.
- The game is incredibly non-intuitive.  You really have to work to learn how to play.
- There's effectively no story to speak of.
- Many skill synergies feel forced and/or meaningless.

Short, but good game. Shadow of the Colossus-like atmosphere but from a bird's perspective.
- First off, I really don't get why some users compare it to the Dark Souls games. It has absolutely nothing in common with them except maybe the "souls" in its title and the fact that it's difficult.
- There is almost no story, but the atmosphere is great. You're wandering through a huge, unpopulated area with long-forgotten ruins etc., encountering big, dangerous enemies. All of that reminded me of Shadow of the Colossus but with different gameplay: You don't climb the titans, you only have one bow and one arrow, and you as well as the bosses die with one hit (the bosses can only be hit on a specific weak spot). (Also it's not third-person view, obviously)
- Checkpoints are a bit rare, and many players seem to be frustrated by the fact that upon dying they have to walk all the way to the boss again. This can be tedious at times, especially if you get killed by the same enemy over and over again, but I think it's a good way to punish the players for getting themselves killed. If you spawned directly in front of the boss again, it wouldn't be as much of a challenge imo, because that's probably the biggest incentive for getting better at this game. And usually, the checkpoints aren't THAT far away from the next boss.
- The controls feel like some kind of Zelda A Link to the Past or similar games, except with less features.
- Completing the game took me less than 3 hours on my first run, which isn't very long, so personally I wouldn't buy this game full price. I got it for 5 bucks, which is a good price for a good game like this.

Alright, let's recap: Titan Souls wants to benefit from the "souls mania". It's an isometric 1 hit 1 kill boss shooter. There are several areas in the game that can be explored, but there is nothing to explore apart from finding the actual bosses to gather their souls. There are a total of 19 bosses I think. The gameplay could not be simpler. You have a dodge roll that serves as a sprint button when held down, and an attack button with which you shoot your arrow. Your one and only weapon. The longer you hold the button the farther it flies. When you don't have your arrow, holding the button pulls it back towards you (necessary for defeating at least 1 boss even).
The bosses themselves aren't terribly designed, they're even fun, but the game is at times too unforgiving and doesn't tell you well enough how you died at times. Couple that with a system that takes 1 shot 1 kill to the extreme and there is way more frustration here than I ever had in any of the Souls games. The game suggests a controller and since I had one plugged in I can't even remember if there is an option not to use one. THAT would make aiming at least somewhat possible. With the controller it's not very precise to be honest, if you only have 1 shot and you have to hit the weak spot on a constantly moving and attacking enemy (at most you have like half a second after an attack to hit that weak point). And you die in 1 hit...as do the bosses. When you do kill one you feel incredible happiness for a short while, but not necessarily because you know you've achieved something, but rather you pat yourself on the shoulder for surviving long enough to take the lucky shot. Shoot just an inch to the side and you're screwed.
But even after criticizing the game's gameplay so much, I still managed to beat it in about 3-4 hours. For a 15 dollar title with minimalist graphics AND gameplay that's not all that great imho. Everybody values money differently, but mine is precious to me, so I noped out at the final (hidden) boss, because restarting a 3-stage fight from stage 1 every time and waiting for the weak point to appear is more pain than I can handle. Give it a go if you like really hard boss fights and nothing more...and when it's on sale.

It's incredible on how this game is so realistic, yet still in it's developing stages. There are multiple maps with envorinment settings. So you can go to one server with a map and it's raining, and as you play in the map the weather actually changes to where it'll be easier to fight, or to where it'll be harder to fight.
-Weaponry/Equipment: At this time, there is only 1 weapon, which is an assault rifle. Yet, you also have the abiloity to activate a lazer for you to help with your accurasy, a flashlight incase it get's dark (game sometimes has you in pitch black darkness), of course you can zoom in by right-clicking, and unlike any sci-fi FPS, you can actually take off your visor. So it'll be like fighting with literally your own eyes. But the game doesn't give you a cursor to aim with like Halo, Battlefield, TF2, etc. You actually have to aim like everyone does in real life when in combat.
-Maps: There are multiple maps that go from the middle of a swamp, to the cold regions, to a colony in the forest. All maps has the ability to change the weather to throw off players.
-Game Mode: So far, there is only one game mode where you hold a certain area for the longest, but as time goes on, the capture zone will move into a different area of the map. In order to win, you must hold the capture zone for the longest when the time runs out, or when the amount of time you hold it reaches it's max. Either way, you have to work with your team in order to win. Cooperation and skill will bring you to victory in this game.
Overall, this game is incredible for it to be an Early Access Game, I recommend this game to anyone that reads this.

Wolfenstein The New Order is an FPS set in a post WW2 world where Nazis beat the Americans to Nuclear weapons and now have total global domination. You play as Classic American blue eyed hero B.J. Blazkowicz a.k.a Terror Billy. You fight your way across europe dealing with super soldiers, robotic canines, missile launching weirdos etc. to beat the Nazi evil scientist Deathshead.
Gameplay:
I've put in around 17 hours on this, and finally completed the mission with around 50% completion rate.  The game does not go dull at any second. You are constantly in the midst of heavy artillery packed action and Wolfenstein TNO is best when you are going double handed all guns blazing into the swarm on oncoming nazi militia. Having said that, the game is equally rewarding when you decide to take things slow and sneak our way behing enemies to silently them down. The game lets you be who you want to be and rewards (and punishes) strength and stealth equally. The guns are all well thought of and you feel like switching between them to handle different types of sitations. The ammo is limited and you need to pick up ammo and health packs from fallen enemies and crates. The game rewards you when you are economical with your weapons arsenal.
The Story:
Quite brilliant to be honest. I was a serial CoD player on console, please don't start hating me already.Though it has gone down the drain in the recent years, I loved the CoD story lines back in the day when it had meaningful characters like Soap and Price and Reznov! While the story of Wolfenstein is good in itself, classic Nazi/WW2 backdrop .. can't go wrong with that (unless you are CoD WW2) what really makes it great is the characters. Each character is well thought of and you start investing yourself in them as you play along. Characters have meaningful backstories and you can really connect to most of them. The game does a nice job of including cliche characters also in its subtle non-pretentious way.
Difficulty:
I finished most of the game in the default 'Bring it On' difficulty. But i did also try the other ones. The game experience does change a lot with varying difficulty levels but I found 'Bring it On' to be right up my alley. Mindless violence would not work in this game as even a lowly soldier who managed to sneak up behind you could kill you with a few bullets. So you can't be stupid. Having said that, every time you die, you feel like kicking yourself and picking up right where you screwed up.
The user experience:
I am running an i7-7700 processor with a 1050Ti - 4GB graphics card. I did not face any lags or stutter at all. The game runs out of my HDD and not the SSD and yet the load times were incredibly fast (looking at you DOOM! ). For a game that came out a couple of years ago this does have pretty neat graphics.
Overall:
If you are looking for some classic FPS action with a strong story line, then Wolfenstein TNO would be a complete must buy. Be aware though that its meant for single player only. I picked it up on the steam sale and I feel like it was worth every penny.

OK I've got to confess, I've played a few Telltale games,
You've probably got me down as a fan boy, who'll rate up anything and say it's the dogs doo dahs, but I enjoy the games. They're formulaic, but ultimately it boils down to the story. The Walking Dead Season 1 was an emotional rollercoatser, The Wolf Among Us had a great setting but failed to attract enough attention to get a second series.
The Walking Dead Season 2 - well, Ive played a few of them.
I've played Borderlands the Gearbox game, it's fun - it appeals to my OCD collecting/grinding streak, but to be honest you could take this story out of the Borderlands universe and it would probably work and that's not a bad thing.  As i played it, I really could see visualise this game as a movie, it had some laugh out loud moments and some quite touching moments.  It really is telltale at its best - and i would go so far as to say better than the Walking Dead.  The key with this franchise, is that they could pretty much do what they wanted - if you've watched Game of Thrones, you know that there is certain stuff they couldnt do/ likewise Walking Dead. Here they have a blank cheque - and though its Borderlands, I get the impression somebody said - do what you want.
I'll be honest, I wasnt sure it would work, but some great voice acting and really good set pieces brought it through. I broke a cardinal rule - I went back and reloaded because I didnt want an individual to die. I'll say no more, but you may find yourself in the same situation, and you'll realise why I should have let it play out.
This is a quality game and I hope it picks up some awards, I am not a corporate executive but I am sure that the licence for this game is less than some other well known franchises. There are some great pop culture references, a pop at street fighter - it left me on a high and I am really looking forward to season 2

So, this game is a Twin-Stick-Shooter that is basically a mash up of Diablo and The Binding of Isaac. It has the persistence of gear you equip that is permanent between deaths, and the rogue-likeness of relics that you collect that add effects or massive stat increases and randomized potions that act on your current run ONLY.
The bugs.... god the bugs... This is a game that has (had?) so much potential but I feel like the enourmous list of unfixed bugs is really holding it back. Many have pointed out that the devs have almost abandoned this game, and it is kinda true. They do still fix things here and there but the backlog of documented bugs is astounding. Some you can exploit to power up, some exploit YOU and ruin your run. This is not an early access game, but if you buy it expect all the things that you would expect of an early access game. Its pretty buggy.
Class balance is pretty... unbalanced. It becomes clear very quickly which classes are god-like and which are terrible. That doesnt mean they are un-playable, but dont expect to be on equal footing in the higher difficulties.
Multiplayer is one of the main draws of this game, but you will need to port forward to host, and the dedicated servers are restricted to Europe. On top of that, the multiplayer server hub system seems to crash often, and player hosted games can also crash for no appearant reason.
Items (relics) are somewhat bland, many are blatent clones of The Binding of Isaac items, some are utterly trash, and some really dont make any sense functionally or thematically.
... I still like this game. This is a nice little loot-grind shoot-em-up and its fun to play with friends or randoms, you get to feel pretty powerful and awesome when you start getting gear and mowing down dozens of enemies at the same time and there are hella explosions and huge damage numbers. It is definitely fun, but at the normal price it is probably not worth it. It has too many bugs and not enough dev support to warrent a full price purchase. If you like the genre, then buy when and if it goes on sale again.

Following the Battle of Three Tribes, there was a brief period of peace and prosperity... but such fleeting luxuries are best never taken for granted. One fateful, dewy morning as Amanda's mother, Arlene, strolled out to the edge of the valley to gather some wild herbs, an enemy faction mounted their attack. Arlene was promptly knocked unconscious, and as one raider whisked her away, the rest continued their assault deeper into the valley.
At the mountainside entrance, Grim took cover behind a tall oak tree and sprung into action with his sniper rifle, disposing of one of the encroachers with deadly efficiency as they all came around the bend. It would be a perilous fight, but the odds would be in Grim's favor just as soon as -
Suddenly, Amanda raced in to join the conflict, not aware of her husband Grim's location. As Grim lined up his next shot and pulled the trigger, a larger blur filled his scope. Lowering the gun, he saw Amanda's falling body, dead before it hit the ground. Grim destroyed the remaining attackers in a fiery rage and then rushed to his wife's side. There was nothing left he could do. He dug a hole in the graveyard and buried her. Maddened by guilt and loss, Grim went completely berserk and assaulted another colonist, who then shot and killed Grim in self defence.
The colony had been reduced to three people once again, but still they prevailed, just as they had in the past. Just as they would continue to -
Then, a noise. A chattering, almost. Coming from deeper in the caves. What could make such a sound? As the colonists gathered around a dimly-lit corridor to investigate, their weapons drawn, a swift-moving shadow leaped out from the darkness. Blood spattered the walls and the remaining colonists dropped to the floor, all dead or dying.
The caves would be home to something else now.

"How creative. Not. Take Limbo's protagonist, throw some of those overused pixel style visuals in there and finish it off with Super Meat Boy's precision platforming." Does my first impression of this game resemble your thoughts upon looking at screenshots or videos of this game for the first time?
While Electronic Super Joy does "borrow" some elements from other games, it's still a well-rounded package that manages to find its own style. The various genres of electronic music blend together perfectly with the absurd story of a butt-stealing wizard and an evil pope, the flashy visuals and the near-constant threat of death.
It's not the longest game out there, but if you're trying to find all stars, get all the achievements, do all the bonus levels, aim for record times and spend some time in the deviously hard endless mode, you are still in for quite a few hours of great fun. The mechanics of jumping, double-jumping, butt-stomping, etc. work well and are varied throughout the stages, you'll always encounter new kinds of hazards and thanks to the checkpoint system, most of the game stays fair. Be warned, however, that the final stages and some of the bonus stages can get REALLY mean.

Bridge Constructor is a brilliant game that puts you in the position of a builder constructing bridges across the 5 islands within the game. Each level tests your skills at being able to solve how to build a bridge in a means to get vehicles across. Anybody who knows of a program called West Point Bridge Designer will find this game to be quite similar, but the achievements and challenges presented will hook you right in. While you are able to build a sensible, well-thought bridge that will do the job perfectly, it's extremely fun to be able to build crazy bridges with massive jumps that still transport vehicles. The physics engine is so fun to play around with through each bridge design - launching cars off your "ramps" in the hopes of reaching the end - and the ability to do what you will when constructing bridges to finish each level is amazing.
A game that I strongly recommend to anybody interested in purchasing this game.

TL;DR I have mixed feelings on RimWorld. I like it, but I don't quite enjoy it enough to recommend it at this time; July 2017.
This game finally brings Dwarf Fortress (DF) out of ASCII graphics. It makes the genre playable, AND it's actually pretty decent! Unfortunatly the fact that it does remind me of DF puts certain unnecessary criteria (a.k.a. self-bias) on this game. It's a bias that actually keeps me from recommending it.
However RimWorld does a d4mn good job at walking a fine line where others have failed. If you haven't played DF then you will most likely enjoy this game. If you've enjoyed Prision Architect then you will enjoy this game. If you see this as the new DF, put it on your wishlist and check back in again a year from now.
There have been other games that tried to do a proper graphicial DF-like game, but failed. Those failures fall primarily into 2 categories: Too Simple or Too Complex. Towns failure was everyone expected more, but got a lot less. Gnomoria tried to do everything and in the end failed to match the expectations it set for itself. These are just two extremes, but there have been a lot of attempts. The problem with trying to clone DF is that the game has 15 years of development. It didn't start off as big as it is. Trying to beat that is like MMO's trying to make a WoW killer. There's just too much complexity and fine tunning to the original. You can't complete.
RimWorld doesn't feel like it's trying to directly compete. Instead it takes the premise of DF, but doesn't exactly clone it. It has world generation. It has colony managment. It has personality traits for each settler. You set jobs and each person has skills that they start off with and learn as they go. There's trade and missions you can attempt. The world does feel alive and yet lonely. The technology aspect of the game brings an interesting difficultly curve for the haves and have nots. The modding community also does a lot to enhance the gameplay.
I like that fact. I enjoy the game when I play it for a few hours, but after some time, I wish I was playing DF.
I hear you say, "So go play DF and stop hating on this game then!"
Yes, I did do that. I hadn't played in a few years, picked up the newest version of DF and started a new world. And therin lies my not recommending this game. It's fun, but it's not AS fun as it could be. I think in a few years this game will be pretty awesome. But how many games would you recommend that, after playing for a few hours, has you load up the game it's based off of and finding a much more enjoyable experience?
Or to put it in another light: I mentioned Prision Architect earlier. That game has a lot of the features that makes DF fun and engaging. But when I play that game, I've never thought about how much more fun I could be having playing DF or anything else.
I plan to check in about a year from now and see how things have progressed.

In 1981, there was a game for the Apple II computer (and a lot of it's concurrents, back when personal computers didn't have software compatible with each other and a multiplatform operating system was the stuff of a madman's dreams), called Castle Wolfenstein. It was a top down action stealth game (way before Metal Gear, by the way), and it was among the favorite classics of some guys called John Romero and John Carmack.
So, skipping to 1992, we have those guys asking themselves the question: "what if we made a 3d version of Caslte Wolfenstein, where the player is put in a first person environment with a gun and has to shoot his way out of the castle?"
Gee, I wonder how this idea turned out.

Bridge Constructor surprised me, it sure looks very casual and is as easy to get into as you'd expect. For veterans of the genre who played some of the old hardcore bridge building games though, it not only has a nostalgic effect, but also kinda kicks yer butt in places if you get too cocky. If you have played bridge building games before, you will have an easy and reasonably fun time flying through the first playthrough of the main campaign, which only took me some 2.5 hours.
The main campaign maps then open up for testing your bridges using the "tank truck", which makes things pretty tough and you have to solve levels differently (with some more budget) compared to your first playthrough! In the Expansion/DLC part of the game, you find some rather different and creative levels that at least to some degree challenge your engrained senses for the rules.
So while the levels in the first run through the main campaign become very much "seen that before", especially if you're playing them quickly, I am still positively surprised by the game overall. If you like games like this and haven't played any in a longer time, give it a go! If you've played them all, then wait for a sale.
Note: The game's difficulty often doesn't leave much room for errors or poor decision-making. Despite it's cutesy appearance, the game would potentially be frustrating for younger kids without guidance.

There's a very good reason why boss rush is a
mode in twitchy arcade games: for newcomers, their conventions work best in standard singleplayer, where non-boss levels and enemies shape pacing and learning curve, and bosses are the ultimate tests of newly learned skills. There's a very good reason why Soulsborne games use one hit kills with a restraint  and generally are quite generous about mistakes: to balance engagement and frustration they provide a ton of opportunities to learn their quirks, and brutal punishment is only a tool to encourage players to fully utilize them all. There is a very good reason why Shadow of the Colossus benefited from vast empty spaces: aside from atmosphere and lore building, they gave some quiet time in between epic, multiphased, often drawn out battles with plenty of opportunities to try and learn enemies' tactics without the need to traverse same areas after every mistake.
Titan Souls takes these and other proven techniques, and throws them onto the wall, without reflecting on how they might (and mostly do) contradict each other. No wonder very little sticks well enough to provide anything but constant irritation.

One of the greatest games of all time.
I played this game for over 5000 hours in the disk version. If I had to pick only one game to play for the rest of my life this would be my choice.
Trackmania United Forever is an arcade racing game. Check out the free version Trackmania Nations Forever, to see if it fits your style before you buy this. In the free version you can only play in the Stadium environment, where you drive a F1 like car in a stadium.
Trackmania United Forever combines all environments from old Trackmania games, like Trackmania Original, Trackmania Sunrise and Trackmania Nations.
This game has 7 environments in total with every one of them having a different car, with different physics. Every environment has an own editor as well, to create your own tracks to race on them, this is what keeps the game alive.
The environments are:
Stadium - F1 like car with a lot of grip and high speed, this environment has the most potential because of the high amount of track pieces. This is the most famous and beloved environment.
Bay - A SUV style car, with a lot of grip and high speed taking place in a city-like setting.
Island - A super sports car, which easily loses traction at high speed and starts drifting. This takes place on an island like the name already says. There are a lot of track pieces you place on the water here.
Coast - A relatively slow car with ultra low grip, you drift all the time if you don't know how to control this car. This takes place in an old village setting far away from big cities, with old asphalt roads.
Desert - A very slim car with high speed. This car has the tendency to only drive on 2 wheels in turns. Takes place in an american desert setting with old roads.
Snow - A pickup car with high speed and a lot of traction. Takes place in a snowy environment with a lot of snow-covered track pieces.
Rally - An offroad-rally car with slow speed compared to the other environments. You drive offroad a lot with not much traction. Takes place in a green countryside.
Each environments has its own "physics", which makes this game very interesting. There are different types of gamemodes:
Race - you just try to get a good time on a track
Stunt - you try to get as much stunt points as possible by performing cool chained stunts
Platform - you try to finish the track without respawning at a checkpoint, usually hard-trial-like tracks
Puzzle - you have to complete an already existing track with a limited amount of track pieces, you have to create the fastest route from start to finish and then drive it yourself.
The editor, where you can create your own tracks is amazing and very easy to handle.
TMUF (TrackMania United Forever) is not like other racing games, it's really arcade and you don't collide with other players, everything is about getting the best time on a track not beating the other players in a race like in most other racing games.
Unfortunately the game doesn't have that many players anymore and the once you are going to encounter are probably very good at the game. There is still a very nice community of very good players who build and race together. This game probably has the best and friendliest community of all games I played.
This game is worth a try if you like fast arcade-like racing games.
Thank you Nadeo for bringing so much fun to my life. I've been playing this game for over 10 years now, and I still enjoy it.

I think this game would have a very bright future if it tried to follow the model of Farming Simulator. Allowing Multiplayer (or at least private co-op of some type) would open up so many different possibilities. With so much to do during the mining process, having multiple people working at once would make it that much more fun.
There's also a LOT of buggy/glitchy things that need to be fixed/fine-tuned throughout the entire game. The overall game mechanics seem to be pretty good, but have a good deal of room for improvement, Being able to hire AI that actually do work on your claim would be a great addition as well, rather than just a simple "Hire a worker to gather gold, but not actually do anything on the claim".
Some of the physics really don't make a whole lot of sense either, like the trailers dropping to the ground when you release them from the truck and then catapulting whatever is inside it at the time once it sets itself back up.
Another aspect that I think would be a nice addition would be the ability to carry multiple items at once, depending on the items... For example, multiple hoses at once, multiple buckets at once (up to 6 unloaded, 2 when loaded)... I just find it a little unnatural and unrealistic to really say you have to carry one item at a time, regardless of what it is, yet if I were actually working in an environment like this, I wouldn't carry a single empty bucket at a time if I had 10-20 buckets to carry in total.
I'm sure once I go forward I'll have more to add to this. Overall it's a pretty good game and quite addictive, has a huge amount of potential, but ultimately the game play also has a bit of an amaturish/unpolished feel to it, almost as if it wasn't out of Beta before it was released, or wasn't tested properly before letting it out into the wild.
Time will tell with this game... For now, it's a thumbs up, solely for the potential it has...

The graphics look amazing and the game is very well optimized for the PC, by which i mean it doesn't take a super computer to run this game at max settings, but even so, there is still the option to change the graphical settings to your liking.
The gameplay is very well done, complex, engaging and it is simply amazing.
There are strong attacks, weak attacks, super attacks, ultimate attacks and evasive moves.
The combos are made up of various combinations of strong and weak attacks.
The combo inputs are the same for every character but the animations are all different and have different effects (some throw you down, some throw you up, etc).
The same combo input that throws the opponet up, with one character, can throw him down, with another character.
There is also "vanishing" (teleporting behind attacking opponent), grab moves and regular ki blasts.
The movement is also a big part of the gameplay.
You can move up, down and sideways, you can quick step (move a short distance quickly) and you can "boost" (become covered in an aura and fly quickly in any direction).
The game has a "lock-on" feature that always keeps your opponent on-screen.
If you deactivate it you can move and look freely in any direction (until the "invisible wall").
Also, you can actually walk in this game.
When you are close to the ground, you enter a running animation whenever you move.
All these different elements combine to make a very complex and exciting experience out of every match.
The story in this game is a very well made spin on the original storyline which mainly involves time travel.
Evildoers are traveling through time and changing things with disastrous results, you know, the butterfly effect, except the butterfly is various characters.
You, with your created character, along with Trunks, will travel throughout Dragon Ball history and correct the abnormalities caused by the evildoers (you get to fight great apes).
The game goes through all sagas, including the most recent "Battle of the Gods" saga.
Then there are "Parallel Quests", which are a variety of missions, each with it's own setting, where you can obtain skills and clothes for your created character and more.
Parallel Quests are like short stories you can play, which i really like.
- Runs great on the great majority of PCs.
- Graphics look great
- Great complex gameplay
- Great story and side missions
I own this game and i highly recommend it.
