TLDR: The biggest problem with the game right now is the servers.  There are some drawbacks in the gameplay department but the pros outweigh the cons.  If you're a fan of the Dragonball series and the world that Akira Toriyama has created then this game is a must buy.  If you don't really care for Dragonball but are interested in the gameplay it is a solid game but packed with fan service that will probably go over your head.  You will also probably be less forgiving of its flaws and may not get enough enjoyment out of the story and the Dragonball world to offset them.   Character customization is definatley the high point of the game, everything from looks to stats to skills is up to the player.
Long review:
If you like the Dragonball universe and the past Dragonball games then there's a great chance that you'll love this game.  There's a ton of fan service here for those that know the story well.  There's also a nice refreshing take on the old story with a new Time Patrol twist.  Your character feels like they belong in the Dragonball universe and they become important to the story of the Xenoverse game.  With the way they did the story it feels like your character is an important part of the Dragonball history and not just some voiceless, tacked on nobody that you get to customize.
The customization is great too.  Being able to choose between human, namek, saiyan, maijin or changeling is a great start and there's a variety of body builds and looks that you can use to personalize your DB avatar.  It probably isn't the most in-depth character creation you've ever seen but it offers enough variety for you to individualize your avatar.  Each race starts with it's own unique bonuses.  Namek's, for example, get natural regen when their health is low.  Saiyans get a bonus to offense but have lower health than other races, etc...
You'll get to dictate what skills are available to your character by earning them through quests or by choosing a mentor.  Your mentor will be a well known character from the Dragonball universe, they include heroes and villains, and they will give you quests to complete in exchange for learning their skills.  After you've mastered one set of skills you are free to move on to the next mentor (or, if you don't like the skills you're getting, you can select a new mentor at any time).  If you want to be a Maijin who goes Kaokenx20 and then blasts people away with Piccolo's special beam cannon, Krillins destructo disc and Vegeta's final flash all in one match, you can.  Feel free to change it up in-between fights as often as you see fit.
You'll also have control over your stats.  Your character will receive 3 attribute points each level to put into Health, ki, stamina, basic attacks, strike supers (which are physical super attacks) and ki blast supers (which are energy attacks) up to a max level of 80.  It's completely up to you what your character will excel in.  You can specialize in ki blasts and have weak physical attacks or vice versa.  Or you can try to be well rounded and do a little bit of everything.  It's completely up to you.
When you finish up the main quest line you'll have access to 55 Parallel Quests with a wide range of difficulty.  Each quest has a random chance to drop skills, items and gear relative to the difficulty and the characters that appear in the quest.  Your reward will be directly related to how well you perform and you'll be given a score that ranks your performance from D at the low end up to Z at the high end.  You can choose to do these offline with NPC teammates or online with other players.  You'll also gain access to pvp battles ranging from 1v1 to 3v3.  This is all in addition to the main quest line which can probably last you anywhere from 10-15 hrs depending on how adept at fighting games you are.  You can easily put 40-60 hours into your first character.
There are some cons.  Right now the biggest con is the server stability.  Sometimes multiplayer is great, sometimes it's completely broken and you can't log in at all.  The game is also a bit grindy.  If you're unlucky you can spend a whole day grinding for an item in the same Parallel Quest over and over again and never get it.  You're also going to run into hackers who are giving themselves godlike stats to cheese you in pvp, but what game doesn't have this problem to some degree?  Very rarely, I've had missions where an enemy npc will get stuck in a mountain, where they aren't supposed to be and I have a hard time getting to them to KO them and finish the quest.  This problem hasn't occured but maybe 2-3 times in 56 hours of gameplay for me.
There's a really good amount of content in this game and for those of us that just want a Dragonball world to get immersed in and be a part of this game will somewhat scratch that itch. The pros outweigh the cons, in my opinion, and there is enough game here to play offline if you absolutely had to to make it worth the $50.00.  More than likely in the worst case scenario, you would be unable to log into the "Multi-Lobby", which is a hub city where you can meet players and form teams.  You would probably still be able to queue up for online Parallel Quests with other players and online battles in a single lobby (a hub city populated by npc's that you can recruit to help with quests) but without the multi-lobby it is a bit harder to keep track of the people that you want to play with again.
Overall this game is still worth the time and the price even if it does have some flaws at the moment.  If you aren't the biggest Dragonball fan and really don't know the story or care for the DB universe too much then I would suggest holding off.  The drawbacks will probably be a lot more difficult for you to forgive if you're not into Dragonball in the first place.  If you're a fan of the series and know the story like the back of your hand then the new "Time Patrol" approach is a nice refreshing take on a very familiar story.  The game is a grind but doing the same quest over and over for gear isn't so bad when your character is so versatile and customizable.  Part of the fun for me is changing up my skills as I acquire new ones to figure out what works best (and you can do this as much as you want in-between quests).  So even if the scenery doesn't change for a bit, your character can, and that can keep things interesting.

I really enjoy Crossout because:
+ You get to design your own vehicle
+ You decide how you play by designing your vehicle
+ Strategies & team synergy
+ PvP & PvE missions and events
+ A lot to achieve
+ Not p2w, and here is why:
Crossout does a great job combatting P2W. Every vehicle has a power score which is calculated from the parts that the vehicle has. You might have a team where there is a fast melee/close range "glass cannon" or slowly moving heavy artillery vehicle that shoots rockets from long range or anything between those two and all within the same power score. It doesn't matter if you buy nice weapons or farm them, either way teams are balanced around power score. The higher your vehicle's power score is, the higher it will also be for the enemies. This also creates a nice variety inside the team.
Tips:
- Don't just aimlessly ride inside the whole enemy team.
- Help your teammates and try to destroy enemies together.
- Be aware of the situations your teammates are in by watching the map and comms.
- Pay attention to capture points.
- Always have some weapons on your car.

The original Borderlands. Also the best overall Borderlands game in my opinion. Despite how many critics/fans seem to claim that Borderlands 2 "improved on the original in every way", I can't help but COMPLETELY disagree with that notion. Yes, BL2 IS more story FOCUSED, that doesn't instantly make it better, though. Also, the original Borderlands by FAR in my honest humble opinion handled the loot system, drop rates and gun manufacturers much better than it's sequels. Yes the guns in the original Borderlands could seem similar at times. But that was made up for with the vast amount of gun types that EACH and EVERY manufacturer made (I'm looking at you BL2!!).
See, In the original Borderlands, not ALL TORGUE weapons shoot explosive rockets, DAHL and Vladof make shotguns! TORGUE makes sniper rifles! Not ALL DAHL weapons have that ridiculous burst fire. Hyperion weapons are actually what they're supposed to be in the first place, ACCURATE! So, you see, Borderlands 2 may have flashier and more stylish and gimmicky guns, but Borderlands 1 had more practical, usable guns with actual substance! And every now and then you could find flashy weapons that had weird gimmicks like the Typhoon SMG for example, but at least it was usable half the time.
People talk about the diversity of weapons in BL2, and I just don't see it. I'm sorry folks, but I'll take substance, usability and consistency over flashy, gimmicky guns that barely have any practical use. Also, drop rates. Borderlands 1 actually rewarded you, the player, for actually, you know, buying and playing the game. Whereas BL2 if you want to find Legendary or even just good purple guns, you have to constantly farm and spend extra money for things that you shouldn't have to if you want to get your hands on some higher quality weapons and gear. By the end of you 1st playthrough and beginning of your 2nd playthrough of Borderlands 1 you'll ACTUALLY have an appropriate amount of legendary and purple guns.
Also, atmosphere and tone. See, something people who've started the Borderlands franchise with Borderlands 2 lack the understanding that Borderlands 1 was about a Diablo II style Action-RPG experience in a serious and bleak Sci-fi Post-Apocalyptic setting that had consistent doses of comic relief and dark humor, and most of the humor in the original stemmed from the DLCs. BL2 on the other hand, started this whole "Everything has to be a stupid pop-culture reference, everythhing MUST have jokes constantly being rammed into your ears!!".
Point being here is this, if you want to find out what Borderlands is REALLY about, you must play this, the original Borderlands. As much as I've bashed the sequels, I just want to make it clear I love BL2, it's a solid game in it's own right, but it's more a completely different game to the original in tone, atmosphere, loot, character, story etc. I honestly hope Gearbox attempts to either make a remaster of the original with just graphical enhancements, or do a Borderlands sequel that actually sticks to the original style. Trust me, this game is great, and IMO THE greatest of the franchise. The original Borderlands is a special experience, so go experience it!
-Tyler

Has more in common with mario kart than with forza. If you're looking for a serious racing game, this isn't it... but if you've already beaten plants vs. zombies and peggle and are looking for something mindless to do while listening to audio books, this will fit the bill perfectly.
The only multiplayer mode is concurrent time trials, which works quite well. Since you're mainly racing the clock, you can restart the race at any time and won't be unduly affected by lag or cheats. However, the lack of variety means the game itself won't hold your interest for long unless you're playing with friends or also listening to podcasts at the same time.
All cars in a given race mode handle exactly the same. There is no car customization outside of your car's paint and model, but that's quite fun in itself. No plot. None of the annoying interruptions that are so common in other racing games such as cutscenes, slow menus, and crash cams. You can jump directly from one lap to the next. There is a 1 minute delay between races every time the server switches tracks, but otherwise the fun is uninterrupted.
There is a huge number of tracks but all are constructed from the same set of sections, so the variety is limited. Most tracks can be driven fairly close to top speed for most of the race - late braking isn't a part of the game. The game is mainly about finding the shortest path through the track that doesn't result in a crash.
The free version requires spectating every few races but otherwise gets access to most of the content. This isn't pay-to-win. Free players don't play at a disadvantage. I paid for the full version and I found it to be worth the price in order to play uninterrupted. Paid players also get access to several other modes including many tracks, different track types, and a new type of car for each track type. Unfortunately, the paid servers are normally empty so you'll still spend most of your time racing the same tracks as the free players.
If you think of this as a casual game, you'll get some fun out of it. If you're looking for a realistic driving sim, look elsewhere.

Titan souls is a boss rush game, plain and simple. But its one of the best out there (Though there aren't many to begin with.).
The story is simple enough, you want something, and in order to get it, you go to a forbidden land to kill about a dozen titans, claim their souls, and then obtain that which you sought after. Its very shadow of colossus if it was pixled, more selfish and without cutscenes.
The gameplay is where this game shines; you are armed with a bow, an arrow, and the ability to recall said arrow with your mind. You can walk, run and dodge roll, but beyond this, you have nothing. Using these basic mechanics, the game creates very enjoyable, difficult boss battles for you to throw yourself at, where one hit on either of you is an instant kill. In a very David and Goliath manner, you are fighting something with one weak spot, which you have to hit perfectly in order to gain victory. Using the simple to learn, but hard to master mechanics, you have to figure out where the weakness is, then, obviously, strike it. Thats it really, but the way its all designed makes every new titan a joy to fight. Every single boss is extremely fun and will take all of your focus and patience to overcome. There are no minions or anything else getting in the way, its just you, and them.
The only big downside to the game is the open world, while it is absolutely beautiful, its also entirely pointless aside from visual splendor. There are no collectables as far as I am aware of, no lore tid bits, nothing to warrent exploring off the beaten path or do anything but go from one titan room to the next in whichever order you like. Combined with the fact that every time you die you return to a checkpoint near the boss room, and it can take anywhere between five to twenty seconds to return to the boss room you just died in, it can be a little annoying for some. I personally didn't mind it, as it gave me time to collect my thoughts, think over where i went wrong and then try to plan for the next round.
Graphically speaking the game is beautiful, its up there with hyper light drifter, owlboy and superbrothers. I rarely care about how good a game looks, but this is one of the rare few times where i found myself just stopping to look at all the effort that went into every area in the game, it is really just that good. The bosses themselves all have this very zelda-esque look to them as well, each one being a cartoonish behemoth which will smother your blood all over its own body many times.
The game also has a great soundtrack, every boss has their own song, and different areas of the map have seperate music scores as well. Each piece matches the locations perfectly, and I loved it so much I downloaded the entire thing. Its all instrumental, But it covers alot of bases. Metal, orchestral, Flute music, with every track bringing something different to the table.
Overall, I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a challanging game that cuts the fat of most titles and skips right to the boss battles. It makes for a quick experience unfortunately, but a memorable one that sets bars.

I love Steins;Gate. It's unique visual style is something that's always a breath of fresh air. Every character that you come across feels very human. Each of the routes are finely crafted. The soundtrack is beautiful. The mood of the story is captured perfectly through it, and I can't be more happy with it.
Enough gushing, though, I have to say that I should bring up that I have 2 issues with this game, neither of which are a very big deal. The first issue is how long it takes to kick off the ground. This can be a turn off for newcomers, as the first few chapters are paced fairly slow, however, I feel that the slow pacing is necessary to build on the impact that the tone shift has on the player.
The second issue that I have with the VN is the requirements for the true ending. You aren't going to get the true ending on your first blind playthrough of Steins;Gate unless your looking it up. That isn't an issue, and I don't think it should be seen as one, but the problem comes that the flags required to achieve the true ending can be seen as a little convoluted.
Aside from those two things, which may or may not even be an issue for some people, I loved this visual novel. Totally worth the price. I'm really glad to see it finally made its way onto Steam for others to enjoy the same way that I have.

There are some interesting ideas in this game. I like the random gun compnents coming together to make a single weapon, unfortunately there are so many guns that the game requires you to constantly change out your weapons. That kind of makes the uniqueness of the weapons loose their flavor. The co-op is interesting and almost the only way you can play, because the world feels a bit hollow. Due to the massive leaning on the co-op the story doesn't seem important. I had to replay levels several times to try and get the story, because all my friends would complete quests, which would mostly nullify the dialog. Oftentimes when playing with other I didn't even know what they did to complete the quests. The other problem you run into is that if you are at the beginning on your game and go join a friends game and get all the way to level ___, it doesn't translate well back to your game. All those quests you completed with so and so don't count in your game. So now you find yourself overpowered to the extreme, having to find a way not to feel bored while going through the level to catch up to where you played to, and so you can get the complete story. I'm a completionists so this drove me nuts. It could be a fun game if you accept the fact that you'll probably never complete it for your character. I found myself playing through the same levels what seemed like dozens of times. In most games that would be an advantage, but since all the opponents are bullet sponges it just leaves you feeling like you're grinding in an MMO. The second game has the same problems as the first. First, this game is a ton of fun but suffers from severe problems:
1. Group size is limited to 4, my friends and I don't see how a game like this should limit your group to just 4 when matches have at least 6 to 8 players per side, and often the game will augment with terrible AI players instead of filling up the room.
2. The pay to win is by far the WORST I have ever experienced in a game, they have Rockstar beat on how much the game requires you to pay to stay competitive.
3. Crafting is limited and the developer expects you to PAY to craft items, you have to 'rent' each workbench for every faction to craft.
4. The resources you need to craft to sell on the market or use for yourself are capped each week, this further reinforces the pay to win aspect.
5. Players that put things on the market overprice their items to further keep the pay to win.
6. The 'bonus' XP you gain from being well rested (taking a break every 24 hours or whatever the time limit is) is very much like a mobile game, which doesn't make sense why you would even put this in a game like this. You will definately play longer than a mobile game, so why the 'cool down'? Better yet, don't have this at all.
7. The progression is entirely too slow, you don't unlock parts fast enough or the ones you need to stay competitive, and somehow you can't buy extra parts on the market. How did this greedy developer overlook this?
8. The power score of your vehicles means nothing, you could have a starter truck and get matched with high levels and be destroyed in seconds. The power scores are over inflated and don't speak to player skills or abilities and only hurt you when you're trying to make a light build (below 3000) or beef up for maximum armor.
9. The maps are small, really small. Usually I don't mind playing them over and over but there are a few maps that are terrible from a design and balance stance.
10. Weapons dictate success, espeically the overpowered drones, which are all nicely behind that pay to win wall. All of the paid weapons quickly destroy your armor and your vehicle, which makes it hard to be competitive since the game punishes you for losing.
11. Parts and vehicles  get caught on everything and sometimes you hit bumps that shouldn't effect your vehicle. This game promotes building monstrosities and ugly things that snag and hang up on the terrain.
If you have lots of time and I do mean a lot of time to waste. You'll need to spend a lot of REAL money to win or just grind it out slowly hitting every cap each day and week. This game has a TON of potential and I would have bought a game like this if it had level progression and no pay to win features. The game needs more balancing and not so much the damn paywall.
Having said this, I will still play the game until I'm not able to play for free, things keep gearing up to a pay to win and I'd like to spend $0 on 'in-app purchases.'

I learned a lot by playing Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3 - Uprising.  I learned that strippers make the best commanders.  I learned that buildings are fireproof.  I learned that the best way to sneak into an enemy country is via tugboat.  I learned that the reason the Soviets lost the cold war is because their controls were so awful.
C&CRA-U is one of those games that's trying to mask mediocre gameplay with eye candy and humor.  Both are miserable failures.  I'm sure having a stripper for a commander appeals to the 15-21 crowd, but it just made me cringe.  The humor is based around really bad Russian accents and national stereotypes.  no game in my list has been more painful to play.
As for what really matters, the game play, it's just the same old RTS mechanics that we've been playing for 20 years now.  Order people around, shoot foreigners, maybe use a special ability, there's nothing new to see here.  In the grand tradition of the C&C series, all the cut scenes are live-action using real "actors.", but really that stopped being novel in the 90s.
If you want to play an RTS, avoid this game and play something like StarCraft 2.  This is just another weak entry in a franchise that's been milked to death.

One of the virtues of Point-and-Clicks like The Silent Age, is that the stories tend to be more original and compelling than most other genres. There are no real mechanics that games like this need to feed to you over time, so the story is the focus right from the get-go, and those stories tend to have a lot more freedom because they are not limited to situations where you can carry a machine gun or claymore around without being capsicum sprayed and thrown in the back of a divy van. And that's what drew me to play The Silent Age in the first place really; I had never played a game set in the 70's, and I desperately wanted to see whether it would be as funky and sleezy as I imagined it could be.
10mins in and I wasn't disappointed, with moustaches, flares, and disco divas all included, but♥♥♥♥♥♥soon started to get eerie as the real meat of the story started to kick in. The protagonist, Joe, isn't the sharpest tool in the shed and there are no shortage of people that love to tell him that on a regular basis, but what Joe lacks in cognitive ability he more than makes up for in fashion sense and interior design. To be honest, I struggled to relate to Joe because he's a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥, but I could really appreciate the character and made sure I looked at everything I could to have a giggle at his commentary on occasion.
The art style was great and well directed, and I think I took more screenshots in The Silent Age than I have in any similar game I've played to date. In particular, some of the lighting effects and larger landscapes really stood out, and the team has done a great job to create a good ambience with the lighting and pallet used. Sound was good and the voice acting was well above average for this genre, which really added to the overall feeling of quality despite the game being realively short.
If you're looking for a game to play on a day off that you can enjoy from start to finish, and experience a story that's nice and original, you'd be hard-pressed to find much better than The Silent Age.

I'd describe Crossout as a combination of the building mechanics of Kerbal Space Program, mixed with the tank combat of WarThunder, all set in a universe that heavily draws inspiration from Mad Max.
The building and combat is fun, there is no denying that. I recommend the game solely on that alone. But....
The grinding can be a bit less fun.
If you treat this not as a F2P game, and instead as a cheap Steam game, the grind is reduced. It's not Pay-To-Win, but it is Pay-To-Advance-At-A-Rate-Faster-Than-A-Snail. Just dropping $3 to let you easily unlock a workbench goes a long way.
There are 4 colors of parts, White, Blue, Purple, and Orange.
White parts are given out fairly common, you win a skirmish, you'll get a white part.
Blue parts are 'rare'. They can be crafted by players with specific white parts, some copper, and some scrap metal (which are earned in battles and raids). Unfotunately, to "rent" a workbench to craft parts, you need to have coins. Coins are earned by either paying real money, or by selling your extra parts, usually for a very small amount. This is where the grind starts getting a bit long, scrouning up the coins to craft a blue part. So, once you get the coins to rent a workbench to make a certain number of blue parts, now you need 3 of a certain white part, 2 of another, 2 of yet another white part, and 450 scrap metal and 50 copper. Then you let that go an hour while you craft, and BOOM! A blue part! Now you can use that for more destruction, or sell it for coins. But say you then wan to craft a purple part. You'll need to rent another workbench, and you'll have to get 2 each of 3 different kinds of Blue Parts, in addition to the scrap metal and copper. So, for those not keeping track at home, One Purple part requires 2950 scrap metal, 450 copper, 750 wires (which are earned through a PvP battle) and 42 various white parts.
You can see how that grinding might be a bit tedious. (Orange requires 5 purple parts and even more raw materials)

Titan Souls is a game which revolves around the concept of "One" - one arrow, one shot, one hit kills you, one hit kills every boss you fight. On Iron Mode you have one life with which to beat the entire game.
The game is nothing but a boss rush with small exploration elements between each boss. It's very similar to a 2d styled Shadows of the Colossus, in terms of being a big empty world with neat little 'things' to see, with big setpiece bosses. The problem is that... well, there's not really anything to see in the world besides the bosses, and the bosses are neither really all that big or setpiece. The fights are swift, often anticlimatic affairs in either direction. While it can be satisfying to achiev a very fast kill on some of the bosses or figure them out, if you die repeatedly, you're making trek after trek back and sitting through loadscreens, rather than respawning at the bosses door. For bosses that can kill you in <10 seconds, it can turn into spending more time running back to the boss than it is actually going in for your next attempt. At this point, when you finally get the shot right, the feeling is relief rather than satisfaction, and that's never a good thing.
The game requires pinpoint reflexes, accuracy, and timing on essentially every boss, so be aware of that going in. The game is difficult because it's very fast paced and the weak point openings for many bosses can be measured in single or lower double digit frames. Fighting becomes trial and error memorization until you get the perfect shot and it's over.
Other issues stem from the fact that besides the sometimes disappointing boss battles, there's not anything else to actually do in the world. There's no upgrades, no abilities, no skills, no stamina lizards to find, no incentive to look at the world, which is actually rather pretty and accompanied by wonderful music. But when you're on your 15th trek back, you don't care anymore and you just want to kill the stupid bomb tossing lava blob, and you can't roll up stairs so you have to do it slow every time. The only reason to hop off the beaten path is to find some of the hidden titans, since you're not required to kill them all to beat the game, merely to get the post-game 'final boss'. This isn't spoilers since there's literally giant lights on every sealed door and rune tile indicating the number of titans in the area, and if you miss some, the last door doesn't open because some of the lights aren't on.
The story is told through actions and suggestions and implications, which is fine for a minimalistic game like this. The end revelation of "TRUTH" is nothing really extraordinary or revelatory, nor has it not been done before in a billion other ways.
I wish there was just "More" to the game. More progression, more Titans, more incentive to play the game. I beat it in a few hours and beyond the achievements felt no real urge to play the game in a harder mode, or god forbid Iron Mode. There's just not enough here, and what is here is frustrating and annoying enough to go through to where beating the gaem was, again, a relief rather than satisfaction, and that's unfortunate, because there's a lot here that would otherwise be very very fun.

This game could be amazing. I have always followed a sort of code for games that have most enemies kill you in one hit, and it is based off of Hotline Miami. That game is hard as balls when you first start, has you killing and being killed in one hit, and jamming music. This game also has all of these things, however there is one key difference. In hotline miami, when you die, you hit "R". No stop in the music, gameplay, or flow; it is very easy to get back into the action. In Titan souls, when you die, you get a slow fadeout to black, a ~3-4 second loading screen, and then a 10-15 second pointless stroll back to the boss, not to mention the same "dramatic" intro you might see 20 times for the same boss. While it seems small in the big picture, it is game ruining, as it makes dying infinitely more frustrating, typically 5-10 minutes of nothing tacked onto defeating a boss who can and will be killed moments after the fight begins once you manage to hit their weakpoint.
Pros:
Great music
Great presentation
Great art
(occasionally) Interesting scenery
Cons:
Incredibly frustrating for little reason other than poor spawnpoint placement and load times
Flow is interrupted every few seconds in what could be otherwise a seamless flow of boss rushes
If things were fixed, I would gladly say its 7/10 or 8/10, however in its current state: 3/10, only buy on sale, or not at all if you are impatient.

This is pretty much the pinnacle of story-driven games, in many areas. The 30-hour length allows for a lot of development of characters and exploration of consequences, while every single question that is raised in the entire timespan is answered somewhere, if you see all of the optional sequences. The writers have done a great job of creating a universe with time travel dynamics that are consistent and generally work out when thought through, then populating it with varied and well-written characters and using the time travel aspect to explore aspects of the characters that wouldn't normally be possible. It was so good that I spent another 30 hours going through a second time to see things I'd missed and the incredible extended ending (which is very much recommended).
My only gripes are a couple of rather cringeworthy moments and some slow pacing in the first half of the game, but after a certain plot point the train comes off the rails and there's 15-20 hours of gripping story until the end. There's also one side character who feels entirely like filler, but is more than made up for by the main character who's a jackass yet also the standout character of the whole game.
If you enjoy story-driven emotional rollercoaster games like Life Is Strange and Telltale's Walking Dead and don't mind dropping the puzzle aspect of them, then this is a 10/10 every time.

Short and to the point:
This game will, at times, leave you wanting to snap your keyboard/controller in half, yet at the same time keep you coming back for more.
Long and detailed:
Over the past four years (release date says Jul 2014, but I have achievements from as early as Jun 2013. Maybe I got it in beta? I don't remember) I've abandoned and returned to this game a few times. Now, you might think it somewhat redundant and/or pointless to write a review years after the game has been released, but I felt it was owed not only to myself but to people who might find this game for the first time in the future, to say something about it.
While the game has many enjoyable aspects, it also has some... curve balls. And boy are they some doozies.
At first, you'll likely be charmed by the game's sense of humour. Right out of the gate this game shows itself to be set apart from your typical Castlevania style RPG, most notably with its "adult" content. Now, that doesn't mean it has nudity and sex on every second screen, rather, it means you won't feel like you're playing a game aimed at twelve year olds. Dialog in conversations and even one particular side quest will have a decidely mature air about them without it feeling deliberate or forced for the sake of the adult content toggle. Another side mission, while not actually being mature or adult in any specific way, can only be truly understood and laughed at by someone who is an adult and therefor understands the situation.
The art style, music and gameplay itself are all very much enjoyable. And as you might expect, there are a variety of methods at your disposal to dispose of the hordes of enemies awaiting you on the next screen. But that is where the norm ends and the unexpected begins. For starters, you do not begin the game with all possible abilities available to you. Some must be unlocked and, if you're not careful, can even be missed entirely. While most bosses are fairly straight forward and easy enough to formulate a strategy for on the fly, one in particular can be nothing short of mind numbingly infuriating in its unorthodox mechanic. Even the finale of the game itself will likely leave you dumbfounded and lacking in colourful descriptive words for the developer as you are left wondering just what the @!#$ are you meant to do now?
It's hard to decide whether or not to recommend this game or not, for the simple fact that, even before you finish it, UnEpic will leave you with a servere case of a love/hate relationship. On the one hand, it has many enjoyable moments and elements, but on the other hand, if you don't know what is coming, it can be brutally and infuriatingly punishing and unfair. Many developers add elements to extend the life of a game and make it replayable. With UnEpic, you need to replay it just to be able to finish it. If you know what to expect, the game will be less aneurism inducing. But if you are unprepared... make sure you have nothing expensive within arms reach.
Finally, while I believe there is a special place in Hell reserved for the developer as a result of this game's creation, I have decided to recommend UnEpic because it is a unique and refreshing experience, even if it may leave you with some PTSD afterwards. The characters aren't generic. The story isn't typical. And if you don't completely hate UnEpic, you're sure to at least hate the fact that you love it.

- Combat is fun, challenging, and fast paced. The beginning is rather simple but the game quickly gets tougher the further you get. I love fighting for my life when fighting against these super strong characters.

CONS

First off, this is another pretty early review for me, however this game really hits you in the face right off the bat with everything it's got, for better or for worse.
I have to say that, like most DBZ games, this game is an absolute blast. There are very few other games that I enjoy to this degree, and the only other one I can think of off the top of my head is Ultimate Marvel vs Capcom 3. The gameplay is fast-paced and you really feel like you're in a DBZ fight - minus the staring at each other for five whole episodes bit (why is that even a thing in the anime? The manga doesn't do that...).
On thing that's a bit different from other DBZ games is that, when you first start up the game, you can't just jump into VS mode. You have to start by creating a character. You have five races to chose from (Earthling, Saiyan, Majin, Namekian and Frost Demon/Frieza's race), and three of those have male/female variations (Earthlings, Saiyans and Majins), resulting in a total of eight different basic characters. Each of these combinations has their own strengths and weaknesses, though are mostly balanced with each other (female Majins are technically a bit weaker than the other choices since their highly defensive racial passive doesn't match up that well with their glass cannon base stats). You also have decent control over your character's appearance - not to Bethesda levels, but it's enough to make something unique. Finally, you can unlock new moves as you play and you have a choice of up to four supers, two ultimates and an escape move.
The story is just a bit more than an excuse plot, and is essentially a re-writing of the original DBZ storyline with your character thrown in - but then again few people play fighting games for the story.
Of course, the music is pretty awesome - but then again that's been a staple of DBZ games.
Now, for the bad. When the game launched, the servers were pretty much slammed. People were constantly getting disconnected, and even then only if they managed to connect at all. This issue has been aleviated but not fully fixed. This game is also incredibly unbalanced at the higher levels, with certain combinations of moves and abilities being much more powerful than others. This issue has also been somewhat aleviated but not fully fixed. Finally, the game has a significant amount of artificial difficulty - there's a large number of escort missions and your ally's AI is practically suicidal in these. In addition, the way Super Saiyan mechanics work in this game makes certain missions where you have to fight more than one of them a living nightmare - luckily those missions aren't mandetory.
Since this is a pretty early review, I'll probably end up editing it later on. Therefore I cannot give a score breakdown.
While I set this review as positive, that doesn't really tell the whole story. If you're used to polished and balanced games, especially in the fighting game genre, you would be best to look elsewhere, at least for now. But if you like Dragon Ball Z, or are looking for a game that's an absolute blast to play, or you are a casual fan of fighting games, then there's a good chance you will enjoy Dragon Ball Xenoverse.
Score Breakdown: TBD
Recommended for: DBZ fans, casual fighting game fans, anyone who wants a fun game that's easy to learn the ropes of.
Not recommended for: people expecting a very polished experience.

I recommend this game but only because I have had so much fun with my friends as we scream and cry at trucks as they fall through our poorly built bridges. If I was an antisocial type who played this game alone, I would have hated it.
The "campaign" is reasonably long, but it gets repetitive. The only way to add variety is to try stupid designs that would not work in real life, but do in game. For example, I used a counter-weight to create enought tension to support my bridge. The levels are very challenging, but not in the sense that they challenge your understanding of physics, because anyone who knows anything about building bridges with get very frustrated with the idiotic placement of build-points in the map. In combination with the restricted use of certain materials, and the third-world budget for purchasing said materials, bridges often can barely stand their own weight, and beating a level often only means that your load got a cross even though the bridge collapsed behind it.
Which brings me to the reason I actually recommend it. The level of challenge results in hilariously inadequate structures that make any educated person cringe. It's addictive to try something hilarious and then watch as cars plummet to their death with satisfying crunches. In a sense, the game is more fun to lose than to win. And if you have a group of friends nearby who can make fun of your attempts to build and when you fail push you aside to attempt their own idiotic designs, it gets fun and competitive. However, this is not a feature of the game, but a feature the way you can choose to augment your experience.
My chief complaint, though, is the lack of a sandbox mode. The game never gives you a chance to experiment with different properties of physics or the materials you are working with without restricting you to a budget and limited build points. And a sandbox mode would not be hard to implement, considering that all it would need is custom maps, build points, and unlimited access to the already available resources.
So, if you are looking for an educational experience that will teach you to build bridges . . . go somewhere else.
If you are looking for a hilarious cautionary showcase of how not to build bridges, particularly with smug friends nearby, buy Bridge Constructor. (Which should have been named "Bridge Destructor")

I play this game like it's a full time job. 26 hours in my first 3 days and loving almost evey minute of it. It's purpose is to tell a story, whether of joy or sorrow, and it accomplishes this well. Let me share with you my favorite story so far, which lasted about 10-15 hours in real life.
I finally made a colony that lasted longer than a year before the narrorator decided that this story was ready for a twist. 3 years in. Population is up to 7-8 people at the same time; work was getting done. Solid defense multiple blocks deep surrounding the entire base. Enough food to last for 2 years. Raiders don't stand a chance.
Randy decides he's been too easy on me. First wave of raiders equiped with heavy artillery arrives. After hours, they blast a crack in my wall and flood in. My colonists have been waiting. Firing commences. Bullets fly, blood spills and bodies drop. The raiders grab 3 of my people before they retreat. I save one of them but the others are gone for good. Time to rescue and restore.
Hours after the first attack, the next raid begins. The crack hasn't been repaired because most of my colony is in the hospital. A few good soldiers answer the call for justice and defend the homeland. They quickly dispense of the second wave but sustain minor injuries. Time to visit the hospital.
Hours later the third strike falls upon us. This battle will be a last stand. I send those able to walk out to the battlefield, likely to take thier last breaths. They meet the aggressors at the door and unleash their weapons. This desperate attempt to save the colony ends like many wars -- neither side claims victory as we all strive to hang on. They capture two of mine, but we take down 3 of theirs.
Only three reamain, wounded and unconcious. Luckily, my doctor is still alive and well, making her rounds amongst the two soldiers. We survived the war . . . or so we thought. The siren wails again as a final wave of raiders enters the arena. These lone stragglers are equipped with shoddy wooden melee weapons, but the odds are five to one. My doctor greets them at the door with an LMG and fights to her last breath. The wounded hear her screams and answer the call. Using their guns as crutches, they hobble to the entrance and face certain demise. Their only thought, "We're taking them with us."
They fight their way through the flames and rubble that they once called home, stabbing and shotting anything that moved. The raiders retreat, but we won't allow them to get far. Not today. They chase the raiders to the gates, cornering them against the wall. The grim reaper is amongst us. They fire as long as thier strength can hold the gun before falling to the ground due to blood loss. One soldier dies while the last man finishes the assult.
With every raider dead, the lone soldier returns to his room, passing his fallen comrades along the way. He eats his last meal and grab some Flake to unwind. He locks himself in the Rec room and lights up to ease the pain. He thinks back to the story that was told within these walls. The crash landing and the first walls. The famines and the feasts. The wars won and the people lost. He finishes his first pipe full and decides to light another dose of flake. His blood is draining as he slips in to an overdosed coma of ecstasy and joins his friends in the light.
With him, dies the legacy of this grand colony. Perhaps some day another weary traveler will stumble upon its walls and take shelter.  Maybe they will wonder of the epic tale that transpired, looking upon the works that his hands created. Or maybe the dust of the mountain will consume this town and its insignificant story. After all, in the end, we're all just dust in the wind.

Alright, quick review after a couple of matches.
The concept, I love it, it focuses around team-work, covering eachother and completing objectives (far as I know there's only a domaination gamemode), not only that it focuses on tactics but your ability to score headshots as bodyshots are practically and as far as I've seen, is the only way to take another player out.
With that said, the difficulty is increased futher the only gun your given (a SMG) is suprisingly unweildy with a "tough but fair" recoil, it seems to be designed around the players skill, like for instance:
It was quite possible for me to perch myself at a vantage point and take headshots from somewhere between medium and long range, it can be, by no means be a makeshift sniper rifle but the reason it's possible for me to pull it off is only because the first shot is percise and the sight is clean and simple.
One thing I also must point out is that the weapon your given has 2 accessory's, a flashlight and a laser sight:
The flashlight is useful for dark area's and spotting enemy's as they don't have any indicator or name-tag appear but doing so might give away your position so sometimes it's better to keep it off and hide in the dark (choice is yours).
Now one thing that took me a while to notice is that there is no crosshair, none (mostly because I don't play games with one where there's alturnatives) you've only got your ironsight for percise aiming but obviously iron sight's impractical if in closer quaters which is what the laser sight is for, it allows you to aim percisely from the him but this also comes with the drawback as enemies will also be able to see your laser beam and can track it right to your position, so both are quite useful but  thourght and caution is needed before using them.
There are a few design choices that I like and dislike but both are by no means should be used for judgement on wether should be considered positives or negatives as they are my own personal prefrences:
Positvies (+):
+ Real emphisis around teamwork, skill and tactics
+ As matches goes on, the level's change conditions (from light to dark, from clear to foggy, from thick updrafts to rain)
+ Gun add-on's gives extra flavor to combat .
Negatives (-)
- Obviously the game is not finished so you will be stuck with the same gun and gamemode but there's some variation of maps that I found quite sufficiant and intresting as well, especially how the level's morph and make full use of the landscape.
- Not as many players as I would of liked to see playing the game
- When you get hit it disables your hud which also means your teammate's indicators resaulting in possibly you accidently killing your teammate.
Overall, a very promising game and worthy of consideration.

I've been working my way through all of the Telltale games. I just finally finished Tales from the Borderlands, and I can't help but feel that, honestly, it deserves a review.
I would definitely recomend it to anyone who likes Borderlands, anyone who likes the other Telltale games, and anyone who likes a good laugh and isn't too squeemish. Telltale typically tells stories that are deep, meaningful, but depressing. You're forced to make choices that are difficult, and usually with someones life hanging in the balance. This is especially true in The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us, where there are times that you quite literally have to choose between who lives and who dies, with the occasional dark humor thrown in.
Tales from the Borderlands strikes a surprisingly different and pleasant chord by still giving you these meaningful choices, still often with the lives of your friends on the line, but making you laugh your rear off in the process. Plenty of references to the main Borderlands games, pop culture, and pure wackiness abound to create a truly unique and amazing experience. (A quick glance through my screenshot collection for the title will reveal a few of these wacky moments). But at the same time, it doesn't detract from the meaning behind them. There were moments where I cried (I'll always love you, Loader Bot), plenty more moments where I laughed (Finger guns, lots of finger guns), and others where I was shocked into stunned silence (and disgusted. Can't forget disgusted. Never let a psycho invite you to a "Face Pizza" party.)
With that all in mind. I loved every second, and I'd do it all again.

I first played this game a long while back.  Playing as Brick the berserker was moderately amusing and had my co-op buddies laughing hysterically as I punched stuff to death, but the game seemed primitive, colorless, and repetitive.  I didn't stick with it long.
So time passed and my co-op buddies got me to play Borderlands 2.  I wasn't exactly excited about it but I humored them and went in with my Borderlands 1 experience coloring my view.  And if you're expecting to not like something, and don't really want to like it, you probably won't like it.  I played BL2 for a couple hours with them and put it aside, and quite honestly forgot about it.
Well, for some reason I got hungry for an FPS and remembered I had Borderlands 2 installed.  So I figured I'd give it another shot, try another class and run solo for a bit to get to know the game.  And I fell in love with it.  I fell so hard I eventually came back to Borderlands 1 to give it another go and see if it just wasn't bad attitude keeping me from enjoying it.  Nope.  Comparing Borderlands to Borderlands 2 is like comparing Pong to Portal.  I got far enough in to recognize a few landmarks when they showed up in BL2 and that was as much as I could take.
So to sum up, save yourself some time and just go straight to Borderlands 2.  Maybe catch a YouTube video for some BL1 backstory.  The only good thing about Borderlands 1 is that its existence made Borderlands 2 possible.

I don't really know who to recommend this to. It's an epic platform rpg with a comical setting. I'd say if you like indie rpgs and you want to play something different, go for it. I fell in love with it and quickly became addicted. I believe it's a must have for any rpg gamers but that's just my opinion.
Pros
Epic: The castle is HUGE. Every area is big, with its own secrets, with its own sidequests, that give you many hard-earned rewards. The story is epic, mixed with gods and spirits and even other realms.
Platforming: That's done really well in my opinion. I never found that "i pressed the button but nothing happened" aspect that i usually find in platform games.
Comedy: The game is funny, but without that "ruining" the epic-ness of it. Let's just say you're an ordinary guy from our world who doesn't believe this is really happening. I thought that was a cool setting. To be honest i still don't know if it's really happening or not.
Bosses: The bosses need some tries before you can win them. This may sound frustrating but the cool thing is that every boss or sub-boss is pretty much unique and needs its own strategy. You can't win a boss by just hacking and slashing and focusing on one area of expertise.
Respawn-grinding: Grinding is not needed if you play in normal difficulty. But i started it in hard++ and you gotta grind a little bit. However you will soon find that it's not a tedious task - you don't have to grind for hours and hours. To be honest, since every area respawns monsters after some time (so when you visit it again after you've been to other areas you have to re-kill the monsters but now they're easier) the grinding kinda happens naturally.
Difficulty: If you're new to games in general, or if you just want to breeze through it, play it on easy or normal. But if you're a proper gamer, play it on hard++ to see what the game offers - i think that was the way the game was intended to be played. It's really not as hard as it sounds, you don't die in one hit or something. Also, manual saving, passive regeneration, and all this stuff that the easier difficulties give you really look like cheating once you've played the hardest setting AND you get +2 skillpoints when you levelup. I really feel i have to utilize all the different things you are given, magic, scrolls, potions, even the fact that when you crouch you light the area below you (before you fall down on it).
Challenges: That was one of the really cool aspect of the game. You find some hidden challenges at some points in the game that - if you manage to pull them off - give you some special points that you may spend at a special trader. The challenges are pretty much as difficult as the points they award. The stuff you get for these points are seriously worth it.
Adult language and humor: Well, the title says it all.
Fast travel: Remember i told you you don't really need manual saving? That's why. Just next to your save point in the hardest setting there is a gate which links to multiple other gates in other areas and you can pretty much fast-travel to the entire castle.
Realism: By this i mean you don't press on a scroll and he just casts it. He has to take it out and read it first. I loved that. He has to actually drink the potion, you can't just spam it like in hack and slash games. You have to find a safe moment. Throwing yourself mindlessly to a myriad of opponents is gonna get you killed.
Choices: The game has choices that impact the gameplay but NOT the story.
Subquests: I thought the subquests are really cool. They are pretty straight-forward, they are unique and the rewards are sweet.
Complexity: So, if you saw the screenshots and were like me and thought "i'm not gonna drag myself in this icon-filled nightmare", it's nothing like that. Although at times i found i really would like to remap the controls, it's not as complex as it looks, and the complexity bar really raises naturally as you play the game.
I think i've covered everything i like about the game here.
Cons
Remapping controls: I thought it's a shame you can't remap skills and spells. I mean, you can, but you can only do it with numbers or shift+number. That's the only keys you can remap. And you have a TON of things you'd like to put on these.
Game-changing challenges: Remember what i said above about challenges? Seems like there's some challenges that you have to replay the game to get. Also, i read about one that you can't get some specific spells in order to complete. I thought that was a bad idea. You don't NEED the spells per se, but it's always nice when you can work hard and complete everything in one playthrough right? Well the game doesn't do that.
Wand recharging: There is, simply, no way to recharge the wands. You get a wand, it has some charges on it, you spend them, that's it. Kiss the wand goodbye. I don't really care so much about that because wands are gamebreaking indeed. I finished a boss with a bunch of wands so i wouldn't really want that power for the entire game. But noone in the game even talks about that. You go to a magic seller, there's not even a one-time event that the character says "i'd like to recharge my wand" where the seller says "that's impossible" or something. I had to look in the discussions to realize that.
Anyway, since i'm struggling to find cons in this game, i'll finish my review here. I think it's a must, there's nothing to say more about it. Just go get it.

I am forced to either recommend or not recommend a game when writing a review. Fine. Not recommended. However, I have a neutral stance when it comes to this game. I can neither recommend nor discourage purchasing this game.
I finally got around to getting into this franchise this past winter, and was pleasantly surprised by just how much fun it was. Co-op was ok to good. Game mechanics were actually pretty good. However, the respawn rate can make the game a little too grindy - even if you play with a friend. Nonetheless, I had fun.
So. Why am I not recommending Borderlands? I don't recall ever becoming so disenchanted so quickly with a game on the basis of just how much better the sequels are (including the much maligned TPS). After playing The Pre-Sequel and starting Borderlands 2, I have zero desire to go back and play the original Borderlands. Almost every aspect of the original seems very klunky compared to Borderlands 2 and TPS. Thus, even though I have a portion of the last Borderlands DLC left to complete, I doubt I ever will. Oh!  And I usually want to try each character class in this sort of game. Not so this time.
Borderlands is worth playing to experience the storyline first hand, but only once in my opinion. However, if story doesn't matter to you, you can probably skip ahead to either The Pre-Sequel or to Borderlands 2. I do like games with a tale to tell, and this aspect of the game appealed to me. The DLC is fine, but might be hit or miss on the basis of theme. Read the description of each before blindly buying. Just be sure you are completely done with Borderlands before playing any of the sequels. As I've said, there is just no going back.
Deeply discounted, this game is a good buy. It is also good enough to give you a relatively inexpensive taste of the Borderlands series; and, if you like what you see, it is a fine appetizer.

Titan Souls is a "just keep trying"-kind of game. You can run, roll, shoot 1 (just one) arrow and retrieve it telepathically. With that, you're off to fight numerous bosses. You die in one hit, and so do they (granted that you hit their one weak spot).
Unfortunately that's literally all there is, as far as I've encountered. You slowly traverse the map to find a boss and you'll probably die a few times before you kill it. Then off to the next  boss, and so forth. There's nothing inbetween. No small enemies, no upgrades, nothing. And if you die, you'll slowly have to get back to the boss to try again. Even if the checkpoint(s) are relatively close, why not just allow me to retry immediately? Spawn me in front of the boss again!
Within one hour I found myself pretty bored of it. I'd probably keep trying if I could retry bosses immediately, though. Imagine if the respawning in Super Meatboy was three times as slow.
Its more of a tech demo for the other two Borderland games.  Also I hate too much DLC.

this game became a sentimental favorite almost immediately. its a really beautiful and unified work of art. the plot is vague and mysterious, and entirely implied for the sake of non-stop gameplay. the tiny size of the child hero on screen perfectly conveys the massive scale of their challenges and surroundings. the peaceful overworld songs are somber and thoughtful, while every bosses' song is unique, exciting, and fun, just like the bosses themselves. the color palettes and designs are really beautiful, and having a 2d hero battle giant 3d bosses just always looks amazing, that is like, so inspired and well executed. onyxia is my favorite.
what really works for me is the way in which the challenges of this game are designed and presented. killing extremely fast giants with only one arrow and stopping whenever you draw your bow is literally as hard as it sounds, and the moment you die you see the hero's tiny child life snuffed out in an instant. it sets in how unlikely you are to succeed by facing you against constant failure, but never a form of failure that actually punishes you for playing: the checkpoints are an equal distance from 2 to 4 boss chambers at once. trying again is always easy, going for a different boss and coming back to this one later is always easy, setting out to find a different set of bosses is always easy. your skill just slowly rises to meet each challenge, and in this way i find the game extremely relaxing.
for me this game was like an indulgent wish fulfillment. i always wished that 2d legend of zelda games were more simple, unified, and truly let you face challenges in any order. i always wished that shadow of the colossus had more variety and challenge and less presentation fluff and complicated scenarios. i personally prefer this game to both. titan souls is just so aesthetically pleasing and so tightly designed and i just adore 2d pixel art mixing with 3d to no end. it's very short and sweet, and slowly mastering each of the 19 bosses is stimulating and rewarding.
also, i can tell this game is designed for a controller thumbstick, but playing with a keyboard is absolutely fine too. aiming your arrow in only the 8 cardinal directions is a bit of a handicap but its actually a pretty fun way to play if you think you'd like it. i promise the game isnt spoiled if you don't have a controller handy. also i'm aware now that this game has a reputation for "hair-yanking hardcore gamer frustration", but i wasn't aware of it when i first played to the end. i just found it extremely chill and was pretty surprised to read the "you will scream at your monitor" response to this game. i guess i would suggest that you stay hydrated and watch your sitting posture if you get upset easily?? idk.
but yeah this game is perfect.

I've been playing Crossout for a few weeks now, and I've got a bit of a different view of some of the others. So, keep that in mind.
First: There is no pay wall. Everything in the game is available just by playing, collecting resources, and... selling them on the Market. Crafting is fine, but it's easier, and less headache-inducing, if you get the things you want from the market. I got my first Rare item within the first 5 days of playing, without ever spending a dime. I have since bought one of the car packs, but only
figuring out whether the game really was some kind of cash-grabbing con. (It isn't.)
Second: The game's mechanics and engine are awesome, exactly what you'll expect for a game like this... but as with anything, there are some good weapons and some not-so-good weapons. It's VERY MUCH worth spending some time in the game's own Forums to get a feel for what is and isn't worth spending your in-game money on. There's also a few good threads to explain how to use the Market effectively.
Third: Don't go whole-hog on building your dream tank. The bigger you make it, the bigger the opponents you're going to have to face, and they are unquestionably more experienced than you... and have better gear. Even worse, they'll be up against you at any power level. So the only way to really mitigate this is to keep your vehicle's power level down. Keep it under 4000, ideally. Keep it under 3000 if you can! You'll have a more enjoyable experience if you don't end up going against the biggest and strongest... and once you pass 5000 rating, you're in the deep end.
Fourth: Not
in the game is on the Market. Most of the core components - the car fragments that you put together to put everything into one functional death machine - aren't available through any method other than knuckling down, playing the game, and leveling up the various factions. You can't throw money at them. Level 10 isn't some end of the game, as some of the reviewers are saying - it's the
of learning how to really play the game. There's a lot of variety in components out there to be had, but some of the best parts are buried deep in the faction trees. And that requires playing lots and lots of games. Thankfully, most PvP fights are short (3 minutes per game, plus loading and unloading time).
Fifth: The cars that are available in the real-money shop are
. Let's make that clear right now. If you buy one and go out in it, you will be shot and killed fairly quickly, because they're meant for looks, not sustainability. Terra Nova: Strike Force Centauri is a mech-action game by the now famous Looking Glass Studios. Much like many of their other games, this one got overlooked at release, but unlike their other non-sports or flight-sims, this one never really did seem to have garnered a huge cult following.
I went into Terra Nova with very little knowledge about the game. Before I got it on steam, I had only seen the box for this game, and never played it, or watched any videos from it. So there are no nostalgia goggles going on here.
Terra Nova was released in 1996, and you can tell that it's an old game by just looking at it. The graphics look pixelated, the FMVs look poorly compressed and are in many cases shown in a smaller window. Many objects are also 2D sprites despite the game being a 3D game.
With that being said, the developers did a really good job working with what they had. The environments feel big, and despite how pixelated things are, it's never hard to tell what things are supposed to be. They also made good use of simple effects in order to convey different conditions, far more so than any contemporary game I can think of. While the game looks old, it does not feel old, if that makes any sense.
The sound is a bit of a mixed bag. Some of the tunes that play are good, but some clearly needed better hardware. Most weapons have convincing sound effects, and the voice clips from the different characters come through clear (even if the voice acting is not always good).
The game does some neat things to make things more believable. For an example, during a thunderstorm, there's a delay between you seeing the flash, and hearing the sound. It's a tiny detail, but it does help build immersion.
In the future humanity has managed to colonize the solar system. Earth decides that it wants to rule the entire solar system, but your group don't want to be ruled by anyone. So they're allowed to leave, and colonize another system. Now earth is once again showing interest in your land, and you're forced to fight the invading earth forces.
There are hints of a really interesting universe in this game, but sadly the setting feels underdeveloped. Had they spent more time fleshing out the game world, the story & setting might actually have been something memorable. It's still better than that of most action games, in particular of the era, but there's so much room for more.
Also, there's one huge inconsistency. How large are your mech suits (or Power Battle Armour (PBA) as they're known in game). In the cutscenes they look like they're about 2-2.5m, but in game you tower over trees and when standing next to a house, they look to be at least 2 stories tall.
For a game released in 1996, Terra Nova feels surprisingly modern. The game uses a form of proto-WASD controls, which are easy to get used to if you've played any modern shooter. There's no mouse look, but that's in part due to you having to use your mouse to manipulate different systems in your suit, and there's at least mouse aiming.
The suits are a versatile and agile lot. There are 3 kinds of suits, light, medium and heavy, and they do what you would expect. The light suits can only have 2 weapons equipped at once (or 1 big weapon), and has far less armour, but  moves faster. The medium & heavy suit can both equip 4 weapons (big weapons take 2 slots), and there are weapons that only the heavy suit can equip. The medium suit is of course faster but less well armoured. All suits are equipped with jumpjets, allowing you to fly several times your height up into the air. There are also plenty of other equipment that you get to use through the game, giving both replay value and variety between the missions.
You also have a squad of up to 3 more members that you sometimes need for different tasks, but often just acts as a bunch of extra guns that can help you out in combat. You can give orders to the squad, but most of the time they behave in a semi-intelligent way. Just don't give them powerful weapons that deal area damage, that's a surefire way of getting killed, or having them kill each other. They're also not very good at self-preservation, but for most missions, losing squad members is not a big issue, they'll be back for the next one with no harm done to them.
Just how good Terra Nova: Strike Force Centauri came as a bit of a surprise to me. While I knew that Looking Glass has a good track record with making games, I did not expect this one to have held up this well. The controls feel surprisingly modern and smooth, and the action is fast paced, but never mindless. There's a good amount of variety between the missions, and the fact that you can bring your own loadout for most missions also makes for some great replay value.
There are also plenty of details in here that makes the game very immersive. This game beats most modern action games in this regard, but considering it was Looking Glass who made it, that should come as no surprise, almost all of their games were great in this regard.
That's not to say that the game is perfect. Sometimes the lack of self preservation among squadmates can force you to restart missions, and the game is both short (in game time after my first playthrough said 2:41:38, but that does not count cutscenes), and relatively easy. Still, the good absolutely outweighs the bad, and the game comes highly recommended.

18-09-2016: Updated review after second playthrough: added some lines, fixed a few errors.
This review does not go into details of how the game works, nor does it mention everything. It only broadly explains what you can expect when playing it.
So, one would hear about this game, and would at first glance think: Well, this game looks interesting, let's give it a try, right? It's made by Looking Glass after all! (sounds a whole lot like me ;)
And then you play it. Holy crap, this game is amazing. Complexity unlike i've ever seen before, to the point that I have learned so much to fill a whole game at my second playthrough alone. one of the best soundtracks i've ever heard (albeit pretty biased), a story that starts very cheesy but then keeps punching you in the face with plot-twists and the gameplay is nothing short of excellent either.
About the story, do your research (in-game), or you won't understand much of it. I highly recommend you to read all of the information they give you between each mission, and before the story really starts, no matter how long it takes. Playing this game without a good understanding of the storyline just takes too much away from the attractiveness of the campaign.
Weapons and equipment that felt useless at the default difficulty setting suddendly become much more important at higher difficulty settings, which keeps the game fresh for at least a second playthrough, although you're still going to stay fairly close to your preferred setup.
Oh yeah, this game is NOT easy, expect to die a lot while you refine your strategies and personal skills.
Talking about setups, this game provides a ton of possibilites to prepare and plan your strategy before, and during each mission, by allowing you to choose your squad members (should i pick a repair or electronics, etc. expert on this mission?), their equipment pieces of equipment, decide in which way they handle combat situations and what they should follow.
This brings us to your squad members. Depending on the orders you give them, they can work greatly to your advantage or get themselves killed in seconds. Per example, "Cautious attack" isn't a "Only attack when it's relatively safe", it's a "Always attack, but through the safest route possible". You can guess, taking the "safest route" to a massive squad of enemies is still going to get them killed very quickly.
So, you take the next option in the list, "Take cover". While this works excellent to keep your squad alive at all times, If your squad spots an enemy just once, and that person doesn't come towards you but runs instead, they will stay at their nearest cover forever. So you walk towards your enemy to engage in combat and wonder where you squad is, to die on your own shortly after.
These are good examples of how good and bad strategies can unfold, and why it's important to be flexible and change your strategy in the middle of a mission, or in combat even. This important decision-making at all times and getting your carefully planned strategy to work (imo) is biggest charm of the game, and is one of the biggest factors to this game's high replay value.
Sounds awesome right, a game with absolutely no flaws! ...Well, even though i would love to say this, there are some tiny nitpicky things i have to mention. The videos sometimes don't play, but a simple reboot (or pressing alt + enter to switch to windowed mode) of the game fixes this 4 out of 5 times.
Afterwards, you start a mission, but i screwed up and i want to retry. Maybe i still need to get used to the quite clunky controls yet (which feel surprisingly natural, but still difficult if you're willing to learn them). But I haven't read this game's 46 page manual to find out where the pause button is (this is mentioned no-where else). Aaaaand, i ran out of explosives to kill myself. So i shoot my teammates excessively, and they call me a traitor and kill me.
...Wait a minute, i can do that? How much attention for detail does this game actually have? I am supposed to talk about the negatives now but i can't even stop myself from noticing even more good points of this game! This should really tell you enough, JUST BUY IT!

Terra Nova: Strike Force Centauri was an immeasurably revolutionary computer game released in 1996.
Terra Nova established the outdoor first person shooter genre with extreme render distances and advanced physics modelling including gravity simulation, water reflections, player movement systems, and weather conditions. Terra Nova also pioneered and perfected squad commanding in an fps environment, with competent, realistic bots. The squad members performed the player’s exact commands, ranging from movement options, tactics, engagement techniques, and special abilities. Terra Nova even pioneered exosuit simulators, inspiring the Tribe series of fps’s. It is a very technical simulation, with the missions requiring strategic planning, in outfitting the squad with weapons, suits, pilots, and, “alternative suit functions.” Alternate Suit Functions, or A.S.F.’s, permitted an operator to perform an ability, including deploying sentry turrets, additional suit shields, demolition explosives, power plants, repair modules, cloaking, and other abilities. On most missions, the player had to rely on the bots to perform tasks for the player, either defending a structure, destroying enemy fortifications, and scouting. The player managed all of these tasks via three multi-function displays, similarly to an aerospace fighter jet. The player had access to a powerful and immersive mapping program, drones, damage outputs, and A.S.F. controls. The player also had access to jump jets. Jump jets were integral to gameplay, allowing for mountains to be scaled with ease and impossible maneuvers to be performed.
Due to Terra Nova having been released on the Microsoft Disk Operating System in 1996, months before ID Games released Quake, technical limitations exist. Terra Nova runs off of a modified version of the System Shock engine, based off of the Ultima UnderWorld engine. To accommodate the long render distances, only a limited area around the player is texture mapped. For extreme distances, voxel rendering was utilized. Because of this conglomerate of rendering techniques, the resolution is limited to 320 by 400 pixels. Based off of the System Shock engine, Terra Nova also inherits System Shock’s controls, lacking mouse look. Due to poor popularity, few mods exist for this game. Joerg Fischer, now a German neuroscientist, wrote a famous mod for Terra Nova known as Operation Stonehenge, available at Rich Nagel’s website. Upon inspecting Steam’s Terra Nova game files, it was observed that Night Dive Studios hadn’t even bothered to extract the game files from the ISO copy of the disc. If anyone intends to modify Terra Nova, the disc’s contents must be extracted. Also notable is the use of DOS4GW instead of DOS32A in the Disk Operating System Emulator, limiting the maximum performance and speed of Terra Nova.
Terra Nova was and is an extremely accurate and enjoyable exosuit simulator. The game had the reputed Seamus Blackley as the lead physics programmer, responsible for dozens of flight simulators, including Flight Unlimited, and was originally planned to be part of the Starship Troopers franchise, hence why the player and his or her squad began each mission by falling from the sky. The character models were based off of a dynamically animated skeleton with bipedal physics simulations that outclass current fps’ movement systems. Similarly to System Shock, Greg LoPiccolo composed and programmed the soundtrack to dynamically react to the player’s status. It was Paul Neurath’s dream, the director of Looking Glass, the team of programmers, artists, and designers responsible for Deus Ex, System Shock 2, Terra Nova, System Shock, Thief, and Ultima UnderWorld. Unfortunately, like their previous titles, Terra Nova received critical acclaim and no popularity. The company went bankrupt and was summarily purchased by Ion Storm. The highly experienced team proceeded to develop the highly regarded Deus Ex and System Shock 2 games. After Ion Storm’s breakup, the Looking Glass team was divided amongst many current developers, with some now returning under Paul Neurath’s new company, OtherSide Entertainment. With the rights to System Shock finally having been purchased by Night Dive Studios, work on remaking System Shock and developing System Shock 3 has finally commenced. If anyone recalls the final scene from System Shock involving TetraCorp, a new Terra Nova might be coming out within the next few years.
