Do you like rednecks? Midgets? Psychotic people? How about the color brown?
Do you really like to shoot things too?
In that case, have I got a game for you.
The pinnacle of almost-good games, and winner of over a hundred "Best Sand of the Year" awards! Borderlands!
What else could combine all the great aspects of rednecks and sand quite like Borderlands? And not only that, it's a pretty decent co-op FPS-RPG. Imagine your favorite shooting game, but when you shoot things numbers fly out. Yup, that's Borderlands. It takes all of your favorite RPG elements and incorporates them into a shooty-killy. Now there's numbers, fetch quests, you gotta level up, fetch quests, kill thing quests, fetch quests. Oh yeah, and midgets.
There's a great treasure somewhere on the brownest planet in the galaxy, and it's up to you to find it. Do you have what it takes to run back and forth across an alien wasteland over and over?
There's a lot done right in Borderlands. And a lot done wrong. Quite a bit done wrong, actually.
There's a lot of sand in this game.
Borderlands is a very special kind of game.
At its best points, it's an incredibly addictive shooter with an interesting loot system. Get your mission from a redneck that wants you to fix something that's wrecked "as bad as his momma's girl parts". Go out into the desert, shoot a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥-face alien dogs. Blast its face off, and watch as a magical rainbow of lights explodes from the bloody stump where its head was. The lights are new guns that have appeared like magic, and you get to take all of them. Maybe one has bullets that explode on contact. Maybe one will melt faces off. Maybe one has a funny name. There's all kinds.
You'll go back and get your reward for completing your mission, use your newly earned cash to buy some new equipment, maybe level up. Learn to melt faces with your hands or something.
But as you set off on your next mission, you'll find that it's more of the same. Different part of the desert, different things to shoot, different redneck to help. But ultimately the same as what you'd already done.
The desert never goes anywhere. You might find a cave, or a run-down building to explore. But there's never anything except brown. Which is actually pretty sad.
Using a lot of browns and greys is incredibly common for your average AAA shooter. But none of those have the level of style and charm that Borderlands does.
Borderlands is a heavily stylized, charming game. The graphics are beautiful, at least until you realize that they're the only graphics in the whole game.
The world that it fleshes out looks like a massive brown turd, but it's the prettiest and most stylish turd you've ever seen.
It's a shame that an art style so good is wasted on the repetitive and dull world that you're given. Not to mention how often you'll need to run back and forth across said lifeless desert.
At points, the map is so big that you'll NEED a vehicle. Which IS usually provided. But if it gets blown up mid-quest, you'll be stranded in the middle of nowhere with a very long and dull trek back to civilization.
And getting stranded is gonna be a really common thing too, with how often you'll be running back and forth for the near endless amount of fetch quests.
Borderlands got a few things right with the RPG mechanics. You have different classes to choose from, each with a couple different skill trees to develop. And the loot system is incredibly fun, and yet a little poorly balanced. I kept one specific gun throughout much of the game just because it could just kill things faster than most higher level guns. It's easy to find one really good gun amongst a ton of crappy common guns and just keep it even while underleveled. Most of the loot you usually get is absolute trash, but it's still fun to pick up a bunch of guns and look through them for anything better than what you have.
Guns can have quite a bit of features to differentiate them. Different scopes, fire rates, reload times, even elemental powers. You can have a shotgun that causes things to burst in flames. Or a machine gun that melts things with acid.
These are some of the things that make Borderlands such an almost-good game.
And then there's all of those things that make it such an almost-bad game. Like repetitive quests that take place in visually identical areas that are supposed to be different.
If there's anything that can redeem it for its poorly executed take on a great concept, its definitely the game's general style and sense of humor.
Dialogue is never dull. Characters are always interesting. The humor, while often incredibly dark or raunchy, is always bountiful. The plot itself isn't anything special in the slightest, and is more predictable than watching bread. But at least the journey is decently entertaining.
If you can immerse yourself in the world of Borderlands, you might just be able to enjoy it. Its co-op features are pretty nice, allowing you to tackle missions together. Let's start on a positive note: Hero Siege is a great, time-killing Roguelike/RPG with a load of potential.
Now for the downsides: No tutorial, a desolate hub, an
amount of bugs that range from minor to game-breaking, an even buggier multiplayer and way, way too many DLCs.
To start, you are thrown into the hub with no idea what the heck is going on. You have to figure out the (non-customizable) controls, and on curiosity, talk to the locals. None of them have anything interesting to say or do, barring Jack the Ripper (who is the one buying your useless crap), some monk in the far corner who wants "prime evil" (primeval?) artifacts, a guy who will give you "excess wool" for an insane amount (5000 crystals!!) and the Sarcaster, whom asks if you want to join his coffee club. At least the last one nets an achievement, although he still asks you to join again, and has no response regardless. This has to be the most depressing and confusing hub I've ever seen.
While there are common exploits in the game (such as the dungeon-hub tp farm), I immediately noticed an issue where monsters and chests would spawn outside (or even within) the boundary walls. On top of this, a plethora of bugs exist in multiplayer. I was quick to notice the insane lag right off the bat, since it resulted in instantly killing me on several occasions, and was several seconds behind in dungeons. On top of this, the dungeon-farm exploit still works, but only for the host player. As the server player, I found myself in an empty version of the overworld, and would teleport around on the host's screen. If I touched the theoretical spot that the ladder would be, it would teleport me out. Another issue I found was having a negative wave count, which instantly spawned the boss and carried on until the next act.
Finally, after beating the game's first four acts on however many difficulties I choose, I find that there's already four (FOUR!) DLC packs, three of which grant additional acts and characters, and one of which just grants a character. Premium versions of these packs exist, and you have to RE-PURCHASE the whole thing to get the premium bonuses (which sucks for early-access players like me, since we got the first DLC in base form). Each regular pack is $3.49, and the premium are a whopping $5.49; compared to the base cost of the game ($11.99, I believe), you certainly aren't getting your money's worth.
In all, I haven't seen much change in the way of bugs or broken mechanics since I bought the game back when it first came out. I thought this game had some real charm, but if you're going to buy it, do it for the offline base-game. Honestly, you'd be better off spending your cash on a game like
or
. Both bring the retro charm this game presents, without the hassle of broken mechanics and crappy dlc expansions. Not to mention, they actually have lore.

This is a worthy successor of Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing. It improves on it and is currently the best competitor for Mario Kart. It may be a little inferior to the Nintendo kart racing, but it's still an awesome game for this genre. Plus, Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed isn't a Nintendo exclusive. Like the title implies, this time around you race in 3 vehicle types: car, boat and plane. And you'll frequently change between these vehicles during the same race. The car plays almost the same as the original title, which focuses on gaining extra speed through drifting and boosting. The car is stable and easy to control. You can also drift and boost on boats and planes, but the boat sections are more focused on hitting ramps to perform stunts to earn boosts and the plane sections are more focused on hitting boost panels in a more straight line, while also evading the course obstacles to get extra boosts. The boat is harder to maneuver because of the water waves and because it's harder to turn. The plane is more straightforward, with the added verticality to control. But sometimes it can be a little stiff, especially during sharp turns. But overall, the vehicle switch mechanic is fluid and the physics are great for all of them. The carrer mode is essentially the same as the previous title. World tour to me felt like the original mission mode, but more organized with added unlockables. Gran prix is just that, a series of 4 races awarding points in each race based on the final position. But this time you can't restart in the middle of it, and that's how it should be to me. Time trials are the same, but this time with added leaderboards. And of course, there's single race. The game is also way harder than the original, and the expert difficulty is hard, with some events being very hard, like some of the time trial ghosts. But it's doable with some practice, and as you play and experiment you'll get better. There's also online mode, which isn't quite dead yet, but i didn't spent much time on it. The character and track selection is also better than the original. While some characters were removed, there's plenty of new ones. Some are from the same game as others, some from other SEGA titles, some 3rd party ones (e.g. Team Fortress), and even a real life rally racer that here drives a Hot-Wheels on land. This selection feels better and more diverse, even with the removed characters. The tracks are also cooler. There's only 16 tracks (not counting 4 returning ones), but they are more diverse, longer and change mid-race, so the 3 laps aren't always the same. Added with the vehicle switch and good design for the most part, these tracks are a blast to play on. They are also beautiful as well as the graphics, a real eye candy. The soundtrack is also cool. This time the tracks are arrangements instead of ripped songs, and they work pretty well (i love the Golden Axe arrangement on Adder's Lair, as well as this course). If you like kart racing games, this is an easy recommendation, even if you think that you may like it. It may take some time for beginners to get good, but it's definitely worth it.

So I picked this up on a whim, because I was bored and then Youtube happened, and... ahh, it's like I've been transported back well over a decade into the past.  Back to a time in gaming that I personally thought was pretty darn great.  Had been a few years since I last really played this, but it's amazing how it all comes back...
I doubt I need to explain what Wolfenstein 3D is, really.  Pretty much everyone seems to have at least heard of it, and it's role in shaping the industry.  This game was a really, really major thing back then, and it paved the way for Doom, which was an even bigger thing.
But what does it play like?  Compared to modern FPS games, well... there's not much here.  This is an OLD game.  Really old.  I mean, this is back from an era where many people still had game sounds coming out of their PC speakers (do any PCs even HAVE those anymore?).  Back when things like Sound Blaster or America Online were big things. Back when all mice were "ball mice".  Kinda glad THOSE werent around.  Used to have to clean the stupid things by stabbing the internal bits with my car key.  Computers of that time could only do so much, and with a genre that had only just started.  And that does show here.
Firstly:  The controls on this game. AWKWARD.  This is something I never really noticed back then, and that's because nobody had really come up with anything better yet.  I honestly dont even remember if the original version of this game had mouse support.  I really dont.  I remember that *I* used just the keyboard.  That's right. JUST the keyboard.  That's how old this is.  And it shows, because there's some very weird things going on with these controls.  Firstly, while you can remap controls, they still wont work quite like you want.  You have a key that you hold to run of course, but you ALSO have a key that needs to be held in order to strafe at all.  While you are strafing, you cannot TURN, because you're using the turn keys to strafe.  This can make things really, really awkward as you move around.
Fortunately there's a way around this:  Look for something called ECWolf, using Google.  It's not a free copy of the game or anything, you greedy snot.  It's something that uses an already existing copy of the game, and adds some "quality of life" features to make it better.  Most important, it lets you fix the controls to be non-awkward.  It also allows you to use a minimap.  That's right, this game didnt have one.  And I know, there's those out there that'd say it "ruins the challenge" to use one.  I say:  No.  Wandering around in areas you've already beaten, over and over and over again, while wallowing in extreme tedium is not "challenge".   Seriously.  Get the minimap.  It'll make your whole experience better, and it WONT ruin the challenge.
And the game definitely has alot of challenge to offer you.   There are not all that many enemy types in the game (particularly in the first episode, as that episode also made up the demo version of the game, so only 3 enemy types appear in there), this is true.  But they all tend to hit like freight trains.  Even the absolute most basic soldier can chop off over 50% of your HP if he gets a hit on you up close. And that's with a pistol!  The closer the enemy is, the higher the damage they'll do to you.  And of course, the more accurate they'll be.  And these enemies arent flinging fireballs and actual "projectiles" at you like in Doom.  These enemies are all using proper guns, which means hitscan attacks.  So once they fire, if their aim is true, you WILL get hit, as you'd expect.  So unlike Doom, just running through like a maniac is likely to get you flattened.  The game does a very good job of creating a challenge though without making it feel TOO hard.  And you have four difficulty settings to choose from.
One defining feature of this game though is the levels.  These places are true labyrinths in every sense of the word.  Doom's levels were never this confusing.  Loops and dead-ends EVERYWHERE.  And secrets?  Oh yes.  There are secrets.  Despite that ALL secret doors work the same way... they look like a normal wall, but when you hit "use" on them they move backwards about 3 tiles or so... they can be amazingly hard to find.  There tends to be alot of them, and the game absolutely will do things like have one secret room that you find, which then has another secret room in it, which then has a third, which leads to a small maze with doors and rooms and things, one of which has another secret room, which has another secret room, and then your head bursts all over the ceiling.  It does stuff like this alot.
While that can be pretty interesting, one thing of note is the game's items.  This isnt Doom where there's all these different powerups and armor and lots of weapons.   There are FOUR weapons... two of which you start with...  and no powerups, no armor.  There are healing items, 1-ups (rare), and treasure.  Treasure increases your score... yes, this game has a scoring system... and counts towards the tally at the end of the stage.  MANY secrets will lead just to treasure.  This game was designed back in a time when scoring systems in games were still a major thing, and when players would go out of their way to get the 10000 points that an extra area might offer.  Because they want the damn points, that's why.   That sort of thing is starting to become more popular again recently, but some players wont really have played any games like that.  And if you dont like things like that, you're likely to find alot of secrets and bonus areas to be, well, not at all satisfying.  But if you're like me, always trying to get scores as high as can be, you'll find alot to search for here.
Though I've always wondered just WHERE good ol BJ stashes the hundreds of crowns and treasure chests that he picks up along the way.
And all of those things pretty much sum up the actual gameplay mechanics nicely.  Everything meshes well together, but be warned that the game can be repetitive.  LOTS of games are like that of course, but for some this one may be a bit too much in that way.  If that's an issue for you, this is not the game for you.  Also, if you need a big story, and talky bits to make a game interesting for you.... this REALLY isnt the game for you.  The story can be summed up like "You're in this castle, built by maniacs.  Run through mazes and shoot evil Nazi jerks.  Find Hitler, who has a mech suit for some reason, and kill him.  Also kill some other bosses, because bosses. Thus the world is saved. The end!"  And that's all there is to the story.  You never even get to find out where he got that mech suit.  What a cliffhanger.
With 60 levels, this is a LONG game.  There are 6 "episodes", with each episode having 9 normal levels, a boss fight, and one secret level (one of which is very unique... you'll know it if you find it).
If you can handle the simplicity and repetition, if you like finding treasure and doing battle against endless waves of evil enemies, finding secrets, exploring... Wolfenstein 3D is a true classic, and should be played through at least once.

I just can't recommend this game. It sounded fun, and the first few bosses weren't bad. They were enjoyable as you died a couple of times, figured out the goal, and then killed the boss.
Later, the bosses aren't fun. They are tedious. Sometimes, you know almost instantly how to kill the boss. However, the hitbox may be tiny, or may move really quickly. It becomes a crapshoot, and you just keep firing arrows around the hitbox, hoping that it hits the spot. Even when I knew what to do, I didn't think it would work until, eventually, it magically hit the target.
Sometimes, the bosses are fun enough to figure out. You finally expose the weak point and take aim... and then the boss recovers within a second or two. This actually encourages you not to aim at all. As soon as the weak point is visible, you let off an arrow asap and pray it hits the flashing mass.
The bosses are fast. Sometimes while dashing or running, you get pegged with a projectile or stepped on. It doesn't seem  fair, because you knew it was coming. You thought the timing of your dodge was spot on, yet you watch as your bloody body sails across the floor.
Finally, there are the poorly placed respawn points. You'd think that walking 5-15 seconds to a boss room wouldn't be a big deal. But when the fights often only last a second or two, especially when you are first learning how a boss moves, that 5-15 seconds gets really old, really fast. In the forest area especially, in the course of 5 minutes, you might only spend 20 seconds fighting a boss, and 4 minutes and 40 seconds walking back to the boss each time you die.

Age of Empires 2 is one of the most popular strategy games ever made, thanks to its large variety in civilisations, units, and tactics that suit many play styles. While this Steam release added some unwarranted bugs and issues, its expansion packs and ease-of-use mod support can make it a great edition for newcomers.
The original Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings and its expansion disk, The Conquerors, remain one of the highest-rated real-time strategies of all time. They feature mechanics that are easy to grasp but takes years to master, and many unique civilisations to choose from—even if all of them share a certain common unit and technology pool.
This variety can easily help anyone to practise different play styles (from slow turtle-like base-building to aggressive rushes) on the game’s several campaign missions and dozens of randomly generated map types, offering nearly limitless replay value even in single-player, let alone in the busy multiplayer scene.
The game proved so popular over the years that eventually a group of fans decided to take over its post-release development, which resulted in this HD edition, where the main feature is its strong Steam integration.
This base game in itself offers little compared to the fan-made free UserPatch (created for the original version). I would still consider AoE2HD the better single-player experience for a newcomer, thanks to some of the small user interface tweaks and many of the gorgeous Workshop graphical mods. However, we have to admit that the game’s real strength lies in its DLCs that add some new and interesting content (and in the multiplayer, but that is out of the scope of this review).

This game was another great entry into the "Tales" series. The art-style was increadible, the story telling was superb, the action was amusing, and the humor was hilarious.
The first chapter did a great job at introducing you to the two protagonists by allowing them each to interpret their own part of the story. Switching between characters did end up disrupting my routine when I finally got into character- but it turns out that's not a bad thing. Having two sides  to the story allowed for the feeling of more variety when many of your choices seem to be rather mundane during the slow moments. It also allowed Tell-tale to throw in more action packed scenes and humerous side characters. I found that the story was quite humerous at times and had me laughing late into the night where I fear I may have disturbed my roomates. Many times, I found the side characters were the best part and far more entertaining than any dialog option I was left to answer with. In addition, each episode increased the series excitement, decision making, and humor at an exponential rate.
My only complaint was that when the two story lines for the protagonists merged together, it seems it favored Fiona's story telling. I would have enjoyed getting to play Rhys more. In addition, occasionally I would answer as Rhys only to find out it was Fiona's response. Also, some of the characters appeared for very short rolls and were quickly forgotten until the last episode when we were reminded they could join our team. It would have been nice if these characters were included more in the subsequent episodes prior to the big finale. There were also some extremely important decisions made in the last episode - yet it occured right at the end so there was no potential for it to have an impact on future events. I just hope that's indicative of a sequal since I would love to see that concluded in a future release.

I grew up on the Twisted Metal games. To me, that series pioneered the car combat genre. So when I first saw Crossout on the Steam store over a year ago, I had been eagerly awaiting a chance to play it ever since -- and possibly relive some of the most memorable games of my childhood in the process.
The combat in Crossout is fun as hell, and speaks to the developer's years of experience making car combat games. Not only that, but I was taken away by the creativity allowed with the game's building system. It reminded me of the early days of RoboCraft. The great feeling of building your own vehicular death machine and iterating upon it further after every new unlock is something Crossout has nailed. Clearly one of the best implemented systems this genre has offered.
However, the fun factor rapidly deminishes after a while. Specifically, when you realize you have to grind endless 4-minute matches for meager amounts of Scrap as a reward so you could then have x100 Scrap to sell on the Market in the hopes of affording a better weapon. When you start from nothing like I did as a humble free-to-play, the grind seems daunting and here's why:
Normally, I would expect the game have you craft your new weapons with Scrap, Copper, Wire, and parts from which then you could keep or sell. Unfortunately, using the crafting system to acquire these weapons is hopelessly redundant in a broken economy. You're better off buying your new weapon from Scrap sales and avoid crafting like the plague. With the new Knight Riders event, the in-game economy has collapsed and has made little room for coin profits besides selling Scrap, Wires, and Fuel.
Raiding is fun, but also redundant. The rewards you get from raiding is not worth the price of admission. It takes 20-40 Fuel per raid mission, and at the end of it you receive 5 Copper if you do well. If your team fails, you get nothing. Copper is required for crafting, and right now crafting is not profitable. See the problem?
TL;DR: It's a good game and is well worth a few hours of your time. Don't plan on sticking around if you don't have deep pockets, however. After level 10, you are pretty much required to fork over your hard-earned shekels for a new weapon to stay competitive or endlessly farm Scrap in order to afford one in this current game economy.

(a megabot is a bot which has more parts attached to it than a normal bot has, giving them a lot of armour and a lot of weapons)
They were readded, but back then, they were a horrible mess in elimination (back the named team death match).
In every match your team HAD to follow the mega, meaning if you don't, it would have meant that you would do horribly if you were alone. Because of "hug the mega" all medics were ONLY around the megabot, which caused problems like if you were disabled because you lost all movement parts, you are unable to help your team. Then again if you ask a medic to go all the way to help you back up if you survived a conflict(there was no regeneration), there will be 1 less person to help out the team which is with the mega.
Another problem can be caused by the megabot itself.
There sometimes were megabots, which did not have any movement parts and spend all the time being in spawn, which made the team stay with it, which ended being surrounded by the enemy. There were also times were the megabot only had 2-4 weapons equipped (a good megabot normally had 7 weapons) which got disarmed very fast and often meaning that the game was lost/won before start.
In addition, there was a pilot seat (destroying it will destroy the entire bot) which could have been very poorly protected causing a mega to die faster, then the other.
A megabot simply carried a huge weight, on which the entire team depended on and if the megabot made a mistake everyone in the team had to suffer from it.

A lot of my gameplay so far has consisted of:
Getting stuck in a bulldozer on a 1 inch high lump of dirt
Getting stuck in a front end loader in a quarter foot deep hole
Getting stuck on foot on a 1 inch diameter power cable
Getting stuck in a 4x4 pick up truck with the diff lock on EVERY F#$@$NG time I drive out of old arnold parcel on a small rock
And countless other bugs...
BUT...
What I've seen is a genuinely half decent EARLY ALPHA RELEASE.
Don't go buying this yet expecting smooth gameplay, because it is still as rough as a badgers ring piece.
Gold panning at the start of your gold mining quest is mind destroyingly boring... six or seven hours of my gameplay time was taken up with hand shovelling then panning dirt to get minor amount of gold (asides from one big chunk put in to help you along to the next tier of mining... as a bit of an OCD completionist I kept going until there was no dirt in the panning area).
However once I had a decent amount of gold I moved on to tier two where the game finally takes shape and it truly gets fun.
I love having a good old fart around with the excavator digging deep and steadily filling up those gold buckets, it must have something to do with digging holes with toy diggers when your a kid that makes it pretty addictive although repetitive beyond belief... hopefully after a while a few more features will be brought in to change things up a bit and keep it interesting, as at the minute the only drive is to get enough cash to buy the bigger equipment... I fear this could be the downfall for the game if it hits the point where you have everything and have no more incentive to keep digging.
The attention to detail is great in terms of setting everything up such as water pumps and generators. The cabling is good as it forces you to think more about how you set up your dig site instead of snapping everything in place (although at tier 3 you have to, as the equipment is huge in comparison to tier 2) but it's SOOOOOOO time consuming although I don't see much of a way around it and I wouldn't really want a solution as it would take something away from the simulation experience.
I've not gone too in depth into tier 3 yet as I have heard it's buggy as hell at the moment and i dont want to risk having to restart my save so ill not comment on that part yet.
So far it's not horrendously bad... I've seen the game getting a bad rap in a lot of reviews...
I've heard a lot about bad bugging and honestly I've not had major trouble... the getting stuck thing is remedied with clicking reset on the map... it's still bloody annoying having to mess around that every ten minutes though.
Is it worth fifteen odd quid? Questionable... it's definitely not really worth the price tag right at the minute but If the developers keep up with the free DLC and iron out the teething problems I think it's definitely a winner with more care and thought.
One word: AUTOSAVE!!!!!!!!!!!! (Needed ASAP)
This game isn't recommended to anyone who just wants to jump in and get on with it straight away... it's buggy laggy and somewhat annoying to play at times but I really want to to work out!
Well done to the developers so far... please keep up the good work and don't let this game not get the hard work it deserves as it's potential is HUGE!!!
Watch some YouTube videos (graystillplays just to mention one channel) and see what you think... so far I recommend it if you're willing to take it on warts and all.
As the bugs get ironed out and updates come in, I'll edit my review either positive or negative depending on what happens

Okay, I've almost got 30 hours into the game at this point and the date is 03/05/2015. I want to say a few things first off. If you watched DBZ when you were a kid this game is just for you. If you have never watched the show you will probably like the game because of how fast and chaotic the controls are. So here are my pros!
- Tight controls, it feels super great to move.
- Power... This game makes you feel super strong at some points and very weak at others.
- Battles are super cool.
- There are many combinations of Supers and Ultimates that you can obtain. Getting them is half the fun because after you toil and fight for so long and you get the attack you wanted it really felt like training.
- The clothing options are cool. Chances are that you will see someone with clothes that look similar to yours but this isn't really innacurate. I mean, if you wear clothes in real life chances are that you saw someone with clothing similar to yours. If you're a nudist then.. well Idk.
- The Character creator is cool. There aren't very many options so far, but I'm sure that they'll do some updates on it eventually. If not, you're gonna have a character that you imagined when you were seven.
- The missions are fun! I won't spoil anything.
- Multiplayer battles are cool. I mean, if you get 3v3 pretty strong characters in a map chances are that you will see some crazy stuff happening. The chaotic atmosphere is pleasing and if you win you really feel like a victor.
- Everything has loopholes; many attacks, supers, and ultimates have flaws for you to find an opening. Granted, you will have to be quick about your actions and careful about your approach.
- My favorite part is that some battles take a bit of strategy. For instance, my buddy and I fight together and we split up to take on separate enemies. We kind of have to plan to switch foes a few times and if we get overpowered its smart to call out that you are being beaten. Sometimes you can have your friend toss the enemy into a blast that you are doing or  hold the enemy in place so that you can ge in an ultimate. When I say hold the enemy in place I mean that he kind of keeps close combat so that the foe won't move from your blast.
- Finally, the story; it's pretty awesome. Putting your character in all of the big events of the Dragon Ball universe really takes you back if you were a fan of the show. For old fans, it's super nostalgic. For newcomers, it's pretty exciting to see a lot of characters grow. The only thing is (and this is for newcomers) You're gonna want some context. I suggest reading up on the events of the show, otherwise some things won't make sense to you.
Now for my cons.
- the servers are pretty bad. I have no idea if they will be updated soon or not. All I know is that they're really rough and you'll probably end up trying a few times to get into the multiplayer time nest thing.
- Super armor. When you become a high enough level or you get further into the story you will notice that some enemies will not flinch. You're gonna be like. "Dude... what?" and you'll probably get your face punched many times before you can power through the armor. You'll find out later that they had super armor on to increase the difficulty of the fight but all it really did was make you a punching bag to an un-flinchable foe. Of course, what they could have done was, instead of creating super armor, factor in new algorithms and fighting styles of characters who are meant to be like a "boss". For instance, you could have the enemy come at you harder and the hits to a bit more damage or maybe an instance where you really have to pay attention to what happens and decide when to block and when to attack. But instead... Super Armor... Which will literally just enrage you as long as you try to bust through it.
That is it for this review. The game is super great and It is worth the money! Go ahead and try it out.

TL:TR; one usage of the r-word. I almost stopped playing because of the ignorance of this remark in an otherwise good game, but I decided to give it a chance.
Short. Cheap (was on sale). Good story.
Occassionally tedious. Felt a bit clunky.
Puzzles boring.
Spoiler alert;
My thoughts on this game, considering I got it for such a cheap price, is that it's a genuinely good point-and-click. I loved the story and was pretty surprised by the ending. Maybe that's down to my poor skills in predicting predictable things, but overall I enjoyed it and found it gripping enough to play it in one day. I'm pretty tired of time-travel story lines as I almost always find loop-holes (why didn't he just do this or that?!) but despite it being purely about time-travel I liked the way it was executed. I like being able to control when I swap backwards and forwards in time, and it's really cool to see how each scene changes depending on what time you're in.
However, there are some things I wasn't too keen on. I've played quite a few point-and-clicks and the clicking sometimes felt pretty sluggish and as though I had to click several times before it would recognise the click. I'm REALLY glad you can run with double-click, if not it would have made the game slower than necessary.
Secondly, some tediousness. The example that springs to mind is having to get Frank a cup of water. Possibly down to my impatience, but I like running backwards and forwards for puzzles, not so much for errands.
Final note; I like the idea that video games can be inclusive. Throwing in one sentence which was along the lines of "she probably thinks I'm r-word" really ruined it. It added nothing and it's just made the creators look, at the very least, pretty ignorant. Please reconsider the usage of it in the future.
edit;
gosh the puzzles do need to be less straightforward or weird.
Why did I need a Katana for the rope to be cut?
Some of the puzzles were creative (soil/apple/tree) but other than that it was all too easy in places, but I didn't mind the easiness of the game as the art style is pleasant enough and the story is enjoyable.
6/10

Wolfenstein 3D is the grand daddy of First Person Shooter games, and here is why it deserves your respect:
1. It may not be the first FPS game, but it's the first FPS game with stealth elements.
2. You can mow down Nazis with a chaingun.
3. Hitler drives a mech in this game, and yes, you can kill him.
4. Every level is full of secrets and treasure to collect.
5. There are 60 levels in all.
6. This game is the predecessor to Doom AND Rise of the Triad.
7. Despite being a run-and-gun game mixed with a stealth action game, the whole experience is very balanced and paced.
8. There are Nazi zombies nearly 2 decades before Black Ops.
9. Two of the bosses are literally Hansel and Gretel.
10. There is a level with 179 secrets in it.
11. There is a Pac-Man level complete with ghosts.
12. The Nazis in this game speak real German.
13. There is a surprisng amount of strategy in everything from how you enter a room to whether or not you fire a gun at a door to alert the enemies on the other side.
14. If you buy this game there is a never ending supply of mods you can play- the roster rivals Half-Life and Doom 2.
15. If you are afraid of being left wanting more, there is the Spear of Destiny expansion pack also available on Steam which includes 22 new levels in the form of Spear of Destiny and 44 additional levels in the form of Challenge packs (which have entirely new graphics).
16. Call Apogee and say "Aardwolf"
If that's not enough to convince you, let me put it this way: the game is a fast-paced shoot-em-up where you use the enemies' awareness of your presence as well as distance and cover to your advantage.  Resource management becomes a real issue as you constantly seek health to survive encounters and ammo to cut through crowds.  If you run out of ammo, you can use your knife to take down an enemy for their ammo, but it might come at a price if they get a shot off while you're shivving them.  Exploring the Castle floors for secrets become a crucial part of survival, as well as remembering locations of supply stashes in case a firefight turns out particularly ugly.  Things can get so tense and feel so rewarding as you make your way from level to level.
Give it a try if you're able to stomach retro graphics.  It's a great gem from another age and there's a reason why older generations of gamers hold it in such reverence.
You need to be patient with this game at the beginning but it is definitely a game worth the patience

Do you like rednecks? Midgets? Psychotic people? How about the color brown?
Do you really like to shoot things too?
In that case, have I got a game for you.
The pinnacle of almost-good games, and winner of over a hundred "Best Sand of the Year" awards! Borderlands!
What else could combine all the great aspects of rednecks and sand quite like Borderlands? And not only that, it's a pretty decent co-op FPS-RPG. Imagine your favorite shooting game, but when you shoot things numbers fly out. Yup, that's Borderlands. It takes all of your favorite RPG elements and incorporates them into a shooty-killy. Now there's numbers, fetch quests, you gotta level up, fetch quests, kill thing quests, fetch quests. Oh yeah, and midgets.
There's a great treasure somewhere on the brownest planet in the galaxy, and it's up to you to find it. Do you have what it takes to run back and forth across an alien wasteland over and over?
There's a lot done right in Borderlands. And a lot done wrong. Quite a bit done wrong, actually.
There's a lot of sand in this game.
Borderlands is a very special kind of game.
At its best points, it's an incredibly addictive shooter with an interesting loot system. Get your mission from a redneck that wants you to fix something that's wrecked "as bad as his momma's girl parts". Go out into the desert, shoot a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥-face alien dogs. Blast its face off, and watch as a magical rainbow of lights explodes from the bloody stump where its head was. The lights are new guns that have appeared like magic, and you get to take all of them. Maybe one has bullets that explode on contact. Maybe one will melt faces off. Maybe one has a funny name. There's all kinds.
You'll go back and get your reward for completing your mission, use your newly earned cash to buy some new equipment, maybe level up. Learn to melt faces with your hands or something.
But as you set off on your next mission, you'll find that it's more of the same. Different part of the desert, different things to shoot, different redneck to help. But ultimately the same as what you'd already done.
The desert never goes anywhere. You might find a cave, or a run-down building to explore. But there's never anything except brown. Which is actually pretty sad.
Using a lot of browns and greys is incredibly common for your average AAA shooter. But none of those have the level of style and charm that Borderlands does.
Borderlands is a heavily stylized, charming game. The graphics are beautiful, at least until you realize that they're the only graphics in the whole game.
The world that it fleshes out looks like a massive brown turd, but it's the prettiest and most stylish turd you've ever seen.
It's a shame that an art style so good is wasted on the repetitive and dull world that you're given. Not to mention how often you'll need to run back and forth across said lifeless desert.
At points, the map is so big that you'll NEED a vehicle. Which IS usually provided. But if it gets blown up mid-quest, you'll be stranded in the middle of nowhere with a very long and dull trek back to civilization.
And getting stranded is gonna be a really common thing too, with how often you'll be running back and forth for the near endless amount of fetch quests.
Borderlands got a few things right with the RPG mechanics. You have different classes to choose from, each with a couple different skill trees to develop. And the loot system is incredibly fun, and yet a little poorly balanced. I kept one specific gun throughout much of the game just because it could just kill things faster than most higher level guns. It's easy to find one really good gun amongst a ton of crappy common guns and just keep it even while underleveled. Most of the loot you usually get is absolute trash, but it's still fun to pick up a bunch of guns and look through them for anything better than what you have.
Guns can have quite a bit of features to differentiate them. Different scopes, fire rates, reload times, even elemental powers. You can have a shotgun that causes things to burst in flames. Or a machine gun that melts things with acid.
These are some of the things that make Borderlands such an almost-good game.
And then there's all of those things that make it such an almost-bad game. Like repetitive quests that take place in visually identical areas that are supposed to be different.
If there's anything that can redeem it for its poorly executed take on a great concept, its definitely the game's general style and sense of humor.
Dialogue is never dull. Characters are always interesting. The humor, while often incredibly dark or raunchy, is always bountiful. The plot itself isn't anything special in the slightest, and is more predictable than watching bread. But at least the journey is decently entertaining.
If you can immerse yourself in the world of Borderlands, you might just be able to enjoy it. Its co-op features are pretty nice, allowing you to tackle missions together. And having friends always makes games better. The amount of content here is pretty massive, and the DLC packs also add even more to it. Including trees!
You really shouldn't have to pay extra to have trees in your games. But still, you can get a crazy circus stripper too. Who doesn't want more of those in their games? Those are worth paying extra for.
Like I said, it's an almost-good game, and an almost-bad game. At the same time. It definitely has its moments, but those moments could've been executed a lot better.
It's a game about rednecks and sand.
If you can be fine with a game about rednecks and sand, I think you'll be just fine.

Both my wife and I are avid fans of the platform genre. It stems from both of us being console gamers from the 80's. The harder the better and there is no shortage of aneurysm-inducing platform games on Steam. ESJ is a perfect example of platforming today. One of the key aspects of the genre should be tight controls and this game excels in that department. You will never complain about the dying because your jump was lagged, or the response time from your controller to the game was delayed by unnecessary animation.  You die because you screwed up, not the game and that feels both comforting and a little saddening. No excuses but bad gaming skills.
Controls are first and foremost for the genre. Everything else is window dressing and depending on your taste will add to the experience one way or the other. Fortunately, ESJ scores well in the other categories. Classic pixel graphics with a unique style are both fresh and satisfying for an old gamer like me. While I'm not a particular fan of electronica or techno music, the game's soundtrack by EnV nails it from the first beat. The music never feels repetitive and is perfect for the setting the mood of the game. The music says, "Hey, here's a tough as nails game, let's go get some!" You jump in and keep jumping because the beat keeps pushing you. Very well done and even worth purchasing the soundtrack.

This game is the post apocalyptic vehicular combat/building game I have always wanted, at the same time it also features many of the things I hate most about modern games...
If you loved the car combat games of the 90s and wanted something that captures the spirit and depth of them made for modern hardware, this is the closest thing I have found in years.
The handling itself is great, feeling realistic enough to pull off some satisfying stunts, but easy enough for new players to get a good feel of the cars very quickly.
It has an EXCELLENT building system in play so you can make almost any kind of land based vehicle you can imagine up.
The combat is very solid, in my opinion it feels very polished, rewarding and is very deep, letting you use countless amounts of different strategies in battle for example choosing whether to dismantle your opponents part by part, or attack their cabin directly and go for the kill, hoping that the parts still attached to their vehicles arent enough to tear you to shreds.
There is a great post apocalyptic atmosphere here, which goes perfectly hand in hand with the building mechanics, allowing you to weld all kinds of scrap parts that you obtain over time to almost any part of your vehicle.
The optimization, oh man the optimization is supurb. The game looks gorgeous, supports DX11 and will run on all kinds of systems at exceptional framerates for the things that are happening on the screen. Expect buttery smooth gameplay throughout the game... until.
...Latency.
The entire physics system in the multiplayer side of the game is processed server side, meaning that when you input a command on your mouse or keyboard, you dont see it happen until the server calculates your command and sends it back to you and to all other players. If you get put in a server with a crap ping, expect to sometimes not be able to take part in the entire battle, watching your car rubber band back and forth to you and not allowing you to do anything but looking like a total idiot to the rest of your team. I can't say if it's this bad in other parts of the world, but I am in Australia, running some of the fastest internet you can get here and as of yet there are no oceanic servers and it's incredibly frustrating to not be able to play the game that you really should be able to play.
If you test drive your vehicles in the garage sandbox area before joining a game, you notice a HUGE handling difference, and it really makes you wonder about the possibilites, such as racing modes and things like that, that would have been possible in this game had the developers chosen to let your actions happen realtime as the server updates and sees them like amost any other modern multiplayer game I have played.
It's also got some pretty decent AI, which I would have loved to see in some kind of single player story mode that lets you build the vehicle of your dreams without having to worry so much about power levels and server side lag.
So, I played and levelled up for a decent amount of time before reaching the point where you pick a second faction at level 10, and this is where the game started to make me a bit sad... You have to pay to rent benches to build new parts for these new factions. I dont mind paying to unlock these features perminently as it's a free game, but paying to RENT it is bad, just like when you sometimes get a loot crate after playing for hours, you get excited and then you open it to find a RARE PART, and by now your heart is racing as you read the description and then part of you dies when you see it only lasts for 2 hours...
...Really? If you are going to award players for playing your game with parts, then let us keep them? It's so pointless just making them disappear, especially when the game encourages you to let your imagination go wild.
I love this game, I really do and I still recommend it as there really is nothing else quite like it, but if you are going into this expecting to feel like the developers care about you, and want them to share the same passion you feel for the game and its unique and fun features, this isn't the game for you.

I'm a great fan of the Dragon Ball series, i've watched Dragon Ball Z as i grew up, and seeing a game that actually pulled it off making such a great fighting game of Dragon Ball Z after so many years with only somewhat decent ones(the old generation had it tough without any proper Dragon Ball  games)
Alright so let's get down to it. The game has a different story than most of the Dragon Ball Z Games, since it adds more history into the Dragon Ball Universe, the game also resembles a MMO, but of course, of a smaller scale, since most of the game is on history and battle/paralell mission parts, and the Multiplayer lobby is what it makes it look like MMO. In history mode you can play all Dragon Ball Z sagas with altered histories due to the power of a force unknown to you. There is also a secret saga, and some new sagas due to the time change. In battle mode you can battle along with 6 friends, 3 people in each team, the battle mechanic is actually pretty decent and you can pull of some awesome combos with it, mixing normal attacks with Super and Ultimate Attacks, you can play with either your custom made character or the characters that appear throughout the game(except the giant ones such as the great ape).
In the parallell quests mode, you can play with 2 other friends and do secondary quests that you unlock throughout the game or playing the quests before the quest you want to unlock, the loot is not distributed, each player has the chance to win items, and they will not be shared between people, but for the positive side, all the players can win loot, instead of only the leader.
The character creation gives you options to change your face and other options common to RPG's, you can choose your race between Frieza's Race, Namekians, Earthlings, Saiyajins and Majin Buu's Race, each has it's own pros and cons. You can further focus on certain skills through the Attribute Point sistem, in which when you level up in any of the modes, you get points to distribute in some categories that change the way you play the game, the max level is 80. In your custom characters you can also get Masters/Mentors, which will give you powerful skills and even an Ultimate Attack with a chance of your own master appearing and helping you do it(making it do extreme damage).
Like most RPG's you can buy clothes, acessories, items and skills.
You can also collect the Dragon Balls and make a wish for sheen long to make true, however they are rare, and you need 7 in total to make a wish, as you make your way through story, you will eventually unlock Characters to play with and the second type of quest in this game, one which you can only finish once, but has the chance to give some very good loot, as well as Mentors.
Currently the game is passing through problems with connection to the server, which to be honest, is a REAL pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but hopefully it will soon be fixed, other than that i'm loving this game, and i definitely recommend it.

Very fun and has lots of replayability with the character races and genders, since each fights a bit differently. Even the male saiyan and female saiyan fight quite a bit differently.
Pros
- Lots of fun, with exciting battles that actually feel like the show from time to time.
- The fighting system is well done, there are one or two things I'd like to see included (like the swift dodging from some of the previous games), but for the most part, once you get your handle on the controls, it's very balanced (provided the two characters have similar stats, though even uneven stats don't effect skill level outcome for the most part... Unless it's something like Broly against Guldo or Hurcule [Mr. Satan])
- TONS of abilities and skills to aquire to make sure you make your character fight just how you want
- (^kind of continued) Which pairs well with the stat building system, which allows you to give your character customized stats based on your playstyle, or character build. Each mission gives experience you use to level up, getting 3 stat points to spend for each level up. Each race and gender has different beginning stats that are built off of, but can vary any way you wish them to, with a maximum of 240 stat points earned by level 80 (max level), allowing for all kinds of builds.
- Battle supports up to 6 players at the moment (3v3), making for large epic battles that can get crazy fast. Don't worry though, as it actually feels quite natural once you get the hang of it (which is one thing I was personally worried about), and fits in to the earlier statment about being balanced, since someone could very well go 2 on 1 against you, but then it will be two of your team members agaisnt one of theirs, or your partner can take advantage of the situation and do a behind attack on both of them to knock them off of you. Also there is 2v2, and the traditional 1v1 as well.
- The story is charming though a little short and unexplained for the most part, but it is very fun to go into the "what if" scenarios and correct them, fighting along side familiar characters.
- There are lots of clothing and accessory items to unlock and get, as well as power-up passive abilities called "Z-Souls", which harbor the spirit of certain characters and give stat buffs and battle advantages.
- Levels are large and pretty well detailed.
- when you create a new character, all the items and abilities and story progression from your first character transfer over. This is helpful for making multiple characters, as it cuts down on grind time getting things and completing the story. Each mission (Including story missions) can all be done over and over too, at any time you wish.
-  The game looks fan-made, and I actually mean that in a good way. Like if fans of the show got a bunch of money and spent it all on getting the original cast and getting some good developers to help with their vision.
- It's neat to see all the different custom characters.
- The player can get certain moves that are exclusive to certain mentors or teachers (one of the characters like goku teaching an ability) that mixes up the usual grinding missions for abilities and Zeni (money). To get them, you have to fufill certain requirements while studying under the mentor.
Cons
- Obvious first one is that the servers are slow and buggy at the moment because of the flood of people for launch playing, but they're working on it, and it will get better with time anyway.
- Only one accessory can be equipped at a time.
- The Levels, although nice to look at for the most part and pretty big too (compaired to previous games), they introduced "zoning", where you can go from one level to another through little warp portals, letting you go to different areas. The reason why this is on the con side, is because although it's a nice thought, you have to lock on to it to use it, which creates problems when you're close to one but trying to lock on to someone else, and it's rather small and hard to find at times, making what should be simple scene transition, turn into an awkward 30 second hide and seek for the portal, or going through the wrong one to find something.
- The TokiToki District (the main district where you get missions, shop, spend time, do story stuff, etc.) is rather unimpressive and falls flat of what it should get across to the player, and looks more like something from a poorly made MMO from 2010. It's rather small, and has portals separating three areas that are small enough that they should all be one large area, making transition to each area a hassle. It's not increadibly pleasant to look at either. If TokiToki District is where the player is supposed to spend time doing things in between fights, and basically be the MAIN hub for all activity, multiplayer or otherwise, they should spend a little more time making it prettier. Fortunately, the TokiToki District stuff, and main gameplay feel like two seprate games all together, making this not effect regular gameplay.
- Character creation is a bit shallow, and there's not a whole lot of options. There is enough to be happy and make something you like, but it's just shy of that mark that makes it feel like a full character creator. The hairstyles are all similar, there's only 3 body types and a few heights, and the faces are limited, as well as no facial hair option, or a few other nice options.
- The writing isn't that good at times, and the voice acting is pretty poor as well, which is depressing since they got Chris Sabat and many of the original voice actors back. It just seemed like there was no voice direction, and everyone was trying to get out as soon as possible. That's not to say ALL the voiceacting is terrible, but there are a few uncomfortable moments where a few extra takes would have been nice.
- From what I can tell, multiple created characters can not be on the same roster. Meaning that whichever character you log in as, takes up the "created character" space in the character select screen. This prevents custom character teams, along with a few other features that would be nice to have, but as of the moment are not part of the game.
- The game is quite a bit buggy at times, with enemies sometimes finding themselves stuck in the side of a mountain, or a dragonball you have to collect that rolled out of bounds, and sometimes the game simply not ending when it should. These are all things that I think will be fixed in an upcoming patch however, so I wouldn't put too much on it for right now.
- The game basically requires internet to play, since it uses servers to transfer information. This means that the story mode will probably not be available offline, or on a bad connection. Or at the very least you're going to have to sit through some boring text boxes about how it's not finding anything. Don't quote me on this, I haven't tried playing it without a connection. It just seems to look like it needs one to work properly.
- The story is a bit bland and not super interesting, which is too bad since it actually has a bit of potential, and unique characters. This is something I think they will fix with the upcoming DLC and the extra story content that will come with it, using all the money they got from how well this game did so far, which is a good thing. I also believe that the voice acting will probably be stronger the second time around with the DLC as well.
There's quite a few more things I could say one way or the other, though I do VERY much like the game, I also think it can be improved. I do fully support anyone who wants to get it, or try it, and hope that many of the issues, however minor they are, will be fixed in the upcoming patches and DLC. Worth the purchase

Sonic All Stars Racing Transformed may seem like a bit of a childish or bad game, due to the title - but do not be fooled. It is one of the best games I've played, and I will be sure to sink more hours into it.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay in this game is crazy - you switch throughout levels to different cars, planes and boats. Remember, this happens in the same level; so you could have been driving one second, but the next, a piece of the cliff had fallen off and suddenly you're in the air, flying. Due to this, I will be splitting the next section of the review into different parts.
CAR HANDLING
The cars feel decent - not the best, but for an arcade racer, it does the job pretty well. I don't really have much to criticise, as all cars are different but there are no major flaws with the handling of the cars.  They feel mildly satisifying to drive, but I would say that the camera shake does make the game feel like it has frame drops.
PLANE HANDLING
The planes in this game are amazing. They feel so smooth, and refined that you will almost always look forward to the plane sections of a level. Mixed with the visuals, they provide a very nice touch to the game that I haven't seen before - although Mario Kart 7 + 8 does have similar sections, ala gliding.
BOAT HANDLING
Not too shabby, I have to say. Boats can be tricky to get right, but this game has done a damn good job of it. It doesn't make you feel frustrated as the glide of the boats are easy to learn and also feel very light. In my opinion this is good, and it makes the transitions feel very nice as well.
GRAPHICS
The graphics in this game are phenomenal - especially for a game with such a cartoonish atmosphere. It looks amazing at 1080p and I'm sure it will look even better at high resolutions - although on my 1080p monitor I couldn't get the game to run at 4K for some reason. Optimisation is decent, but I believe that the frame rate is locked to 60, which is a shame, especially for those of you with 144HZ monitors.
LEVELS
The levels are well done, and feel amazingly detailed compared to what I've played recently. I can blow up parts of the map with powerups, and they will let me get to a shortcut or past an obstacle if I was about to crash, and that makes me smile as it truly feels like the developers have thought about their consumers.
MODES
I have not had a chance to delve into the multiplayer, but the Grand Prix mode is very nice, although the 3 laps can get a little boring. Still, I like that mode a lot more than the world tour mode. I feel like the World Tour could have been so much more, but that is just me. Single race is, well, a single race, and I believe the game has 4 player split screen - BUT don't quote me on that.
OVERALL
This game is very nicely done, with lots of intricate details and decent optimisation. It's visuals are very pretty to look at, as well as it's cars and characters being detailed. The gameplay is a breath of fresh air from the pile of garbage that game developers seem to class as games these days. I would recommend it, especially on a sale.

This game is amazingly fun.  The plot barely exists, but the gunplay is so great you wont even worry.
My favourite part is, of course, the loot system.  The RPG elements in this game make it feel akin to a lighter version of Skyrim, but the loot system is what hooks you.  Instead of starting off the game with all options in front of you and slowly narrowing your playstyle throughout the game, you are at the mercy of what guns you can find.  If you find an amazing shotgun but haven't found that highly accurate sniper you've wanted, you had better learn to use shotguns in the meantime.  This creates very diverse gameplay, where you're always learning how your unique weapons work and adapt your fighting style on the go.  By the end you will have proficiencies with the weapons you liked the most, and will most likely have powerful weapons in that class, but there is always a chance of finding a super rare, super powerful gun of a class  you've yet to use.
If you're looking for the story to be anything but a general compass showing which area has similarly levelled enemies, you will not find it here.  In the end, this game is to be played for the great gameplay and the excitement of finding rare loot.  But that is more than enough to keep you hooked on multiple playthroughs.

Highly recommend this game, read on to see if it's a fit.
Overall - This game is a clever mix of puzzle-solving and boss fighting, wherein you're doing both at the exact same time. Once you've "figured out" the boss, you work on executing it. My time to complete was just over 2 hours, YMMV.
On the "long walk" comments - I didn't find any of the walk-backs (well, run-backs) to be longer than ~15 seconds, it's the perfect amount of time to think about what you just experienced / how you can improve your micro (or come up with a better solution that's easier to execute). If you find yourself running a long way, you probably didn't stand on a checkpoint circle.
On patience required - I didn't find myself getting frustrated until the very last few bosses, where the controls start fighting you. Deaths are usually funny and most bosses have a solution that's easy enough to execute on, and the fun of analyzing/strategizing while dodging/testing ideas -> I beat the game in one sitting, never had a thought of wanting to take a break, loved every bit of it (except when that damn roll button fought me).
To the devs -- Aside from the implied compliments of the above, would love to see the control scheme improved. I'd recommend just taking out "run" so that button can only be roll and the responsiveness/cooldown can be made very clear. I haven't tried the "no run/roll" mode, but I'd just settle on one movespeed to have at all times during combat, and perhaps allow "sprinting" when outside of combat (also helps with all the 'long run back' complaints, two birds one stone! :P )

The pixel art creates a familiar game style as well as a clean and beautiful design. It's easy to grasp the basics, yet the detailed physics engine, creative stages and lots of diversity in enemies and friends show how much thought went into the creation of this game. The game is easy to get into and play for short amounts of time but has a lot of depth and complexity to explore that make you play it over and over again. There's lots of ship customizability that makes the game accessible to different playing styles - you can play fast and action-packed, slow and calculated, or luck of the draw by stocking up on weapons that allow you to run around in a confused panic and then deploy all your ammunition at once. The amount of variation between the different ships and types of levels allows for all sorts of challenges, and the ability to save up and unlock new options means that you never get stuck doing the same thing over and over with no progress.
Also, the game has a lot of style. Both the graphics and music are really captivating. There's a wide variety of ships, weapons, and enemies to interact with. If you feel like tutorials are for chumps you can get pretty far just by ramming into your enemies (and fist-bumping your friends). If you like figuring out the intricacies of a game there's a lot to explore here, from critical hits to reflecting lasers off of inanimate objects and shields to creating your own levels. If you despise fighting and just like drawing cool contrail patterns, you can usually pull that off too. Your onboard computer, who narrates much of the game, has plenty of snaky comments to make when you fail. The allies you can acquire will have conversations with each other, making it fun to gather different groups together. Sometimes, there are biscuitfish, which are like biscuit-shaped cuttlefish. They float around in packs and trill and cycle through the colors of the rainbow. I don't understand them but they make satisfying sounds if you blow them up.
I would definitely recommend this game! It's well worth the price and a great game to come back to again and again.

Sonic All Stars Racing Transformed may seem like a bit of a childish or bad game, due to the title - but do not be fooled. It is one of the best games I've played, and I will be sure to sink more hours into it.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay in this game is crazy - you switch throughout levels to different cars, planes and boats. Remember, this happens in the same level; so you could have been driving one second, but the next, a piece of the cliff had fallen off and suddenly you're in the air, flying. Due to this, I will be splitting the next section of the review into different parts.
CAR HANDLING
The cars feel decent - not the best, but for an arcade racer, it does the job pretty well. I don't really have much to criticise, as all cars are different but there are no major flaws with the handling of the cars.  They feel mildly satisifying to drive, but I would say that the camera shake does make the game feel like it has frame drops.
PLANE HANDLING
The planes in this game are amazing. They feel so smooth, and refined that you will almost always look forward to the plane sections of a level. Mixed with the visuals, they provide a very nice touch to the game that I haven't seen before - although Mario Kart 7 + 8 does have similar sections, ala gliding.
BOAT HANDLING
Not too shabby, I have to say. Boats can be tricky to get right, but this game has done a damn good job of it. It doesn't make you feel frustrated as the glide of the boats are easy to learn and also feel very light. In my opinion this is good, and it makes the transitions feel very nice as well.
GRAPHICS
The graphics in this game are phenomenal - especially for a game with such a cartoonish atmosphere. It looks amazing at 1080p and I'm sure it will look even better at high resolutions - although on my 1080p monitor I couldn't get the game to run at 4K for some reason. Optimisation is decent, but I believe that the frame rate is locked to 60, which is a shame, especially for those of you with 144HZ monitors.
LEVELS
The levels are well done, and feel amazingly detailed compared to what I've played recently. I can blow up parts of the map with powerups, and they will let me get to a shortcut or past an obstacle if I was about to crash, and that makes me smile as it truly feels like the developers have thought about their consumers.
MODES
I have not had a chance to delve into the multiplayer, but the Grand Prix mode is very nice, although the 3 laps can get a little boring. Still, I like that mode a lot more than the world tour mode. I feel like the World Tour could have been so much more, but that is just me. Single race is, well, a single race, and I believe the game has 4 player split screen - BUT don't quote me on that.
OVERALL
This game is very nicely done, with lots of intricate details and decent optimisation. It's visuals are very pretty to look at, as well as it's cars and characters being detailed. The gameplay is a breath of fresh air from the pile of garbage that game developers seem to class as games these days. I would recommend it, especially on a sale.

So, I havent had all that much time with this game just yet, but... even after just 90 minutes, I can honestly say, I think this game is brilliant.  It's good enough that it leaves this impression on me that quickly... for me, this is very rare.
Starship Rubicon is an interesting beast.... it uses a whole pile of different elements that were inspired by many seperate games.  But the thing that makes it so good is that it takes all of these disparate elements, smashes them together... and they WORK together.  They dont conflict with each other at any point.
At it's base, this game uses Asteroids-style gameplay and controls.  You have a "thrust" button to move your ship forwards, and then other buttons to turn it left or right; you also have a "boost" function that you can use.  There are even actual asteroids floating around in many areas, which work pretty much as you'd expect, and generally making your life that much tougher.  From there though, the game goes in it's own seperate directions.  Your ship is not static, but is instead made of various "parts" that you can equip, that give abilities or change stats, or things like that.  This includes changing both your basic weapon (and you can have more than one) or your special weapon, an activated ability that has a cooldown and also knocks out your shields for a bit upon use.   You cant just equip everything though; each piece of equipment has a shape to it, sort of like blocks in Tetris.  You have to fit these blocks inside the ship properly, or they cannot be used.  What's more, some items are meant to modify others, and will only work if linked to the system they're modifying, which means you have to place it adjacent to that system for it to function whatsoever.  So this can create some interesting decisioni-making when you're changing your equipment.
Equipment can be either found in battlefields, or bought in stores. Stores are easily the most frequent way to get equipment.  The rate of equipment actually being FOUND is very low... a bit TOO low in my opinion.  You end up not getting all that much total, which is a shame, because it reduces the amount of interesting decisions that you'd need to make.  There's no need to decide between two items after all if both of them easily fit onto the ship.  If you're not getting enough items, you wont be filling it.  So there's a bit of RNG issues here with this system, but it's not enough of an issue at all to detract from how well it works.  There are many different weapons and things to find, so look for them, and try them out, and see what kinds of builds you can make for yourself.  Most of these different items and such are also just plain fun to use.... that's ALWAYS a plus.
Between missions, you're sent to sort of an overall sector map.  It's very similar to the map that FTL uses, in that you move forward from one node to the next, with each individual node having specific links to other nodes to choose from.  Around each node, you can see icons representing the different enemy types that are going to appear in that area, so it's important to learn these and have a look as you make decisions.  Other things will appear here too, such as hazards, or the existence of items or "money asteroids" or shops or various other things.   You can also find other ships to rescue, and if you are successful in saving them, they will join you on your quest.  Each one provides a unique ability that becomes active whenever they participate in a battle with you, and you choose when to bring them in by clicking them on the sector map.  They have a cooldown time afterwards, and can also be knocked out by enemies during battle... so take care of them, when you bring them with you.   The one big problem with them though is that they just arent very bright.  Asteroids in particular will give your AI allies alot of trouble as they repeatedly crash into them.  By the late game, these guys arent as useful, simply due to the fact that they'll be knocked out of the fight too quickly to help much.
And on the note of the enemies you face, each type is different from the last, and you quickly learn to recognize each by it's appearance, which is very important.  There are different approaches that you should take depending on just what you're fighting, and what weapon you're using, and there can be many enemies at once.  Some enemies may have beam weapons, or maybe homing missiles, or shields, or even the ability to shield other enemies.   And of course, it wouldnt be a shmup of any sort if there werent gigantic bosses to fight at the end of each sector.
All in all, there's alot going on for this game, and I think there's plenty of replay value; naturally, everything is procedural when it comes to the maps and sectors and such, so each game will be different.   The campaign is short, but that's typical for this genre, and probably for the best.
Is it worth your money?  If you like shmups at all.... I'd definitely say yes.  It easily lives up to it's asking price and more, I think.   I can definitely recommend this one!

This game is hard. Like, really hard. It probably took me a good 10 hours to beat the first three worlds the first time through. So, I've told you it's hard and it's good, now onto the gameplay. Electronic super joy is a side-scrolling platformer where everything is a silhouette on a bright colored, sometimes flashing background. It's fast, intricate, frustrating, and engaging, and it's set to some awesome tunes all made by the talented EnV.
I managed to snag this game while it was on sale (for under $1), but I would gladly pay full-price for the game and DLC (just $15, and I've put in a bit over 16 hours of play now, so < $1/hr). This is one of the games I would recommend to pretty much everyone regardless of their taste in games.
A few things to note though, just so you don't go in without knowing... the colors and contrast and flashing lights may make you nauseated and probably don't mix well with epilepsy. Also, one of the bosses in the game is the pope, so if you're not okay with a bit of mild blasphemy, it might not be your thing. Still though, play it and decide for yourself.

The upsides:
• Unique and evocative visual aesthetic—the anonymity of the faceless character models (and the fact that the main character is named Joe) give the story an eerie, could-happen-anytime-to-anyone vibe.
• Engaging story that sometimes stumbles over familiar time-travel paradoxes, but generally keeps things moving with interest. Resists taking the easy way out in the endgame.
• Minimalist ambient soundtrack suits the doomsday mood.
• Voice acting is decent, and not overused.
• The use of chapters for gameplay means the adventure is neatly bundled: no objects left from the beginning chapters remain in your inventory to muddy the waters later on.
• Hidden Back To The Future reference.
Good or bad? You decide:
• Simple, straightforward point-and-click adventure... sometimes too simple. Usable objects are never far from the place where they're to be used, and the chapter system means all puzzles are compartmentalized within sometimes very short chapters. Objects don't need to be combined, only used with the thing they were (obviously) meant to be used with. While this makes the game suitable and enjoyable for the casual player, experienced players may find gameplay occasionally tedious as it's reduced to switching times in all available locations to make sure you've found all there is to be found.
• Achievement hunters can pick up a relatively easy and short 100% here.
Downsides:
• Short game for the price tag.
• Not sure how the assets for this game add up to 4 GB, but they do.
