This is going to sound like a cop out but:
Go back to the store page and read the "ABOUT THIS GAME", the full description, not just the blurb up at the top of the page.
This is probably one of the only games where the description is pretty much spot on.  There's almost nothing I could tell you about the game that is not already in the rather lengthy about this game description right on the store page. It's not lying, it's not making anything up.
Take a close look at the pictures too, it's not hiding anything. This is a minimalist graphics game that uses cute icons to get it's point across. There's no impressive 3d visuals and there never will be.
From the ground up this is a colony management sim. You have some crash landed survivors, well; go survive. If that's not enough of a hook to get you interested, skip it.
Everything else the game does is predicated on that scenario. What makes the game shine is the size and scope of what you can manage from there. It literally generates an entire planet. Every square block of the entire planet. Let the magnitude of that sink in.
Beyond that it's a story simulator only in the loosest sense. Your colonists will have events happen to them, natural disasters, invading raiders, animal attacks and so on. In vague terms you could sum up every story as "life happens, deal with it". And how you deal with it is mostly up to you.
Or at least it would be if your colonists didn't all have minds of their own. You can give them directions, you can lay out plans, you can set out a path to bring your stone age campground back to a proper civilizations standards. And you can watch it all burn down when one of your colonists goes nuts after having his arm torn off by a hungry monkey that used to be his pet.
The size and scope of the life stories that can be told are basically endless.
If there is any major flaw with the concept... well, it's the same thing: the life stories that can be told are basically endless.. but that generally means they are also going to end in tragedy (forced start over) or go on in tedium without any goals beyond what you set for yourself. And once you reach those... then what? Keep surviving for the sake of surviving.
Winning basically either puts you in an endless loop of treading water until the end of time watching colonists give birth to new generations of colonists. Or it all just comes crumbling down as you decay into random methods of failure whether that's on week 1 because you lost all your food and there was nothing to hunt, or it's year 3000 and your colony despite many generations of growth is flattened by some invading aliens who want to build a hyperspace freeway through your home and demolish the planet.
The game is simultaneously one of the most boring and exciting games I've ever played. The scope is incredible, the scale enormous. And the random nature of event's is only as profound as it's tedious repetitive treadmill that is survival.
The bottom line, if theoretically massive scale colony building in a massive world filled with random events sounds like a good thing to you and you are willing to sludge through a very repetitive early game no matter how many times you lose, you are going to find several thousand hours of fun here.
On the other hand if you are easily annoyed because you laid out a godly plan on how to build an entire civilization only to have it foiled by a stupid monkey. This might not be the game for you.
Now excuse me, I need to go start a new colony and this time we're shooting all the stupid monkeys and eating them instead of trying to make them into pets....

At the time of writing I have 9 hours played on this game, and I think it is important to capture the feeling around 10 hours of gameplay as many people may only be asking for this much time from a game. I'm going to also preface this review with the fact that I am a massive Dragonball Z fan and have not owned another DBZ game, though I have played a couple.
Pros:
-The game is very stylistically in keeping with DBZ and it transitions a 2D anime into a 3D playable game very well. I think that all the attacks look great, and the scenery is pretty nice.
-The story is an interesting take to a very cemented series. Adding in behind the scenes villains allows everyone to play out their favourite fights from the series while also giving new circumstances.
-Once you've figured out combat you can have a good deal of fun with it. It's pretty satisfying landing a Gallick Gun on 2-3 enemies at once and seeing them fry.
-The game has a lot of potential for online capabilities and a succesful competitive scene. Also there is room for lots of DLC.
-Movement is very smooth, I have always though it would be difficult to implement DBZ style flying into a game but the boost system is calibrated perfectly.
Cons:
-The combat is too repetitive for the difficult nature of the game. That is to say that the game is naturally hard to complete story missions without grinding your character up, and to grind your character up you have to play story missions already available to you. There's not enough varience in combat to keep this all interesting, and fights often play out the same which can get very boring if you have to keep retrying levels.
-The menu level (i.e. TokiToki City) is just pointless and long. Having to physically run to a loading screen to have access to the shops is thoroughly pointless. It feels as if the developers are trying to make it into an open-world RPG but there's only one of each shop (item, clothing, accessory) so that falls flat. I would rather have that space allocated for something more interesting and put the shops in the menu.
-All story and mission oriented features are weighed down heavily by clunky and outdated UI stylings. This feels like lazyness on the animators part, they could quite easily (just for the main storyline) put everything into cutscenes which would then play out like the anime, the reason why the majority of people have bought this game. Instead you have to sit reading bland text that doesn't even auto-finish, you literally have to press a button to get the next sentence. It doesn't even have a roundup (what I mean is a game like Skyrim you could skip every word of a conversation and be told what to do next in your journal, in this you are forced to read to know what's going on).
-I don't know what's going on with multiplayer but they seem to have the slowest servers. Searching for a match takes an age and so far I've only managed to join two games, one was a co-op parallel quest which played out great and the other was a vs match which was laggy. I put in the pros that it has potential, which is certainly does, but right now it looks like a mess.
-The game needs more flavour to battles. The choice it gives you at the start is 'do you like to be up close punching or at the back with Ki attacks', but surely you could add in at least one more choice? Unless using your specials (granted you can do it a lot if you just land a few punches) Ki blasts consist of weak short bursts that go in straight lines, not exactly the most riveting part of the game. They're only really effective for staying back if you've got someone else on your team holding the enemy still. The game could do with more 'stuff'
Overall I'm saying don't get this game unless you're a fan of DBZ and are going to anyway. I've had fun, and am actually having more fun the more I play, but if I wasn't a massive fan of the series I would have stopped playing after an hour.

Pros: Fun, retro, great control scheme (and in-game reminders of how to control your ship)
Cons: I can't really think of any. The game's difficulty could go here, but it's not horrible. Many improvements have been made over the course of development to ease the game's difficulty.

Starship Rubicon is a fun and challenging game, which was inspired by Asteroids. This takes many players back to their childhood playing classic games, something that's missing from many modern day games. However, this is not simply a clone.
Essentially, the player is a lone pilot out to defeat an alien nemesis in space. At the beginning, the player is given the option of a few different ships to use, each with it's own attributes. Over the course of the game, these ships can be upgraded by purchasing parts at a ship or by finding equipment stashes on the map. Other ships can also be unlocked.
The game is challenging, but by participating in the progress of the game, I've seen vast improvements to help make the game a bit more easier.  While defeating enemies, the player will notice blue orbs dropping from defeated enemies or by shooting blue asteroids. These are the currency for the game and it is best to collect as many of them as possible. Luckily, the Steam version has made these center toward the exit upon completion of battle.

I'm terrible at this kind of game, but at least with Starship Rubicon it's fun while I'm repeatedly dying. The difficulty curve ramps up nicely, and the controls are stellar. It's got a bit of everything; the classic space shooter mechanics you'd expect, with semi-FTL-style upgrades, ship unlocks, etc.
It's a roguelike-like, so you're expected to die and start over, and it doesn't hurt to do so, death just makes you want to get further next time.
It has gamepad support if you need that, but I find I prefer the mouse controls, which is a first for this kind of game.
The graphics and soundtrack are top-notch, and really  help set the mood. You have a funny AI companion through the whole thing as well, adding more charm. As someone in another review said, the screenshots don't do it justice.
The Windows, Mac, and Linux versions look and feel identical, I had no issues running either version.
Highly recommended to anyone who loves space shooters, or those who have been frustrated with space shooters in the past, and think they would love them with the right controls.

Loved the anime adaptation and decided to buy the VN when it came to Steam. Probably the best ~30€ I've spent. This is the first version of this visual novel I've read so I can't do any comparison between this and earlier releases. There are a lot of other rewiews that do that so you should go to read them if you're interested in that.
Many of you (like I was) are propably thinking: "Is it worth buying if you've already watched the anime?". Simple answer: Yes. Why? Let me tell you shortly.
While the main storyline is the same the visual novel has a lot more content in it. It gives much more insight in the eight main characters' backgrounds, reasons to their actions and interactions with each other. What the anime especially lacks is the most of Okabe's (main character's) inner monologues. They give so much info about his character and why he acts and behaves like he does.
The anime series has only one ending aka "true ending" of the VN. Well it would have been very confusing (and silly) if they'd have done all 6 endings in one series. Even when you follow the true ending storyline the story is more detailed and a bit different in a few scenes. I must say that I learned a lot more about the universe of Steins;Gate (and the whole Science Adventure series) when I read this VN. The anime apadtation was great, heck it's #4 top rated anime at MAL. But there's just so much you can fit in 24 episodes.
- A well written story about time travel, decisions and consequenses, the cause and the effect...
- Well explained and beliveable theories about time travel.
- 6 different endings depending on your decisions throughout the game.
- Interesting characters with lots of character development.
- Well made voice-overs with the same voice actors from the anime.
- Amazing soundtrack.
- Took me ~70 hours to 100% complete this so there's a lot of content.
- It's a visual novel. Lots of reading with little interaction.
- Starts slowly with lots of science stuff about time travel.
- Different art style than the anime series.
- Only Japanese voice-overs.
- Not enough トゥットゥルー
- Seriously, can't think of any flaws since most of the bugs/translation errors have been fixed.
Highly recommended to the fans of the anime series and those who like sci-fi, mystery/thriller and a bit of romance. Worth every €/$/£/yen even at full price.

Holy cow, I just realized I've played about 7 hours of this game. The time really flies...
Everything I want to say about this game has already been said via other reviews, but I want to throw my vote into the pile of 100% positive reviews that this game has at the time of this review.
This game is about forward progression through zones, exactly the way FTL plays. The zones split off, you can choose to pick which direction you want to go. You'll even be granted preview of what types of enemies will await you should you choose any specific direction. Note, like FTL, there is no backtracking, so the choices in direction you make will matter. You might find items on certain paths, new allies, bonus cash, or shops. Each zone is guarded at the end by a boss, so make sure you beef up as you go.
The ship customization is pretty terrific, it's extraordinarily simple, yet deep. You have limited space on your hull, and all customizable parts are in configurations of shapes, which you can rotate to make fit as best you can. The more parts you can pack into your ship the better. You will be pleased to know the weapons, abilities, and effects you can add to your ship are quite large in number, so the replay value is pretty huge. Some attachments can alter how weapons work, boosting various attributes.
This game has Neutonian physics, so you can turn on the thrusters, suddenly shut them off, then spin the ship around to fire at enemies behind you, while still gliding in the same initial direction. The combat system is great, everything feels fluid and polished. When you beat the game, you can bank the cash from the campaign, use it to unlock powerful new weapons, or even ships. You can also access a hangar to customize and build your own ships with access to all parts.
Great game, good story, good shooter. It needs a little help with moderm systems (like Win10), but nothing serious, nothing broken.

If you like FTL, SPAZ or just arcade space games in general, this game will hook you. Each level has forward-moving, branching pathways for you to choose. Guided by Control, your AI helper/ dictator, you'll encounter Nemesis (your enemy), ships in distress that will become fighting companions to an extent should they survive the skirmish (some of them offering some kind of beneficial boost), cryopods to be rescued (the number of those rescued goes toward unlocking many upgrades and ships), armaments, cash-flow, and space anomalies, rocks and intriguing organisms. The story is simplistic, but thought-provoking and hinting at something sinister afoot.
At first glance, the encounters seem similar, until you realise there are various kinds of space rocks that react differently when fired upon; anomalies that affect your ship in a variety of ways and anomalies that can appear owing to results from specific recipes of mayhem; and organisms that may or may not be eye candy or passive-aggressive. A boss fight awaits you at the end of each level, and your ship and its armaments
matter. And speaking of ships, the outfitting is really fun and different, requiring thought and puzzle piece-placement with some restrictions - it's very creative and it really just adds to the game in a great way.
Despite being rogue-like, you do feel a progression in your skills as a player. Your deaths, and there will be many, do not feel out of your control. To the contrary, if you do die, it is solely your fault, and not some random roll of an ether-die. Like me, you may approach this game in a casual mood but it always turns into determination, bursts of triumph and ending with
ooooooo defeats. Upon defeat, you may choose to continue for cost, and you will if it's an encounter you just need to get out of your system; but mostly you will Abort because in doing so, the game is at its most rogue-ish (as well as the money you make stockpiling toward unlocking ships and upgrades eventually).
There are so many fun mechanics going on here, reminding you of this or that game; but honestly, Starship Rubicon is a game in its own right. I would be floored if it doesn't become a cult classic. The developer is friendly and involved, proud of his work, and he should be. I look forward to what he may develop in the future and wish him and Starship Rubicon great success.

I want to recommend this game, it has some nice ideas and could have been excellent, unfortunately it weds itself too much to it's own mechanics, doesn't provide good enough puzzles and the story doesn't really go anywhere interesting enough.
First off the mechanic, time travel, whilst the idea of being able to move back and forth in time to provide different paths, objects and interactions is interesting, being forced to jump backand forther every room so that you can pass through a door that is/will only open in one timeframe is annoying as heck, especially once you have to retread your steps back and forth.  The house section is by far the worst for this but the whole game suffers from it.  Had it been used more sparingly, especially in the mid-game it would have been welcome, instead it becomes a chore as your immediate reaction every time you are blocked is "time travel" and 99% of the time it's correct.  Additionally the very last chapter requires so much stupid walking back and forth (was it really necessary to ask for a cup of water and retread the whole level before moving the plot on to it's already more than obvious next stage.
Second the puzzles are really quite simple once you find the objects needed to progress and the fact that several are reused a number of times (dark corners etc.) doesn't help.  Then there's the overkill of using a chainsaw to enter a home and a few others that just didnt sit in the right tone.
Finally the story, I won't spoil it, ut it's csuch a time travel chiche that you will see it coming well before the end of act 1.
It will take you 2 hours or so and if you really like this kind of game then feel free to pay a few £s for it, but you'd be far better off spending your time doing something else.

I first met with The Silent Age back in 2013 on iOS and I really enjoyed it - You can never have too much good games on mobile devices. Then I bought it here on Steam, when it was discounted, but haven't played it until yesterday. Now I have to say, that this is one of the best invested 1 Euros in terms of story driven games. So let's go to the facts:
Storyline: 10/10
Well well well, in the first seconds of gameplay You will never think that this will be one of the best written scripts in indie games. The storyline isn't very innovative when it comes to the main plot - extinction of mankind and post-apocalyptic vision of future, but when joined with really marvelous system of time travelling it really becomes one of my favourites worlds created in games. There are also some plot twists, that You can't predict from what You have seen earlier. That adds some points to the overall grade, but the most important thing is that I really wanted to know what will happen next, to discover what devs prepared for me, I was really absorbed by the plot, and this is the thing that describes good story driven game. So, it's 10 out of 10 for storyline of The Silent Age.
The World: 9/10
I really like time travelling in this game - between the Seventies and post apocalyptic Seventies,
but I had to remove that one point because in the end, the reason of apocalypse was not so innovative. Everything else is good, especially the feeling that You really are wandering in the Seventies. There are also some good easter eggs, even in the achievements, that only make this feeling of Seventies better.
Gameplay: 9/10
Everything is correct for an adventure game. Items You find and their interactions are intuitive and quite simple (unless You want to get all the achievements, but just look at their description, and You will find out what to do). The only problem for me is that the game is sometimes sluggish, I mean, You have to click on something one more time, because game was busy with something else and didn't notice that You want to do next thing. But hey, come on, this is point n click game, so I can get with it. You surely won't die because of it. Well, You won't die at all, and that's good because...
Graphics: 9/10
...You can stop and admire these unique, but really beautiful graphics devs prepared for You. Honestly, I really like the style of this game. It's some kind of cartoon, but made with its own unique style. For me it perfectly fits the world of the Seventies presented in the game. For me the only weakness are eyes of some of people - but it's a matter of taste, maybe someone will find them matching with the world.
Sound: 6/10
No fireworks here. Just correct. Music could be better, but the game depicts post-apocalyptic world, so those tunes fit it.
Voiceacting: 7/10
Correct, but one person should speak with strong accent in certain time of plot, so this is why I give only 7 points. Every other person has voice that fits them perfectly.
Overall: 9/10
The Silent Age is just like a movie - very good adventure for short amount of time. You can end this game in one evening, and play it once a certain amount of time, because it's really good piece of game developing, and You won't get bored, trust me. The only disadvantage of this game is its price - 10 Euros for 3 hours of gameplay is just too much, especially that the game has almost 5 years, so I strongly recommend buying it when its on discount.

Wolfenstein 3D is clearly a rough predecessor to DOOM; there's a lives system that doesn't make sense considering the save function, there's only one ammo type, the levels are of a uniform height and are easy to get lost in, there are fewer of DOOM's level design tricks (that is to say, putting an enemy in a corner you normally wouldn't look in), both you and the enemies are far easier to kill, and there's just less content overall. In addition, it helped popularize first person shooters for an audience that probably hadn't seen one ever before, but then DOOM came along and...well, you know. For pure quality and importance to game history, DOOM is superior in pretty much every way.
However, on its own merits, it's a decent game that drags a little too much in the middle and was enough of a hit at the time to allow id Software to go onto bigger and better things. Also, it makes fun of the Nazis by portraying them as straight-up cartoon villains with mech suits and swastika-shaped bases and Hitler vampires, so that's good. I'd say buy it to experience a piece of gaming history, 'cause that's what I did.
EDIT: I did not play the Nocturnal Missions, because 1) they didn't come with the original release, and 2) once you've killed Hitler, you've won the game as far as I'm concerned.

Senran Kagura: Shinovi Versus is a 3D hack and slash game, where you find a horde of mobs of female ninjas, before fighting a boss. Unlike your typical hack and slash game, in this game, whatever damage done is being experienced by the clothing worn, thus the more damage a ninja takes, the more parts of their clothes fall off. In other words, ripping and tearing fabrics is the name of this game, in a manner of speaking.
Basically, like normal hack and slash game, you have your weak attack, strong attack, guard and parry and transformation. Weak attack is fast but its deals little damage, while strong attack hits hard, but are slower. Charging it up will also allow you to break the enemy's guard, in case they are too block happy. Guarding is basically to reduce the damage taken, but it can be broken by guard breaking moves or ninja arts. Parrying, is basically guarding done at the right time. If you block at the right moment an attack lands, it will counter and stun an enemy. Some guards just stun, while some guards will launch them for a juggle. Nevertheless, it will give you a meter of ninja energy.
Transformation, boy this is where it gets interesting. You have two forms; one is the ninja transformation, which require a ninja meter to do so. This transformation will change the girl's appearance into another outfit (or for a certain girl, bust size), which some nice camera shots on their bust and hips. The other one, is the Frantic mode, which basically strips your character into their underwear. In this form they take more damage (obviously), but at the cost of improved offense. Both have their pros and cons, and have certain unique traits. In both forms, they can use the ninja super art, which is basically a super move. Depending on which super move used, it can basically inflict enough damage to rip a part of their clothes off. Special mention to the ultimate ninja art though, as it's only available at a certain point in the game and when you are low in HP. If you finish off a person with this move, and they are in their undies, prepare for their undies to be ripped and teared into oblivion.
Basically, there are two type of story modes, which are the school one and the character one. The school one is about 24 chapters (except only a certain school have 25), while the character one are only 5 chapters. Each school storyline is supposed to tell what happens in that school and are supposed to be interwoven together. By playing through those story modes, you can level up your character stats, where depending on the transformation mode you stay in (default, ninja transformation, Frantic), it will up your stats for a certain area. For example, if you max out your Flash stats, which is for staying in default outfit mode, you can do an infinite air juggle.
This game itself is a massive fanservice. Pervs... ahem, people who like this type of game will really love it. You can dress up the girls with whatever outfits, hairstyles, ninja outfits and lingeries that you want. It's practically a semi-Barbie doll simulator. Plus, there are many type of lingeries, you name it, conventional, G-string, thongs, C-strings, etc, you name it. Also, you can, err, "play" with them in the dressing room. Clothes? They are meant to be ripped and teared, if you know what I mean. Combat wise, there are plenty of mobs to kill. Air combos, super moves, parries, it's pretty fun and frantic, especially on hard modes, where mobs start to inflict massive status debuffs and have increased aggro. Story wise, it's quite decent, as there is a total of about 99 chapters for the school, and about 110 chapters in total for the character stories.
There is also online mode for this game, where you get to duke it out with other characters. There are 3 modes, which are deathmatch, capture as many panties as possible and strip as much clothing as possible. They either come in individual mode, or team mode. I didn't tried it out much, but oddly, while doing an AI battle for this, it actually lowers my FPS badly for some reason, despite the fact that there are not many mobs on screen.
Though, in hard mode, sometimes the leap in aggro is a bit too much. In normal difficulty, they are pretty docile, however in hard mode, they will spam attacks like no tomorrow. Special mention to a certain mob that ONLY blocks in that mode, so you have to continuously guard break them or use the ninja arts just to kill them. If you are in Frantic mode, one slip up will get you killed. Also over time, the game gets practically repetitive. It's basically hack and slash until you meet the boss, and defeat her. Levelling up a character to max level is not so bad, as you can reach max level just from playing in normal difficulty. However, levelling up all the character stats will be a chore. Doing all the character story quests and school story quests in both normal and hard difficulty mode, will most of the time, not max all of your stats in one play through (unless you are Hanzo Academy though, especially that certain chapter which is really useful for grinding), thus you need to replay certain valuable chapters just to max them. If going for all of the character stats, it will be a massive grind and chore. Enemy boss AIs, on hard difficulties, will have additional bonuses, such as a longer period of i-frames, easier to escape juggles, and consistently do air clashes, which makes it quite irritating. Worse offender is easily the DLC final character chapters, where the boss is practically a huge leap from all the other character story chapter. Heck, it's even harder than the final battle itself! The biggest issue this game have, are the input displays. I want to see what my buttons corresponding to A and B is during the info prompts, not see just "press A/ B". I don't know which button is A and B when the keyboard binding option doesn't state it!
Overall, I would recommend this games to people who like a decent hack and slash, with a huge dose of fanservice. Though I would admit, get it during the sales, as it will be more worth it's price. However, if you are ripping and tearing clothes, make sure your parents or younger siblings are not watching you doing so. Overall verdict: 6.9/10.

Pros:
- the building part is easy and don't take too much time, while being very valuable. I have seen people putting weapons put on top of fuel tanks, which, when hit, exploded with the weapon on top of it. On the other hand, you can protect your weapons with armor parts wisely placed.

Cons:
- the winning strategy is to move around the map in the biggest convoy possible. Otherwise, you are dead.
- the con that made me give this a negative review: you can get starting weapons and parts by winning battles or at the base workshop for free. However, to get higher stuff, you either need to buy it with credits on the market from other players, or build it and pay some credits to use a higher-level workshop. How do you get credits ? By selling stuff on the market or by spending real money. Yes, the entirety of the mid and end game is only accessible if someone spends real money. Either you, or the guy who is buying something from you.

Overall, Xenoverse is a good game. Moving away from the style of their previous games (the Budokai series, Burst Limit, Infinite World), Dimps crossed the line from 2D-Fighter to a Tenkaichi/Raging Blast-esque 3D fighter. Despite this, it remains a completely unique experience - whilst it certainly appears to be inspired by Tenkaichi, it plays a lot different. The emphasis is shifted from extensive combo strings to simply chaining short combos together (at least, if you're not a Saiyan, but more on that later).
Character creation is a welcome addition to any DBZ game, and the level up system borrowed from RPGs lets you differentiate your fighter from those of other people by letting you use stat points gained each level however you deem fit. The races are for the most part well balanced, each with perks and cons, but this is only until the Saiyans gain access to their Super Saiyan transformations, which allows them to spam any super and ultimate attacks for free until the transformation ends. Expect to run into Super Saiyans firing off their ultimates many, many times.
The Mentor system is overall a good addition to the DBZ gaming franchise, letting you train under iconic characters from the show and gradually learn their techniques and eventually their ultimate attacks. Why is this such a good thing? Mentors and the Skills Shop are the only places you are guaranteed to find skills - yet the skills you can obtain from these two sources probably don't even amount to half the skills in the game.
Which brings me to my one gripe - to get the vast majority of skills available for you to collect, you have to grind through every single Parallel Quest multiple times. The expectation would be that if you meet certain requirements within the battle, the skill you desire would drop, and you'd retire from a hard day's work. This is not the case. The way it works is, meeting the requirements only gives you a chance of the skill dropping - not a guarantee. As a result you'll find yourself grinding for hours on end hoping to obtain any of the following: Super Vegeta, Super Vegeta 2, Ultra Fighting Bomber, Giant Storm, Kaioken X3, Kaioken X20, Maximum Charge, Spirit Sword, and even more.
This is, of course, ignoring the other items you must grind for, such as the Z-Sword...and Dragon Balls. However, these items (and, if you think about it, most skills) aren't really essential for success in the game, and for some this will be a minor problem.
Xenoverse, despite its tedious amounts of grinding ultimately gives a fresh new experience in its excellent new combat system. If you're a fan of the previous console-exclusive DBZ games, or you want a fighter with a radically different combat system, this game is for you.

One of my favorite anime of all time. The basic story revolves around time travel and potential consequences of having such power, to say much more would spoil it. To those that have seen the anime I would still recommend this as it gives further character development and shows some potential storylines via alternate endings. I think playing this after having watched the anime makes the visual novel even better with being able to pay extra attention to foreshadowing and hints knowing the major plot points that are coming up. The anime follows the "true ending" so it's worth exploring all the other endings for new content. And despite revolving heavily on supernatural elements like time travel, it stays relatively grounded by clearly establishing the rules of time travel that this universe decides to follow.
The actual gameplay is that of a typical visual novel. It's a lot of reading with voice acted dialogue and a handful of decisions that determine extra scenes/the endings. The choices in this game come in the form of cell phone text replies. So gameplay is minimal, but is expected of the genre. Like any other games of the genre, the draw is the story and character interactions.
As for negatives, it's still a visual novel. A lot of people don't enjoy the genre for the lack of gameplay and this story isn't amazing enough to turn people into fans of the genre. There's still the anime if you want to story. The start of the story is also extremely slow, but necessary. The format of being a visual novel makes it even slower than the anime (which is often the biggest criticism). It's worth it for the payoff in later chapters though.

I have mixed feeling towards Titan Souls. It often feels very satisfying to finally kill a boss, but at the same time I don't think the concept of "one arrow, one life" was that well mastered.
Since every titan has only one life, the developers couldn't make it too easy to hit them. Their solution on most titans was to make their week spot very hard to reach or vulnerable for a very small fraction of time. What I find interesting in boss fights is mostly to figure out how to defeat them. In Titan Souls, I almost always know in no time how to kill the boss; the challenge is to be able to hit it on the right spot in the small amount of time where it's vulnerable. This is not a very epic or interesting fight, as opposed to many bosses in the Zelda series or in Shadow of the Colossus (to name a few).
I also met the opposite problem, where I'd be able to hit a titan at the right time in its week spot in a few seconds, after let's say two or three tries.
In the end, the number of bosses I found genuinely interesting is rather small. I played the Ludum Dare prototype when it came out, and I found it worked better as a short browser game. However, I am very fond of boss fights and still enjoyed it, and would recommend it to anyone who's ready to fight a series of bosses far more powerful than their character. Its minimalism is charming, and even though I don't think the developers did that well with their constraints, they still made a decent game about fighting titans with only one arrow. I'd just suggest to not expect too much from it, and to play in small game sessions.

With a name like Titan Souls, I came in with high expectations, but soon found out it’s more of a Shadow of the Colossus clone than a Souls game. There some aspects of this game that I think are done well, but an action-adventure title falling short in the gameplay department hurts it greatly. It has other issues too, unfortunately.
You’re a little archer in a nice looking, pixelated world taking down titans with a single magical arrow because you want their succulent soul juice. You can run, dodge, fire the arrow, and call the arrow back to you. You’ll have to read the Store Page to sort of understand your purpose because the game doesn’t tell you anything itself. After doing that, you’ll know that you’re on some quest for truth and power. Fantastic! Except there is no character progression of any sort present in the game so gaining power is mostly story related. I also still felt like I was killing titans for the sake of killing titans.
The truth isn’t very helpful since there’s virtually no plot in the game unless you’re really into theories and analysis. Dark Souls is explicit in comparison. The little crumbs of plot present in the game are found by observing the environment or are obscured by a fake alphabet that are present for 17 of 19 boss names. You’ll have to beat this difficult game first in order to have them translated for you which means you’ll need to beat it twice if you really want to know whom you’ve been killing or just look it up. That’s not a great way to tell a story which means Titan Souls is pretty much about the gameplay.
Prepare to die repeatedly in order to play this game where you die in one hit. There are no enemies except for titans and you have to find their rooms around the world. Most of them are straightforward, others might have a minor puzzle blocking the way to the fight. Once you find one and start the fight, you’re greeted by good music and death. The game will kill you repeatedly until you finally understand how to win. You must first observe the boss’ pattern, die, figure out how to expose its weak spot, die some more, and then plant your arrow deep inside in order to collect the titan’s soul. Titan Souls doesn’t allow moments of respite and can be quite demanding on your reflexes with some weakness windows ranging from .2 to .5 seconds before death if you’re taking the shot. It’s an extremely punishing and frustrating time, especially when trying to be precise when aiming with the gamepad.
One of the fights had such bad RNG with the boss’ moves that it could either take 20 seconds for it to expose its weak spot or up to 3-6 minutes of kiting before letting me have an attempt at killing it. That’s immensely irritating and a big waste of time. Some bosses have much better patterns than others. More than a handful of my victories boiled down to luck because the titan positioned itself just right, but without me really doing much to manipulate it. I wasn’t gaining satisfaction from completing many of these fights.
I just wish the game were less brutally difficult by being much more polished and reducing random behavior. I wanted proper patterns and not so many homing attacks. A couple lesser enemies populating the overworld and some new skills would have been nice too. I’ve seen evidence of TS being capable of providing good gameplay with the plant titan fight. I had to avoid a multi-tentacle slamming attack pattern, play keep away with the slow-you-down gas that homed in on me, shoot the arrow in the glowing spot, recall the arrow to peel the plant open to expose its core, and then stay alive while firing off the kill shot before it closed up again.
Maybe respawning in the boss arena would have been another improvement instead of making me waste 4-8 seconds to walk back to the same fight over and over again (I died several hundred times). Only 3 of the bosses had good checkpoint locations. The optional final boss that unlocks the translation for the game had three forms that would make you fight from the first stage again if you died. I lost 25 minutes to that terribly thought out boss fight where only the first form was good. The other two would spawn minions that functioned like homing missiles that loved getting in the way of the weak spot.
In conclusion, Titan Souls turned me into a bitter, broken soul. It’s a game for people that enjoy difficulty for the sake of difficulty, are borderline masochistic (Iron Mode is a post-game unlock that grants you one life), or gaming savants. Hyper Light Drifter would be a much better alternative as it handles difficulty well while also being great looking (it’s still a hard game).

Look, no game is for everyone, and that includes Titan Souls. If you don't enjoy accomplishing hard challenges, exploring a (for the most part) non-linear world to defeat bosses, and ESPECIALLY if you despise backtracking, don't buy this game. There is an easy mode, you could use a guide to find bosses, but NOTHING will stop backtracking. I personally loved the backtracking. It calmed me from the boss I either killed or was killed by with a beautiful world and an amazing soundtrack. Some get frustrated by the backtracking since they just want to get to the next area and or kill that boss that killed them. I actually got frustrated when there WASN'T any backtracking. I just saw the backtracking as a relaxing and calming walk before the storm. Oh yeah you also have 1 arrow the entire game to use to kill bosses........
Titan Souls has 2 basic movements besides walking around. You can roll/run and shoot/retrieve. When you roll you go to that direction you were running at but there is a little delay like a cooldown once you roll, so you can't spam it. After you roll if you hold down that button you can run. These controls are more focused for boss fights. Running around the world itself may be tedious if you don't enjoy the atmosphere. When you shoot your bow you aim it the direction you're facing, and the longer you hold the more power to the arrow, making it go farther and faster. Once shot you press that same button to
retrieve the arrow. This also can damage bosses.
Titan Souls has a
and
world. It was diverse enough for me never to get bored and big enough for me to run around and explore until i stumble upon my next area. The sountrack really is amazing and (to me at least) makes a mood that is the calming before the storm.
For the most part they're unique and interesting and fun. Thats pretty much it. Oh and almost every boss has a corrisponding achievment on how you kill it or mess with it.

After you beat the game you unlock hard mode, iron man mode, no roll mode, and if you beat the secret boss you unlock truth mode that translates ingame text.
If you liked Dark Souls, exploration games, and games that had backtracking then try Titan Souls. If you don't then play something else, I dunno.

Positives:

I am not one to write long reviews, but i am gonna make an exception here.
Senran kagura Shinovi Versus is basically a beat em up/hack n slash where you defeat enemies and bosses while playing as one of 22 ninjas...who are also busty schoolgirls...well...most of them. Bossfights are against the other characters and defeating them ends the mission, giving you exp and cool new moves.
The biggest elephant in the room is the fanservice, and it is a bit of an acquired taste to some but i bloody love it. I mean, the very non subtle perverted humor is plain hilarious and the girls transforming and getting their clothes ripped is quite a pleasant sight to see. Then again, you are not me (be glad) and you might not enjoy all the boobs jiggling before you. But the game is not just a mass of giggly♥♥♥♥♥♥ i can assure you.
The gameplay is pretty solid and fast paced. You can dash, heavy attack, weak attack, jump and block and more stuff i might have forgotten. The characters' playstyles are quite diverse and some have attacks that are marginally different from the rest. They can also transform into their shinobi outfit or go frantic. Both heal you completely, but while transforming allows you to create more flowing and powerful comboes and aerial raves, frantic is all about brute strength and speed while sacrificing defensive prowess. After launching enemies in the air you can chase after them and combo them further (known as an aerial rave) and you can do heavy attacks in comboes to change up your combo or simply make it shorter. You can also charge up the standard heavy attack for a breach art which instantly knocks enemies flying and breaks their guard.
Depending on what transformation you used (or did not use) you gain yin, yang or flash affinity which gives you bonuses for the transformation that fits them (yin=frantic, yang=transformation, flash=none of them).
As for the story it is actually pretty damn intriguing. It takes place after the events of Senran kagura burst (which i have played before shinovi versus as well as deep crimson) and it introduces the Gessen academy as well as a new Hebijo after Homura&co became renegades. The stories revolve around them and each school has their own story you can do as well as each girl having their own story known as shinobi girl's heart. While the shinobi girls' heart stories are lighthearted and pretty meaningless, the main story is pretty good and exceeds expectations. It even gets surprisingly dark at times, although i already knew it can enter those grounds as i have played Burst and 2 before. The characters are also pretty well written, making them less like dolls you wanna bang and more like actual humans you care for (and you will do so in the story...trust me).
As for any other stuff, it does have a dressing room. In it you can outfit the girls with accessories and touch them from every angle you please, as well as fondling, pulling up skirts, staring and ripping. So if you take a liking to one of the characters you can get a bit more personal if you wish, or just touch every one of them...i ain't picky. It also features a store where you can get lingerie and other cool stuff.
It does not have a lot of replay value though, it does have hard mode and the previously mentioned shinobi girls' heart but that is about it honestly. But i recommend anyone to give it a try. Even if you are not a pervert who just wants to stare and fantasize (like me), you will still like the gripping stories and the overall satisfaction of slicing, punching or bucketing your enemies' clothes to pieces.
Final verdict: Good game, i recommend it to anyone.

What immediately sets
apart from its predecessors, is the fast paced & frequent action sequences. Much of the game feels like it is a rollercoaster ride, with the polish of a Hollywood blockbuster. It is evident from these sequences that Telltale have come a long way in creating ever more complex scenes to immerse the player.
is a tale of two. Uniquely, the narrative has introduced two protagonists, Rhys
& Fiona
. As you progress through the story, you frequently get to replay the same ‘scene’ from each of their perspectives. This is creatively woven together with an over-arching storyline & flashbacks. Although it does jump around quite a bit it remained easy to keep track due to the well-crafted story & dialog. I think it was a bold move from a story-telling perspective but this spin works surprisingly well.
The chemistry between Rhys & Fiona makes for some great verbal jousting, often bickering like an old married couple arguing semantics with some witty banter. The jokes come thick & fast between all the characters interactions, many of which had me laughing so hard! The bro-tastic scene was terrific & some of the other embellishment ‘dream’ scenes were hilarious! It’s not only in the dialog that holds comedic value, but also in the physical comedy that ensues throughout, from the clever facial expressions to the crazy antics in the all-out action scenes.
All of the characters introduced through the episodes were memorable, great personalities & well voice acted.
was one of my favs, voiced by Patrick Warburton,
along with the ever-so-adorable
; it’s certainly not hard to become fond of the characters you encounter.
I found myself with many ‘WOW’ moments like you see above, that just were begging for a screenshot to be taken! The world is saturated with colour & rich in detail, with many scenes
used providing something interesting or hidden to discover
. I expect there is more Easter Eggs I didn’t even notice
being a player of the original
. Rhys has cyborg implants to add another layer to what you can see in the world, which also introduces a number of other gameplay elements that I won’t spoil for you. :)
My leisurely play though took around 10 hours for the 5 episodes with no real technical issues to report. I did see a couple of minor texture popping issues & the odd clipping issues but neither lasted long enough to detracted from the experience.
Only two really minor improvement suggestions I have is that
, unlike many games, does not pause the game when wireless controller loses connection or has dead batteries. With timing a big factor by design it would be nice if it was better supported for those that do not have a keyboard handy
to pause automatically so none of those precious seconds are lost.
Secondly, there are scenes using a new, more ‘fighting style-esque’ multi direction responses. The response time of the game was slow when having to hit multiple directions or buttons, often resulting in having to hit them several times before they register.
I did really enjoy the more complex fighting/action sequences overall; it felt at times like a 21st century version of a
or
game! Just wish it was harder! After seeing what was accomplished in the action scenes here, I would love to see a pure action game from Telltale in the future with a stronger focus on timing & precision.
My minor gripes aside, there is really is nothing to fault in this excellent action adventure game
. I enjoyed this one so much I played through the last 4 chapters in the same day.
I didn’t want the rollercoaster to stop!
I laughed, I had fun .. I had a blast!

*This review is based on a pre-release version.  Some of my issues are related to the engine used to build the game, rather than the game, per se.  But many fans of RPG may be used to the engine*
This is a good RPG to pass the time. My initial attempt, like other reviews, ended in death after about 2 encounters, and the User Interface was also a bit of a bind to get used to as I am not used to this style of RPG interface.  However, I'm glad I pursued this game because the next game I was able to progress a good way through, got much more used to the UI  and really enjoyed the variety of monsters, characters and the story.  This game has about 3 hours of enjoyable gameplay, but if you play again certain elements are random such as treasure chests and encounters.  I do recommend this as a good casual game for RPG fans who want a few hours of entertainment within a new story.
Positives:
- Atmospheric epic opening screen.
- Random loot, different every time.
- Good achievements - positive for achievement hunters.
- Varied characters who set a good few quests.
- A good selection of monsters / combinations of monsters to fight.
- Good developer who listens to fans and cares about the games.
Improvement opportunities:
- The game is pretty linear with lack of freedom to fully explore, though gives some feel of free movement.  The quests dictate how to move backwards and forwards down the same path in order to progress.
- Music a bit too modern for the setting in my opinion, though dramatic in encounters.
- Lack of tutorial and help in initial battles. For example I didn't know you can choose to leave the encounter.
- UI takes time to get used to i.e. right click to exit, to equip items you have to click on item twice - too many clicks.  Also the quests don't tick off distinctly enough.
- Screens cutting to battles lag on my PC.
- The difficulty needs work - the first game was too hard in initial encounters, but the second game once used to the game too easy as I had loads of potions, weapons and money that I'd never need.  I easily won every combat.
- Quite basic combat, two options initially, extra attacks are quite expensive to purchase.  i.e. an early mystic wants 100's of crowns, but early on in the game you wont have that much money.
- Levelling up doesn't increase stats automatically, but you get points to spend.
- You have to pay in game money to save the game, I believe the system is.  Not a fan of that as I prefer saving often.
Overall - a very good effort at developing a nice little adventure RPG with a good amount of variety. Despite some concerns, it's fairly easy to see past these as the game is very enjoyable.  This game is very fairly priced as I think it's worth about £5/$8, but is available for less. Thank you to the developer for creating this game and giving me a chance to review.
My rating 6.5/10 - 65%.  Recommended for RPG and adventure fans.

Telltale Games does it again.
TL;DR: This is their best story since Season 1 of The Walking Dead. Final recommendation: pick this up at full price as soon as you can. You don't need any prior Borderlands knowledge to enjoy this story.
Story:
As someone that hasn't played any of the Borderlands games (save for about 10 hours or so in BL2), I was kind of scared going into this that I wouldn't understand anything. There are a few little references here and there, but a complete Borderlands novice like myself was able to grasp everything and fully enjoy the story.
You follow the story of Rhys, a Hyperion company man looking to screw over a higher up who screwed you over, and you also play as Fiona, a Pandoran-born con artist that's always looking for the next big deal that'll set her, her sister, and their con-artist mentor up for life. Without giving away much of the story, you end up making new friends and enemies from both Hyperion and Pandora, your little ragtag group of friends up in a race for a Vault against bandits and corporations alike.
Critically speaking, there is actually quite a bit of character development here, especially with the way you can control the way your characters develop. Are you a cold-hearted, callous, and overall ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kinda guy? There's dialogue options for that. Do you want to create more enemies than friends? Go right ahead. Your choices in this actually effect how everyone reacts to you, and Telltale has masterfully worked choice into this story. Because of the development of the characters, you'll definitely get attached to them. When a character dies that was kind-hearted and didn't deserve to die, or one that you particularly liked, you'll feel really sad. I actually cried in the finale. Real tears.
Oh, and did I mention humor? There's TONS of it. And it's very tastefully done; many a time was I laughing out loud.
Gameplay:
The standard point-and-click adventure that is Telltale's trademark. If it ain't broke, don't fix it. The quicktime elements are smooth, and while they aren't particularly challenging, they're definitely fun.
What I hated:
Uh, there's no Season 2 of Tales from the Borderlands announced. That's literally it. I honestly can't think of any negatives to this game.
Final recommendation:
110% worth every penny at full price. Pick. It. Up.

March 7th: The review has been updated. Check the bottom of the review for more details
Have beaten the game a few days ago. Now, if you are looking for a review with some details, and if you are still not sure whether you should buy this game or not, then read on.
First, many people seem to be talking about the whole connection issues, and yes, it appears you need to be connected to the Xenoverse server in order to even play offline. But do you get disconnected so often that, it is almost unplayable? Not really. Most of the time, the offline mode works without any issues. But usually the online mode is off, and you most likely will end up seeing the message stating that the Xenoverse online is currently off. But yes, this game basically requires you to level up and all anyway (Unfortunately I have not done the online mode yet, so I might add some more to this review when I get my hands on it), so in the end, you should have no problem playing the game, at least the offline mode. And I will explain why the game is made like an MMORPG later in the review.
Now, let me point out the things that make this game "good".
First, the combat system. If you are thinking this game might be the Battle of Z 2.0, then please give it a chance. This is ABSOLUTELY nothing like the Battle of Z, and feels nothing like that game, either. First, Battle of Z, as far as I know, is pretty slow when you want to rush right into the enemy, in fact, you can't really do that. And many people complained how the game feels a lot more like a strategy game. But thankfully, as the game was made by different company (Dimps, the company that made the most famous DB game ever, Budokai 3), this game really focuses more on action, and the game is quite engaging. Many of the missions can be pretty hard, in fact, you must keep grinding in order to even stand a chance against stronger opponents and beat harder missions (So yes, this game is like an RPG game). And you might be thinking "Are you serious? I am not buying a game like that, that sounds like wasting a lot of time", but it shouldn't take much time to level up fast, only if you knew where to level up. But yes, just like an RPG game, there are status effects like poison and such. Probably this is the first fighting game that has so many RPG elements in it.
And yes, the game might be hard, but compared to the Battle of Z, this game is very forgiving and a lot easier to unlock more characters. The game is challenging, but it is challenging enough to make you come back and grind more, so if you like the Dragonball franchise and good fighting games, you will most likely be playing this game for hours.
There are many (But not THAT many as far as I know) clothes that you can buy, and also there are many skills that you can buy as well. And getting trained by the DB characters and get new sets of skills is pretty interesting, too.
Now, on to the problems of the game.
As I have mentioned, the whole combat system is fun and engaging. However, in most cases, the environments can not really be destroyed. Sure, there are houses and many places that are breakable, only making the game look far more fancier during the battle, but when you use wave-style beams and such, you can see the ground being destroyed due to it, but the destroyed part disappears instantly. It is pretty much a small thing to think about, but I really wish the destroyed parts could just stay destroyed.
And I wish I could see how big the map is. When I try to run away from strong enemies, I end up finding myself pushing the invisible barrier, as the barrier does not appear until you are right near it. This can be pretty irritating, as the enemies can come right at you pretty fast and you just don't know how big the stage is. Well, probably you will understand when you play the game, especially when you want to run away from real tough enemies.
And now, I really am not sure why Dimps had to just put the elements of Dragonball Online. Towa and Mira, the main enemies of Xenoverse are basically the original characters that first appeared in Dragonball Online. And the whole character creation idea and such basically is from the DB Online as well. Dragonball Online is the Korean-made MMORPG that failed to be successful, and probably Bandai Namco just could not let go of the elements from DB Online, so I am assuming that led them to make the Xenoverse like a "successor" to the DB Online. But in reality, because of this, basically there are times that you can not even play offline since you need to be connected to the Xenoverse server. The chance of not being able to play the offline is around 10%, which is not a lot (And most of the time you can just log in when you just try again anyway), but it still can be pretty irrtating for many players. And since the game functions more like an MMORPG, if you want to play 1 vs 1 or 3 vs 3 type of game modes, you must first "log in" and then go to the place where there are robots and ask them. I am not really sure why anyone needs to be walking all the way just to play those modes (Even though it takes around 10 seconds to get there from the starting point, if my memory serves me correctly).
I mean, I can see Bandai Namco wanted an MMORPG type Dragonball game, but I think they could've made this a little bit easier and more convenient.
But honestly, as you can see, my complaints are pretty much minor things. The story mode is all about a new story, so you will enjoy the story mode if you are a fan of Dragonball franchise, and I believe as a Dragonball game, I can just tell you that it is very entertaining.
And I can say personally, this is "the Game of the Year".
And maybe I could say, finally "the Game for the Dragonball Fans".
530,000 out of 10 (You'd know what 530,000 is, if you know DB)
*UPDATE*----
Let me point out some more things that I forgot to mention.
*Graphics: 9.5 out of 10
Now, many people have wondered what kind of graphics it will get. A PS3 version or a PS4 version. Turns out, both versions are not all that different in the end. The main difference between them was the FPS. And guess what, the PC users can enjoy 60FPS, so I would say the PC version is as good as the PS4 version, if not the same (My Steam FPS counter usually says I get around 58~62FPS). So, if you are worried about the graphics of the PC version, don't be. In fact, I never really cared about the graphics throughout the entire game, and I bet no one really does.
*Gameplay: 9.5 out of 10
The Battle of Z felt really slow, weak and the difficulty of the game was a nightmare. I personally liked DB Raging Blast 2, but I actually like this one more since the game can be a lot more chaotic once there are so many enemies against you or when it is 3 vs 3. I just beat the secret campaign which unlocks two of the very famous Saiyan characters and the first mission, my goodness was it hard. But that mission surely tested my skills fully, and when I beat the mission, I was pretty happy with the fact that I could've finished it. It really is that thing that makes this game so fun. Wolfenstein 3D was the game that brought the FPS Genre on he map. At least until Doom came out then everyone forgot about it. You play as William B.J. What a pleasant surprise! The initial pitch made me stay away: that it was a game just about boss fights, all of which required fast reflexes to avoid one-hit death, all hinging around their weak points. That is all the game does, yet it does this brilliantly. Bosses obey very different rule sets, some mirroring how you use the bow and single arrow, others being giant mimic chests or tentacled plants, requiring very different approaches. It's a game with one weapon, the bow, and you only have one arrow which you'll have to retrieve if you miss. Yet the versatility of challenges in the boss fights with that one weapon are inspiring. It's all done with remarkable pixelart and a soundtrack that often draws on Transiberian Orchestra and Legend of Korra. By the end, it oozes style and begs you to hunt down the hidden titans. I had a blast.

Based on the full price, I wouldn't recommend the game. But if on sale, I would.
- The atmosphere/music/art is wonderful.
- The storytelling is my absolute favorite type (tells a story through atmosphere, and things you see/interact with, not through dialogue, this leaves wonderful things to the imagination).
- Games that just have boss fights are great. I only say this because there are not many. If this market because oversaturated it would get tiredsome.
- You are astonishingly squisy (this would be bad exept for the next point).
- Bosses are astonishingly squishy (they are intimidating and take figuring out, and even once you do, learning proper execution is a challenge).
So because bosses are so squishy, and boss fights are so short, it works that you are so squishy. What doesn't work is the tedious nature it takes to restart a boss fight. Spawn points are typically better than in the demo thankfully. We're only talking double digit seconds to start a fight after dying. But, when boss fights are so lethal and so short, the time it takes to retry turns into quite a turn off. The world is great to explore, and the first ~3 times entering the bosses lair are great and atmosphereic. But if your like me and average over a dozen deaths per boss fight, it just starts to drag. Problem is, you are pumped and anxious to get another high adrenaline try, not to switch gears to the more medatative walking down the peaceful entry path, making it jaring. And with the bosses being a puzzle to figure out how to beat them, it encourages experamentation... but then the fight restart time feels like it's punishing any experamentation that results in a quick death (quite likely when experamenting). It gets discouraging to turn the game on because of this. Between this, and the price being a little too high for what it is, I don't recommend it. But I also don't think it's bad to get, particularly on sale. I just have to lean one way, so it's leaning towards the "no" side, but not by much.
Even though I like that this is all boss fights, if you had non-boss enemies, this actually might be more bearable. I understant that sounds silly since it would increase the time between boss fights. But it's be action challenge time, not tedious restart time. There's a difference between a game being work, and a game feeling like work. "Being work" example: walking through a level with enemies to fight. "Feeling like work" example: walking down a path of. I'm not suggesting non-boss enemies be put into the game. Just making a point about why it feels so painful to restart a fight to many here (see other reviews). Better than adding non-bosses, have respawn be at the boss chamber entrance.
Tips if you get this game:
- Don't watch how to beat bosses on youtube. The main part of the game is the puzzle. If you are the type of person who wants the puzzle nature solved for you, so you can work on just the technical execution, there are far better games for that.
- Don't go for the quick kill. When you meet a new boss, first just try to survive in their presense.
- When you shoot your arrow, wait to pick it up. Most early game deaths for me were showing no patience to get my arrow back because I had the delusion it made me safer. Pick it up, but use that time to just try to dodge the boss and learn their ways.
- Those last 2 bullets wouldn't be my natural style of play, but with the time to restart a fight issue, it helps the fun play time to tedious restart time more bareable.

Then noteably there's the music, which easily invokes the same space-western fantasy of Firefly fame which pulls you in even more. Rimworld doesn't stop at selling you a challenge or even a story - it's an environment for for producing stories.

Okay, I thought I'd just share my first impression of this.
Make no mistake, this is a highly unfinished game. They describe its current state as beeing "pre-alpha". There's not a whole lot of content here. As far as I know, there's just one multiplayer mode available at the moment. There's also some singleplayer training areas and a sandbox mode of some sort. There's currently only one weapon available, which is a submachine gun with a holographic sight. There are no customization options, I'm afraid. You can't crouch or climb either. A few snags there.
However, what you do have is a basic, fairly good-looking multiplayer shooter. It's quite playable and somewhat addicting, actually. I like the environmental factor to the game. Sometimes it's sunny, sometimes it's raining, and sometimes it's completely dark. I particularly enjoy the last one, where you must be careful not to use your flashlight more than you absolutely have to, or the enemy will spot you. Sneaking around in the dark and ambushing people is a lot of fun. When it's raining your visor gets blurred, so you might want to open your helmet to see clearer, and sometimes there are gases that, I assume, requires you to have your visor down. Additionally, some of the maps physically changes between rounds, introduciong yet another variation. The very minimalistic hud is also quite nice and realistic. That's right; no fancy mini-map here, although you do see icons if you have your visor down. Sounds of footsteps and weapons is also important when you're sneaking about. All of these things makes this an interesting tactical game.
So, what is my early verdict? It has some potential. In its current state it's a fair multiplayer experience, with some interesting aspects. However, there are a lot of shortcomings in the form of missing features. I got my copy as part of a cheap bundle, and if you happen to come across a deal like that or a sale on Steam, I suggest you grab it and try it out. Otherwise, I'd recommend holding onto your money for a while yet to see how it turns out. Unless you don't care about money, that is.

I thought I would edit my review, seeing as I had been playing it a bit more over the past few days.
Interstellar Marines still is very much in Early Access, and has been for as long as I can remember, seeing it pop up on Kickstarter some years ago. Though fear not, though we've had some shaky EA games recently, the attention to detail and updates coming to this game show no sign of slowing down. We received a campaign type map mode to play either singleplayer or cooperatively, there's also another more linear map that can be played singleplayer or cooperatively, and then there are the whole host of survival and extinction maps to play either singleplayer or cooperatively. This is all on top of the previous PvP game mode that was already implemented.
The coop and singleplayer have you facing against both armed and unarmed CTRs, or Combat Training Robots. There is a small bug where when you kill an armed one it still comes up saying unarmed, and it says +15 points for killing one when you only get 5; but they're minor issues.
The dev team at Zero Point Software really know how to do atmosphere. In some of the survival modes, near the end of the sequence the whole map goes pitch black, you HAVE to use your flashlight. Of course, this means you can only see in the direction you're facing, it also means that when you reload the light points into the air somewhat as it's an underbarrel mounted flashlight. This makes for super intense moments when you can hear the unarmed CTRs running towards you, but have no idea where they are.
The environments are also amazing, the rain and effect it leaves on your helmet visor, the fog, the alarm lighting, and just the areas you're dropped into in general. Definitely a fantastic game, if you ever see it in a bundle, I would buy it without question as you will not regret it, even the Steam store asking price isn't bad for what you're getting, especially with the stream and quality of updates.

WARNING: THIS REVIEW REFLECTS MY PERSONAL EXPERIENCE DURING THE ALPHA STAGE OF DEVELOPMENT, UPDATE 12
IT IS IN NO WAY A FULL PRODUCT REVIEW AND IT WILL BE UPDATED IN THE FUTURE AS THE GAME EVOLVES
UPDATE: CHECK AT THE BOTTOM FOR UPDATE 10, 11 and 12!
Interstellar Marines is a tactical shooter which aims to innovate several aspect of co-operative teamplay, and succeeds in doing so.
While it's still in a very Alpha stage, (there's only one gun, the assault rifle, and there's only one game mode, king of the hill domination) it already started showing why this shooter brings something new to the table.
In this game, your helmet is your UI. You take your helmet off, and you resign seeing tactical info like scoreboard, ammo, health, shield, teammate positions, next rank, and so on. The thing is it also gives you advantages. While using your helmet provides good info like that, it also muffles the sounds surrounding you, which makes it hard to hear if there's someone walking nearby. Also, when fighting in some scenarios with weather like raining or snowing, or while looking straight to the light, your sight will get blurried, either by the raindrops falling on your helmet, or because of the cold, or because of the light refraction. Also, your helmet will get dirty as you go through the map under different effects so it will get blurrier and blurrier. Taking your helmet off and putting it on at the right times gives you tactical advantage.
Friendly fire is always on and at 100% damage rate, which is great because that is the way it should be.
While the game currently lacks of many standard features like crouching and going prone, it already shows promise.
CURRENT STATUS AS OF FEBRUARY 11, 2014
PROS
- Innovative helmet UI system.
- Great settings, from storms to dark caves.
- EXCELLENT, and I can't even begin to describe how good they are, SOUNDS. I mean, you feel like you're really there. I dare you stand under the rain in this game and not loving how it sounds when it falls on your suit.
- Fair and balanced gameplay (seriously, the most balanced shooter I've seen so far).
- Each match has several rounds changing the setting of the map (it can rain, it can become dark, it can be under a bright sunlight, it can snow, and all during a single match, making taking the helmet on and off something necessary).
- Optimized engine, no FPS drops so far, while looking beautiful at the same time.
- You can play with lag and almost not even notice it.
- Shadows and body immersion is really good. You can see your own body looking below, and you can calculate if you're hiding well or not.
- Great hitboxes. No refrigerator box here.
- The best online community I have ever found around a game. No hate, just good people. Really, I've never had so much fun talking with people inside a game until playing this. I must congratulate every single one of you guys for being so awesome!
CONS
- No ducking at the time. (ADDED IN UPDATE 10!)
- No proning at the time. (ADDED IN UPDATE 10!)
- Only one weapon (assault rifle) at the time.
- Only one gamemode (king of the hill team deathmatch) at the time.
- Few servers (all official alpha servers) at the time. (ADDED MORE SERVERS IN UPDATE 10!)
Is it worth its full price at the time? Nnnnn... maybe. I'd say wait before going full price on it.

Absolutely hilarious if you're into political / cultural satire, more so if you've ever worked for a bureaucratic organization and were frustrated with your inability to get anything done. The game uses traditional point and click adventure mechanics, and the puzzles are all fairly logical within a limited set of environments, so it's not too hard to figure out what to do. You can fail the game by making the wrong choices, but failure is always rewarded by a humorous description of why your quest has ended, and choosing "Continue" from the main menu puts you right back to just before your ill-fated decision, which makes failure itself enjoyable.
It's a short game, about 2-3 hours play time. As such, I recommend it at the $3 price point, and only for people who enjoy its satirical subject matter; this game is not for children or those desiring a cute Sierra or LucasArts adventure.

Or you're making a japanese game. That said, TPAoE is a very conventional and unconventional game. From the technical and mechanical side, it's an adventure game. .  Credit where it's due for having so much dialogue written for all the combinations made, though...only in these areas will you find partial voice-acting.

For as far as shooters have come, they can still be boiled down to their fundamentals. Shooting and navigating levels. Wolfenstein 3D set the groundwork for a genre that hasn't ceased being the most popular in the world. If you enjoy shooters in any capacity, you owe it to Wolfenstein 3D for popularizing them.
Does the game hold up in the modern era? Yes and no. No in that it's incredibly simplistic. It's nice to have something with such a clear goal, but playing through a single episode is all it takes to see the entirety of Wolfenstein 3D's bag of tricks. Other than different boss characters and one new enemy, you can fully understand this game in about 30 minutes.
The level designs start off fairly obtuse, but get refined as the game progresses. The prequel episodes, for instance, are very concise and fast. Things are laid out in a more logical fashion and the levels don't take more than 5 minutes (save for a few agonizing levels in Episode 6). The earlier levels suffer from being sprawling and lacking definition in their textures.
The weapons are definitely limited, but it's cool to have everything utilize the same ammo. Whatever weapon you decide to go with is more like an optional challenge than anything. Trying to knife everyone may be futile, but it can be done. Getting that gattling gun is like putting the game on Easy mode, so it's hard to not default to it.
As for the boss battles, they range from hilariously easy to pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The first boss is a push over (and he comes back for Episode 5), but taking on Hitler is a different story. He has hit-scan weapons that basically hit you with 100% accuracy. He also has floating magicians and a second form. It's insane.
Some of the levels are also overloaded with enemies. You start off with basically a pistol and have no possible way to take them on, unless you are astute enough to find the secrets. Secrets were basically half the game back in the day, so it's not hard to understand why valuable items were placed there.
What isn't acceptable is how some necessary keys and a few exits are stuck behind "secrets". That is just cruel. I guess level design standards were more based on finding secrets back in 1992, but it doesn't hold up well.
In every other regard, though, Wolfenstein 3D is solid. It was a groundbreaking game back in it's time and it still remains a rather fun and glorious romp through Hitler's castle. ID Software would later perfect the formula with Doom, but it's always cool to see where things began.
