Graphics-wise this is one of the most varieted 2D platforms I have seen, almost every 2 level (of 104, 8 per console) have a different theme, and this is one of the main motives to keep you playing, but it ends as a shot on the foot as the game doen't have enough material to make not make it look generic. it can be clearly noticed how the developers didn't have a focus when you notice that some music creators didn't know what felling to work (there's musics called amiga and snes...)
Gameplay suffers of this lack of definition, it has the same feeling all the time because the main obstacle, the
, it really bogs the pace of the game and makes a lot of cheap kills (and the game is proud of it)  as it lacks previous warmings. Most enemies act similar, but has the two most anonying elements to have: Following and randon patterns. Sometimes you can be locked because of bad placement and insistceny of a eneny on a place. There's inscontancies about game rules (sometimes, crytals fall, sometimes don't, sometimes no floor means bottonless, sometimes doesn't)
Level design is another poor thing, it many times doesn't know what it's doing it certaing platforms, but in special it doesn't know sometimes where to place the player, putting you in places where you need to go forward and back, making you go zig zag. Almost every level has the same challange (something related with spikes). The game boasts about having secrets and collectables, while some are well made, others are really blalant and makes me think that they were added for display only... But the top goes to the delay bonus you can have to jump off platforns you don't are on, necessary for two levels and the guide dang it! Some levels lack old-school good sense, as not having enemies go thru scenes if you are making a game with locked cameras, or having visual references for bigger than one screen jumps.
The game is very buggy, I found random grapical lag, the game drawing stuff off-screen (you can see extra stuff up and down, problems with getting off of the airship, pressing anemies with pushables, You following the platform acceleration you jumped off (visible on the first amiga level, probably a feature, but makes jumps a lot harder), and bugs about tile collision on the first console (you will sink on water even if you are more than half sit on a solid tile).
In the museum aspect the games mess-up badly (and this is main motive for a negative review). To start, we have a widescreen resolution when you are playing consoles of "square" resolutions (the resolutions are even display in the info charts...). We have a mario sound effect play on every console who has a time switch (including Sega ones... really?), grapics quality that suspicily overpasses the original systens..., lacking caracterization for 16-bit console graphics. Thinking that showing that you will die a lot is retro... And only tecnical information about the systens, almost ignoring historical placement of the consoles... (where is the console wars between Sega and Nintendo?, main inovations between platforms?) even more salty because of all the useless apearences of the professor in the levels.
I feel sorry about pixel, he went out thinking that he discovered his past, but he doesn't really know why it was awesome.

The game as it is now is very well polished, looks, sounds and 'feels' great and will only get better, (and more expensive), as more stuff gets added.

Pick this game up and it's unlikely, in time, you'll be dissapointed.

Fun game for oldskool players. Just like back in the old days, this game shows why good gameplay doesn't need to be complex and why simple graphics are not an issue when you have something called replayability. That replayability comes from classic best time lists for both the single levels and all level times combined. Hi-score liste and best time lists - that's what caused players back in the 80s to replay the same games and levels, and try and optimize your own performance. Who cares about achievements? Okay, the game also has achievements (for younger players, I suppose?), but that's really just a sidenote.
As for the game itself, you are a pixel that plays 8 levels each in the style of a "historic" computer/console. It's basically a platformer and the double-jump feature is a nice touch. Collisions sometimes seem to lack a little bit in precision, but that's not an issue really. You'll get the hang of it.
However, there is one sad issue with this game: There's a pause bug/glitch, which you can use for cheating. The game devs don't care, which is sad, but most players seem to be competitive enough not to make use of that glitch. Otherwise I wouldn't be number 10 in the overall level times list right now. ;) So, those best times list would be a little bit more fun and increase replayability a bit further, if the devs coded a proper pause function, but oh well ... they probably didn't want to have to reset the list times, because they don't really seem to believe in the replayability of this game themselves, but I do. If they fixed the pause function and reset all the times, I would happily go on the same journey again. ;)
About the level designs and if you can actually recognize old games: There was one level which instantly reminded me of a Simpsons game. There's also a tavern called "Joe's", so I'm probably right about that level. While I played this game on C64, this level is not part of the C64 levels.
The shop site also mentions Turrican, which is one of the most famous C64 games, of course. Don't bother looking for anything Turrican-esque in the C64 levels though, you won't find anything. Basically, the graphic style that Turrican made famous and the graphics revolution that came along with it, can't be found in any of the C64 levels. There's an Amiga level though that has Turrican in its title. I've never played Turrican on Amiga, so I can't say if that level actually is Turrican-esque. It doesn't look like the original C64 Turrican at all though.
Oh, one Master System level clearly is Sonic-esque. I've played Sonic on Mega Drive, but there's not a big difference, really. So, apart from those 3 classic games, I couldn't really recognize any of the games I used to play back in the days. Of course, I haven't played all classic games. But it doesn't really bother me that I don't recognize more classic games in this new game. The important thing is that the classics have the same charm as back then and that the sound is awesome! Now THAT is how game music should sound like!
All in all, a nice game. If you love classic platformers, you can't make anything wrong here.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is one of the best Dragon Ball games to come out in a long time. The battles feel nice, the character customization does it's job well, and the story adds a new interesting spin on the DBZ story we all know. They did a good mix of fighting, and rpg mechanics. You are able to equip up to 7 skills, and put skill points into 6 different stats. The skills are easy to use, but it is when to use them that takes skills. The hand-to-hand combat feels nice, and you can string together nice combos, that can string into more combos.
The story is nice, but really short. There are few missions in the main campaign, and they don't cover most of the story. They hit all the main points of the DBZ story, but they leave out things like cooler, and most of the movies besides broly, and bardok. They are costumes from other movies, but no missions/characters.
The multiplayer is fun, and works farly well. The servers are haing problems right now, but that will be fixed soon. There are some cheap tactics that people can use, and are annoying to deal with. Most of the time though you will have a far fight.
The game is not perfect though. Some missions have you fighting a 3-5 on 1, and the computers will stagger you, and basically make it impossible to move. It is possible to deal with it, and win but it can be very annoying to the player.

What can you say about Borderlands that hasn't already been said? Well, probably a lot, but I doubt much of it would actually be relevent to this game. I've only done one playthrough which spanned 19 hours of actual gameplay over 2 or 3 months, because my guild in WoW had me raiding so damn much. That alone should speak to how great this game is. Think about playing a game off and on over the course of 2 or 3 months. For many games, you might lose interest. I certainly lose interest in most games if I'm playing like this. However, Borderlands kept my attention throughout. The funny dialogue, the very fun combat, the excellent equipment and inventory system, and the "comical" look of the game kept my interest and kept me coming back expecting (and receiving) lots of fun. One thing that almost everyone seems to agree on would be the ending. I'm not going to go into specifics, even though at this point if anything gets spoiled it's your own damned fault. However, I'm hoping that maybe people who have not yet played Borderlands might read this review before deciding whether or not they want to buy and play it. As epic as this game is, the ending seems to be quite anticlimactic. Throughout the game, things tend to pick up steadily. Then, you get to the final boss, and you're left wondering....ok, where's the epic boss I've been expecting in this game? Well...unfortunately, it's not really there. The final boss is kind of out of place according to the story of Borderlands. This final entity definitely could have been referenced better in previous parts of the game, leading up to a more "expected" final boss, which in turn would lead to more satisfaction upon defeating it. That said, I still absolutely love Borderlands, even with my one playthrough. I've told my friends many times that I plan to play through this game on each of the other classes as well (first time was on Lilith the Siren) but, other games keep on taking up my time. Now lets talk a bit about DLC. Buy it. Buy all of it. Now. I was completely satisfied with every bit of DLC for Borderlands. It was all very fun, very intense, and very awesome. That's really all I can say about it, because it's just so simply amazing. 9/10 for Borderlands, 10/10 for Borderlands DLC. If you decide to go ahead with this game, good luck and have fun, Vault Hunters!

1992 ID software released the "Progenitor of First Person Shooters", it is still remembered as one of the greatest classical games of all time. I resently played this using one of its numerous ports, namely ECWolf. It added support for several control schemes much like in a modern shooter, giving me a good reason to jump back in and play it.
And bhoyo.. Was it hard. I almost immediately cranked the difficulty to "Death Incarnate" and I have currently blasted through 5 of the 6 total episodes and during that time of pixelated and very profound carnage, I realised something.
I was enjoying the game. It was a rather strange feeling, mostly due to not having it happen in a long while. The last game that I remember doing it was Mafia and yes, I realise that it is an entirely different game and it is very narrative driven, but I enjoyed it. Something that cannot be said from some of the games I have resently reviewed. (Fkng Bureau..)
Anyway, back to the matter at hand.
Although Wolfenstein 3D has aged, it still looks great. There is something about this early-age of computing graphics, that is just amazing. The way they had to work with hardware limitations, limited colours and not to mention floppy drives. Ughh.. I tell you, I resently got one of those cheap USB ones and I suddenly remembered how moody those fkrs are.
Where was I? Oh yes.. Even with the age of the game, its pixely graphics and all. It still manages to stay relevant, even after 23-Years. Let's think on that number there for a minute.. 23, a lifetime ago for some people. Including me and for everyone who grew up during the 90's.
I keep digressing, I apoligize. But this is partly why people appreciate these games, they are part of their past, their childhood and that is just way too important to ignore.
Let's talk about the actual game a little bit, now that I've got the nostalgia chip off my shoulder.
The game is an FPS, I can't really explain more than that. It is the most basic of things, get gun, find secret, get bigger gun, kill everything.
The game is silly, very much so and it does not give a f**k. The story is the most basic of basics, yet again.
The biggest issue that I have with the game, is the level layouts, they are mazes. I remember a wonderfull story of being stuck in one level for a day, just because I could not find the door and to make it better, there is no map system.
There is very little that can be said about the game besides these two things, yet again, it is the first. I know that tere are other FPS games before Wolf3D, but this is the one everyone remembers so.. Meh.
I don't think I need to pad this out any longer, I think you got what I'm saying here, right?
But to recap.
Wolfenstein 3D is a worthwile classic. Even for something of its age, it manages to stay entertaining. The modding and source-port community keeps the game alive, there are numerous mods on sites like ModDB. That can be used to enhance the experience or change it completely. I would highly recommend the ECWolf mod, it is easy to install and only reguires a copy of the game files found in the program folder. Similiar to Brutal Doom in that respect.
The game can take a good number of hours to finish, even with the mods making it more playable. But the enjoyment is there and for those brave enough to go-a-romping through Castle Wolfenstein,
stay calm,
keep a gun handy,
and always eat the dog-food when at low health.

This game is a great example of Steam's quality control, because they can't hide behind anything else. They can't say anything like "It was on greenlight and the public voted for it, so that means it's the public's fault." The only reason that this game was put onto Steam was because it was made in the source engine, yeah, imagine if you made the worst game ever, put no amount of effort into a game, most people would say that it's terrible, but Valve/Steam would accept it because it was made with their engine, but the trouble is, you can't, because Dark Arz Entertainment beat you to it.
If you can't tell by the screenshots, this is a clone of Left 4 Dead but is set in what was supposed to be the year when the world ended, as predicted by the Aztecs. Now, that doesn't sound like a too bad a concept but it's the execution and the laziness of the whole game here in general.
You all know that the source engine gives off good graphics and are the type of graphics that will still live up to any day, as shown by games like Half-Life 2, Left 4 Dead and Garry's Mod. The graphics in Revelations 2012 look like the were done in the earliest version of Source engine, I'm talking the original Half-Life's graphics. If you're saying "they used an older version" because they didn't, the setup of the game is done in the Half-Life 2 and Left 4 Dead style, so there's no excuse for the game to look this bad.
The gameplay is marginally the same as Left 4 Dead but add in some unresponsive controls, unneccesary controls that overlap the necessary controls so the game doesn't know which action you want to perform so it's madatory that you rebind the keys before playing. The most handiest key in this game is Alt+F4. They also somehow manage to take the once addicting gameplay of Left 4 Dead and make it boring with no AI director so you're experiencing the same thing over and over again.
The sound is also terrible. Imagine the horrible sound of a guy throwing up his lunch into a bugle horn, proceeding to make a sound out of it and then proceeding to throw up into a trombone and playing them both simulatenously. The sound in this game is unbareable to listen to.
Revelations is a chunk of boring mess, cobbled together with bad graphics, disgusting sounds and taking a beloved engine and abusing the hell out of how it's used, get a grip Valve, don't make yourselves grow a boner just because someone else is using your engine. Actually ply the games yourself and see what they're like or stick it on greenlight and hide behind someone else.
Pros
+ Nothing
Cons
- Bad graphics
- Unbearable sound
- Misuse of an engine
- Boring gameplay
- Repetitive
Final verdict: 1/10

First off ignore the time you see as played on steam.  You can check my achievements if you desire to get a better idea of how much I've actually played.  I played this game before it was out on steam, and stopped when it did.
The combat is this game is fantastic.  It's a lot of fun, and it can get you hooked.  The balancing can leave a bit to be desired sometimes, but overall the combat is brilliant.

The game has daily login rewards, a daily bonus xp cap(that you'll need to advance), biweekly missions, monthly brawl collections, daily raid caps, and weekly resource caps.   Some of that may sound good, but what it comes down to is that the game feels like a job, and often you'll feel like you need to play even after you're getting almost no rewards from doing so.
For me the devs sucked out the fun in this game, and after watching them do this repeatedly despite the community begging for them not to, I decided to leave it behind me.  It's a shame, as the combat was a gem.

The game's format is very typical for the otome genre - an early branch onto different love interest paths with a more or less linear plotline post-branch that can reach different endings depending on combinations of choices made.  It does better than many examples of the genre in making the different love interests, as well as their plotlines, quite distinct, but I wish the choices had a little more impact on the story prior to when the ending is triggered, and/or that they seemed to have a more strong tonal connection to the highly-divergent endings.
The central conceit is a fun one, and the writers used it well in the sense that the available endings are so very different from one another.  I'm somewhat curious as to how obvious What's Really Going On is to other players prior to the game spelling it out in exposition - I figured out what was up pretty quickly, but still enjoyed the reveal.
The love interests are all well-written, and I really appreciate the diversity of gender options.  That said, particularly since Lyall is my favorite, I wish the editing had been a bit more careful/thorough, as it seems that Lyall was originally written as male and then changed to be nonbinary somewhere later in development - they are erroneously referred to many times with masculine pronouns instead of they/them, and I found that rather jarring every time it happened (both because not misgendering people matters to me, and just because it often made the narrative confusing, as I'd see "he" and think another character was being referred to).
All in all, the game's a really solid effort for a free indie VN, and I'd still be recommending to others who enjoy the genre if it wasn't free.  I'm looking forward to more from this studio.

As a kickstarter backer, I'm nothing but proud.
The community still grapples with growth and mass influxes of players when there are sales, however as time goes on, the community seems to find a really good parity between jokers and tryhards. I tend to be more the latter, but its healthy for the community to retain both.
Why talk about the community in a game review?
Because the community is here because of the game. The mechanics of teamwork, dependency on others, it -creates- community. I have no doubt that there are people who have bad experiences with this game or community, but I do think that the majority of players get to see something in this game they have a hard time finding other places, and that is a driven interest in learning, winning, and seeing others do better because it makes the team do better.
Developent:
I was there for the closed alpha, the pre-closed alpha, and the pre-pre closed alpha (golden dogtag wooo!). Naieveity is what I would describe as the early forecast. "It'll take about 2 years." and its going to take well longer, but. I'm glad they were naieve, because if they knew how much work it wouldve taken from the start it wouldve been more likely to be passed up. They've had hard times, but they keep working. They've never disappeared and left us with a steaming heap of sh-t for a game. Sometimes it takes a while for that fix to be found, but, anyone who's every worked a real job, especially in construction/production understands sometimes sh-t goes south, and not as planned. The good ones are the ones who fix it and finish it regardless, and that is something I think that OWI has done.
Thanks to them for not hosing their backers, and proving our investments in them, as sound.

My review of Gold Rush: The Game... I do enjoy this game. I recomend this sandbox type of game to the videogamer that might enjoy high, HIGH... detailed focus in how processes work with machinery in order to gain more gold. "Mr. Murphy" is built into this game BIG TIME!
I must start off by saying I am a gold (hobbist) prospector and have been since 1988. Growing up in Nothrern California and going to all of the 1894'er mining towns; gold can do this to some people ( I mean, I got bit by the gold bug).  I know this game is in it's infancy. Computer bugs are abound... but the concept of this is amazing! The charm of going out into Alaska and finding gold in a video game is a perfect match for those who like to get the gold. It is also amazingly difficult for the developers to get all of the mining nuances correct. For what I have seen after playing this game for a week is that you are the soul survivor and boss of an invisible workforce who build you wealth once they are assigned to a certain peice of kit or machinery. ( This will change in the future per the game designers modifications).This gold wealth must then be taken to a smelter and turned into ingots which then you have the choice of hoarding it for your greedy little self, or selling it on the gold market at the bank or through your tablet or at the bank. This is all very cool and has a realness to it. I also enjoy that when you go to the stores to buy supplies, you really get to load all that gear into you Army truck and haul back to home base. Minus the heavy vehicles, those are delivered with a fee.
Getting down to the nitty gritty of gold panning...sigh. It's kind of a let down. By the way, the controls make you act like a drunkard after last call. Every action is overly done. Get ready to knock everything over that is not bolted down. Luckly gold in buckets and water in buckets cannot pour out. I hope the developers continue to redevelop this section of the game. First off, the art of panning is that, an art. Every panner has their own way to shake that gold free.  If I was to practice how the game pans gold in real life I would not find any gold. The specific gravitiy of gold in water is 19.7 times heaver than water itself. Int he game it makes gold act like it is 8 times heavy. The rocks flow around like they are 7 times as heavy. The rocks should flow off the top as the pan is being dipped at 22 degree angle ( roughly, the sides of the pan should be level with the water line as it is being slowly dipped in and out of the water). Flushing a pan of gold bearing soil in water in this game is too easy. Another flaw in the game. Second the rocks and soil should not look like Kibbles and Bits dog food. ( this too is temperary) There are no "blonds" (light colored silica sands) or "cons" (black "consentrate" sands holding your possible gold). I hope in the future this is added for reality.  I have run across a silvery gold or amalgumated gold...it turned out to be a computer flaw. I was hoping for it though... it could more reality to the game. I was also hoping to walk up to the waterfall at the Old Arnolds claim in the creek and try gold nugget sniping ( not a chance!).
This game will crush your expections for the thrill of finding gold in the mountains. Gold hunting exploration is non-existant in this game.  You will only find gold where it tells you to find gold. You cannot read the rocks and try to sample certian areas other than those plotted out. (Sorry Geologists.) I did read that the game developer has made certain hotspots in the flood plains of where to dig. Reading the rocks in the landscape can create intrest to acutal prospectors. I hope in the future the game designers might add that feature to the game.  The other aspect I found wrong is that the gold bearing soils looks like overburden soils (the useless top soil trees grow in.) And the over burden soils look more like the actual workable gold bearing soils with stones and dirt. I hope this gets reversed and revised.
Is this game worth buying? If this is the type of game stlye you like then, YES!
The things I love about this game:
The Alaskan environment... A+!
The realistic machines...A+!
High focus of realism within the game (minus death, and sleep)...A+!
The work stations and shelving for equipment..A!
The gear to get the gold...A+!
The processes to get gold with machines...A+!
The physics in the game (minus the gold specific gravity)...A+!
The future intentions of the game designers...A+!
I look forward to this game maturing into an amazing gold adventure.

Squad is like ARMA minus the bullcrap. No remembering dozens of specific keybinds, no weird menu you use your scroll wheel for, no installing a bunch of mods or searching through countless servers to get an experience you enjoy. Simply open Squad, join a server, and instantly you are thrust into an intense open-world conflict in which you along with 8 squadmates can set your own objective in accordance with your team's strategy and attempt to win the game by any means necessary.
Being a squad member is fun, but the true fun of the game, at least for me, is being at the head of the action, and directing the rest of your body (your squadmates) on how to proceed. Being a squad leader in Squad is truly an incredible experience that no other game can truly match, not even ARMA. You've got eight people under you that will (usually) listen to your commands, and you've got four or five other squad leaders to communicate with so you can develop the best strategy.  There is no greater joy than leading your squad to victory, going into the next round, and having people wait for you to create a squad because you did so well. Squad Leaders can also set down Rally Points for their squadmates to have a temporary spawn point, set down FOBs to hold vital chokepoints or provide a permanent spawn, as well as other fortifications around FOBs. Squad Leaders truly control the flow of the game, and a good or bad Squad Leader can mean the difference between a victory or defeat in Squad.
But do not fret if leading is not your strong suit or your thing; every role in Squad has it's purpose. Obviously there is the important "Squad Leader" role, but the roles of Medic, Autorifleman (Machinegunner), Marksman, Anti-Tank, even Rifleman are all important and have their roles. Medics keep the war machine going, Autoriflemen provide a base of fire to cover their fellow squadmates, Marksman take out enemies from afar in accordance to the squad's objective, Anti-Tank take out those pesky and vital armored vehicles, Rifleman can set up barricades as well as act as the all-important point-men and primary attackers, all with the SL leading from the back (or on the frontlines.)
If a Squad is malfunctioning, deformed, or simply unable to work with each other, the game is simply not fun. The Squad Leader is vital to keep the squad pushing forward, but the Squad Leader cannot put down much of anything without squad members at his side. Communication and teamwork is VITAL in Squad, and without it the experience will not be enjoyable. However, whenever a Squad gets it right - they are communicating, helping each other, working together, listening to each other - the game is like none other. Luckliy, the game makes it easy to make sure Squads do have cohesion.
The only issue I have with this game is it's fierce optimization problem. Even at low settings I struggle to keep 60 frames on most maps, and I don't have a bad rig. That, along with some map glitches that involve going through the map and having to suicide to keep playing.
All in all, I have never played a multiplayer game more rewarding than Squad, and I'm excited to make this game my next primary experience and design a community around it. I would truly give this game a 10/10 if the game was optimized, bugs were fixed, and other quality of life issues were resolved. For now, I give the game a 7, but the devs are working hard on the game and I think it'll hit a solid 10/10 (meaning the game delivers 100% on its promise and is fun to play, easy-ish to run, and chock full of features) when the game is fully released.
If you are looking for a realistic first-person-shooter where communication and teamwork is required for success, look no further. Buy Squad.

Everyone else has great points. I figured I'd throw in a unique reason why I really enjoyed and recommend this game.
I have a love/hate relationship with point & click adventures. The stories are usually much better than a normal game and I really enjoy that. But many games of this type use bass ackwards logic to solve problems i.e. You have to break a window to get outside, but you can't use the hammer, that's to bash open a chest to get a piece of cloth, to clean a picture frame, to discover a key hidden behind it, to open a drawer, to find a jewelery box with a missing windup piece, to find the piece, wind up the box, to find a glass cutter... WTH did I just do?
Silent Age does not fall victim to this trope. At first I couldn't understand why. But the reason is it's episodic adventure. Each part of the story is separated by chapters. Each chapter focuses on only a few different rooms. Most adventure games open up the entire world for you to explore. That leaves lots of oportunity for frustration as one puzzle's solution would work with another IRL, but not in game.
Breaking down each part of the story into smaller pieces allowed the developers to really hone in on the puzzle aspects of the game. This is a mechanic not seen very often in adventure games and I really wish other game devs would take note. I throughly enjoyed playing this game and only once did I even need a hint as to what to do next. Kudos to these guys!!

Controls: 10/10
Being a point-and-click game, the controls are very easy to understand.
Gameplay: 10/10
This game is the embodiment of what a point-and-click puzzle game should aspire to be like. The story is not hard to understand, considering the time-travel shinanigans, however, it maintaints a compelling story throughout the entire game with elusive clues and engaging puzzles.
Atmosphere: 10/10
Though the art-style may be minimalistic, what this game achieves through level-design and ambient music really contributes to user-immersion and an eerie atmosphere.
Replay Value: 2/10
Being a game with an extremely linear story line and no alternative endings, there is minimal replay value. That being said, the game, as with most games, does come with flavorful achievements that can be earned through in-game easter-eggs.
Price: 3/10
While I do respect the game in its entirety,  I feel like the $10 price tag is too much for this game, especially considering the minimal replay value. That being said, if you are able to get this at a discount of under $3, like I did, then I highly recommend playing it. Even if the game only lasts you 2 or 3 hours, It will have been 2 or 3 hours well-spent.
Conclusion: 7/10
I was tempted to give this game an initial 9/10, but that is only because I purchased this game at a significant discount (-90%). Taking the lack of replay value into consideration, I really do not believe the $10 price tag is justifiable. That being said, if anyone picks this piece of art up for under $3, then it will be worth the time and money. *I recommend this game only if it is discounted.*

The game is a solid platformer, especially the retro graphics are what catches the eye as they are copying the graphic possibilities of all the featured consoles very well, which gives you a feeling of what it was like way back in the early days of video gaming. HOWEVER: I am a completionist by heart and while I enjoyed grinding for all the achievements (especially the additional hardcore ones) there is one particular level that is needed for the latter that is not only extremely frustrating but also sort of "unfair" and I am going to explain why (I am not going to be too precise but it is a level you unlock pretty early in the game).
In order to get the final achievement you need to collect everything there is to get in all levels which feature extra collectibles and finish them in one go - meaning that if you die you have to collect everything in the level from scratch.
This level incorporates a secret dungeon of sorts that is fairly long and features quite a few rooms compared to the size of pretty much all the other levels/secret areas in the game. I am just going to jump to the area that was bugging me.
After you got the special pickup you have to press a switch to get out of a dungeon of sorts, but the path is of course plastered with spikes and enemies, nothing unusual for a game like this if it wasn't for a final "tunnel area" with robots walking left to right. They are blocking your way and it is too narrow to evade them by jumping, forcing you to either play it smart and wait until they leave the tunnel so you can pass them or just rush through and sacrifice one of your two health points in the process.
In order to reach the exit in time the only option is number two. Of course this whole feat is by no means impossible as I got the achievement eventually but in my book this sort of breaks a rule in video games. A level can be hard as hell but still has to leave you with the possibility of finishing it ungrazed, which is not possible in this case (at least for me).
Sorry about my whining, apart from that the game was fun to play and enriches the genre.

Words cannot describe how much I wanted to like My Own Little Planet. The art is fantastic, the character designs are great, and the soundtrack is top-notch. Taken together, the game succeeds in producing the creepy, yet aesthetically appealing atmosphere it seeks to create. However, what matters most in a video game is the gameplay, and that's where My Own Little Planet suffers. Greatly.
Creating an action platformer sans attack button is not necessarily a deal-breaker, but when your defenseless character's only means of survival is to run and jump a foot off of the ground, the fun factor diminishes by several orders of magnitude. This is compounded by a complete lack of power-ups and usable items. The game's most significant shortcoming, however, is the level design.
Unlike most platformers, My Own Little Planet places the player in numerous situations that he/she cannot possibly react to in time. Put another way, the game relies on repeated attempts to complete most levels. This essentially requires the player to memorize each level's layout, as well as the locations of traps and monsters, rather than hone his/her skills to address them. This shortcoming is most evident during the giant moth "battle" in stage 5. The player is given no warnings as to where the moth will appear, effectively forcing him/her to replay the long, arduous level over and over again. Such gameplay is not skill-based and is definitely not fun.
I admire the vision you had for this game, Mr. Parise, but I cannot honestly recommend it to anyone at this point in its development. That said, I think a patch rectifying some or all of the shortcomings I addressed could make My Own Little Planet a memorable game worth playing over and over again.

The game is a very basic platformer with the same aesthetic as Don't Starve (so much so that the main menu looks like a carbon copy). Your character lacks the ability to actually kill anything so the killing of enemy comes from luring them into the traps that would normally kill you.

The principle is good but the actual gameplay not so much. There is a lack of an ability to peek around the edges so a lot of times you are stuck just jumping into an area you cannot see at all and dying on a trap. Most of the difficulty in this game seems to stem from this die until you have seen  the entire stage aspect + the extremely jenky hitboxes. Traps that have already activated can still kill you before disappearing, the first major boss will kill you even if it is clearly not hitting you on the screen, enemies that kill you on touch will hit you when you are visibly out of range. Basically Flappy Bird in terms of hitbox accuracy.
The music is pretty decent, most of the tracks feel like a rehash of something else but different enough to not feel like a total ripoff. The aesthetic is the same fun Don't Starve style, some of the sprites are pasted on a bit poorly but you aren't likely to run across them except during deaths.
Not sure if the game will actually run you 5 hours as the dev claims considering I reached the boss of the first of 5 worlds in under half an hour with my poor platforming skills.

There are unlockables in the form of new bits of clothing ranging from lingerie to maid outfits, etc. As you play your characters gain experience and level up and unlock new abilities as well.

So this game is going to get compared to 'robocraft' allot... because it is in so many ways, a 'robocraft' clone.  You get a bunch of vehicle pieces either with a kit, or buy buying the pieces individually, and then assemble them into working vehicle kit to fight to death against other people who did the same thing.  Sounds awesome right?  right... but everything sounds awesome till you find out how much you have to pay for it.  And that is why this game is not winning allot of recommendations.  The real issue is this game needs to be compared to 'world of tanks' and the pay method used in that game vs this one..
The way the game's pay method seems to works is you buy coins to buy parts for your crafted vehicle.  The more you spend the further up the tier ladder you can be placed and theoretical if you spend a good amount of money, like all the money in the world... you end up at the vary top and if you did your research well, you will have a vehicle that will be vary competitive at the top.  but if you don't spend enough money you start playing lower and lower in the salt pits where you do not have the opportunity of being just as competitive as everyone else.. but a support fighter to the biggest badist guy on the battle field in the biggest toughest tank..
And that is the main problem why i would not buy this game.   Unless everyone can only spend so much money to be on equal ground with everyone else... I don't think its fair to use me as cannon fodder for your whale spenders.  This is the same exact thing that world of tanks did to lower level people and I hated it.  On top of that your whale spenders.. they are really big fish.  Right now at the vary top of the tier listing you can buy a Porcupine mine layer for 18000 coins, or hope some one will sell to you for over 7111 coins.  the Firebug flame thrower is on sale for as little as 17989 coins, but the best offer to beat is 8200 coins...  and the legendary scorpion Pulse accelerator, some one is selling for 18500 coins, while someone is offering to buy it for 14210 coins..
7500 coins cost 99.99 us dollars.. to get one gun in this game someone expect you to pay as much 200 us dollars for that.  That is outrageous and no way should you pay that much to play a game.  Even the next tier down from this where you spend 2600 coins for a Reaper mini gun is not what I think of as a bargain.  maybe these prices are subject to change but even then that begs another question.. what if the meta changes?   Do you really want to spend 30 bucks on a single gun only for it to later on change and become  the nerfed gun everyone got and then got nerfed because everyone has it?  that is exactly what is going to to happen once everyone researched what to spend there hard earned cash on..

Some of the players are so angry! While there are things that need work I do not feel its worth getting as salty as they do. 
Here are my opinions, some of which echo what others have stated:
Overall this is a fun game, love the setting, creation of vehicles and quick vehicular combat. 
Matchmaker - all mmo games struggle with this but there are simple things that seem like they should be enacted. I do not feel there should ever be a match of 3 platooned 12k players fighting a team where the highest is 9k. This is inexcusable. Either that platoon needs to wait longer if there is no one in that bracket or they should have to fight outnumbered. The total PS should be similar on both teams at least. This isn't a huge issue but annoying when it happens. Usually I feel most games are winable from either side.
Raids - I am afraid to click battle solo for raids, I try to create or join a group now....,there have been so many times on hard raids where I am stuck with only 2 people even been a couple where it was me and one other. I don't care how long the queue is, a full team should be required prior to the game taking my fuel for sometimes a certain loss. If the team is less than 4 then the number and strength of enemies should be adjusted. And minimum PS for hard/medium raids should probably be bumped up a little. 
Weapons - I usually do not care about the weapons. There will always be adjusting to be made and that is fine. Drones were a little cheesy and OP so I built one and rolled people with it for awhile. Glad they were adjusted. It is a living game and the tinkering will never be done. 
Crates- Hate the timed item stuff - Taking time to build and design a car is fun but I will not build a car around some random item i get for only 2 hours. Even if it was days I would not build a car around it. But alas, I stopped opening crates awhile back due to the low chance of non-commons. 30+ DIY crates with one blue was mediocre. If it is a market problem just make the items "soulbound" so they cannot be sold and only used for fusion or scrapping. A crate with resources or maybe getting 3 items and choosing one or choosing the type of item from a crate (wheels, guns, decor, etc) would be interesting. 
Workbench - Seeing how the premium money is so hard to earn the workbench rentals are artificially high. If I did not spend $30 on this game which included 1500 C,  the grind would be pretty intense. However, timing it out people underestimate other free to play time slots. I calculated the time to get a tier 10 tank in world of tanks versus the amount of time it takes to get a solid vehicle in this (epic weapons and gear) and if I recall it wasn't that much different. But I dunno, lots of variables and hard to remember all the details that went into my crude comparison. 
Save slots and storage slots are annoying and seem like you are just creating those as a resource sink. In hearthstone back when they only had like 8 deck slots it was absurd. This feels just like that. And the high cost of expanding the save slots and storage slots for such a small increase is also prohibitive. I mean the work around is publishing the blueprints which is cool and maybe that was what you were aiming for. But storage should be higher especially if you are forced to keep so much as you level factions. 
When I want to salvage a part for scrap please give a counter or slider ----- there are times when I have like 30 of something and i want to keep about 5. So I am forced to salvage one at a time! 
Sound effects/music - A+
I love the theme, idea of the game, building vehicles, and the creativity the game allows. 
I enjoy the quick pace of the game. Getting eliminated early is not that bad when the battle is only 3 minutes. Having to wait it out is ok most the time. Sometimes if i get out super early its a bummer to have to sit but not the end of the world. 
Rep Gain - killing blows are over powered - its pretty much all about the kill - not damaging the enemy - I can de-arm and enemy and deal a bunch of damage exposing the cab only to have someone sweep in and take all the rep points by getting kill shot. Re balancing this should be simple and looked into. 
Anyhow good work on the game, I hope it continues to grow in player base.

This is the kind of game which unfortunately gets a lot of discourse on the net. Everything i have to say is that if you're not its core demographic, better to simply ignore than make social statements against it when there's WAY, WAY, WAY WORSE sexualizing issues. But on the other side of the coin, don't defend it just for the fanservice as if is something sacred.
With that put aside to the review itself.
This is a franchise which is mostly known for its absurb boob physics and character dressing. However, even if you're not into big anime tiddies or not into (anime) women, the game offers a steady gameplay where the goal is to keep long combos against swarms of enemies and bosses. While the first stages might seem a way too easy game, if you leave the guard down enemies can easily drain your health with their own loops and combos. So pretty much you're in the same position as them. Once in a while bosses and yourself will end stripping clothes, and while is a novelty and probably welcome to fanservice fans, it feels intrusive in the middle of combos or will completely interrupt the game's pacing.
Unless you're uncomfortable with breasts zooming on screen and such, there's really not many negatives with this game. Yet, there's a really huge problem with this port as your computer might or might not run it. Some like myself will crash on certain missions or after certain time playing, while others will be unable to play even a second. It really depends of what computer and/or OS you're running, and until the devs releases an assured fix you better prepare to refund the game if something goes wrong. I also had a few framedrops, but is mostly after performing a super and isn't really much of a deal.
In resume. If you're into the fanservice genre you will like the game, but if you are looking for a beat'em-up you will also find something in this game. But as said, is an unstable port and you might get few or no experience from the game.

First thoughts on Crossout:
Read a ton of negative reviews about people who would appear to be playing their first f2p game ever. Most of the negative reviews are about people far away connecting to US national servers and experiencing lag OR how you can buy anything with real$ and♥♥♥♥♥♥on everyone. After nearly 10 hours I have never experienced this. You start out fighting bots on a team of real people until you get to level 3. The matchmaking appears to be level based and not power based; but let me elaborate further...
Certain items have a level requirement so trying to buy gold and building the best early level vehicle is meaningless. After spending no money whatsoever it can be said that patience and sensibility wins the early matches over money. Sit in the fields around corners and take pop shots when you can, and when your team has weakened the other team find the weaker targets and take them out at your leisure.
Moving forward to level grinding: Items are awarded on winning; building smart vehicles increase your chance at staying alive and staying alive improves your score dramatically. Stay alive and take shots at those unaware to your presence. A high accelerating vehicle can outrun enemies visions when performing in-and-out cornering combat, only shooting when you CAN shoot. This increases the points you get at the end of the match, which will increase your level. Try to build something wacky and unpractical will make you useful but don't be afraid to experiment. You never know which build will perservere to your playstyle and you can save up to 5 blueprints.
Market System: Every win early on gives you 1 token. View your inventory after quite a few wins and attempt to sell these with a simple right click. I have nearly 10 hours on account right now and almost 18 gold after selling these tokens. Blue items (rare) sell for quite a moderate amount each so buy with intelligence. If you are winning matches because of your playstyle better items won't make you better. Sometimes it's better to play with a handicap to improve your personal skill level.
Graphics and loading: Loading is instant graphics are subpar. The maps are pretty small and the cars dont move so fast. There are some choppy moments but it's sort of to be expected in a beta game.
Thanks for reading

The first time I saw UnEpic I thought to my self, not another one of those retro looking games. That was one of the major points why I waited so long to pick that game up. But then the Steam Sale came and for a few bucks I took the risk, because everyone and their mother praises this game and they are right.
Well for the most part at least. I mentioned already the graphics, but they are not that bad as they look in those previews. When you get a bit used to the look and feel of the game, they are rather pretty and make an excellent job to convey the "dungeon feel" of the game.
The biggest problem I have with this game are the controls. They are not fluent and every now and then you are not fighting the game, but the controls of it (I played with a xBox 360 controller). After a while you know how the charakter handles itself, but even after close to 20 hrs of gametime, there are situations where I almost rage quitted the game altogether. The Moments were triggered mostly by two situations:
1. The Target Lock will not work for whatever reason. If you have, for example, a flying enemy and he is high up. You need the target Lock function to shoot him with magic or arrows. If the enemy is out of reach for your melee attacks and you cannot lock him on, you are forced to jump around and hope to agro it into melee range.
2. The Platforming is for the most part enjoyable, but here comes the controls you have to get used to. You have almost no control over you character mid jump and without a impulse in either side you just jump up. So to jump sideways, you need to get a bit of momentum and then jump. The margin for error in the platforming is rather small, but that is personell preference if that is good or bad. It only infuriated me in the later part of the game, when it took way to long to make that jump.
The pacing of the game is rather good, and except of the late game I enjoyed it quite a bit. Starting with "The Halls" it felt forcefully drawn out. There are two Enemy types there that annoyed the hell out of me. The Harlekin mage that transmogrifies your drawn weapon in a joke weapon that does 1 dmg, if he hits you with his range Attack and the blobs. If the blobs make contact to you, they get you a debuff named "slippery hands". While this is active, you will drop your weapon. I have no problems with strategic situations, but if you have hallways filled with blobs, it is more a test of Patience to finish this section. But all of this is a thing of the past when you start the "final level". I do not want to spoil anything story wise, but this is a cakewalk and way to easy.
Even if I only complained up to this point, that does by no means mean that the game is bad. It is good. The music is enjoyable and compliments the feeling of the game and the situation at hand and never felt out of place. This game has a ton of replay-ability with all the secrets, challenges and different character builds and difficulty setting. Apparently it also a multiplayer mode, but I did not test that.
Just buy it.

Why I dislike this game:
Titan Souls is difficult simply to be difficult.  Your attacks are slow (compared to enemies), you only get one health, and the bosses are overpowered for no other reason than because they can be.  I understand that some people enjoy that kind of game, but I am not one of those people.  I'd rather play a game and have fun with it than try for hours to defeat a tough boss and ultimately wind up feeling frustrated and empty.  Even after beating a boss, instead of feeling any sort of triumph I only felt a sense of annoyance that I'd have to move on to the next extremely powerful enemy.
Why you might like this game:
If you're a glutton for punishment and enjoy playing a hard game because of the difficulty level and bragging rights, this might be a game for you.  While the bosses are tough, there is a pattern and strategy to each of them.  You'll likely die your first time against each new boss, but as you continually challenge them you will learn from each death and adapt for the next round.  Each fight is not perfect however.  One boss I was able to defeat by simply standing out of its range and firing my bow at it; another I defeated by accident within 30 seconds of our encounter (don't worry, I died plenty of times before against it).
What I still enjoyed about this game:
While I disliked the gameplay, I very much enjoyed the art and music in Titan Souls.  The graphics designer is very talented and the music is great.  While the gameplay wasn't my cup of tea, the mechanics were fairly solid.  If the context of this game were different and it was more an adventure than a torturous boss run, I'd likely have enjoyed the way my character moved and attacked in the vast environment.

This is going to be an odd review, for the reason that I will mostly be reviewing this game with the idea that one is playing with a mod to polish this game a little bit, as the steam version feels very blurry and dated, and makes this game feel a lot less timeless than it really is. If you end up buying this game anyway, and try the mod I recommend, it's a good idea to view this as the 2D maze-like puzzle game where you have some sort of fog-of-war, because most can relate to a retro game rather than viewing this with the same standards of call of duty. This game has one serious flaw, and it's that you almost can't play the original version that steam sells.
The mod I recommend here is called ZDOOM, and while it's for Doom, it can be used for this game with a few tweaks. Overall it makes this game feel less like it did in 1992, and gives it the polished feel of a retro game made in the 80's that everyone can play, like Mario. ZDOOM fixes polishing issues in the game, such as resolution fixes, mouse and keyboard if you wish (even though I don't recommend it), texture fixes, and overall gameplay fixes that make this game a lot more timeless while still keeping the original atmosphere. I usually strongly dislike revamping old games (for example, SkyWind makes me cringe), but this fixes key issues that make this game not fun, while stuff like SkyWind just makes the game pretty, killing its original atmosphere and feel of the game.
Now that I've discussed how to be able to play this game with minimal frustrations, I'm going to be straightforward and tell you this is not a good game. I have about 15 hours off steam on this game, and based on my experiences, this game still has some serious problems that can't be fixed with something like ZDOOM. It's really obvious that this game is dated as hell, as it was the grandfather of FPS. You'd really think it's not that bad, but it is. It's a truly unplayable game when you get down to it; it's just not fun. A pros and cons list would be a good way to show this game's worth since ratings for games can be pretty subjective.
Pros:
- Managable fighting mechanics, ZDOOM gives this game simple controls and easy-to-learn combat. At first I didn't enjoy keyboard controls, but this game's map design really gives an interesting idea with it. The fact that you have to turn left and right does add a bit of challenge since the devs like putting enemies on both sides, and gives strategies that also include a mix of strafing (with alt key), and add a little more extra fun to the table, and trust me, you need that extra fun.
- Has creative map layout at points, and the maps that try to be memorable (like secret levels, bosses, and aardwolf maze) are very memorable and I could still point them out. The did some interesting choices with the actual combat itself, and gives a more fun idea of fighting that really gives strategy. Like Doom, this game is known for having some serious consequences for not thinking and responding fast, and really gives some emotion out of the game.
- Pretty playable, it's easy to beat a chapter in a day since missions are short and the game can be not enjoyable or bad, but just generic, so you can sometimes play a lot.
- Uses an atmosphere and a premise of why you're fighting rather than a linear story, so you can get right into the action rather than having a boring, linear game with no thought put in yourself.
- Better mechanics than a lot of modern games (difficulty in this game has more factors for it than Skyrim, and gives some variety there)
- There's fun in the idea that there are a lot of modders that add their own flavor to some of the maps, and create their own original weapons and maps, and it's fun to play at least a couple. I'll send one to start with at the bottom of the review.
Cons:
- 4 types of enemies, most chapters don't show all at once. This really kills a lot of the fun, because it's just you doing the same thing over, and over, and over again, and I can understand that this game was made in 1992, but it just lacks polish for such a big game.
- The normal levels really aren't memorable and it just seems like there lacks care in the level design, everything is bland and the same, and it's nothing exciting for so long.
- Generic weapons that do the same amounts of damage and use the same ammo, just have different fire rates.
- Can feel a bit clunky at times with movement, and looking around.
- Overall a generic game, nothing seems exciting, and some points you just get so bored you quit and don't play the game for the rest of the day. All of the missions feel like the same thing over and over again, there's no interesting gun variety, no enemy variety, no variety for any factors in this game, even health and ammo drops are the same over and over again. I'd really say that doesn't make this game bad, but it's just not exciting. It would be different if there were a small amount of weapons but each were very unique, but each small variety of items adds nothing new to the table and feels the same as the last. If you're dealing with small variety and blandness, there's not only no content, but no fun with it, and that's just done poorly.
Overall, I'd really say this game isn't terrible, but it lacks map, weapon, enemy, health, and ammo variety, and ends up feeling like the same game over and over again. I'd personally recommend this over modern day Call of Duty because they're essentially the same game; a generic game with nothing really new or exciting in it. This game is somewhat timeless with ZDOOM, but movement can feel seriously clunky at times and it's just more of "not fun" than a "dated" or "hard" game with today's standards. If you're one to enjoy FPS and don't really care about variety then this game would be playable and pretty interesting to play, especially since you can be the guy who said "I beat Wolf3D on 'I am Death Incarnate'!" like me, but really, this game is nothing more than that, a game you can say you beat as bragging rights.

EDIT: After beating Doom Shareware and Doom 2, I realized that I was a little harsh on keyboard controls when I first played the game, especially since the game is 2D and it's kind of fun to use left arrow keys to turn and then use a mix of strafing. Regardless, the controls are still kind of dated, and ZDOOM is still essential for making the game feel less old, especially the blurry graphics and bad resolution, plus slow turning and all that. You have a lot of choice in what controls you want to be and generally the game's just better with ZDOOM, so still pick it up.
Also, as another edit, this game's map design isn't terrible, but it sure seems bad if this is the first old FPS you're playing. They have some originality, and you can tell there's some care, but overall it's not too original and not too hard. These games aren't that casual but they're not too hardcore either.

Also, it automatically recognizes the files from your steam folder so there is no set up; just extract and play.
If you're a purist, it might not be for you. I would wager that ECWolf is the way to go for 90% of gamers, though.

Squad is like ARMA minus the bullcrap. No remembering dozens of specific keybinds, no weird menu you use your scroll wheel for, no installing a bunch of mods or searching through countless servers to get an experience you enjoy. Simply open Squad, join a server, and instantly you are thrust into an intense open-world conflict in which you along with 8 squadmates can set your own objective in accordance with your team's strategy and attempt to win the game by any means necessary.
Being a squad member is fun, but the true fun of the game, at least for me, is being at the head of the action, and directing the rest of your body (your squadmates) on how to proceed. Being a squad leader in Squad is truly an incredible experience that no other game can truly match, not even ARMA. You've got eight people under you that will (usually) listen to your commands, and you've got four or five other squad leaders to communicate with so you can develop the best strategy.  There is no greater joy than leading your squad to victory, going into the next round, and having people wait for you to create a squad because you did so well. Squad Leaders can also set down Rally Points for their squadmates to have a temporary spawn point, set down FOBs to hold vital chokepoints or provide a permanent spawn, as well as other fortifications around FOBs. Squad Leaders truly control the flow of the game, and a good or bad Squad Leader can mean the difference between a victory or defeat in Squad.
But do not fret if leading is not your strong suit or your thing; every role in Squad has it's purpose. Obviously there is the important "Squad Leader" role, but the roles of Medic, Autorifleman (Machinegunner), Marksman, Anti-Tank, even Rifleman are all important and have their roles. Medics keep the war machine going, Autoriflemen provide a base of fire to cover their fellow squadmates, Marksman take out enemies from afar in accordance to the squad's objective, Anti-Tank take out those pesky and vital armored vehicles, Rifleman can set up barricades as well as act as the all-important point-men and primary attackers, all with the SL leading from the back (or on the frontlines.)
If a Squad is malfunctioning, deformed, or simply unable to work with each other, the game is simply not fun. The Squad Leader is vital to keep the squad pushing forward, but the Squad Leader cannot put down much of anything without squad members at his side. Communication and teamwork is VITAL in Squad, and without it the experience will not be enjoyable. However, whenever a Squad gets it right - they are communicating, helping each other, working together, listening to each other - the game is like none other. Luckliy, the game makes it easy to make sure Squads do have cohesion.
The only issue I have with this game is it's fierce optimization problem. Even at low settings I struggle to keep 60 frames on most maps, and I don't have a bad rig. That, along with some map glitches that involve going through the map and having to suicide to keep playing.
All in all, I have never played a multiplayer game more rewarding than Squad, and I'm excited to make this game my next primary experience and design a community around it. I would truly give this game a 10/10 if the game was optimized, bugs were fixed, and other quality of life issues were resolved. For now, I give the game a 7, but the devs are working hard on the game and I think it'll hit a solid 10/10 (meaning the game delivers 100% on its promise and is fun to play, easy-ish to run, and chock full of features) when the game is fully released.
If you are looking for a realistic first-person-shooter where communication and teamwork is required for success, look no further. Buy Squad.

Though it would seem self-evident from its nostalgia based advertisement, proclamations of historical knowledge, and general retro theming, I remain unclear as to what Life of Pixel actually wanted to be.
As a minimalistic platformer aiming to present itself through the lens of 13 dated gaming platforms, the immediate answer would seem that Life of Pixel is trying to encapsulate the evolution of gaming from its inception up through the 16-bit era. Except that here that evolution is personified as solely the product of graphical improvement without any of the underlying design principles of a particular era. Life of Pixel would propose to say that gaming’s heritage is rooted solely in the capabilities of a given platforms hardware, spouting off wiki-like tech sheets as if the only significant element of any given period of gaming is how many pixels a machine can push.
This seems an especially shallow understanding gaming’s history, because it neglects the ways in which those recognizable graphical aesthetics were so entirely linked to and created out of the ways developers were forced to compromise in all areas of design based on the limitations of the machine they were working with. One can’t begin to accurately recreate the technological development of videogames without first understanding how, in the presence of such limited resources, developers had to devise intricate and convoluted workarounds in order to have their games actually run on such low-powered hardware.
At no point does Life of Pixel manage to shake its artificial nature. It attempts to step back in time but one foot is always stuck firmly in the presence, creating a bizarre dissonance between the era Life of Pixel is attempting to replicate and the one it actually exists in. But let’s suppose Life of Pixel only ever aspired to chronicle the visual progression of games, entirely removed from any other variable but the most iconic graphical style of a platform’s lifespan. In this Life of Pixel fares much better, often coming close to approximating a memorable historical look even as everything underneath it feels wholly out-of-place.
But if Life of Pixel is solely a visual showcase then it is again betrayed by its adherence to modernity. Though it may appear to align with the graphical identity of whichever platform it is attempting to recreate itself upon, it doesn’t go far enough to actually represent that platform authentically. The resolution is too high, the frame rate and animations too smooth, and the amount of information on-screen too extensive to feel believable. It is unlikely many would like to play a modern game running at the same resolution as the Apple II or C-64, but with the graphics of those systems being so defined by the same capabilities that Life of Pixel ignores it is hard to accept it as a legitimate visual chronology of gaming history, rather than merely another game attempting to ape the appearance of games long past in order to sell itself on the basis of nostalgia.
But let’s again qualify Life of Pixel’s attempts at historical recreation by considering it as its own game that simply wishes to borrow the aesthetics of gaming heritage in such a way as to be recognizable, rather than genuine. Once removed from its attempts at creating a technological timeline, it seems crucial to consider whether Life of Pixel’s various aesthetics can really be considered retro anymore. Within the context of the game they are of course attempting to align with a particular era of gaming, but once we move beyond that (for reasons already discussed), what separates Life of Pixel aesthetic from any number of modern 8 and 16-bit games? With how extensively modern games (especially within the indie spectrum) have revisited and repurposed graphical styles originally synonymous with 80’s and 90’s game systems, it feels as if we have long since moved beyond the point where every gaming using pixel-art should be categorized as retro. I feel the distinction is necessary because while we continue to view pixel-art as inherently dated its usage will always seem driven by nostalgia, rather than being an intentional aesthetic decision chosen for reasons beyond its historical context.
So returning to Life of Pixel with this in mind, setting aside its middling attempts at historical authenticity, we are left with an entirely inoffensive but unremarkable platformer. Its visuals might be varied, but the art direction is routinely mundane, seemingly driven through a desire to exist within a given style of pixel-art but not do anything interesting with it. There is a solidity to Life of Pixel’s mechanics, but also a pervasive tepidity brought about by its simplicity and tedium. Early levels are dull for their basic, tutorial-like nature, where later levels are tiresome in their difficulty, becoming larger and more prone to cheap deaths while retaining the same meandering level designs of the more manageable early game.
From all fronts it would appear Life of Pixel fails to find its footing. Its historical pursuits lack nuance, its visual replication proves inauthentic, and beneath all its appeals to nostalgia there is little to find but an overwhelmingly ordinary platformer, becoming then indistinguishable from so many other pixel platformers. And I don’t think that’s necessarily fair to Life of Pixel because it is at least trying for something more substantial in trying to pay tribute to gaming’s heritage, but its attempts are so sterile and superficial that they provide little to distract from an otherwise decidedly plain experience.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a good game, and I recommend it.  I've heard quite a bit about it and the prequel and I think I expected more of The New Order, due to getting a variety of information.
But at the same time, I really like Wolfenstein: The New Order for the most part.  My real problems come from expectation and a few issues with difficulty.  The fact is I found the game to be harder than most players seem to, I started on Uber, and went down to medium, before the halfway point, and finally on the final boss I dropped it to the easiest mode just to get through it (more because I was sick of the repetition).
That's actually a big of a the problem of this game.  You really only fight about 3-4 enemies and they just keep coming.  It's not that the level design is bad, or the game is bad, but the enemies that you fight stay generic from beginning to end.  You fight nazis, robots, and dogs, and more of each of the three of them.  There's some cool fights, there's a couple boss fights, but ultimately they fit in those three categories, and that's a bit of a shame.  There's also no real mention of Hitler (which does get mentioned in the sequel that just came out) but I have to admit I'm curious about the Furher, even if it was to know he's alive and that means I might have a chance to kill him in another game.
The other issue with this game is that while I REALLY liked the characters in the game, and the life bred into them, the story feels almost like it's lacking something.  There's two real problems with it.  First the story seems to be building to a big twist.  You black out at times, you switch from a sex scene to action relatively quickly, you clearly form these emotional relationships with people we don't seen.  If they told me "You never had any friends" I'd believe it.
Problem is, there's no really big twist in the game, the building and the awkwardness of some scenes are just awkwardness.  The love story doesn't really pay off, and I've heard people saying the sex is appropriate in this game... sorry no, it's just sex for sex sake.
The other problem is the story seems to be written by someone who didn't really see the action until after they finished writing.  BJ Blazkowicz, the man character is a rough and tough bad♥♥♥♥♥ and in the cutscenes they try to make it sound like he's a gentle man, there's even points that show him in the first chapter chastising someone else "Another dead because of you." or something.  Again, these things are never paid off. We play him as a total badass from beginning to end, and that's the game.
The world is interesting, if not really explained.  The game starts in 1946, Nazis ultimately win world war 2, the world is run by the Nazis, and everyone stops fighting... There should be good stories here...
And the thing is I LIKE Blazkowicz, I like the female character, I like almost every character in the game.  I felt horrified by one character in the game.  Oh god she kind of scared me and that's a good thing.  So I like the characters, I like the setting a lot, it's a great alternate history, but the narrative itself was lacking.  Well that and the fact that the end boss is ... not who it should have been.  It makes sense who the final fight is against but there's another villain that the game has built up, why not use the villain you developed verses the villain who only appeared once and only had a little development?
But ultimately I liked the game.  Killing Nazis is fun, there is good level design like I mentioned, and the mixture of action to stealth was good, and even the stealth felt right most of the time.  Sometimes a level started and I wasn't sure if I could stealth it, but most of the time the answer was "no, go kill Nazis."  And so I did.
There's a fantastic perk system, where you complete little feats and get little perks, maybe an addition 10 bullets in a magazine, maybe less damage from X, and so on.  None of these are game breaking, but they're a lot of fun to earn, to the point I farmed a number of them on the first stage.
The collectibles were done well, the only real issue I had is some levels had a "commander" that if you kill stealthily you get to see where collectibles are.  A great perk (earned on the first stage farming) but some levels don't have any commanders, so you're eventually going to need a guide for those levels.  Why? Why is the system that's developed to help the obsessive people only available on 90 percent of the game.   The collectibles themselves are great.  Nazi gold, enigma tapes that unlock bonuses, and letters and records.  All good additions to the game and mythos.
There's good action, good amount of violence, nazi killing (which should always be acceptable), good characters, so all in all I like the game.  The gameplay is a mixed bag that worked well.  My trouble came from the fact that the cover shooting isn't my favorite thing.
Well the game surprised me.  After playing doom I love run and gun and wanted it back.  Wolfenstein looked in it's bag and with the first enigma code I got from the collectibles, I got what was called the 999 mode.
You see when you die, you normally revive at a checkpoint, in 999 mode, you revive at the last checkpoint but you get 999 health that will slowly fall back to your max).  Oh and infinite ammo, but the gameplay is on the hardest difficulty (Uber).  THIS right here is a game changer in every meaning of the word.
No longer is cover "mandatory".  No longer is the enemies as dangerous, with 999 life, you can just run and gun the game, and just have fun killing everything you want and ignoring those who you don't care about.  The game changes from a cover based shooter that people are used to, to just a pure action game and the results are glorious.  It's the perfect way to do a second playthrough and I love it.
So without 999 I would still recommend this game because it's good, and while the story tries to be a lot more than it is, it's still a very good game, but with 999 mode, I absolutely adore this game, because they found a way to make it more fun.
And yet you kill Nazis, and if you are a person who dresses up in Hugo Boss uniforms with Swastikas on your shoulders and talk about the master race and how other people are undesirable, and do nazi salutes, and threaten to kill "unworthy people"... yeah you're probably going to be offended by the game (even if it is about a world which has Nazi's winning world war 2).  If however you've been called a nazi, but don't believe in any of the actual Nazi German crap, I'm sorry but this game isn't insulting you.  The German Nazis that this game are about, are a specific group and the game is about killing them.
And you know what?  It's damn enjoyable no matter how many times you do it.

It didn't affect my enjoyment at all.   However it's sad to see the game in a state where I knew for a fact the game was causing more issues than it should have.

The game itself is a neat, well designed classic platformer, with just the right amount of challenge to keep you muttering curses at the screen but still keep trying until you get it right.
The beautifully recreated style for each system is what sets it apart, though. It goes well beyond merely imitating technical specs: it actually manages to get close to the actual look and feel commonly expected of games released on that particular era and platform; enough for many of them to feel instantly recognizable, even familiar. And it's a pleasant surprise to see usually overlooked classics get featured - even the ZX81! You can tell so much love and detail was put into this.
Bonus points if you can get to play it with a classic controller of some kind (I used a Konix Speedking - best joystick ever!)

The trailer is a bit misleading. You don't spend the entire game chasing some guy in the future, but you stumble around traveling back and forth from post apocalyptic future to the present. The story was almost perfect. It had a creepy, mysterious vibe, which resulted in 2 satisfying twists I did not see coming. However, the final end was a bit of a letdown leaving me thinking "that's it?". Regardless, The Silent Age is a very good dark sci-fi narrative adventure that will ultimately keep you intrigued.
Like any point-n-click, you go on a scavenger hunt, looking for items from both present and future, and solve puzzles, talk to people (with decent voice acting), no timed puzzles (no pun intended) and no combat. Minimal animation but it suits the minimalist art style. And the eerie atmospheric audio is very well done. I really loved how the developers handled time travel logically.Definitely worth an afternoon of your time.
