Life of Pixel is a very enjoyable platformer that takes a trip through the history of video games, with a particular focus on the early PCs of the 1980s. The gameplay itself is decently challenging and a lot of fun, but the main attraction with this game are the visuals and the sound. The visuals of this game make you feel like you are actually playing a game on one of those old systems, and the soundtrack is great and fits in with each system that the levels were designed for.
As I said before, the gameplay is a lot of fun, a lot more fun than the "collect all x doodads in order to advance" structure of each level would imply. Each system that you play on in the game has it's own set of mechanics that make each level interesting in its own right and a lot of fun to play.
While you can learn about the systems that you are playing on before you start the levels of the system you are playing, it presented as a paragraph of text that is easily skippable, which makes it both avoidable and not a good way to convey that information. However I feel that the purpose of the game wasn't to teach people about the old systems, but to let people be nostalgic about the old systems, and with the wide variety of systems in the game, there is something for anyone who grew up in the 8-bit or 16-bit era to be nostalgic about, plus the developer is British and they included UK exclusive systems in the game, so unlike a lot of nostalgic looks back to the past games, there is something there for people who grew up with a UK only system.
Due to the quality of the game and it's low price point ($6.99 full price), this is a game that I can wholeheartedly recommend regardless of whether it is on sale or not. At the time of writing, this game is 50% off ($3.49) and at that price, picking up this game is a no brainer.

As someone who grew up with the early 80s of video games and onward, I always thought it would be neat to have a video game showcasing the progression of gaming technology.  Apparently the developers behind this game thought the same thing, because that's exactly what they have made.
For gameplay, this is a standard platformer.  You need to collect various gems to unlock the exit and progress to the next level, while avoiding traps and enemies.  There is not much mechanically to do.  You can jump and double jump; that's it.  The control is spot on and the game relishes in its simplicity.
Graphically, Life of Pixel is quite good.  If anything, the various renderings of older technology look better than I remember.  Fortunately, there is an option to apply various filters to recreate the feeling of playing old games on a washed out CRT monitor, scan-lines and all.
The best for me, though, is the audio.  The game recreates the old-school chiptunes style soundtracks of games of old.  Just listening to the music for the various levels is the best part of this nostalgia trip for me.
Overall, if you grew up through the 8 bit and 16 bit eras of games and want a dose of nostalgia, this is a worthy game to get.  At full price, it's a bargain.  On sale, it's a downright steal.  Definitely recommended.

The most beautiful pixel art game I have played so far. And although it is visually stunning it lacks depth and a story to follow.
You start a game as a nameless hero who embarks on a quest to slay all the titans. Why does he do it? What is his goal? You will never know because game consists mainly from boss fights and there is literally nothing in between. Just some walking simulator elements where you explore different areas and you do a little sightseeing. You stop your hero at an interesting looking location and you think to yourself "it's a shame that there is nothing to do here, no NPC to talk to, no secret to discover."
However, if you are interested in playing this game it is because you want to kill some f***** titans, not to enjoy the view :)
It is easy to find a titan, it is a lot harder to kill it because what you need to do is to kill it in one shot (most of the time in the♥♥♥♥♥. No health bar, no stages. Just a puzzle what and when do you need to shoot to kill him before it kills you. And don't be afraid to die. This game rewards efficiency. If you figure out a trick, a quick way to kill him (and there almost always is one) it is faster to try over again than just running around a titan and not getting slammed to a pulp. You get used to it and it gets easier with time because there are some small similarities between the titans.

In the end it is a fun game to play.

My brother ended up winning four copies of this game during some summer/winter sale a couple of years back. He insisted that I play with him and our crew. The problem is that the three of them played it once when I was at work and never played it again for some mysterious reason. I finally put this thing on my computer and found out the reason they never touched this game again: this game is abysmal in every category.
You start the game out with three other players , but this game came out two years ago, i.e. more than enough time for people to try the game out and decide that they've had enough of it, so you'll probably end up playing the single player version of the game with your teammates being played as bots. Your choices are a noble hick, a British historian, or two hot chicks. You illustrious four have been warped from wherever the heck you were to some part of Central America by a Mayan priest, have been given futuristic weapons and armor (which he states were worshipped by the Mayans) and you must stop the 2012 apocalypse from happening by essentially murdering the Mayan people. Or at least I think that's what happens. I kind of stopped playing after half an hour and have no intention of continuing whatsoever.
The concept is a lot like the Left 4 Dead games (four players slaying a swarm of enemies), but the gameplay is very much along the lines of Painkiller (swarm of enemies with limited weapons and powerups to kill them in a very linear area). The only difference is that Painkiller and the Left 4 Dead games all have very well written stories, interesting characters, professional voice acting and superb graphics, whereas Revelations 2012 has none of that. The story sucks, the voice acting is laughable at times and the gameplay is boring and intellectually devoid. Skipping over such trivialities as the PLOT or the DIALOGUE to get straight to the action can be a good thing, as the Unreal Tournament series has so often shown us, but the gameplay in this one justifies nothing. And the graphics, ZOMG the graphics! The graphics look like they were made by a two man independent development team from a third world country who were trying to make a video game where all the characters have vision problems...for the SEGA SATURN!!! I usually don't dwell on the graphics of the game so long as every other aspect of the game is amazing, but the graphics of Revelations 2012 deserve a special whistleblowing.
In conclusion, you want to stay the hell away from this game. I was literally given a copy of it completely free of charge and I still feel like I've been cheated. I doesn't matter if the game is only $2.49, no price is low enough to blemish your STEAM account or your hard drive with this genital sore equivalent. If you want a four person game where you run around and kill stuff, play Left 4 Dead. If you want a game with a Latino presence, play any of the Tropico games, Grim Fandago, Black Ops II, or hell, play as the token latino guy in any of the Rainbow Six games. Even that will be more culturally enriching than this abomination. You may think that I'm not warranted to speak about this game having only played a half hour of it, but just trust me on this one, okay? This isn't about me being right, even though I am. I'm looking out for YOU.
In fact, let me show you something. Scroll up a bit on this page. See the one critique listed by Valid Gaming? Click on the hyperlink "valid gaming". It took you to a web domain that no longer exists, didn't it? Want to know why? Valid Gaming:
a.) didn't know what the hell they were talking about and because of that was ignored until they were forced to quit.
b.) was Dark(f)artz Entertainment secretly inventing a publication that would actually give their game a thumbs up.
or
c.) was purged from existence by the powers that be for supporting this game.
You decide! Any way you slice it, this game is cursed.
The game is now free to play, so now everybody can experience this game the way I did- paying nothing and feeling owed something. Also, cross platform multiplayer is available. Like the Star Wars Christmas special being leaked onto the internet, I feel that exposing something this bad to even more people should never have happened.

This is a difficult game to review because I have mixed feelings about it. There are so many great things about it and yet there are also a number of huge flaws. In the end, I tentatively recommend it, especially if you can find it on sale. I bought it for about 3 bucks from the Humble Store and I'm happy with what I got for that money. I don't know if I'd feel the same if I had spent 15 bucks (or 16.99 CAD). I'll list the pros and cons below and you can decide for yourself; like I said, this is a tentative recommendation that really depends on whether you can A) get it on sale and B) how much you can stomach a game that is great fun at most times but has really frustrating drawbacks at others.
Oh, and my final death count was 525.
+ The core gameplay is absolutely very, very fun. The central concept is kind of genius: you die in one hit, but all of your enemies also die in one hit. The trick is figuring out their weaknesses and looking for an opening to strike. When you finally nail those weak points, it feels great. It takes a combination of strategy and a little luck (sometimes a lot of luck). Battles can take several minutes or they can be over in a matter of seconds, it all depends on when you let your arrow go. It's an addicting formula, and after killing a titan, you definitely get that feeling of "Ok, let me go kill just one more."
+ The bosses are all really well-designed and unique. Each one has a special pattern and set of attacks that you'll need to figure out and they each require a different set of skills. For some of the titans, it's about split second accuracy, for others, they've got some sort of gimmick where you need to lure them into a certain area or destroy their armor before they're vulnerable. The gimmicks can admittedly be very annoying at times (like the fire blob) but for the most part, these bosses are very satisfying to figure out and kill.
+ The graphics are good but simple, they look kind of like an early 16 bit game. Think a low rent Hyper Light Drifter plus the old Ys games. The art direction here won't set the world on fire but it gets the job done and can be pretty evocative at times. The designs of the bosses are pretty simple - they are mostly blobs, bulbs, and big stone heads (someone on the art team was a Zardoz fan), with a few cool exceptions - but the simple designs suit the streamlined, minimalistic look of the overall world.
+ The music is really good, it's aiming for a sort of Joe Hisaishi/Miyazaki movie vibe and I think that it humbly succeeds at it.
= The story is minimalistic. You play as a kid who wanders through a mysterious land and hunts down the titans, which seem to be some sort of primeval gods. When he slays one, he gets some sort of power or knowledge. Except for a few lines of dialogue and a couple of other things that are implied, that's about all you get as far as story goes! Personally, I think this is a strength and it's cool, but you might want more context to your game. This will really depend on your taste.
- The game demands precision play and split second accuracy but this is hampered by a lot of glitches and clipping. There were so many times that my arrow clipped through a titan's weak point, so many times that I got smashed when I had definitely avoided an enemy's attack. There were also times when I *should* have been killed but wasn't. I also glitched through walls and got stuck in corners during boss fights...at one point I glitched through a wall and the boss couldn't touch me, but I also couldn't move, so I just had to restart the game.
- The arrow can be kind of sluggish and isn't always that fun to use. It gets stuck pretty easily and is extremely slow to start to come back to you. One of the major gameplay mechanics is that you need to psychically draw your arrow back to you after you shoot it, and you can use this mechanic to nail an enemy's weak point on their back. Great idea but the low speed and clunky nature of the arrow means that this mechanic isn't as satisfying as it could have been.
- There's no map or beacons or even a compass, you wander through the land and just need to find your way. You walk around with no sense of direction and no idea of where to go. I see what the development team was going for, but this was ultimately just frustrating to me instead of mysterious and atmospheric. Plenty of mysterious and atmospheric games give you at least some way to mark your journey, even the relatively spartan Shadow of the Colossus gives you the ability to use your sword as a beacon to generally point out the direction you should go next. I don't think that the lonely atmosphere of the game would have been appreciably harmed by including a subtle way to direct you or at least mark where you've been.
- The camera is really awkward during boss fights and at some points becomes a true obstacle. There were moments where the camera tracked the boss and left me off-screen so that I couldn't see where I was moving and couldn't dodge attacks, and there were times where the camera tracked me in such a way that I couldn't see the boss even though it was close by. These weird camera tracks killed me several times. If you're used to games with a similar perspective like Zelda or Secret of Mana, you'll find some of these camera movements really odd and counterintuitive.
- I'd like to point out one last weird design decision. Before each boss fight, the name of the boss will pop up, Zelda/Dark Souls style. Instead of just staying for for a second or two while the boss does a little animation, the name actually stays there at the bottom of the screen for several seconds into the fight itself. This doesn't sound like a big deal but there were actually a number of times that I died because my character was covered by the big white text and I couldn't see where he was in relation to some projectile. You start each fight at the bottom of the screen, so the text is really poorly placed...

Aiming and shooting takes longer than you think when you have a split second gap for hitting the weak point.
Know when to collect your arrow. Collecting your arrow at the wrong time and place will lead to death.
I strongly recommend a controller for your game for better aiming, but it is possible to win with keyboard, just very hard.

A Rimworld Tale...
Our escape pods crash landed on a tropical Rimworld. Just Doc, Miss Farmer and Chef on a strange world.
We gathered what resources we could from the wreckage and slept the night rough on the floor of a cave.
The next day we started building a lavish stronghold before planting a few crops.
Before we knew it the rations we scavenged were gone, (should have planted crops first). So we were forced to hunt the local wildlife for food.
A cry for help came over the radio. It was Doc's sister, Princess, she'd also survived planet fall and was being chased by raiders!
We set out in force and rescue her and bring her back to the fortress. We celebrate with a hearty meal of our first crop.
It turns out that Chef is a nudist. In a bid to make her more comfortable we let her spend her days o'natural.
Everyone is fine with it.
Our home of Fort Haven is finally finished and we start researching upgrades.
Chef makes a statue of her self striding around in the nude and we use it to decorate the guest room.
Another escape pod crashes down. We rescue the occupant, some guy called Aiki. He's a junkie with violent tendencies.
We patch up his wounds, give him a hot meal and send him on his way.
Both Doc and Princess catch plague! I bet it was that space junkie. They're instantly confined to bed.
It take some doing but Doc treats Princess and Princess treats him.
Raiders attack with half our crew bedridden with disease. We push them back but Chef is badly injured.
Miss Farmer carries her back to Fort Haven and heals her wounds.
Through sibling compassion, and their medical know how, Doc and Princess survive the plague and Chef is also restored to full health.
Realising how vulnerable we are we start building defensive gun turrets. We need more metal so everyone heads off to mine.
Princess doesn't like mining and, for some reason, she snaps. She runs around setting fires all over the place.
Doc and Farmer knock her out and put her to bed, but not before the fires spread taking out a huge section of forest to the North.
A huge army of raiders attack. Perhaps they saw the fires? The attack our walls and devastating most of our crops. The new gun turrets come online and we mow them down.
With our crops in a bad way and our food supplies low Chef recommends eating the would be raiders...
A fun game. Would crash onto a Rimworld and eat man flesh again...

The father of all First Person Shooters. Although not id Software's first FPS, it certainly paved the way for a long-running succession of amazing games over the years. id's passion for details makes this game a valuable piece in every gamer's collection.
Just imagine that in 1992 all offices in the world still worked on text-only interfaces, However, id Software came out with a game that further extended previous FPS's capabilities, such as 256 colors (instead of 16), textures, incredible sounds, voices, an excellent music that immerses you in the gameplay and sets the perfect mood, and detailed animated sprites for enemies, as well as an amazing level design throughout the whole game that makes you feel as if you were actually within nazi premises, trying to escape. Basic and easy controls, a choice of only 4 weapons (sharing the same ammo) and a nice amount of secret walls and treasure on each level make this game very rewarding and loveable. id's typical sense of humour can be witnessed throughout the complete gameplay in inter-episode texts, the enemies' speech as they see you and as they die, as well as Wolfenstein's famous PacMan secret level, make this game unique and amazing.
Although it is possible to download the game for free, you will be glad to have paid some money for it.
Where would FPSs be nowadays if id Software had pursued a different path and never developed Wolfenstein 3D? Would have another company dared make an incursion into FPSs? Would the 2398 Call of Duties of today exist? Or Half-Life?
Every FPS in the shelf today owes its existance to this game. And you will not regret having played it.
Update: I have happily nominated this game for "The Test of Time" Award for the December Steam Awards :) It is still as good (or maybe even better) as the day it came out.

Squad is the most realistic shooter I have played. Teams are broken up into up to 40 person teams consisting of squads of up to 9 players filling a variety of roles with different weapons, skills, strengths and weaknesses.
Communication is so incredibly important to doing anything successfully in Squad. A mic is all but needed in this game, as swift communication of various things are necessary, emulating real military combat.
The sound efects are so loud and terrifying and they make a physical "THUMP" thatsounds so damn real and has a real effect on the game. It truly is something that must be played, heard and FELT to believe.
One of the coolest moments I ever had was hiding in a building while mortars blew the crap out of everything around me, including all my allies. The loud "THUMP"just kept going off from various mortars, and our base was compromised. Someone I survived it all, but our FOB was lost, and soon so were my nearby allies. I let my team know I was still alive and could defend the base. The mortars started firing and 4 enemies walked right by the building I was in. I gunned them all, halted their offensive, and allowed my team to setup a new FOB and save the game, which we barely won.
Moments like these make Squad. And you can get moments like these manifest themselves so many different ways in Squad.
-Sneaking up on enemies or being snuck up on
-Scouting enemy soldier, vehicle, FOB, and/or rally point positions and planning them
-Rushing bases and capture points down in a vehicle with a full vehicle of soldiers
-Slowly but carefully as a squad (and hopefully a team) trying to take a capture point
-Setting up a defensive perimeter and then defending it as it if were inpenetrable
There's nothing quite like being in a good squad slowly achieving the objectives you or your squad lead gives out. It truly is satisying achieving that and doing all of the little things along the way.
The community is generally great, although again I must mention a mic IS just short of required (I couldn't play without one). Please have a mic before you play this game.
Despite the Alpha status, some cleary bugs, and somewhat lacking optimization (if you have a weaker rig you may want to wait a while), this is definitely a game worth looking into. Squad is definitely shaping up to be a fairly unique video game more than worth your attention.

Wolfenstein 3D is the game that first defined the 1st person shooter genre, a true classic. Although extremely basic compared to more recent games, Wolfenstein 3D still provides challenging gameplay, a variety of difficulties, secrets and peculiar Nazi bosses up to a vampire / robot Hitler, all drawn in fantastic golden age pixel art! Wandering around mapless mazes and pressing on walls looking  for secrets passages, all while killing pixelated nazis with limited vocabularies make this a great classic to playthrough.
Pros:
+ 6 Episodes, with 9 levels each provide plenty of gameplay
+ Multiple diffculty settings for those wanting a real challenge
+ Runs perfectly on Steam, as well as saving on the cloud
+ Save the game anytime to start where you left off
+ Awesome bosses like vampire / robot Hitler with death replays
Cons:
- You die in a few hits depending how close the enemy is
- Mazes can be hard to navigate as there are no maps available
- Enemies always lurking behind hidden corners can wipe you out with ease
- Not a big variety of weapons (but that's understandable)

The Silent Age is a 2d point-and-click adventure game all about time travel, and big scary corporations. In the game, you star as a bland janitor to a corporation that works in national security, you have just been "promoted" when you discover a dying old man who tells you the world is close to ending and that he is from the future. The plot is pretty good, but the world building is where this game really stands out. the feeling of oppression and bleakness is used extremely well to build an almost unsettling atmosphere around the game.
The art style is very complimentary with this, as it is very minimalistic, and bleak. This causes the colorful things to stand out, leading the player to believe it is of some importance. The puzzles introduced in this game are often of the variety of finding something and then using it later, which works well with the color scheme, to help point out objects of importance to the player. This can be quite frustrating, but the game sets an example to puzzle games of how game design should be done, by holding the player's hand just enough, so that he gets it. That AHA moment is something you want to garner in your player as a game designer, and The Silent Age does this fantastically.
The game is fully voice acted by quality voice actors that help bring life to the game. The protagonist is also voice acted, but you have no input into what he says. This actually ends up as a positive quality, as this adds to that atmosphere of hopelessness.  This game is extremely subtle, from small hints in puzzles. To little jokes in the dialog if you do something right. The game is fantastic at subtlety. The littlest things like the sound of a fan moving help build the atmosphere very well in this game.
This game is a must have, if you don't want to spend $10 for it on Steam, pick it up for free on mobile (though I highly recommend the Steam version) The silent age sets an example for other point and click / puzzle games to follow and earns itself a 9.5 out of 10 with a label of "Unsettling".

If you want a game like Mario Kart on the PC, but more skill-based and rewarding, definetely buy this! Got this for € 4,99, it's an absolute steal. I haven't experienced any glitches or bugs as of yet (EDIT: Did get stuck for a bit in a weird spot in a certain map) and the online community is active enough. I'm usually able to find a match for Race mode, all though not for Arena or Mixed.
In a race the laps are able to change and parts can swap between normal, arial and water terrain, giving it some extra variety. You can gain boosts by performing acrobatics when you're lifted in the air by car/boat or barely escape getting hit by an obstacle with an airplane (risk boost) and also by drifting. While most of your performance relies on your skills, there are enough luck-based elements to keep it interesting: like item pick-ups and a slot machine. There are ways to evade attacks, so you aren't automatically screwed when someone locks a drone to you and most weapons require good aim (can also be shot backwards) All-Star is SASRT's equivalent of Bullet Bill, all though it doesn't break the game nearly as much as its effectiveness relies on your All-Star stat (which would cost you points in other areas) and you still need to controll it. It changes your vehicle in an airplane (the fastest one in the game) and makes you indestructible for a short period of time.
There are lots of different game types, including: ring race, boost race, drift challenge, versus races (multiple 1v1), timed race, traffic challenge, battle race (+ 3 lives) and fighting a freaking tank. The maps and characters are all from various SEGA games; some characters are also really funny to play with. The maps look absolutely gorgeous and vary greatly in play style. The difficulty is easily accesible, but hard to master. And if you think you're good, try Expert once you unlock it and get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you once again.
This game supports 4 player split-screen (even online!) and controllers. However I had to look up online what the controls were as there seems to be no keyboard controls configuration. If you opt out of a race online, you'll receive a ranking penalty. I like this idea as it prevents some cheating in ranking, but I had it happen to me when I accidently got disconnected and one time when the race hadn't even started yet and I realized I didn't have enough time. There isn't an easily accesible menu in-game as you'll have to manually go back, which can get annoying because you'll get spammed by an overly enthousiastic commentator voice. These are about all the pet-peeves I have with this game.
Since spoilers don't matter for this, if you concider buying this I'lld suggest first watching a gameplay vid. If you do end up buying it you'll be sure what you're getting and would greatly learn from it, which would immedietely enhance your gaming experience. I usually don't play race games, but for this I easily make an exception. Overall this beats my nostalgic friend: Mario Kart. 10/10

I feel like this game did a lot of things right and twice as many thing wrong, but if you came for a good story about time travel you won't leave disappointed.
This was by far the worst part of The Silent Age for me.
Now, I'm not the biggest fan of "Point 'n Click" games, but I still expected to have a good time.
I... did not...
At least with the gameplay I didn't.
Things took too long or were down right ridiculous!
For one, I did not enjoy the fact that you couldn't solve problems in more than one way.
There was one part of the game that you had to get a scientist out of the lab he was working in by... giving him an apple... Really? I can't knock him out? I can't set off a fire alarm? I can't just tell him that someone in the other room wants to see him?
No.
You have to take a rotten apple core and a pile of dirt from the future put it in a file cabinet underneath a dripping pipe SO YOU CAN GO TO THE FUTURE AND GRAB HIM AN APPLE FROM THE TREE! WHAT?! WHY?!
Not only was this part ridiculous and felt tacked on, I couldn't even figure it out until I found a walkthrough on the internet!
Another problem I had was a level where you had to get to a room in a guy's house. You find an ax which you are going to use to BREAK DOWN A DOOR TO A ROOM YOU NEED TO GET INTO. Meanwhile, I have to keep going to the future and past, because THE GAME WON'T LET YOU BREAK DOWN ANY OF THE OTHER DOORS IN YOUR WAY BECAUSE "WHY DO THAT WHEN I HAVE A TIME MACHINE?"! REALLY?!
The gameplay was boring and uninteresting, except for the things you didn't have to do!
At one point in the story you find a screwdriver in a subway. A blind veteran is playing a guitar nearby and if you try to use the screwdriver on him Joe, the main character, says something along the lines of:
"By the way he's singing I think he's had enough of that from Uncle Sam..."
Best part of the game!
This was the part of the game that really stood out to me and I really enjoyed it.
The Silent Age's plot a classic "TRAVEL THROUGH TIME!" story that takes inspiration from a lot of similar stories, but never feels like it's copying them.
I don't want to spoil too much, but I did have a few problems.
I, for one, felt there weren't NEARLY enough characters and the ones that were there varied from downright uninteresting to "meh".
The ending was also visible from a mile away, but I still thought it was pretty satisfying.
Altogether though, this complaints are minor. I would recommend you play the mobile demo and if the story interests you I would tell you to pick it up.
I immediately fell in love with the graphics of The Silent Age and it was probably the key factor in me picking this game up.
The minimalist style was cool and made it feel unique, if not a bit artsy. Heck, the developer even made fun of it as Joe looks at paintings around the world and says that he really doesn't understand it.
Listing more minor complaints, the animations often felt cheap when picking up or handing objects, but I digress.
Oh, boy...
In my opinion this is where the developers REALLY messed up.
While going through the game the background noises are always on point. Very early on in the game you here a ceiling fan overhead and it really immersed me. I loved hearing the sound of Joe picking up items and it kind of made me appreciate the The Silent Age's name!
Then I talked to the secretary a few seconds later and immediately was pulled out of my immersion.
They added voice acting...
I like having to read the text when I played the mobile demo! It gave it a retro feel and let ME decide how everyone sounded!
Joe's voice sounds nothing like how I pictured and you can tell that the dialogue was written BEFORE the voice acting!
There where moments when the actors change what's written on the dialogue that's in front of you when there was really no reason too!
Right in front of me it says. :
Listen, man, you need to chill!
But, instead the voice actor says! :
Listen, you need to chill, man!
(This exact dialogue was not in the game, but this sort of thing happened multiple times.)
The voice acting broke my immersion multiple times and was an overall bad design choice for this game.
I don't have many, because I'm really don't play these types of games often, but, while I'm not finished with it, Broken Age is great so far! (Not to mention it has Elijah Frickin' Wood!)
Well, I know I've complained a lot, but I only paid $1 for it.
It's usually $10 and I could NEVER recommend it for this price, but for a $1 you get a pretty good story.
This game would have been much better off as a short comic or animation. If you're looking for a good story for $1 you could do a lot worse, but for $10 you could do a lot better.

I've reached a point where I dread seeing time travel show up in games. It's hard to do right, making it complex enough to be interesting but without completely borking causality between events. The Silent Age certainly doesn't make it too complex, and in fact doesn't make anything about itself too complex at all. It's a very straight-forward adventure with straight-forward puzzles and a just-clever-enough story, It may err on the side of simplicity, but there's enough going on to keep it from getting boring.
You play Joe, a simple janitor at looming megacorp Archon in the year 1972. A dying man leaves him cryptic instructions and a gizmo that propels him to 2012, a barren hellscape of abandoned cities and moldering skeletons. It's up to you to help him puzzle his way to some answers, following the story as it careens between the grooves of the 70s and the desolation of Obama's America. You'll meet a few funky characters along the way, and find plenty of items to open doors, cross pits, and power things up with.
Joe is going to need a lot of help, because he's probably one of the dumbest adventure protagonists I've ever seen. He picks up on absolutely no nuance, he cracks wise at the wrong things, and barely has the gumption to stand up to the crazy events that unfold around him. I wish I could say it was refreshing to have such an obvious everyman dealing with temporal conundrums but really his dopey ways start to grate after just a few chapters. You really have to keep in mind that you're the driving force here, not him, and start to brush off some of his dimmer observations.
The challenges that face Joe aren't the toughest either, but that's more of a blessing than a simple-minded protagonist. Plenty of adventure games have puzzles that require bewildering arrays of items assembled in sequences that only make sense to those who coded them, but that's not the case in The Silent Age. Puzzles here are simple and clear, with a limited inventory to use on logical barriers to progress. Not once did I come across an obstacle with a confusing solution, and the only times I got stuck at all were when I forgot to use the game's time travel mechanic.
If you want complexity you'll find it in the story, which tends to be unavoidable in time travel tales. It's the good kind, though, with an existential threat that needs to be stopped through comprehensible means. There's a bit of dialogue that works well enough but most of the story comes in two big plot dumps that put Joe on the missions he needs to complete to save the world. I wouldn't call it the best way to get the point across to the player but it fits with how simple and direct the rest of the game is. And if nothing else, it does a good job of building stakes and tension all the way through to the finale.
The game looks about as clean and simple as it plays, with untextured shapes and bold colors painting the world in stark contrasts. The sound design is fine as well, but ironically is the only place the game doesn't go hard on the 70s themes as every other aspect will remind you constantly of lava lamps and the Cold War. What The Silent Age lacks in subtlety and depth it makes up for in playability and quality, so if you're here for a steady, entertaining tale you're sure to get it.

Wow, the end is really cool!
With roughly 30 hours of content (give or take, depending what's your approach on challenges/achievements), the single player is really captivating and interesting. The "Deadpool" approach of 4th wall being constantly broken (the nature of the game, not a spoiler!) works surprisingly well.
The game plays excellently with a controller (did not try keyboard at all, so can't comment on that), the combat works really well (the only issue is targeting - you lose target if you take damage, and it does not remember last target, so at a certain point in game it's a bit spammy - however, you do not need targeting for 90% of the game, so it's fine) and there's definitely enough reason to replay it (various endings and character builds).
My only complaint would be that it's a little too melee/ranged focused in the beginning of the game, so by the time you get to a point where a mage build would be viable, you're already 10 feet deep into building your character for melee or range. Can't really experience a mage build until either second play-through by going out of your way to neglect building your character for a while, or by resetting your stats (which, word of warning, you only get one free chance at, so save up some money for spells, robes and staves if you plan to make use of it).
Overall, a great game, and I strongly suggest it to anyone who's interested in Castlevania style side scrollers.

This is a challenging platformer about a pixel that is tired of his humdrum life and decides to explore various systems in gaming history.  The worlds are divided by computer/console, and include many classics like the C64, Atari 2600, Spectrum ZX, Gameboy, NES, SNES, Amiga, Apple IIe, Sega Master System, and Sega Genesis (or Sega Megadrive).  I know there's more, I just can't think of them all.  Each world has its own graphic style, music, and sound affects that reflect the system you are "playing in."  It's a unique twist for a game, and it gives the little pixel a lot of character.  If you like platformers and are familiar with some of the classic systems... I think you'll enjoy this game!

Interstellar Marines is a early access game which only has limited multiplayer modes and maps. But it presents what they have in a way that makes it fantastic. The game is going to add a co-op campaign which is bringing inspiration from System Shock. The multiplayer is extremely different to Call of Duty and Battlefield which makes it already a great game. There is lots of recoil and cool tiny things like ligting up your masks for no reason at all. The developers have made it so you can see the outline of the mask over your face. Tiny things like this make the game realistic and makes you feel like you are a marine. There is only one gun which is a assult gun which you can play with at this current time of writing. I hope they add new guns soon to add to the experience. The graphics look amazing for an indie title. Sun glair reflects on your visor aadding to the experience. I would also like to note that Interstellar Marines is harder then it looks. It is extremely hard to kill people and there is a lot of recoil. I would recommend this game to anyone which wants a challenge or is a sci-fi fan such as myself (reminds my of aliens).

Life of pixel does a very good job at encapsulating the feel of the different old school systems it emulates.
It's a platformer in the vein of Meat boy and the likes which means it's quite hard and with a lot of retries and new strategies.
It features some old computer systems which made me very happy, since I feel a lot of gaming history focuses mainly on the video game consoles.
Although I thoroughly enjoyed this game, I cant help feeling like it's a missed oppurtunity. Although the graphics are often true to the system it's supposed to look like, the animations are still too fluid and the music for the systems are a generic 8-bit sounding tune. (with exceptions like the C64-stage.)
I would love to have a bit choppier animations on the older systems and sounds more connected to the platform.
It's also a bit buggy. I wanted to check out the control bindings. Did so and accidentally pressed enter to back out. It selected a control to change and waited for input. Instead pressed ESC to back out which was all good and well until I wanted to use the menu again. Had to alt-tab out and force quit the game to end it.
All in all it's a feast for the eyes if you love retro gaming, and I hope the devs get all the love they need to expand this concept into a more faithful adaption of old computer- and video games.

Despite it's art style which can turn as much people off as much as it does turn on, I honestly had fun with it. What you basically got here is a basically a Dynasty Warriors style game mixed with Dead or Alive-tier girls, it's a basic button masher where you fight through loads of enemies and occasionally clothes get ripped off. It's goofy, it's very Japanese, and it plays good, especially with a controller, and though the PC port is barebones as far as customization options go (some anti aliasing would be nice) it runs pretty well.
If I had to find some complaints with the game, despite the large roster of playable characters the game can get repetitive because you're mainly fighting in the same environments against the same characters over and over again. Though there are 4 story modes the plot isn't that interesting compared with it's sequel Deep Crimson on 3DS and you'll forget about it eventually. And the transformation/clothes ripping scenes get annoying when you do side stories as they cause the dialogue to repeat again and again.
But in spite of those faults, I'd recommend the game, provided you like beat em ups and can look past the artstyle, as there's a ton of content, and because it's a port of a handheld game, you can easily pick it up and play it whenever you want due to the fast missions. If you're still on the fence, I'd recommend picking it up for $20.

I wont be including the connection problems in the review because you can avoid these in offline mode, and theyll probably be resolved soon.
Graphics - 7/10: The graphics are great and fitting of the DragonBall Universe, and considering the development team were working with a completely new engine they have done pretty well, with all characters looking very well shaded and the motion blur/bloom with other effects makes for a very visually appealing improvement from other DBZ games. Loading screens in this game are super short which is a good thing to have in a game where you are constantly transitioning into different stages. Framerates are high and my computer was running the thing very cool. My only graphical complaint is, sometimes you might have to deal with bad camera angles.
Sound - 6/10: The musical score is pretty awesome although can be quite repetetive as there isnt that much variation. All of the classic DBZ sounds are there. Theres just 1 thing really bothering me...is that some of the voice actors have changed and their replacements, arent that good.  Frieza's new voice actor for example just cannot cut it, English Frieza sounds baaaad. Why dont our characters talk! :( i cant stand nodding no-brains characters.
Gameplay - 7/10: The combat experience is great, and even better that you can now play alongside your friends with Online Co-Operative missions (Yes Online Co-op in DBZ, finally!). You can learn tonnes of abilities from the other DBZ fighters as you develop your character and fighting style, and there is plenty of activities to do. My biggest concern is the PC (keyboard + mouse) controls, theyre very poor and difficult, almost impossible to play the game with, so i strongly recommend playing with a controller. The tutorial isnt that great, so its best to just press every button and learn by finding out. Biggest complaint is the lack of variation in missions as you need to repeat them over and over and over for small amounts of XP in order to continue the story if you have made a balanced character.
Overall - 7/10:  Above Average!
The game requires you to repeat content a lot in order to level up your character so be prepared to invest time into this game if you wish to become really strong. Besides that you have a solid DBZ game here with a good story where you play alongside your favorite DBZ heroes and villains, though i do feel that our custom characters should have been given the opportunity to talk in cutscenes to truly make us feel apart of the world. With lots of customisation and a good combat system, you have a pretty good game. I still think Budokai 3 on PS2 is still the best though.

This was a challenging game. If you dislike dying in a very simplistic fashion, play something else. Toss aside your pride and try to tackle the bosses. They aren't impossible, but it requires skill and timing. Each boss was unique and had their own exploitable weakness. The only question is how long can you dodge and attack before you win or die. There is a tiny bit of story, but the main focus was explore and kill bosses(or die trying). In its very essence, Titan Souls is a game and it requires focus or it will unforgivingly punish you.
I have yet to finish off the secret hidden boss. Current overall death count: 300. Would die again.
Edit: He's dead now. Death Count: 350
Tips:
Aiming and shooting takes longer than you think when you have a split second gap for hitting the weak point.
Know when to collect your arrow. Collecting your arrow at the wrong time and place will lead to death.
I strongly recommend a controller for your game for better aiming, but it is possible to win with keyboard, just very hard.
Dodging is more important than getting your arrow for the most part. There are some bosses that get harder if you don't start shooting more and quickly though.
Each boss can potentially be killed in 40 seconds. Just know what their weakness is and aim properly.

TL:DR
The game is fun but is hampered by the normal issues of grinding in F2P modeled games and easy pay to win buttons. Need some balancing fixes on match rewards.
5/10
-Good Game
-Long Way to Go to be a Great Game.
----------
The Good, The Bad, The Trap of F2P
So first the good:
Great gameplay. The fast pace matches and good vehicle battles are nicely done and controls feel right and intuitive.
Good Controls. Good controls, they can be tweaked with ease and if you don't like the default firing controls, you can remap each weapon on your car if you want.
Customization: Damn straight, the main appeal of the game they deliver on.
Player Base: Longest wait time I've had was 10 seconds to get into a match. Most of the time 2-4 seconds is all you have to wait with many matches just throwing you in the moment you click the button.
The Bad:
Unbalanced Match Rewards:
I understand rewarding the winning players with something extra, however this game doesn't do that. It awards the winning team period. The only way to get something if you where on the loosing team is to be lucky in a match, with requiring around 3 personal kills and 4 match awards to net you 13 scrap....and nothing else. If you win a match and didn't do a thing to help your team you will still get 15 scrap. >.< If you did litterally anything at all (land one hit on an enemy, help with capture etc) then you are gifted with around 15 scrap, event drops, fuel (If you have a fuel tank however in the beta this is sometimes spotty), and a full part!
As a result, you're just rolling the dice on a match to get anything.
Poor resource management:
The game is split mostly into Matched play and Raids. Raids are where you get your harder to find materials (supposidly, honestly just about everything you will need this stuff for to build) like copper, however it's locked behind the fuel system. While neat in theory, the cost for the cheapest raid is 20 fuel! and you get 100 in your tank. That would be fine if there was also a natural timed way to get it, however no, you can only refuel on gas by doing and WINNING matched play against players with a gas drum on your vehicle. Did we mention this drum is for the most part a death sentance for if its destroyed, it deals 500 dmg straight to you! Most vehicles early on (rank 10 and bellow players) will be one shotted by this and the drum only gives you 5 if you win. There are better drums out there however they are going to take a long time to get with the base gameplay as they require parts, scrap and our lovely copper from the raids. How fun!. Oh and for your hard work you will usually get maybe around 5-10 copper on a raid early on. Most  early projects require 50+ copper to build.
The Symptom of F2P:
THE GRIND IS REAL!
While at first you'll get things fairly quickly, enjoy this while it lasts, it wont last long. Moment you reach rank 3/4 it will drop! Like a lead pipe on your head. The vary nature of the game's custimization leads to some problems in balancing, but at about rank 3 you are thrown out of the new player pool and into the 'everyone!' pool  so good luck, as mentioned before rewards for completing matches are slim if you aren't lucky to be on the winning side or j ust epic at the game. Having said this for anything beyond the starter gear (so common items) you will be on the grind heavily to get the required parts, most items beyond common require not just resources like scrap and copper (Copper can only be grabbed from raids as far as I've found so far). So strap in for excessive grinding that simply pads the game out and after a while starts to detract from the gameplay.
Pay to Win:
What you thought I'd let this go un noted. Now not as bad as other games the pay to win is still present. If you have an issue with any of the grinding, farming, building, fuel, hell even the whole thing and just want to skip to the end goal for most stuff. All you have to do is drop some cash. About 50 bucks should do if you want to jump to the later parts of the game. 10 if you just want to feel good briefly before it crashes down on your head.
Purchaseable In Game Currency:
Main source of infliation since MMOs began. The in game currency which is used 100% in the player shop as I've seen it so far and is the ONLY currency/shop in the game as well can be purchased with real world money. As a result it has caused some major inflation on a lot of fronts, mix in that there are some parts that can only be purchased through the packs that cost real money but are still trade-able in the market and you get a very skewed market place full of infliation.

This is a fun little arena shooter. Definetly worth trying for the price of free.
Crossout is fairly shallow. PVP (which is 95% of the game) has several modes but most come down to 'kill the other team/trucks.'  I keep thinking the game doesn't have much to it but I keep doing another match, and another, and another.
The vehicle builder is very simple to use. Start snapping some parts together, give it a test drive and you're done. Weapon and loot progression is fairly slow. They do give you basic items in your first 6 hours of play but expect to be using those for quite some time. It's a fun trial and error system. You see some crazy constructions - some of which give you some good ideas on how to improve your build.
The market lets you sell extra loot you can't use for credits (that are also buyable with real world cash).
The PVE is called raids and are fairly shallow and quick. There is little reason to do more than 2 per day, they take about 5 minutes each. Maybe this progresses to more meaningful PVE later but in the early game expect to spend almost all your game time in the PVP arena.
I suggest you try it, if you don't like it by the end of the 1st hour, uninstall it - that's the majority of the game.

I've, for a long time, been searching for a game which would present itself in a professional yet fun manner when it comes to modern conflict. And I've finally, after at least 10 years of searching, found it and am extremely content.
Although still in Alpha, the game is extremely polished compared even to some triple A games which attempt to do the same thing this game does, but fail miserably. Where did this game go wrong? Nowhere. Perhaps it appeared in the wrong place at the wrong time, perhaps the marketing for this game is lacking, as not many people have heard of it. So if you're reading this and wish to buy the game, do it. If you're reading this and already have the game, then send to all the world a message, and that is that this game lives and marches on.

What happens when you combine Arma 3's realistic feel, Battlefield's graphics, and add DCS/MilSim-level teamwork/coordination?
SQUAD is JUST not quite a MilSim, but it's close. While the Arma series focuses on a gigantic map where you can launch corps-sized operations over a hugly flexible and moddable system, SQUAD is focused more on... well... Squads.
You fight on a set of slightly less gigantic maps (still huge) in roughly platoon-sized teams of several squads of players. SQUAD is objective-based, meaning it is not as open-ended as Arma, but it feels more realistic due to (in my humble opinion) better graphics and effects (such as a suppression system), better/realistic gunplay, and much higher teamwork requirments.
Although not (yet) as moddable as the Arma series, it is a very impressive game, and I will go into an atypical length to review it. WARNING: Long review, I'm sorry... this game deserves it.
How I saw it early on, is that SQUAD essentially has the "ACRE" radio mod from Arma built into the game, and microphones/headsets are almost mandatory, as communication and teamwork is SO important that NOT having a mic can actually prevent you from playing in certain situations (Squad Leaders (SL) who do not have a mic are kicked from the SL position automatically).
I have yet to see or play a game where communication and teamwork is so vital that the team with the better-coordinated squads will always win. Thus, it is needless to say, this game is quite intense.
Time for the overused Pros and Cons list (Hooray!):
The Good Stuff:
* Very realistic
Again, not quite MilSim, but one of the closest games that is not DCS. (Unlike DCS though, SQUAD uses this realism in a fun and engaging way... not boring at all)
* Great gunplay
Takes some time getting used to, but the guns are realistic and they feel right. LMGs take skill to not blaze away uslessly over the enemy's heads due to recoil, and not everyone can be a Marksman (I am one of those few "good" DMs in this game). Bullet drop (applies to rockets too) is present similar to the Arma series, and you move slightly different depending on what weapons you are carrying.
P.S. Sick of OP snipers in other FPSs? In SQUAD, marksmen play a role in the fight, but are quite difficult to use right, and are by no means overly powerful. Being a marksman is actually frowned upon in a lot of in-game situations. I usually play Anti-Tank when we don't need a marksman.
* "Battlefield-level" graphics
Which, coupled with the level of realism similar to Arma, makes this game a joy to look at. You will get immersed in the battle very quickly due to this and the level of interaction the game requires. This game does not have the destruction system of Battlefield or Rainbow 6 Seige, though, but certain obejcts can be shot through by certain weapons.
* Communication and Teamwork matter...
A LOT!! You WILL lose if you don't communicate, making this not only a realistic game, but also a interesting social experience. The stress of realistically-simulated combat, the importance of leadership, plus the unobstucted use of voice comms, means you get to really meet people, and you will make a lot of friends in this game.
* No hackers.
(read that again in disbelief)
Hackers are evidently non-existent on the official servers due to powerful anticheats and the game's own mechanics. And at the moment, admins are usually on-call and will quickly deal with griefers, teamkillers, and radio-spammers (a big offence in a game that focuses on communication). I have yet to run into a hacker in this game, which is a first for me in my 15+ years of gaming.
To any hackers reading this, I can actually tell you honestly to go somewhere else. Not because hacking is bad anyways (which it is), but because you really will not last long trying to hack this game. I'm sorry.
* Leadership roles are, due to the game's realism and need to communicate, quite challenging. Not eveyone is cut out for squad leading! Learn "people skills" while playing this game!
* SQUAD was unbalanced early on (regular armed forces [RUS and US] tended to win a lot against the irregular forces [insurgents and militia]), but recent updates have balanced the factions, vehicles, and weapons out quite nicely.
* Very good options, settings, and keybindings.
* Players tend to be more willing to work together
Than in most other games, since this game forces you to do so. You can do very little by yourself, however, those rare moments when you do pull off something impressive by yourself or with a buddy, you really feel like heroes!
While you always have your bad apples, I would consider this game to have (so far) a better player community than most.
* Game Updates happen pretty regularily (slow but steady)
And each one adds important content such as bolstering the anticheat further, optimizations, bugfixes and graphic glich removals, game content such as new vehicles and soldier types/weapons, game balancing, and framework for future updates.
While helicopters (long anticipated) have not been added due to game balance considerations, the game's current state, etc., they may be seen in the future once SQUAD's few kinks get ironed out. The Devs appear to be intent on building and upgrading a working system first, then adding content. Good Work to them so far!
Not-so-good stuff:
* IMMENSE learning curve.
Getting used to the realistic movement, being able to (and forced to) communicate realistically, having to deal with the minimalistic HUD, and getting used to the idea of not being able to go rambo, will take a lot of patience. Once you learn the ropes, though, what you learn will pay off.
* Game takes a while to download and uses a bunch of memory space
That said, the game itself runs very smoothly for most PCs despite the intense graphics.
* Official Servers are few, and they are usually maxed-out on players
So finding a game can be tricky. However, joining a server has been simplified in a recent update.
* Near Arma-level controls
A tad complicated, but you will get used to it pretty quickly (especially if you have played any of the Armas before).
* No avatar customization (as of 08/31/2017)
SO FAR, you can't modify what you carry/use, which is great since the game is going for realism, but what I don't like is that you can't change your soldier's face, his skin tone/color, and his hair (for insurgents, who have beards. Everyone else is clean-shaven and wears helmets or hats, so the latter matters little). Although the uniforms, helmets, and vests are not (and shouldn't be) customizable, it would be nice to be able to customize small bits of clothing like scarves, sunglasses, and such to add a little bit of variation to the avatars.
I would entirely recommend this game to any miltary fan or anyone who is serious about teamwork and coordination. I wholeheartedly DO NOT recommend this for people who like individual-focused games like COD and Battlefield, as SQUAD is among the most severe team-oriented games I have played, and you will be destroyed time and again if you do not work together!
SQUAD is one of my favorite games right now. Joining a random squad at the start of a match, becoming good friends through shared hardship, and combining your team's diverse skillsets and personalities to win... there are few games that evoke this kind of comradrie with other players. Friendships you make in a battle will carry on to other battles, and even to other games!
I just wish they had more Official Servers, because the 20 or so available right now are pretty packed most of the time!

Overall, it’s an almost decent game. I didn’t get that far, but it shows. You get several different methods of gold mining,  Flying, however, is a fact of life around here, especially when you are trying to load something on your car while holding it down – it will propel you up in the air; and remember to never, ever, drop a panning system on your pan, they will become one and break your game if you don’t have enough money to buy new ones. The panning mechanism is so picky that sometimes the gold nugget is the ONLY thing left in the pan, and it still won’t let you pick it, you have to play with it for a while and then maybe it will let you get it. Otherwise, tough luck buddy.
I refunded it while I still could. I don’t want to encourage this kind of behavior on the part of the developer, who is asking a full price for what represents EA levels of broken.
1.	The setting looks pretty nice and I really love Alaska.
2.	There are quite a few kinds of equipment.
3.	Deformable terrain is nice.
1.	With a pan, unless the gold is in what the game deems an appropriate position, you can’t pick it up. It doesn’t matter that it’s inches from other stones, you can’t pick it up unless the game allows you to do so, which is annoying and sometimes leads to losing valuable stones. The first time I was not even sure whether this was a nugget but wanted to make sure – moved it around for maybe two or three minutes and the game finally realized that I want to pick it up.
2.	I accidentally closed the pan while having a nugget inside. Do you think it was still there? Wrong. All the other stones were but the nugget was gone.
3.	There are no people anywhere. The place seems like a desert. It would have made sense if you were living in a cabin in the middle of nowhere and only trade with a bush pilot or someone every once in a while, but the game is set in a small town, with a factory nearby, and the smoke indicates that the factory is working. What the… are human models too hard to make? This is disgraceful.
4.	Physics is broken like you wouldn’t believe. Flying all over the place because what you’re carrying has touched a fence or something, buckets don’t lose their content after falling almost flat on the ground, bottom up, holding an object down while trying to jump on the car will make you fly. This is inexcusable.
I’m sorry but I don’t want to lose my ability to get a refund to try other tiers when the first one is such an awful experience. Stay away from this game, at least until it is patched and made acceptable. I really don’t want to encourage releasing games in this state.

I wont be including the connection problems in the review because you can avoid these in offline mode, and theyll probably be resolved soon.
Graphics - 7/10: The graphics are great and fitting of the DragonBall Universe, and considering the development team were working with a completely new engine they have done pretty well, with all characters looking very well shaded and the motion blur/bloom with other effects makes for a very visually appealing improvement from other DBZ games. Loading screens in this game are super short which is a good thing to have in a game where you are constantly transitioning into different stages. Framerates are high and my computer was running the thing very cool. My only graphical complaint is, sometimes you might have to deal with bad camera angles.
Sound - 6/10: The musical score is pretty awesome although can be quite repetetive as there isnt that much variation. All of the classic DBZ sounds are there. Theres just 1 thing really bothering me...is that some of the voice actors have changed and their replacements, arent that good.  Frieza's new voice actor for example just cannot cut it, English Frieza sounds baaaad. Why dont our characters talk! :( i cant stand nodding no-brains characters.
Gameplay - 7/10: The combat experience is great, and even better that you can now play alongside your friends with Online Co-Operative missions (Yes Online Co-op in DBZ, finally!). You can learn tonnes of abilities from the other DBZ fighters as you develop your character and fighting style, and there is plenty of activities to do. My biggest concern is the PC (keyboard + mouse) controls, theyre very poor and difficult, almost impossible to play the game with, so i strongly recommend playing with a controller. The tutorial isnt that great, so its best to just press every button and learn by finding out. Biggest complaint is the lack of variation in missions as you need to repeat them over and over and over for small amounts of XP in order to continue the story if you have made a balanced character.
Overall - 7/10:  Above Average!
The game requires you to repeat content a lot in order to level up your character so be prepared to invest time into this game if you wish to become really strong. Besides that you have a solid DBZ game here with a good story where you play alongside your favorite DBZ heroes and villains, though i do feel that our custom characters should have been given the opportunity to talk in cutscenes to truly make us feel apart of the world. With lots of customisation and a good combat system, you have a pretty good game. I still think Budokai 3 on PS2 is still the best though.

This game was really well done. Unlike a lot of point-and-click's where you end up in a cycle of trial and error, the logic behind each next step was quite intuitive and for most instances it didn't take too much to work out the difference between a situation in which you didn't have what you need yet or you just hadn't worked out how to put it together yet. I've found that to be a common problem in other point-and-click games.
Mechanics are simple and well done, nothing moves very fast but it doesn't really need to. The whole thing revolves around time travel, so there are several sequences in which you are searching through the same locations but in two different time zones decades apart which adds some really interesting aspects to the problems you need to solve.
*Spoiler Alert*
This time-travel aspect really comes into the story. I found some aspects of the ending a bit predictable (a guy at the start has been shot, you end up being the one that shot him) but then it took it to much greater heights that I hadn't expected. Sort of didn't feel like there was a huge amount of story at the start (or any story was incidental to put you in the situation of the game) but then it all came together at the end really well.

Life of Pixel is a cute platformer that guides you through a period of video game's history : you will see the evolution of this kind of games through different machines, from 8-bit to 16-bit.
There are 104 levels divided into 13 "worlds" (= machines). For each level, you have to collect all of the crystals to open the exit door. Then, you can look for a special gem and, sometimes, a fruit/candy/cake ... Getting all of them will unlock lots of things, so you might try to catch them all !
Regarding the difficulty, this game is more or less easy, getting more challenging if you want to unlock all of the achievements. You are going to die a lot, especially trying to beat specific levels (this fire level ...), but do not worry, this is how this game is supposed to be :)
Finally, if you are looking for a fun platform game that proves to be challenging for achievements hunters, you may want to buy it, it will take you ~7-10 hours to unlock them all !

I really really wanted to like this game.  I absolutely love the idea behind it, but the execution is so flawed it is not worth playing.
As I am sure youhave figured out from the trailer, life of pixel is an old school platformer that takes you through various generations of games.  The game starts out in black and white, one room levels with very simple graphics.  As you progress through more and more levels you open up new systems which open up better graphics and more complex levels.
The problem is the levels are incredibly poorly designed.  The later levels are broken down into rooms and there is some exploration involved.  There is no way to look up/down/left or right, which in turn leads to an enormous amount of leaps of faith.  For example in one level you are on top of a cliff in a cave, you cannot see anything below you but the only way to go is down.  So you go down and are on another level of the cave, again you see an opening in the floor, and the assumption is to go down again, but this time it leads you to a pit with instant death.  The game is littered with moments like this where you blindly leap onto the next screen only to instantly die and have to redo the level, and there are no checkpoints so you always have to redo the level from the beginning.
This game desparately needs  a feature that allows you to look around the levels so you are not blindly running into things that you had no idea were around.  If the developers added that I would give the game another go, but as it stands the game is too much blind jumping to recommend, especially given how many other vastly superior platformers exist on steam.

Life of Pixel is a platformer for Steam that has a dual purpose. On one hand, you have a nice little platformer boasting over 100 levels with simple controls, and sometimes challenging gameplay as you control a little green block face thingy (as best as I can describe it) as you dodge enemies, jump over pitfalls, make sure not to get hit by spikes, and collect jewels in a standard fare that you would expect from an old school platformer. It’s simple basically. And on that alone, just a basic (but sometimes challenging) game. Luckily, Life of Pixel has an ace up its sleeve. Its other purpose is to feed you a heaping dosage of gaming history, as each of the worlds is themed after a different classic gaming console or computer. You’ll be playing levels with graphics, sound effects and music like they were pulled from your childhood. Pixel includes a load of systems ranging from the Spectrum ZX to the Super Nintendo to the Commodore 64, and a heck of a lot more that inspire each of the worlds.

Fun combat and a steady flow of rewards make this journey a massively enjoyable one, especially with some fellow mercenaries along for the ride.
On the hostile, bandit-ridden planet of Pandora, there is one thing that draws off-world attention: The Vault. This mysterious alien structure is rumored to hold treasures of fantastic power and wealth, and so it attracts fortune-seeking corporations and individuals alike. In Borderlands, you are one such individual, but the satisfaction of unlocking the Vault's secrets pales in comparison to the rollicking good time you'll have on your way there. Borderlands is all about the journey, not the destination, and like most trips, this one is much better when you have some friends along for the ride. Solo players can still have a good time, because the bloody and entertaining combat is paired well with rewarding loot and engaging experience systems. But Pandora is a lonely place for a solitary mercenary, and lone wolves will find the pace deliberate and the friendly characters too few and far between. Those who take advantage of the four-player online cooperative mode will experience the game as it's meant to be played. The pleasing rhythm of killing enemies, gathering loot, and cashing in is punctuated by fighting bosses, completing quests, and leveling up. As a solo merc, this rhythm is slow and methodical, but as a team, the pace quickens to an invigorating clip and pretty soon you've spent hours having a riotously rewarding time.
The world of Pandora has a dusty, run-down feel, yet it manages to be vibrant and eye-catching at the same time. The art style features black-line borders and a colorful palette that give the game a not-quite-comic, not-quite-cel-shaded look. It takes some getting used to, and its technical execution is less-than-perfect . Yet what Borderlands lacks in precision it more than makes up for in style, and hours into the game you'll still be appreciating the thoughtful design touches that bring this world to life. Though the different environments occasionally feel too similar, there is enough distinct detail to keep them from blurring together. Your vanquished enemies also do their part to keep things visually interesting by dying in a variety of gruesome and entertaining ways. Bodies explode, limbs fly off, and burning enemies occasionally disintegrate from the ground up until only the mask of their face is left hanging in midair. It sounds (and is a bit) horrifying, but when the mask drops comically to the floor and finally burns up, don't bother stifling that chuckle. The art design resonates well with Borderlands' irreverent sense of humor, and the game is playful without feeling too goofy.
You travel through this world as one of four characters, each with a unique look and attitude. You don't really get to appreciate the character designs if you play solo because you have no AI teammates, but you do hear frequent quips that give you a little bit of character-specific flavor. The most important difference between characters is the action skill, which is a special ability that can give you an edge in combat. The Hunter can release a vicious bird of prey, the Soldier can throw down an automatic turret flanked by shields, the Siren can turn invisible and speedy, damaging all enemies in the vicinity, and the Berserker flies into a damage-resistant rage and delivers brutal punches to his enemies. You unlock these abilities after playing for a short while, and not only are they all fun to use, but each one can be customized in a couple of strategically distinct ways. You can tweak and upgrade your ability by investing skill points in appropriate skills. So, for example, upgrading the Hunter's bird of prey not only can increase the amount of damage it does, but can make it attack multiple targets, steal health from them, slow them down for easy sniping, and cause them to drop more loot. Expanding your action skill makes you more deadly in combat, and it's one of the most rewarding parts of leveling up. Killing enemies, finishing quests, and completing in-game bonus challenges earn you experience points, which in turn earn you a new level. Leveling up boosts your overall fortitude and grants you a precious skill point to use however you see fit.
You can also spend your skill points on other improvements, and each character has three different skill trees that highlight different tactics and abilities. So the Soldier can essentially become the team medic by developing the skills that allow him to shoot teammates to regenerate their health and that make his turret create a healing radius. Or he could choose to become more deadly, increasing his turret damage and combat rifle performance. Though your weapon proficiency improves based on how much you use a given weapon type, different characters have skills that favor different types of guns, so it's to your advantage to play to your character's strengths. The Berserker can certainly become proficient with the sniper rifle, but his melee-focused action skill and preference for rocket launchers make him a better choice for wading into the fray. Though the branching skill trees offer intriguing ways to specialize, your initial character choice has the biggest impact on how you'll go through the game. Fortunately, each character is fun and deadly in his own way, so you can't choose poorly, and you'll probably want to experience what each one has to offer. Playing cooperatively allows you to enjoy and benefit from the other characters' abilities, something you don't get to appreciate when playing solo, unless you start a new game.
Expanding your abilities and leveling up is one of the main ways that Borderlands consistently rewards you. Loot is another. Loot can be found in containers, dropped by enemies, or given to you as a quest reward. It includes money, ammo, shields, mods that boost and alter your grenades, mods that boost your skills, and, of course, guns. Guns are classified in familiar categories: pistols, submachine guns, shotguns, combat rifles, sniper rifles, rocket launchers, and so on. Each class feels distinct, and the shooting mechanics are well tuned and satisfying, which makes it fun to blast baddies. Base damage, clip size, fire rate, accuracy, and bullet spread are just some of the variables within each class, and some guns have more exotic features, like bladed pistols that increase melee damage or a shotgun that also shoots rockets. They can also do elemental damage, which comes in a variety of flavors that put a special kind of hurt on and can even do damage over time. Equip an incendiary gun if you want to burn flesh, or a corrosive gun if you want to deal extra damage to creatures with tough hides.
The Good
Satisfying gunplay
Tons of weapons, shields, and helpful items
Four unique and equally fun-to-play characters
Distinct, appealing artistic style
Great system of rewards
The Bad
Lonelier, slower-paced for a solo player
Massively unsatisfying
Lackluster loot sharing system

Ah, Wolfenstein 3d. Many, incudling myself, would say that this game helped establish the First Person Shooter genre. Why would we, in 2015 (as of writing), want to play a 23 year old relic of gaming past? Well, it's because despite its age, and its primitive appearance, everything that makes the genre what we know it to be today is here. After all, this is the blueprint to the FPS genre. The gameplay is here, and there's a certain freedom that this and many games like it have that more modern games seem to lack. Sure, as I said before, the graphics are dated and it looks like a mess someone drew in MS Paint compared to pretty much anything since then. Wolfenstein 3d is a game that doesn't take itself to seriously and doesn't expect you to either. So, as inexpensive as it is to have one of the most vital pieces of gaming history to enjoy for yourself, you would be kind of silly not to get it and try it at least once.
