Did you ever hear the tragedy of Moonloop the Isloated?
I thought not. It's not a tale the internet would tell you.
Moonloop was a community on Pathos II, so small and self contained, it could defend itself from anything, so long as it posed no physical danger. Moonloop hosted three survivors: Gerda, Satriki, and Rogesh. Gerda, the computer. So skilled and precise, she could save anyone seconds from death. The other two were pointless horrible people, a father and son escaped from the orbiting prison.
Our story begins with the creation of a simple barracks. Each of our survivors built their own beds with wood harvested from the nearby woods. ''Twas a small thing, but well lit and joyful. The cat slept next to Gerda. Over the next few weeks, the team established themselves. Gerda researched advanced technology, while the other two focused on brute work, either collecting and rearranging their belongings or hunting.
One day, one rainy summer day, Gerda set out to construct a new system of production to keep the community alive. She collected the silver she needed, then walked across the map to her workplace. Satriki and Rogesh left for a hunting trip. The cat seemed to have bonded with our terrible excon friend Rogesh.
You see, Gerda never liked security. She saw beautification and benefits as crucial to survival. Make it pretty, she insisted, and nobody will attack it.
As those ♥♥♥♥ing awful people marched on toward their hunting spot, tragedy struck the beautiful roadside community of Moonloop. A deranged leopard, driven to madness by the excon's effective hunting or, rather, extinctification, of the local wildlife, approached the small research facility built within Moonloop. Gerda looked on at her work as the omniscient god they called "LunaticS0UL" helped the excons hunt. The leopard approached slowly.
The excons returned home hours later, tens of bodies stacked on their carrier. The two collapsed on their beds after dropping off the corpses in the processing room. "Where is Gerda?" they must have wondered. The answer would not wait to show itself.
The following morning, Rogesh awoke early, realizing he hasn't seen the cat since returning home. He wandered about the camp, spurred on by his god. In the top of the screen, a splash of blood. He approached slowly, then faster, then faster still. Drops became puddles became a pool. In the pool laid a pile of bones.
Cat bones.
He turned on a dime, scanning the nearby research room for any sign of help. He found Gerda lying in a similar pool of blood, claw marks covering her weak body. She was still breathing. She still had a pulse. He picked her up and sprinted back to the barracks, dropped Gerda in a bed, and searched for a medkit. The last one was several units away, on the other side of the map. He dropped everything, waking Satriki on his way out. Satriki would watch her and keep pressure on her wounds. Rogesh sprinted to the medkit, grabbed it, and sprinted back. But, as he entered the barracks, he realized that he had forgotten a crucial detail.
Satriki and Rogesh hasn't been trained in medical techniques. They could not help. They could only watch as Gerda passed on.
Gerda's death, stacked with the cat's death by leopard, broke Satriki. He took out the knife he always kept on him since escaping the prison and looked at his father. With fatal precision, he killed his aging father and ran. He reached the edge of the map and stopped. What now? Satriki stayed there for a while until he could think again. Satriki couldn't do anything outside of hunt. His whole life he had been a slave to Gerda. He couldn't survive without her advanced machinery which, for some reason, only she seemed to understand. Satriki spent his last few days attempting to scrap together a refinery table in order to eat. He died of food poisoning and starvation where he stood.
Ironic. Moonloop could protect its inhabitants from boredom, but nothing else. Nothing real.
RimWorld is drop-dead (pun somewhat intended) amazing. It uses AI to create events (like the leopard spawning) then you create your own story by reacting to it. If Gerda hadn't been a moron and would've invested some time in a trap or two, the story would have been completely different. It's AMAZING. Buy it.

Tales from the Borderlands is a five part episodic game series from Telltale Games. Just like any Telltale game, your choices affect how the story is tailored and delivered. Unlike previous Telltale titles, Tales from the Borderlands lets you play with two protagonists, Rhys, a Hyperion ‘suit’ with dreams of being the next Handsome Jack, and Fiona, a Pandoran con artist looking to score her biggest ever swindle. As you progress throughout the story, you'll be switching from Rhys and Fiona. The two protagonists have their own unique skill that sets them apart as individual characters.
Tales from the Borderlands properly portrays the Borderlands atmosphere. From the presentation of the unforgiving wastelands of Pandora to the humor and comedy expressed by the characters, even someone who hasn't even played Borderlands can totally relate and appreciate the game. It's awesome soundtrack pumps up the atmosphere with life. The voice acting is very good that you could actually feel the transition of emotions from drama, action and comedy. The characters are also very likable as each one has their own personality and that as a certain character continues to develop, their presence just becomes more vital as you go deeper into the story.
As for the gameplay, it's a classic Telltale gameplay with times that you'll be choosing how you want to respond, there will also be times that you'll be given a decision that has consquences and a big load of Quick Time Events. Compared from the previous TellTale titles, Telltale did a new style of QTE on this one with multiple buttons that pop out during certain specific points in the game and not just one button to mash.
Story/Plot: 10/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Music: 10/10
Graphics: 8/10
Overall: 9/10
I recommend this game to big fans of Telltale games and to those who love games with a great and solid storyline. Though your choices affect only the flow of the story and not the ending, Tales from the Borderlands is must play for its masterful combination of drama, comedy and action. If a game's story really matters to you, then this is the game for you! Let the Tales from the Borderlands be heard!

"It's the break of dawn. July 16, 1946. Everything's gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥ The Nazi War Machine is advancing at an astonishing rate. We can't catch up. Our tactics are failing. Outclassed and outgunned, and nobody knows why. People are getting desperate. Not me, I'm here to meet an old friend and settle a score, Turn this thing around."
Wolfenstein: The New Order is set 3 years after the events of Wolfenstein (2009) and set instantly after the events of the Prequel Wolfenstein: The Old Blood.
The New Order portrays a what if scenario (alternate history) Where the Nazi's drop the A-Bomb on the US causing them to surrender and thus winning the war. Which then leads the whole world to be conquered by the Nazi's. The game goes across two different times in history. The ending of the war in 1946 and then in the 1960's where the Nazi's rule with fear. Bethesda added a lot of nice features with the alternate history, with famous songs being sung in German or Mount Rushmore being destroyed etc.
Unlike most sequels The New Order can be played without having to play Return to castle Wolfenstein (2001) and Wolfenstein (2009). If you are a returning player you obviously will understand character relations quicker. Also when Caroline and BJ are reminiscing about injuries you will understand what they are referencing.
The graphics and gameplay are fantastic. The world is great, spanning from the beaches of WWII in the 40's, The middle of Berlin and occupied London to the Nazi lunar base in the 60's.
Combat is brutal and satisfying. Either go in silent and perform brutal knife take downs or go in guns blazing even dual wielding weapons and blowing limbs and entire body's to pieces. The New Order introduces a new type of weapon much like Half-Life did with the gravity gun. The New Order has the LaserKraftWerk. A weapon that has the capability to cut new paths through metal and act as a high power killing tool with multiple upgrades along the way.
The characters have a lot of depth and interesting stories. The main protagonist's William Joseph Blazkowicz, Anya Oliwa, Caroline Becker, Fergus Reid & Probst Wyatt III. etc. Because of the way the narrative plays out you end up caring for them and how the story unfolds.
The main antagonist's, Oberstgruppenführer Wilhelm "Deathshead" Strasse, Obergruppenführer Frau Irene Engel & Hans "Bubi" Winkle are fantastically portrayed offering tense moments and a real sense of threat every time they are on screen.
The story is fantastic. Amazing cutscenes and BJ's inner monologue keeps the story advancing all the time. Thought provoking as well. Genuinely makes you think how different the world could be.
Great amount of collectibles for re playability. Ranging from Nazi gold, Enigma codes, Health & Armour upgrades to Records and Letters. Also combines a chapter select and two story lines. The story lines don't differ too much but you get to see some other people perspective etc.
The perk system is great and combines the achievement system into it. For example perform a certain amount of stealth kills and unlock throwing knives etc. etc. So BJ becomes more efficient at shooting, stabbing and strangling Nazi's as the story progresses.
The music for the game is also another great aspect, the soundtrack is provided by the awesome Mick Gordon. Who did DOOM. He is definitely up there as one of my favourite Rock/Atmospheric game music producers. Up there with Frank Klepacki for sure.
The New Order is a fantastic story driven game. I would recommend this to any fan of story driven shooters and returning fans of Wolfenstein. Machine Games & Bethesda has done a great job on this game and I cannot wait to play The New Colossus.

What happens when you combine Arma 3's realistic feel, Battlefield's graphics, and add DCS/MilSim-level teamwork/coordination?
SQUAD is JUST not quite a MilSim, but it's close. While the Arma series focuses on a gigantic map where you can launch corps-sized operations over a hugly flexible and moddable system, SQUAD is focused more on... well... Squads.
You fight on a set of slightly less gigantic maps (still huge) in roughly platoon-sized teams of several squads of players. SQUAD is objective-based, meaning it is not as open-ended as Arma, but it feels more realistic due to (in my humble opinion) better graphics and effects (such as a suppression system), better/realistic gunplay, and much higher teamwork requirments.
Although not (yet) as moddable as the Arma series, it is a very impressive game, and I will go into an atypical length to review it. WARNING: Long review, I'm sorry... this game deserves it.
How I saw it early on, is that SQUAD essentially has the "ACRE" radio mod from Arma built into the game, and microphones/headsets are almost mandatory, as communication and teamwork is SO important that NOT having a mic can actually prevent you from playing in certain situations (Squad Leaders (SL) who do not have a mic are kicked from the SL position automatically).
I have yet to see or play a game where communication and teamwork is so vital that the team with the better-coordinated squads will always win. Thus, it is needless to say, this game is quite intense.
Time for the overused Pros and Cons list (Hooray!):
The Good Stuff:
* Very realistic
Again, not quite MilSim, but one of the closest games that is not DCS. (Unlike DCS though, SQUAD uses this realism in a fun and engaging way... not boring at all)
* Great gunplay
Takes some time getting used to, but the guns are realistic and they feel right. LMGs take skill to not blaze away uslessly over the enemy's heads due to recoil, and not everyone can be a Marksman (I am one of those few "good" DMs in this game). Bullet drop (applies to rockets too) is present similar to the Arma series, and you move slightly different depending on what weapons you are carrying.
P.S. Sick of OP snipers in other FPSs? In SQUAD, marksmen play a role in the fight, but are quite difficult to use right, and are by no means overly powerful. Being a marksman is actually frowned upon in a lot of in-game situations. I usually play Anti-Tank when we don't need a marksman.
* "Battlefield-level" graphics
Which, coupled with the level of realism similar to Arma, makes this game a joy to look at. You will get immersed in the battle very quickly due to this and the level of interaction the game requires. This game does not have the destruction system of Battlefield or Rainbow 6 Seige, though, but certain obejcts can be shot through by certain weapons.
* Communication and Teamwork matter...
A LOT!! You WILL lose if you don't communicate, making this not only a realistic game, but also a interesting social experience. The stress of realistically-simulated combat, the importance of leadership, plus the unobstucted use of voice comms, means you get to really meet people, and you will make a lot of friends in this game.
* No hackers.
(read that again in disbelief)
Hackers are evidently non-existent on the official servers due to powerful anticheats and the game's own mechanics. And at the moment, admins are usually on-call and will quickly deal with griefers, teamkillers, and radio-spammers (a big offence in a game that focuses on communication). I have yet to run into a hacker in this game, which is a first for me in my 15+ years of gaming.
To any hackers reading this, I can actually tell you honestly to go somewhere else. Not because hacking is bad anyways (which it is), but because you really will not last long trying to hack this game. I'm sorry.
* Leadership roles are, due to the game's realism and need to communicate, quite challenging. Not eveyone is cut out for squad leading! Learn "people skills" while playing this game!
* SQUAD was unbalanced early on (regular armed forces [RUS and US] tended to win a lot against the irregular forces [insurgents and militia]), but recent updates have balanced the factions, vehicles, and weapons out quite nicely.
* Very good options, settings, and keybindings.
* Players tend to be more willing to work together
Than in most other games, since this game forces you to do so. You can do very little by yourself, however, those rare moments when you do pull off something impressive by yourself or with a buddy, you really feel like heroes!
While you always have your bad apples, I would consider this game to have (so far) a better player community than most.
* Game Updates happen pretty regularily (slow but steady)
And each one adds important content such as bolstering the anticheat further, optimizations, bugfixes and graphic glich removals, game content such as new vehicles and soldier types/weapons, game balancing, and framework for future updates.
While helicopters (long anticipated) have not been added due to game balance considerations, the game's current state, etc., they may be seen in the future once SQUAD's few kinks get ironed out. The Devs appear to be intent on building and upgrading a working system first, then adding content. Good Work to them so far!
Not-so-good stuff:
* IMMENSE learning curve.
Getting used to the realistic movement, being able to (and forced to) communicate realistically, having to deal with the minimalistic HUD, and getting used to the idea of not being able to go rambo, will take a lot of patience. Once you learn the ropes, though, what you learn will pay off.
* Game takes a while to download and uses a bunch of memory space
That said, the game itself runs very smoothly for most PCs despite the intense graphics.
* Official Servers are few, and they are usually maxed-out on players
So finding a game can be tricky. However, joining a server has been simplified in a recent update.
* Near Arma-level controls
A tad complicated, but you will get used to it pretty quickly (especially if you have played any of the Armas before).
* No avatar customization (as of 08/31/2017)
SO FAR, you can't modify what you carry/use, which is great since the game is going for realism, but what I don't like is that you can't change your soldier's face, his skin tone/color, and his hair (for insurgents, who have beards. Everyone else is clean-shaven and wears helmets or hats, so the latter matters little). Although the uniforms, helmets, and vests are not (and shouldn't be) customizable, it would be nice to be able to customize small bits of clothing like scarves, sunglasses, and such to add a little bit of variation to the avatars.
I would entirely recommend this game to any miltary fan or anyone who is serious about teamwork and coordination. I wholeheartedly DO NOT recommend this for people who like individual-focused games like COD and Battlefield, as SQUAD is among the most severe team-oriented games I have played, and you will be destroyed time and again if you do not work together!
SQUAD is one of my favorite games right now. This game was really well done. Unlike a lot of point-and-click's where you end up in a cycle of trial and error, the logic behind each next step was quite intuitive and for most instances it didn't take too much to work out the difference between a situation in which you didn't have what you need yet or you just hadn't worked out how to put it together yet. I've found that to be a common problem in other point-and-click games.
Mechanics are simple and well done, nothing moves very fast but it doesn't really need to. The whole thing revolves around time travel, so there are several sequences in which you are searching through the same locations but in two different time zones decades apart which adds some really interesting aspects to the problems you need to solve.
*Spoiler Alert*
This time-travel aspect really comes into the story. I found some aspects of the ending a bit predictable (a guy at the start has been shot, you end up being the one that shot him) but then it took it to much greater heights that I hadn't expected. Sort of didn't feel like there was a huge amount of story at the start (or any story was incidental to put you in the situation of the game) but then it all came together at the end really well.

Maybe if the controls were better and some of the other gameplay elements were polished I would let this pass as okay, but the game makes no effort to impress early on and presents itself in a way to make me think it's not going to get better. If it does, perhaps it should have put some of that creativity in the beginning. I've played dozens of Metroidvania games and I've been doing tabletop roleplaying for over a year, and even at low levels there are opportunities to showcase interesting creatures, unique weapons and cool environments.

Life of Pixel is a 2D platformer that takes you through video gaming history; from the ZX81, all the way up to the 16-bit era,  Life of Pixel's charm is absolutely dear.
Every machine is composed of eight levels, each stylized with the graphics and music of their respective machine. The ZX Spectrum levels, for example, have the maximum of 15 colours, just like the actual machine; in fact, the colours even clash, further like the Spectrum! It's amazing how much care the developers put into the game to make the levels feel as if they are being played on the computers and consoles. Even the music for the levels is quite reminiscent of what was capable.
There are over 100 levels in the game, with a special gem in each one that help unlock more machines once collected, and some levels even have extra items to collect. Further in the game, the levels do get quite difficult; not near impossible, but certainly enough to make you frustrated.
All in all, I would most definitely recommend Life of Pixel, especially if you grew up with the consoles and computers it features. Hell, even if you never grew up with them, you will absolutely enjoy the game if you're a fan of 2D Platformers and games with a bit of love put in.

First time I'm writing a review and mostly due to having ridiculously mixed feelings about this.
Let's go through the Pros and Cons one by one.
Pros.
Create your own character. - This one is definitely a win a huge leap away from the original series, a good one in my opinion.
Customization in general. - On top of being able to create your own character and race, their move sets are completely customizable excluding the basic attacks which are tied to race. Not to mention the huge load of outfits you can piece together.
Battles. - The entire gameplay of it is a lot of fun, and I mean a lot of fun, The actual quests can get really tough too!
I do enjoy the challenges even when they can get awfully frustrating sometimes! The way they intergrated the skills, to balance stamina/ki usage and all that, while having a wide array of Z-souls to pick from changes a battle and strategy completely.
Z-souls. - Brilliant, a Z-soul is an equippable item that gives procs based on certain situations and gives certain buffs.
Anything from faster ki regen all the way to starting with some Ki, all the way to never flinching in battle if your health is above 90%, each Z-soul carries with it a whole different type of playstyle, one would most certainly find something suitable for them.
Cons.
Game Server. - Constant disconnects due to servers being full a lot. You can bring steam offline to play it offline but still, it doesn't change the fact that the game servers need quite a big push for it to work out as intended.
RNG. - A lot of drops and battle events are based on RNG and sometimes it can get really, really, really bad. Right now I'm actually farming an outfit piece and have already been trying for 10 hours, it takes about 1 minute to take out the boss that drops it, so do your own math there, no drop so far. This is the biggest letdown for me, I sincerely do not believe the RNG should be this bad. There are players trying to get super vegeta or super saiyan to which they keep failing to due to RNG based events that did not happen and even if they did, RNG drop rates to top off that event is just ugh. DIMPs should really really consider boosting the RNG significantly.
Outfits. - While there are a plethora of outfits, the biggest problem lies in the fact that the game boasts customization and yet most outfits you obtain, particularly outfits based on other characters cannot be recolored. That is a rather silly way to limit things.
Create your character. - Still having not enough options on that end.
Fightings styles. - I vaguely remember seeing it on a stream but I might be wrong, there seems to be a way to change fighting styles in beta but it was taken out? Now assuming I'm wrong, there should be the option in my opinion or at least be able to change fighting stances for some variety.
Game score: If not for RNG and server issues I'd give it 8/10. But right now, I'mma give it a 6/10 until these two factors get fixed hopefully! I hope this helps!

Fun combat and a steady flow of rewards make this journey a massively enjoyable one, especially with some fellow mercenaries along for the ride.
On the hostile, bandit-ridden planet of Pandora, there is one thing that draws off-world attention: The Vault. This mysterious alien structure is rumored to hold treasures of fantastic power and wealth, and so it attracts fortune-seeking corporations and individuals alike. In Borderlands, you are one such individual, but the satisfaction of unlocking the Vault's secrets pales in comparison to the rollicking good time you'll have on your way there. Borderlands is all about the journey, not the destination, and like most trips, this one is much better when you have some friends along for the ride. Solo players can still have a good time, because the bloody and entertaining combat is paired well with rewarding loot and engaging experience systems. But Pandora is a lonely place for a solitary mercenary, and lone wolves will find the pace deliberate and the friendly characters too few and far between. Those who take advantage of the four-player online cooperative mode will experience the game as it's meant to be played. The pleasing rhythm of killing enemies, gathering loot, and cashing in is punctuated by fighting bosses, completing quests, and leveling up. As a solo merc, this rhythm is slow and methodical, but as a team, the pace quickens to an invigorating clip and pretty soon you've spent hours having a riotously rewarding time.
The world of Pandora has a dusty, run-down feel, yet it manages to be vibrant and eye-catching at the same time. The art style features black-line borders and a colorful palette that give the game a not-quite-comic, not-quite-cel-shaded look. It takes some getting used to, and its technical execution is less-than-perfect . Yet what Borderlands lacks in precision it more than makes up for in style, and hours into the game you'll still be appreciating the thoughtful design touches that bring this world to life. Though the different environments occasionally feel too similar, there is enough distinct detail to keep them from blurring together. Your vanquished enemies also do their part to keep things visually interesting by dying in a variety of gruesome and entertaining ways. Bodies explode, limbs fly off, and burning enemies occasionally disintegrate from the ground up until only the mask of their face is left hanging in midair. It sounds (and is a bit) horrifying, but when the mask drops comically to the floor and finally burns up, don't bother stifling that chuckle. The art design resonates well with Borderlands' irreverent sense of humor, and the game is playful without feeling too goofy.
You travel through this world as one of four characters, each with a unique look and attitude. You don't really get to appreciate the character designs if you play solo because you have no AI teammates, but you do hear frequent quips that give you a little bit of character-specific flavor. The most important difference between characters is the action skill, which is a special ability that can give you an edge in combat. The Hunter can release a vicious bird of prey, the Soldier can throw down an automatic turret flanked by shields, the Siren can turn invisible and speedy, damaging all enemies in the vicinity, and the Berserker flies into a damage-resistant rage and delivers brutal punches to his enemies. You unlock these abilities after playing for a short while, and not only are they all fun to use, but each one can be customized in a couple of strategically distinct ways. You can tweak and upgrade your ability by investing skill points in appropriate skills. So, for example, upgrading the Hunter's bird of prey not only can increase the amount of damage it does, but can make it attack multiple targets, steal health from them, slow them down for easy sniping, and cause them to drop more loot. Expanding your action skill makes you more deadly in combat, and it's one of the most rewarding parts of leveling up. Killing enemies, finishing quests, and completing in-game bonus challenges earn you experience points, which in turn earn you a new level. Leveling up boosts your overall fortitude and grants you a precious skill point to use however you see fit.
You can also spend your skill points on other improvements, and each character has three different skill trees that highlight different tactics and abilities. So the Soldier can essentially become the team medic by developing the skills that allow him to shoot teammates to regenerate their health and that make his turret create a healing radius. Or he could choose to become more deadly, increasing his turret damage and combat rifle performance. Though your weapon proficiency improves based on how much you use a given weapon type, different characters have skills that favor different types of guns, so it's to your advantage to play to your character's strengths. The Berserker can certainly become proficient with the sniper rifle, but his melee-focused action skill and preference for rocket launchers make him a better choice for wading into the fray. Though the branching skill trees offer intriguing ways to specialize, your initial character choice has the biggest impact on how you'll go through the game. Fortunately, each character is fun and deadly in his own way, so you can't choose poorly, and you'll probably want to experience what each one has to offer. Playing cooperatively allows you to enjoy and benefit from the other characters' abilities, something you don't get to appreciate when playing solo, unless you start a new game.
Expanding your abilities and leveling up is one of the main ways that Borderlands consistently rewards you. Loot is another. Loot can be found in containers, dropped by enemies, or given to you as a quest reward. It includes money, ammo, shields, mods that boost and alter your grenades, mods that boost your skills, and, of course, guns. Guns are classified in familiar categories: pistols, submachine guns, shotguns, combat rifles, sniper rifles, rocket launchers, and so on. Each class feels distinct, and the shooting mechanics are well tuned and satisfying, which makes it fun to blast baddies. Base damage, clip size, fire rate, accuracy, and bullet spread are just some of the variables within each class, and some guns have more exotic features, like bladed pistols that increase melee damage or a shotgun that also shoots rockets. They can also do elemental damage, which comes in a variety of flavors that put a special kind of hurt on and can even do damage over time. Equip an incendiary gun if you want to burn flesh, or a corrosive gun if you want to deal extra damage to creatures with tough hides.
The Good
Satisfying gunplay
Tons of weapons, shields, and helpful items
Four unique and equally fun-to-play characters
Distinct, appealing artistic style
Great system of rewards
The Bad
Lonelier, slower-paced for a solo player
Massively unsatisfying
Lackluster loot sharing system

A delight, even for non-fans of the Borderlands games.
When I first heard that this game was being made, I rolled my eyes. Who could /possibly/ have wanted a story-based adventure game based on Borderlands? It sounded as bad an idea as that time they made a movie based on Street Fighter.
And yet, somehow, Telltale have really delivered here. I have a hot and cold relationship with Telltale games - sometimes their stories really hit the spot (The Wolf Among Us really satisfied with its pulpy detective fiction), other times they just leave me frustrated (The Walking Dead's constant attempts to suggest you were making meaningful choices just fell flat with artifice), so I was pleasantly surprised to find Tales from the Borderlands becoming one of my favourite interactive narratives of all time.
It's a game filled with warmth and friendship, even as it throws in ultraviolence and gross-out situations. It's a game where betrayals sting not because of their extremity, à la Game of Thrones, but because you genuinely want to like all (well, nearly all) of the characters. And it's a game where, though the ending itself won't have much flexibility, your choices do feel like they have at least a localised effect.
If you want a game filled with charming, well-realised characters, a game that will leave you with a warm, contented feeling, then you want Tales from the Borderlands.

Wolfenstein 3D is single-player First Person Shooter that was released on PC MS-DOS in 1992. It's somewhat official sequel to Wolfenstein game for older computer, a top-down stealth game, yet W3D is neither of those. It wasn't the first FPS ever, no. Few were made before this one. It wasn't the most advanced engine-wise either, it was beaten easily by Ultima Underworld. What matter though, is that it was the first FPS that made the genre popular, as it was all about fast-paced action, running quickly and shooting everyting, exploring mazes, and not requiring a top-computer to be able to run.
It would then later recieve more love, get expansion pack and be ported onto consoles and other computers, with some version being inferior and Mac family ports were almost superior to DOS. Superior ports got higher resolution graphics and two additional weapons, with levels remixed. DOS only got 8-sided sprites of enemies, while other ports have 1-sided only, which doesn't matter so much in this game. Oh, and differences in soundtracks and levels too.
Now, with it being quite an old game, how Steam version was handled?
The game itself is almost same as original DOS version and comes with all 6 episodes. The slight difference is a change of "Apogee" to "Activision", game being brought to Steam at around 2007 year. And they removed help/instructions completely for whatever reason. Probably because ordering info was beyond outdated. Thus no intro story for you.
id software screwed up on DosBox part. It lags heavily. But you can fix it, you just have to go to game's folder and edit DosBox config file for Wolf3D, to make it run with OpenGL renderer.
Shame that gameplay didn't age well, but it is most eye-pleasing WW2 shooter around from colorful design side, with memorable music being upbeat or funky suspense.
The original release of the game had 3 episodes only, each having 8 normal floors, 1 boss floor and 1 secret floor:
Escape From Castle Wolfenstein - Classic episode, which came fully with Shareware. Which was like, 1/3 or 1/6 of a game. One heck of demo.
Operation: Eisenfaust - In this episode you explore some nasty dungeons only to find a secret entrance to nazy base. This is the only episode which has Mutant enemies, who are just plain nasties, providing a huge difficulty spike, for they are completely silent and can have zero reaction time. Good heavens they weren't used in other levels.
Die, Furher, Die - Back to good joy again, this one introduces white officer nazis, who's only advantage is their speed. Still more fun than mutants. And in these set of levels you get to kill Hitler. Even "few". So it's awesome. And secret level is Pac-Man parody.
Now, after original release, publishers figured out that id can quickly make additional 3 episodes themed after chemical war, Noctural Missions, and sell them as well. The results are 3 additional episodes that are quite meh and don't provide any new content, aside from bosses and textures:
Dark Secret - Not much to be said there, it feel like direct continuation of episode 3, having harder and more complex mazes. Though I doubt that you would more of them.
Trail of the Madman - This is where you see id starting to tire out and their creativity starting to sink. It provides simpler mazes than Dark Secret and you can see graphical themes of rooms starting to get even less interesting.
Confortation - This is where developers got completely tired and are going to make players tired as well. Design of levels became completely lazy. First floor has you travelling corridors that have sideways every step and you have to check every one so you will not get bulet into back. Later level layout is nothing but nazi cross repeated few times and connected with each other by doors. Final boss is quite generic and is no match for Hitler encounter.
After choosing your episode, you have to select your difficulty out of four, all of which have phrases as name, so you wouldn't be able to guess which one is "Normal". I recommend you to pick the second to top, as it will still get difficult at the end and you will not die as much. Due to realistical/hitscan nature of enemy attacks, you often will feel that you died in a cheap way.
The game uses keyboard mostly, not exactly comfortable. Buttons it uses are arrows and right shifts, alt, ctrl, so it's kinda cluttered. It also has just one "hold this to strafe" button, so you can't circlestrafe around. Though, in this kind of FPS it would be useless. It also allows usage of mouse. Not for mouselook, nope. More as a replacament for arrows, it's used for movement. Yep, mouse back then was viewed as gimmick and not everybody knew how to make use of them.
Your mission is to find exit elevator, while staying alive. To do this, you have to epxlore 1-floor maze of blocks, that are full of enemies, bonuses and doors. As well as 2 keys and locked doors. You know what to do with these. It's also littered with secret pushwalls, where you have to press "open" on a wall that you don't like and it may open, being pushed away for two blocks, revealing a secret passage. But there is no way to tell if this wall is a secret, as some of pushwalls have interesting texture while others aren't marked at all, thus creating uncertainty. Thus the only way to find them all is to hump all walls you see and that's tedius, not fun. MS-DOS version doesn't have any maps, so good luck navigating.
The game uses scores and lives system that feel out of place in this not-so-arcadey game. You collect many treasures to increase your score. Nope, High Score Board sure isn't going to make you compete with Steam friends, it's as usual full of blank jokeyish entries. At least it saves your score. It also has lives system, where after death you will begin level again with only pistol and if you run out of lives, you get classic game over. But because you can save and load anytime and anywhere, no one cares.
The selection of huge-pixeled (feature of DOS version, by the way) weapons that you get are simple. Way too simple, actually:
Knife - Useless.
Pistol - Fires bullets.
Machine Gun - Fires bullets fast.
Chaingun - Fires bullets very fast.
You are going to use Machine Gun all the time anyway because Chaingun eats ammo too fast, not being able to shoot just one bullet. So it's pretty poor on thinking.
And sure thing fighting enemies if main part of game. Soldiers are preplaced on the maze, standing and sometimes patrolling around, reminding that Wolfenstein 3D was supposed to be stealth game at first, as they take extra damage if they aren't aware of you. Once they notice you or hear you, they will let out some sort of "achtung" voice and start to chase you in a direct way. Nope, their footsteps are completely silent, so on some levels you should listen to doors opening carefully. Rarely it leads to fun mouse and cat scenarios, in which fun suddenly ends by getting shot into back. Most often it means a lot of dead bodies around nearest door. Actually, most often best tactic is to come into room, give a shot and then run back behind doorway's corner, as you just sit and camp, shooting enemies one after another. Not most exciting thing.
Main problem comes from the fact that every enemy has only hitscan-based attack. So it's a game more about camping then running out and shooting everybody in a fair fight. And it's randomized in no end, bringing quite a frustation, as each bullet may either poke you slightly or completely kill you. It all depends on distance though, same for your bullets damage. Close range is deadly.
Boss fights are disssapointing for video game. All of them are same. Pop out, shoot until they decide to shoot back, hide.  Go to secret stack of supply if it goes bad.
So, a game that didn't age well, with cheap core gameplay. Still classic. If you want history, just play Shareware though. And if you do want full game, then only play first 3 episodes in short bursts.

Waste Walkers: Deliverance is an addition to the Waste Walkers world.  You play a new character scavenging around the town of Fair Place about a year after the war.
Unlike the original game, where you start out and have to find survivors and a community, you are already a member of a group of survivors who are holding out in a mental health asylum.  Your character, Screw, is a soldier who fought in the prior war and may or may not have been a resident of the place (being treated for PTSD) when the bombs fell, though he doesn't seem as homicidal as the other former residents you run into (Well, I guess there's a few places where you
make him be like that.)
If you liked the gameplay and style of the original then Deliverance should be up your alley.  It is a bit harder since there's not as many 'shops' available and supplies are harder to find.  This is especially true for ammunition.  If you help resupply your group, some basic ammo for simple handguns might be available but you still won't be running around with an assault rifle firing full auto.
Also there isn't a line of survivors waiting to join up with you like in the original.  You can't just run to where you know an NPC will be, do a little errand, and grab a partner to soak damage and double up attacks.  You don't find a teammate until well into the storyline.  So you need to be able to handle enemies on your own (SAVE OFTEN), or learn to avoid them on the map.  There are also rare instances of random encounters, but you can probably get through the game with, at most, 4 such encounters.  They're just enough to keep you from getting complacent but not enough to be aggravating (unless you forget to save because you thought you were just gonna dodge around all the bad guys.)
While this DLC gives up some of the connection (I want to say 'empathy') that comes from naming, building (at least the 1st level skills and traits), and choosing the appearance of your PC that the original game had, it does allow for a more focused character story in the form of your survivor's past.  The developer has learned a few things from his first game and, this is good, since you can't fall back on the 'it's a good first effort' cushion.  Enemy speeds have been tweaked, environmental sounds have been upgraded, and the map is a whole lot cleaner, better laid-out, and labelled.
About the only thing I have to begrudgingly point out is the mention of 'Dungeon-Crawling mechanics'.  I know of only two 'subterranean' areas; the crypt and the sewers.  While they are significantly different in style and both contain some new things (burning out nests and new enemies) I'm not sure I'd comfortably agree that any mechanics are significantly different enough, though again, I did like going through them.
This is a sound buy for any player who wants a game that sticks with something they know and will give them a few hours of entertainment.  If you can take advantage of the frequent sales Corrosive Studios participates in then it's an easy 'Yes' for a player who enjoyed the original.

To start, Waste Walkers Deliverance can be considered an expansion add-on which runs alongside the original Waste Walkers universe. It uses the same Waste Walkers gameplay elements and setting, but you play as a different character in a different map. This game is separate from the original.
The map in this expansion is smaller than the one in Waste Walkers, but is full of threats to be wary of.
You play as Screw, a war veteran who served overseas. You are part of the community called Tranquil Grove and you one of their best scavengers. You provide them with supplies that they need and overall help everyone there. In return you have a place to keep safe from the dreaded wastes.
Within my first hour of playing, I died by walking into a minefield. Afterwards, I checked the map. Everything on the map is labelled for you, so it's easy to navigate this small city. I found that helpful when I realized where I should be going to help out my tranquil little home. There were some new monsters that I saw, which I avoided due to the fact that they look absolutely terrifying and I decided I'd rather not learn what they were until I could just throw bombs at them. Some of them had skulls for heads. These must be the crazies that once made up the population of the ward known as Tranquil Grove.
I continued to play for a little longer and made some progress towards helping out my group of survivors, but ultimately had to turn the game off because I have other things to do. I'll play some more of this later, for sure.
Overall, I would recommend Waste Walkers Deliverance if you enjoyed Waste Walkers. Of course, the only way to play Deliverance is to own Waste Walkers. I want to say this is a game that could be a separate game with its own distinct store page, but perhaps that would leave some people clueless of the world setting Waste Walkers provided to begin with. This game stands strong as an expansion to the original game and is worth the purchase.
don't get me wrong, this game will set you back if you're a budget gamer, the price is steep for an indie title but it is worth every single cent with lots of replay value.

In short, if you like DBZ at all, you will like this.  Just don't buy the season pass unless you plan on playing it for a while and like the developer.  The game has it's flaws, mainly with the way difficulty was handled and general balancing, but so much time was spent of the core gameplay that it overshadows these flaws.
Pros:
- Combat IS DBZ.  Probably the best it's been since Budokai 3 which is why I got it in the first place.
- Story is not just rehashed, thus interesting to sit through.  There were moments where I said out loud "Well that's different..." but in a good way.
- Roster is decent and includes many of the favorites, ALL with different playstyles.
- TONS of fan service.
Cons:
- Online fights in my experience are HORRIBLY unbalanced.  Instead of fighting people who just use their favorite moves from the show, you will fight people with armor, regenerating hp, and moves that stun you for entire seconds, leaving you wide open for a flashy combo.  Netcode also needs some work but it's a new game so hopefully nerfs and patches will come.
- The story has some major difficulty spikes and does not stop to tell you that you should probably grind a bit first.  I'm fine with having to progress this way, but if the game simply allows me to have my♥♥♥♥♥served to me on a platter first instead of warning me, it can be frustrating because there's really no way to know if you are the right level for a particular stage until you finally beat it.  Many of the missions are also needlessly difficult almost forcing one to spam their ultimate as it's the only way to deal any real damage to the hordes of enemies the game feels so inclined to throw at you or the single enemy with ludicrous amounts of armor AND health.  The enemes are not just really good at the mechanics of the game, they straight up have huge advantages over you and that's not good in a game based on a universe where, with enough training, one can overcome just about any adversity because said training evens the playing field.  Many of the parallel quests fall victim to this as well, though not to quite the same degree.

I think this is a must-buy game for anyone who likes teamwork in a first-person shooter game.
Interstellar Marines has a lot of feature I have never seen in any other FPS before, like changing weather patterns, lighting, and even near-total darkness in a single map, changing between various settings.  This game keeps you on your toes, and gets my heart-racing with intense king of the hill combat.
I'm still playing the game, so that probably says something.
Since my initial review they've added crouching, and jumping; as well as two new weapons, three new game-modes, co-op and singleplayer missions.  The communtiy is still one of the best I've ever been a part of, and the gameplay is still fun, and enjoyable.
I've probably bought 20 or 25 copies of this game for friends of mine over the past two years.  As of now, the Dev team has shrunk a lot, and they're looking for a publisher before they start doing any major updates; but if you're fine with just a smei-competetive shooter, and some neat co-op on the side with a fun community, you're $10 will be well spent.
I've gotten over 250 hours of enjoyment (and counting) out of my $10; that's a pretty good return if you ask me, since it took less then an hour for me to make that $10...
Every purchase helps this company, ZPS, continue pushing forward to creating and polishing up an amazing game, and if you're okay with mostly multiplayer now, and are hopful for more in the future; I'd highly reccomend picking this one up.

FADE IN:
EXT. THE SCOTTISH COUNTRYSIDE - DAY
Epic beauty: cobalt mountains beneath a glowering purple sky
fringed with pink, as if the clouds were a lid too small for
the earth; a cascading landscape of boulders shrouded in
deep green grass; and the blue lochs, reflecting the sky. We
hear a voice, husky, Scottish...
VOICE OVER
I will tell you of William Wallace.
EXT. MACANDREWS FARM - DAY
A farmhouse and a large barn lie nestled in a Scottish valley.
Riding down the roads that lead in from opposite sides are
Scottish noblemen in full regalia: eye-popping tartans,
sparkling chestplates. Even the horses are draped in scarlet.
Behind each nobleman rides a single page boy.
VOICE OVER
Historians from England will say I
am a liar. But history is written by
those who have hung heroes.
Another noble rides in from the opposite side. Two more appear
down the road, converging on the barn.
VOICE OVER
The King of Scotland had died without
a son, and the king of England, a
cruel pagan known as Edward the
Longshanks, claimed the throne for
himself. Scotland’s nobles fought
him, and fought each other, over the
crown. So Longshanks invited them to
talks of truce. No weapons, one page
only.
The nobles eye each other cautiously, but the truce holds.
They enter the barn, with their pages...
EXT. SCOTTISH FARM - DAY
Nestled in emerald hills are the thatched roof house and
barn and outbuildings of a well-run farm. The farmer, MALCOLM
WALLACE, and his nineteen-year-old son JOHN, both strong,
tough men, are riding away from the farm. They hear hooves
behind them and turn to see a boy riding after them.
VOICE OVER
Among the farmers of that shire was
Malcolm Wallace, a commoner, with
his own lands and two sons: John...
We FAVOR JOHN WALLACE, the nineteen-year-old sitting easily
on his horse, beside his father...
VOICE OVER
...and William.
WILLIAM, a skinny eight-year-old riding bareback, catches up
to his father and older brother.
FATHER
Told ya to stay.
WILLIAM
I finished my chores. Where we goin'?
FATHER
MacAndrews'. He was supposed to visit
when the truce was over.
They ride on, over the lush hills.
EXT. THE MACANDREWS FARM - DAY
The horses are all gone; the place looks deserted. UP ON THE
HILL we see the three Wallaces, looking down.
FATHER
Stay here.
He means William. He and his elder son spur their horses.
AT THE BARN - DAY
The Wallaces ride up, looking around.
FATHER
MacAndrews!... MacAndrews!?
Malcolm finds a pitchfork, John the woodpile axe...
INT. THE BARN
POV from within as the door opens and a widening block of
sunlight illuminates the dusty shadows. Malcolm and John
Wallace step in, and are shocked to see...
POV THE WALLACES
Hanging from the rafters of the barn are thirty Scottish
noblemen and thirty pages, their faces purple and contorted
by the strangulation hanging, their tongues protruding.
Malcolm stabs the pitchfork into the ground in useless anger;
John still grips the axe as he follows his father through
the hanging bodies of the noblemen to the back row, to see
the one man in commoner's dress, like theirs...
FATHER
MacAndrews.
A SHUFFLE; John spins; William has entered the back door.
JOHN
William! Get out of here!
WILLIAM
Why would MacAndrews make so many
scarecrows?
Before his father and brother can think of anything to say,
William, with a boy's curiosity, touches the spurred foot of
the hanged noblemen we first saw riding in. It's too solid;
he takes a real look at the face, and suddenly --
WILLIAM
R -- real!!!... Ahhhhhgggg!...
He turns to run, but knocks back into the feet of the hanged
man behind him! In blind panic he darts in another direction,
and runs into another corpse, and another; the hanged men
begin to swing, making it harder for William's father and
older brother to fight their way to him.
FATHER
William! William!
Then, worst of all, William sees the pages, boys like himself,
hanged in a row behind their masters!
Finally his father and brother reach William and hug him
tight. There in the barn, among the swinging bodies of the
hanged nobles, Malcolm Wallace grips his sons.
FATHER
Murderin' English ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
CUT TO:
EXT. WALLACE FARMHOUSE - NIGHT
The cottage looks peaceful, the windows glowing yellow into
the night. From outside the house we see John rise and close
the shutters of the kitchen, where men are gathered. We PAN
UP to the upper bedroom window...
INSIDE THAT BEDROOM
Young William is in nightmarish sleep. He mumbles in smothered
terror; he twitches. We see
HIS NIGHTMARE
In the blue-grays of his dream, William stands at the door
of the barn, gazing at the hanged knights. We WHIP PAN to
their faces, garish, horrible... Then one of the heads moves
and its eyes open! William wants to run, but he can't get

Biggest issue with the game so far is saving problem. As you might have read some people have outright lost their saves entirely. This game is really more of an RPG than a straight up action game so loss of saved data is harsh.
Anyways, that's the biggest bug so far. Other than that the animations are rigid, and not really quite as spectacular as you'd expect these days. It does look okay though, and there are little flairs that make you really feel like a DBZ character. For instance if you execute a fully charged energy/spirit attack on the ground it lives a giant groove in the ground. The sound effects are great, and the soundtrack is decent, but hilariously enough the VA is really bad... even with veteran VA from the series, and even one of the abridged guys on the team. The entire feel lands somewhere between MMO, and Action RPG/Fighting game. This is as much a fighting game as the Naruto "fighting games" It's more of an RPG and that's fine, and it does require a little skill in it's competitive format, but you're not going to be beating a high level character right off.
It plays pretty similarly to the Tenkaichi games if you were wondering about the action portion, but you're equipped with power scanning abilities, and a scouter early on which makes for a fun immersive feature.  Using your scouter/power scan you can can explore areas and obtain items to mix together and make skills, healing items etc. So there's some minor exploration in the game too. You can pick your race which is neat, I wasn't sure what they were going to do with that, but it's an awesome feature. Essentially if you ever got to play the MMO it's basically that but more of an action game, and less MMO-ish. The hub world REALLY feels MMO-ish though... and because of that you'll feel little empty as you around a giant map filled with maybe a handful of NPC's to talk to. It's a lot of fun, but again it feels like assets from an MMO recycled into an action game... PC options are nearly non-existent, and it's really only playable on a pad.
I like it, and feel like it has a lot of stuff to offer, and the action is a lot fun when you get the hang of it. Co-op is fun when it works, and the versus system is interesting but again not really worth your time. It's really a single player experience, with multiplayer feeling like it should belong but doesn't quite fit in the games gutted form. Oh forgot to mention, the game uses a lot of assets from the old MMO, soooooo yeah. There's a ton to do, and the story is a lot of fun but again it's awkward, good, but awkward. If you choose to buy though remember there is a save issue, and the servers are janky as hell... so you're not really guaranteed a flawless experience.

There are no good Senran Kagura games except for the rhythm game Bon Appetit. I've played them all and they're all terrible. Shinovi Versus is no different.
With double the girls of the previous in the series (Though technically this is the second of five games, chronologically fourth...), Senran Kagura manages such little variety, and such little combat depth that even the weakest musou games look down on this mess. XXXYBXXXY. Bam, that's the game. Period for all 22 or so girls.
Don't worry about the chronology nonsense, the game does a respectable job catching you up. "But wait," you say, "Nobody plays a titdees game for the plot." Shut up. Literally half the gametime is plot. VN segments bookend every level with hokey tragedies (And hokey rehashes of tragedies we had LAST game.) pasted on to each girl so you're asked to pretend the girl who literally lusts after other girls boobs in so crass a way as to make Master Roshi blush is somehow a deep and fulfilling character. The only narrative trick on offer is juxtaposing the monstrous and the cutesy. Let me summarize how awful the writing is in this game with a straightforward example: The good girls team's story has them learn the lesson that zealously rooting out and combatting evil is itself evil and you're just a big mean stuck up jerk if you do that. The evil girls story? They kill every one of the good girls one by one. KINDA AT CROSS PURPOSES, HUH.
By now, you're asking, why the thumbs up? Well, I'm dumb enough to keep buying and playing these games for one. They are certainly doing something right. For all the crappy content in this game, and there is a lot of rehashed content, something like 80+ missions across 8 or so actual levels using all the different girls, for all the bouncy boobies, all the underwear you're collecting, all that waifu dress up you're doing, all the boring ninjas you either shred through or spam supers through... at some point the sum of all its crappy parts come together as an all-purpose otaku package. The girls are absolutely adorable, and when the game doesn't take itself seriously, it is so ridiculous as to be worth a laugh.  It helps that the port is solid, too.
I will never defend Senran Kagura. The series is trash. It fails as a musou, fails as a brawler, fails as a VN, but somewhere at the intersection of all this madcap failure and all these boobies and waifus and shredded clothes and this bombast, it is still fun to muck with in small doses. So yes, it's worth playing even if it is absolute garbage in every individual regard.

Reviewing this is a pretty contradictory thing. As a piece of nostalgy and the feeling that the right kind of musical and visual style give this is something I do recommend (even though the visuals are partially better than they would have been on the actual old machines). But as a game I'm disappointed with it and wouldn't recommend it.
In my view the level design is the biggest flaw in the game. Sometimes the levels are boring collectathons, sometimes it seems that they weren't designed for the double jump mechanic in mind which means you get through them in a way that just doesn't seem right for the level. In general the levels feel uninventive or include a mechanic that doesn't feel like it belongs to a level (like having to bomb a wall).
Regarding level design, it's not that the levels would be too hard, it's just that they challenge you in the wrong way. One of the most annoying things is that the emerging spikes are used as a recurring thing throughout the systems. They often kill you for two very wrong reasons. For one the player maybe didn't wait to check where the spikes are. Well, waiting is boring (which by the way applies also to levels where you have to wait a long time for enemies to go out of the way too). The second one: the player didn't know how far inside the ground the spike needs to be in order to not be killed. Not really fun discovering this rule. And well, as an extra reason: I found a bug that the spikes are active even when you pause the game.
Verdict:
As there is no neutral option, I'll give this a thumbs up, as the price isn't that high and you get a nice feeling of the old systems with even some trivia. But if you're looking for a good game, interpret this as a thumbs down.

A fun romp through old computer and console nostalgia that still holds up even if you haven't played all of the things it references, Life of Pixel is a solid platformer with responsive controls.
It's a fairly challenging game, with its 104 levels ranging from 30 seconds to 3 minutes in length, with no mid-level checkpoints and most things killing you in one hit and the rest in two. This can get frustrating with some of the longer levels, but none are so long that it felt unfair - Burning Down the House was about the worst it got. There's some glitchy behavior with instant-death water that's level with the ground (where sometimes you "fall in" and die despite being still visually on the ground), as well as the potions (which let you kill enemies by jumping on them, but sometimes you just die anyway), but none of it's game-breaking because the potions are never required and water that's level with the ground is rare.
Life of Pixel is pretty amazing in terms of recreating the visual and audio styles of 13 different consoles and computers from the 80s and 90s. Whereas some other games (like Syder Arcade, for instance) had different classic visual styles as something of a gimmick, in Life of Pixel it's not just a gimmick where you can make the game look worse if you want, it's actually the game, and it generally stays fairly good looking even on the more limited systems.
While you're likely to most fully enjoy the game if you've played at least some of the systems and games it attempts to evoke nostalgia for, Life of Pixel is pretty fun even if you just want to see a bit of what games looked like back before you started playing as well, and gets a solid recommendation from me.

Not for the faint of heart, for those who expect a checkpoint, or those who can't beat an emulator without the constant use of save states. Life of Pixel is remniscent of the days when console games didn't have battery backup for saved game profiles, it uses the elements of game design to teach the player how to play the game, and even mirrors some of the graphical glitches present in old consoles. For someone like myself who started with an Intellivision, and played various Apple ][, DOS, NES, SNES, Atari, Colecovision, etc., I felt right at home with this game right out of the box. Literally everything about this game was well engineered to mimic the feel of retro gaming, and for that it serves it's purpose extremely well, better than most games that attempt to be "retro". I highly recommend this game for anyone who has played lots of old platformers, but I do not recommend it for those who have only played modern games and expect a pat on the back.

Where do I start?
I just switched my account over to steam since spending a few months in crossout, so please disregard my hours played for now at 0.3. I also have payed for some coins so I have spent real money on the game.
Let me start by saying that I like this game very much. You can build your own vehicles, whether they are practical or not and there is some nice depth to this aspect of the game. There are some limits in place but you do have room to get creative.
Being free to play you can get your hands dirty and really see what the game is about before you have to plunk down some money to access the workbenches. These benches allow you to create higher level weapons and car parts to enhance your gameplay. The in game money can also be purchased by selling your loot, but this is not an efficient way to make the coins you need for the work benches. In the end you will hit a wall so to speak if you do not spend real money, although that will take a while to hit.
The game is a mashup of different play styles, you have PVP that is 8 on 8 with BOTS to backfill game slots although sometimes you will find you are missing 2 or 3 members of your team. As new players join the bots are replaced. you get loot for playing these matches. There are CO-OP RAIDs where you and 2-5 players play together against BOTS to beat an objective. the BOTS range from easy to crazy boss level vehicles. Brawl is deathamatch and then there are CLAN battles which were just added.
The PVP matches in particular are very short <7min. There are lots of explosions and parts of cars being blown off and similar to Hawken, World of Tanks or World of warships, if you want to go it alone you will most likely die. You really need to fight as a team during the match.
Right now the only issue I have with the game is the weapon balance and the formula they use to calculate your combat value. The CV (Combat Value) does not do a good job of rating how deadly a vehicle is esp. when BLUE and PINK weapons are in use.  Otherwise the game is very stable and I have also had very few instances of lag. I def. think it is worth a try as a free to play game.

I want to make it clear that this is not a carefully constructed review, but more of a summary of what made my experience enjoyable versus what didin't.
First of all: do NOT play this game if you are easily frustrated, and/or do not enjoy the process of trial & error and attack pattern memorization involved in beating a very tough boss.
Now, the positives:
+ A unique and responsive one-hit-kill combat
+ Very detailed pixel art (especially when it comes to the enemies)
+ Nice alternance between calm moments of exploration and frenetic boss battles
+ Good variety in both the appearence and the attack patterns of the bosses
+ Hidden secrets around the world that, while being few in number, provide clues in regards to the lore of the game
+ The possibility of completing the game without killing every boss (allowing more casual players to avoid the toughest fights), while rewarding those who do complete all the bossfights with a special secret at the end of the game
The negatives:
- The deliberate difficulty of the bosses, together with the amount of time required to travel from the checkpoints to the boss arenas, make the frequent deaths a frustrating recurrence
- The game areas outisde of the boss arenas are completely empty (the bosses being the only type of enemy encountered in the game), thus making the time spent traveling from a group of bosses to the next little more than a scenic route through deserted enviroments
The subjectives (these are elements of the game the enjoyment of which is highly subjective):
= The game has both lore and a story, although they are more 'hinted at' than told in a classical manner most of the time, which might displease those seeking for a story-heavy adventure
= The bosses are extremely difficult to beat, and while learning their weaknesses and using them to achieve victory fills the player with satisfaction, the process of trial and error through which this victory is obtained is a very frustrating one
= Both the player and the bosses have a single health point and will die in one hit (do keep in mind, however, that most bosses have to either be hit at a specific weak point or posess multiple stages), this makes the combat more tense and adrenalinic, but also means that a single mistake can lead to a failed attempt
These are my considerations on the game, and even though subjective, i hope they will be helpful.

I saw this about 3 years ago, thought it was a really fun Idea, since it made constructing vehicles much more than just selecting a type of unit (where the parts were, what kind of mobity, tech, and weaponry). Recap - this was back when railguns were coming out, as well as shields, and when there were still tech trees and robot tiers. I respected the thought of the game back then, and then recently looked here and saw all these bad reviews. I took a good, hard look at what was available. Tiers system is gone (you can go against guys 4x your cpu, though there'll probably be one nub on your level  on their team and another guy 4x your cpu on your team), and so are tech trees. This actually makes getting into the game a lot easier, since you aren't gated by the tech trees or tier progressions in the slightest. Back then, you got your tech points/ exp/ robocurrency twice as fast if you were premium.... guess what, you -STILL- get exactly twice as much when using premium, only that you end up getting twice the amount of random parts/dust from the lootcrates. (and since tech was replaced with random probablility you get a legendary part OR that you find yourself enough dust, this is particularly the same). So the premium value really hasn't changed much (you probably didn't realize how helpful 2x everything might actually be...). In fact, there's nothing exactly stopping f2p from getting legendaries after enough drops: if you do well enough and fight a hard,long battle and go commando all game, you should be able to get that purple-tiered box (two, even) which gives extremely good loot, even when you can only access half of them. "But what if I can't do well with a beginner bot?" umm, if you look at the damage statistics of the SMG's, the lowest tier can actually output close to the same dps as the highest tier even though the highest tier costs more.... it's just that the highest tier has more overall health and is more compact. So, there's nothing stopping you from -killing- another person and gaining points. Otherwise, the parts that distinctly matter in a cost-to-numbers game are mobility pieces, sheilds, nano-repairs/teslablades, and legendary blocks... the first two are still not too badly priced (Legendaries are the only real whale-items I think...I landed myself a shield generator, and I can safely say it's more than necessary) Now, I was fortunate enough to keep some nice parts on me when I came back but those parts were cheap enough to get factory-produce entire sets out of one day of f2p dust (with a bit of skill and luck, tbf). If anything, I would have to start from scratch and see how difficult it is to get myself a full set of beginner smg's, a full set of non-bottom tier tires, and a couple of shields. Otherwise, so far even with a 500cpu hovering skiff with tier3 guns (out of 6 I think) I was able to give 1500cpu bots a hard time because SMG's are pinpoint accurate (but nobody believes in them T_T), even hitting top score in a winning game. Now, if you want to pin on the community, I have no idea what the metagame looks like or what the salt content is, since most people are silent in my experience. In any case, my respect for the game's concept and implementation hasn't faltered, so I decided to get lifetime premium (I don't think that was even an option 3 years ago, so... not bad).
If I had one gripe that might totally turn off new players though, it'd be the lockon missles. Still don't know how pricey they are but you can come across planes who use that and you won't know why you're being blown up full salvo after you observe yourself being called out (jk, calling targets doesn't exist anymore, you're just being locked on!). It's interesting, you can actually dodge the missles if you run yourself into cover, even after the missles are sent out. Still, that's a pretty horrifying experience till you learn you can deal with it. My other gripe might be micro-transaction $$$ loot crates, but like I said you can make do with what parts you can scavenge till you gather a whole collection of parts.
TLDR : The game is -technically- at LEAST what it used to be, it might have a different crowd, but it is still possible to f2p, build beautiful bots, silly gimmick bots, run/fly/drive, and make do with the parts and resources you have.
PS: I think this is the first time I've seen so many people with nastolgia-tinted lenses. Really, I don't think anyone realizes this really is the same game even by money-model, maybe minus the community.

Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is the new and improved follow up game to Sonic & SEGA All-Stars Racing. Transformed introduces online multiplayer, albeit a fairly buggy connection at times, a mode where you can play with friends in traditional racing or arena matches. Local split-screen mulitplayer is also an option for those that are interested.
It's hard not to compare this game to Mario Kart, and Transformed is as close to Mario Kart as you can get on Steam (since you won't see any Nintendo games here). Transformed has the traditional Grand Prix, World Tour and Time Attack modes we are all accustomed with. Familiar item pickups are also present, including a sort of "Ultimate" move for each character. The animation, graphics, art style, gameplay and optimization are all extremely well done. and there isn't really a weak point to be found in this game.
The karts are fairly customizable, and the driving mechanics are very fluid and polished. Drifting is smooth, allowing for extremely precise maneuverability. Transformed also employs water and air kart transformations in each level, changing up the style of the race, much like the newer Mario Karts. With so much similarity, it's hard not to like the game, assuming you liked Mario Kart at all.
Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is truly THE kart racer to get on Steam.

This is the first Dragon Ball game I have played since Budokai 3 on the PS2 and I am thorougly impressed. I wasn't sure if I'd like the new (well, new to me) fighting style but it is extremely smooth in this game. The story line finally wanders away from the "playing along with the story... again" and brings a unique spin to the story that I know and love. Plus, being able to create eight of your own characters is always a plus.
This game has a nice MMO-ish feel to it without sacrificing it's fighting core. You can party up with people for ranked matches, casual matches, side quests, and the main story. If you don't have internet, it sets up AI that would act like other people, just with a little "hire to join" system. You can customize your character and if you want to get a certain Dragon Ball look, you can get it. The difficulty in this game is perfect. You can cruise through a couple missions but then spend ages trying to beat the next few, or grinding side quests to make it easier.
This game isn't without its flaws though. There is a vast lack of tutorials for the online play. Constantly I see people asking for people to join their party, and others saying they want to join. But none of them know how to join. So the chat is constantly just spammed with people trying to join/start parties (for people that don't know how, pull up the pause menu and go to the 'Player List' selection and look at parties that you can join). The customization seems to be mostly for looks instead of actual stats, save for the Z-Souls. My one big complaint is the heavy reliance on RNG for the side quests. I don't mind if the bonus fights at the ends of missions happen only 50% of the time, and in fact, I enjoy the feeling of randomness and having to play through the missions multiple times. However, when things like an "Ultimate Finish" are random even after having done all the bonus objectives in a certain amount of time, which already requires luck with RNG. If I had to beat a rare bonus RNG'd fight in under five minutes and finish it with an Ultimate Attack, it should automatically give an Ultimate Finish, and not just roll again for the hell of it.
All in all, I am really enjoying this game. I plan on working on 100% this game (we'll see how dedicated I can be) and seeing how♥♥♥♥♥♥I am in ranked matches. 8/10

I picked up ESJ in a steam sale because it was 80c and sure, I had a buck to spare for a platformer. Even though the game only took a few hours to complete, I don't think I could recommend it even at the price I paid - there are just better games out there for your time.
On the plus side, the game is visually appealing, and sometimes there are clever elements that alter the level in sync with the techno music. They show almost all of those clever moments in the trailer.
Beyond that, the game just feels generic. The platforming is sluggish, occasionally demanding pixel-perfect precision to make a long jump or two - hardly the 'hardcore' experience it's been touted as in other reviews. The complete lack of momentum doesn't help things along, and the level design, while varied, doesn't tread any new ground.
On the sound design, the music is bland techno that starts off promising, but if you listen to the trailer you've pretty much heard it all. Also, it sounds like every checkpoint ♥♥♥♥♥♥s, so that's a thing.
That leaves the game with its humor, which induced the occasional smile but mostly fell flat. The pope gets CROSS. The evil wizard stole your BUTT, and you want revenge... FOR YOUR BUTT! Cute, but nothing special.
If you want to spend a few hours on a generic platfomer, save yourself a few bucks and go find something on Newgrounds - there are flash games out there with platforming and humor equal to or exceeding this, and those ones are free.
